bottom_line: Ten sources endorse a single structured intake and governance review for all AI tools, including procured, embedded vendor, and legacy tools, but no supplied study tests whether such review reduces unreviewed AI use or patient harm. The recommendation rests on framework and commentary consensus, and no supplied study documents the hazard either.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice, and none measures how often AI enters use through procurement or vendor updates without review. The ten endorsements consist of two frameworks and eight commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not count as evidence of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The endorsements describe a plausible failure mode in which embedded or updated vendor features reach clinical use without anyone assessing them. No supplied study measures how often this happens, what harm follows, or whether a central intake catches such tools before they affect patients. The safety benefit therefore remains an untested expectation.

One commentary proposes an intake form that yields a risk tier in minutes, and another describes clinicians building tools outside any governed pathway. Neither claim comes with workflow data. No supplied study reports intake completion rates, review turnaround, staff burden, or whether clinicians route tools through intake once it exists.

The HEAAL framework calls for applying standard procedures to all AI tools, whether they already exist or are proposed. No supplied study examines whether a single intake process surfaces equity concerns for tools used with Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

research_gap: Studies should compare health systems with and without a single intake process on the share of AI tools in use that received documented review, the time from vendor update to review, reviewer staffing costs, and downstream safety events tied to unreviewed tools. A baseline audit of how many embedded and legacy AI features currently operate without review would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. One commentary addresses resource-limited settings but reports no data. Safety-net systems may carry more legacy and vendor-embedded tools with fewer governance staff, and whether a single intake process is feasible or effective there is unknown.

bottom_line: Nineteen sources, mostly voluntary frameworks, professional guidance, and commentary, endorse documented lifecycle gates and recurring reviews of deployed AI, but no supplied study tests whether the practice keeps AI under oversight as performance or context changes. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus rather than measured effect.

perspectives.view: No study testing the practice and no study documenting the hazard was supplied. The endorsements consist of frameworks, guidance, and commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Agreement across 19 sources shows consistency of opinion, but it cannot establish that recording owners, evidence, approval status, and review triggers changes outcomes.

The CHAI guide describes checkpoints during silent deployment, pilot, and at regular intervals afterward. The logic is that scheduled review may catch performance degradation before patients are harmed. No supplied study measures how often such reviews detect drift, how quickly they do so, or whether detection prevents harm.

The radiology multi-society statement leaves the definition of sufficient monitoring to each local oversight group, case by case. This suggests that review content and frequency may vary widely between sites. No supplied study reports the staff burden of lifecycle gates or how faithfully organizations carry out scheduled reviews.

The supporting sources are voluntary. CHAI playbooks rate intake and lifecycle documentation as a must, while the NIST generative AI profile and most guidance rate related activities as should. None of the supplied endorsements comes from a binding regulation, so adoption depends on organizational choice.

research_gap: No study compares organizations or AI tools with and without documented lifecycle gates and recurring reviews. Useful designs would measure time from performance degradation to detection, the share of deployed tools with a named owner and current review, patient-level harm events, and the staff hours and cost per review cycle.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether recurring reviews, as practiced, examine performance in these groups or whether safety-net systems have the staff to sustain them.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether an accountable, multidisciplinary AI governance body improves safety, equity, or performance of AI in care. Five descriptive and qualitative studies suggest that AI oversight is often fragmented or absent, and 77 sources endorse forming such a body.

perspectives.view: None of the five studies compares organizations with and without a governance body, so none tests the practice. All five are level 3 qualitative or survey designs that document the hazard. They show consistent reports of fragmented or missing oversight, but they cannot show that a committee reduces that problem. Certainty about benefit therefore cannot be rated.

In one survey, 66.7% (36/54) of hospitalists used AI in clinical work with no institutional oversight, and 86.1% used it for differential diagnosis. This suggests that unreviewed tools may already be shaping diagnostic decisions. No study shows whether a governance body would catch these uses or the errors that follow from them.

Professionals and innovators in England reported unclear governance as an implementation barrier. Texas focus group participants described insufficient systematic governance for validation, auditing, and clinical use. These reports identify where governance may be needed in workflow. They do not measure how a committee performs, what burden it adds, or whether its decisions are followed in practice.

Among 19 organizations, 78.9% reported using steering committees for AI oversight, and some of these were combined with IT, research, or innovation teams. The authors still found fragmented approaches. This suggests that having a committee may not be enough by itself. The studies report no data on staffing, cost, or which committee structures worked.

Five safety-net organizations named AI governance structures as a key barrier during integration and lifecycle management, and the study reports no numeric results. This indicates that governance capacity may be thinner where resources are limited. No study tests whether a governance body improves equity outcomes for Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

One endorsing source cites a federal final rule that requires reasonable efforts to identify and mitigate algorithmic discrimination. A governance body is one way an organization could document those efforts. No supplied study examines whether a governance body helps organizations meet this or any other regulatory obligation.

Patient advocates and patient and public involvement participants took part in two of the qualitative studies, and the participants described unclear or insufficient governance. Neither study reports whether patient members on a governance body changed decisions or affected patients' trust or their ability to reach a human.

research_gap: The evidence base lacks comparative studies, even before-and-after or multi-site observational designs, that relate the presence, membership, and decision rights of an AI governance body to measurable outcomes. Candidate outcomes include unsanctioned AI use, detected safety events, completed validations, and equity audits. Such studies should also report staffing and cost.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study drew on five safety-net organizations serving low-income patients and reported governance as a barrier. This suggests that the organizations most likely to lack governance capacity are also the least studied in terms of what helps.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether a formal AI decommissioning protocol reduces disruption, data leakage, or lost records, and support for the practice rests on six frameworks and commentaries. Two staff surveys from one UK radiology deployment show that retiring an AI tool produced mixed effects on workflow and staff attitudes.

perspectives.view: No study compares decommissioning with and without a formal protocol. The two available reports are descriptive surveys of 40 UK staff, and they may draw on the same respondents. They describe perceptions after one tool was retired and cannot show that any protocol step works. Certainty about the practice cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

Staff-perceived patient benefit stayed near pre-implementation levels after retirement (70% vs 71.1%), and 35% of respondents reported logistical burden. These figures suggest that retirement carries some disruption. The surveys did not measure missed findings, lost records, or data exposure, so the harms the protocol targets remain unmeasured.

After decommissioning, staff reported relief at reduced workflow disruption alongside regret over lost patient benefit. Comfort with AI on their own imaging fell to 25.6% from earlier values of 31.1%, 48.3%, and 47.2%. This suggests that retirement affects staff attitudes as well as workflow, though no study evaluated transition planning or staff notification.

Reported logistical burden was 35% after decommissioning, compared with 51.7% in early implementation and 26.4% in late implementation. Retirement may therefore create a workload increase smaller than adoption does. No study reports the staff time or cost of running a formal decommissioning protocol.

NIST AI 600-1 states that protocols should allow generative AI systems to be deactivated when necessary, and the governance frameworks list decommissioning as a lifecycle step. None of the supplied sources specifies record-retention periods or notification duties, so health systems will need to map these steps to their own legal obligations.

Both surveys asked staff, not patients, about the effects of retirement. The chatbot equity roadmap asks health systems to identify alternative services so that patient care continues, and the pediatric framework calls for a planned move to a non-AI workflow. No study reports whether patients were told about a retirement or lost access to help.

research_gap: Studies should compare AI retirements that used a structured protocol with those that did not, and they should measure care continuity, record completeness, data exposure incidents, patient notification, and staff time, across several sites and tool types.
underserved_note: Neither hazard survey reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and both surveyed only UK radiology staff. The effects of AI retirement on patients who rely on chatbots or language support, which one endorsing commentary raises, are therefore undocumented.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether designating an authority to pause, restrict, supersede, or deactivate AI systems reduces harm, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on 26 endorsing sources, mostly commentaries and frameworks, that agree on the principle but offer no outcome data.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsements are consistent in direction, but consistency among expert opinion does not substitute for comparative data. Some listed excerpts, such as the CHAI model information sheet and the NIST response-plan item, address adjacent practices rather than stop authority itself.

The radiology multi-society statement and several commentaries describe stop authority as a way to keep a failing tool from producing unchecked errors. This reasoning follows standard safety practice, but no supplied study measures how often halts occur, how quickly they take effect, or whether they prevent harm reaching patients.

Commentaries from intensive care, trauma surgery, and nursing education call for predefined thresholds tied to drift, calibration, or subgroup performance, and one asks that deactivation not disrupt routine care. No supplied study reports how such thresholds were set, whether monitoring triggered them, or what fallback workflows cost clinicians in practice.

A commentary on the EU AI Act states that oversight personnel must have the authority and technical means to adapt or deactivate a system, which suggests a legal basis for this practice in that jurisdiction. The supplied sources do not describe comparable U.S. FDA, ONC, or state requirements.

One governance commentary calls for subgroup-based suspension thresholds and authority to halt use when equity criteria are breached. No supplied study shows whether such thresholds detect performance gaps in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups.

research_gap: Health systems need studies that track AI deactivation or restriction events, including the time from threshold breach to halt, the harms observed before and after the halt, and the clinical workflow impact of fallback procedures, compared with sites that lack a designated authority.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Systems serving these groups may need to set subgroup-specific stop thresholds without outcome data to guide them.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether defining AI risk tolerance, holding deployments within it, and signing time-bound residual risk acceptance reduce unacknowledged exposure to AI risk. Five frameworks and guidance documents endorse parts of the practice, so support for it currently rests on expert consensus rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no certainty rating can be assigned under GRADE conventions. The five endorsements are consensus statements. They can indicate agreement among bodies, but they do not estimate whether the practice changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes.

The endorsements emphasize different elements. The CHAI guide asks that risk tolerance be determined and expressed, and the CHAI playbooks ask that high-risk AI appear in risk registers with escalation to executives or the board. The FDA draft guidance asks that unacceptable risk be reduced to acceptable levels. None of the quoted passages addresses the time-bound sign-off element.

The AMA principle quoted here concerns a patient's option to request review by a licensed clinician. It does not speak to enterprise risk tolerance, so it offers indirect support at most. No supplied evidence shows whether board-level risk acceptance affects patients' safety, trust, or access to a human.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without formally defined AI risk tolerance and expiring residual risk sign-offs. Useful outcomes include the number of deployments paused or withdrawn, the time taken to re-review expired acceptances, and AI-related safety events. Descriptive studies that document how often AI risk is accepted without formal acknowledgment would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Governance bodies have no data on whether a risk tolerance set at the enterprise level accounts for risks that fall unevenly on these groups.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether a documented, per-tool risk assessment and management plan reduces harm from AI tools in health care, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on 22 endorsing sources, including federal draft guidance and consensus frameworks, rather than on outcome data.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Support comes from guidance documents, frameworks, and commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence of effect. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative or before-and-after study measures outcomes of documented risk plans.

FDA draft guidance states that sponsors of AI-enabled devices must maintain risk analysis and documentation consistent with 21 CFR Part 820. AMA principles note that EHR Predictive DSIs face mandated risk management practices. These duties fall mainly on developers, so a health system plan may duplicate or supplement vendor files rather than replace them.

FUTURE-AI and the Mayo Clinic case study describe risk files that assess likelihood, effects, and mitigations before deployment and after changes. No supplied study shows that such files catch errors before they reach patients, so the safety benefit remains a plausible mechanism that has not been measured.

HEAAL and the RUAIH guidance ask governance groups to identify risks that may limit access to care and to plan interventions in advance. No supplied study examines whether risk plans surface or reduce harms for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or AI deployments with and without documented per-tool risk plans, measuring detected risks, safety events, time to mitigation after model or workflow changes, and staff burden. Evaluations should also test whether named risk owners and reassessment triggers are followed in practice.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether risk plans capture the harms most likely to affect their patients and may need to add equity-specific risk items on the basis of framework guidance alone.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether publishing an acceptable-use policy and approved tools list reduces unsanctioned AI use or exposure of patient information. Seventeen surveys and interview studies show that clinicians and trainees commonly use unapproved AI tools and sometimes enter patient data, often where no policy exists.

perspectives.view: All 17 studies are level 3 surveys or qualitative studies that document shadow AI use, and none compares settings with and without a published policy. Nine endorsements, mostly commentaries, support the practice. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about the effect of the practice cannot be rated because no study tests it.

In a survey of 146 hematologists, 48.6% had entered patient data into non-approved public chatbots, and 8.2% had entered identifiable data. Among 388 French students, 23.5% of GenAI users reported disclosing patient-identifying information. These figures show that the exposure exists, but no study shows that a written policy stops data before it leaves the organization.

Among US hospitalists, 48.6% cited uncertainty about institutional policy and 43.1% cited lack of secure applications as barriers. Swedish and Chinese clinicians described unsanctioned tools filling gaps in institutional systems. These findings suggest a policy may work only when paired with approved tools and a low-burden intake route, as the CHAI playbook advises.

Among 63 UK health professionals, 70% said they would use AI if officially approved, and 11% reported institutional guidance. Among French oncology pharmacists, 65.3% worked within shadow AI and 17.3% had access to validated tools. These data suggest that most of the cost may lie in supplying vetted tools rather than in drafting the policy.

NIST AI 600-1 advises updating generative AI acceptable-use policies to cover proprietary and open-source tools and third-party personnel. The CHAI playbooks rate policy dissemination as a must. Reported coverage is low, with 6% of 685 Swiss clinicians and 9.9% of 767 Asia-Pacific rheumatologists reporting workplace guidelines or policies.

The reported rates at which clinicians and students enter patient information into public chatbots point to a privacy risk that patients have no direct way to detect. A published approved tools list would give patients a basis to ask which tools handle their records. No study has measured whether publication changes patient trust or data exposure.

None of the 17 hazard studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A framework for Somalia and low-resource settings recommends an approved-use matrix, but it is a commentary and not a test. Whether policies reach staff in under-resourced settings has not been examined.

research_gap: Controlled or stepped-wedge studies across several health systems are needed to compare unapproved AI use and PHI exposure before and after publication of an acceptable-use policy and approved tools list. Outcomes could include audited data-loss events, self-reported unapproved use, and uptake of approved tools. Such studies should separate the effect of the written policy from the effect of providing secure alternatives.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies also do not report on these groups. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence on whether a published policy reduces shadow AI use among their staff or protects their patients' data.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether identifying and managing conflicts of interest in AI adoption keeps patient safety ahead of commercial, engagement, or throughput incentives, and no study documents how often such incentives have overridden safety. Support for R012 rests on one state statute, several guidance documents, and a larger set of commentaries.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Most endorsements are commentaries or position statements that use "should" language without reporting outcomes. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an estimate of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

Utah HB 452 (2025) requires mental health chatbots to prioritize user mental health and safety over engagement metrics or profit, which makes the practice a legal duty for that product class in one state. The other sources are voluntary guidance, including a multi-society radiology statement calling for ethics codes that block data use for financial gain without patient benefit.

The sources propose mechanisms such as conflict-of-interest disclosure for developers, internal ethics committees overseeing procurement, and incentive policies that do not reward throughput alone. None of the supplied material reports the staffing, cost, or time these mechanisms require, so a health system has no empirical basis for budgeting them.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI procurement and deployment decisions made with and without formal conflict-of-interest processes, such as disclosure requirements or ethics committee review, and that measure downstream safety events, vendor claim accuracy, and whether engagement or throughput targets shifted clinical behavior. Descriptive work is also needed to establish how often commercial incentives have influenced AI adoption decisions in health systems.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer staff to run disclosure and ethics review and may depend more on vendor-supplied performance data, so the absence of evidence leaves their specific risks unmeasured.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether assigning named accountable owners to AI solutions reduces unaddressed failures, although 34 frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries recommend some form of it. Two qualitative interview studies suggest that responsibility for AI harms and upkeep is often unclear in practice, which shows the problem exists but not that named ownership fixes it.

perspectives.view: Zero studies compare outcomes with and without named AI owners. The two available studies are qualitative interviews (n=40 developers; n=21 experts) that describe the hazard. They cannot estimate an effect, so certainty for the practice is rated as no direct evidence. The endorsements reflect expert agreement rather than tested results.

Interviewees described maintenance and monitoring as poorly defined and inconsistently performed, a condition they called a responsibility vacuum. Among 40 developers, recognition of their own duty to address harms varied widely. These findings suggest that model drift or errors may go uncaught when no one is assigned, but no study shows that naming owners catches them sooner.

The interview data indicate that monitoring tasks are undervalued within health system workflows. A named owner may exist on paper while the work goes undone if time and tools are not attached to the role. No study has measured whether ownership assignments are kept current or carried out with fidelity after deployment.

The recommendation covers six responsibility areas for every AI solution, which could require multiple staff per tool as portfolios grow. The finding that upkeep tasks are undervalued suggests these duties may compete with other work unless they are funded. No study reports the staffing cost or the time burden of maintaining owner assignments at scale.

NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to define ownership of generative AI incident response, and CHAI guidance asks them to specify who is accountable and to whom. A multi-society radiology statement calls for named vendor contacts for error reporting. These are voluntary frameworks, and the supplied sources cite no binding federal or state requirement for named AI owners.

Several endorsing sources, including CHAI guidance, tie accountability to knowing whom end users should contact with concerns and who will act. The hazard studies suggest that such a contact is often missing today. No study has examined whether named owners make it easier for patients or clinicians to report a problem and reach a responsible person.

research_gap: Health systems lack studies that compare AI programs with and without named owners on measurable outcomes such as time to detect performance drift, time to resolve reported incidents, and completion rates for scheduled monitoring. Pre-post or stepped rollout designs across several systems could supply this evidence, along with data on staffing hours per owned solution.
underserved_note: Neither hazard study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study tests the practice in any setting. Safety-net systems may have fewer staff available to fill six ownership roles, so the feasibility and effect of the practice in those settings remain unknown.

bottom_line: Nine frameworks and commentaries endorse formal, risk-tiered approval before deployment, and two studies suggest the process can run in practice and that patients may prefer locally certified tools. No study shows that formal approval reduces patient harm or improves tool performance after deployment, so confidence in the benefit is very low.

perspectives.view: Two studies test the practice. A pre-post study without a comparator, conducted in a real U.S. deployment, reported that 50% of tools were approved, 34% conditionally approved, and 13% rejected. A vignette survey measured stated patient preference. Neither study measured patient harm or post-deployment performance, so certainty is very low because of study design and indirectness.

Across 64 evaluations, 13% of tools were rejected and 34% received conditions. This suggests the review step may stop or modify some tools before they reach patients. The study did not report whether rejected tools would have caused harm or whether approved tools performed safely afterward.

The review ran in a real deployment, with 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions. This suggests a structured approval process can operate in practice and that some tools may return for repeat review. The study did not report review time, clinician burden, or how consistently risk tiers were applied.

No supplied study reports the cost or staffing required for governance review. The count of 64 evaluations for 55 solutions suggests that repeat review may add work beyond one decision per tool. Leaders may need to plan committee capacity for conditional approvals that require follow-up.

In a vignette survey of 3,000 respondents, local hospital certification increased preference compared with uncertified tools (AMCE 0.078, 95% CI 0.068 to 0.088). A recorded approval may therefore support patient trust. Stated preferences in a simulation may differ from the choices patients make in real care.

Neither study reports whether Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations were represented among patients affected by reviewed tools or among survey respondents. No study tested whether approval criteria examine tool performance in these groups.

research_gap: No study compares health systems or tools with and without formal approval on post-deployment safety incidents, tool performance, or equity gaps. The supplied evidence also does not report the cost, staffing, and time to deployment of a review process, or whether risk-tier thresholds assign review intensity appropriately. Comparative or stepped-wedge designs across several systems could address these questions.
underserved_note: Neither study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The approval rates come from a U.S. deployment whose setting and patient mix are not described in the supplied data, and the survey sample's composition is also not described. It is therefore unknown whether formal approval works the same way, or builds the same trust, in settings that serve these populations.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether a written, leadership-approved AI policy reduces inconsistent or outdated rules for AI use, so the recommendation rests on 11 endorsements and seven studies showing that such policies are often absent. In five surveys, between 4.8% and 37.6% of respondents reported a formal institutional AI policy or guidance, while AI use was reported far more often.

perspectives.view: No study compares organizations with and without a written AI policy on any outcome. The seven hazard studies are six level 3 surveys and one qualitative study of self-reported policy presence. They establish a governance gap, but they cannot show that writing, versioning, or disseminating a policy changes staff behavior or patient outcomes.

In the Türkiye survey, 87% of hematologists reported clinical AI use in the prior three months while 4.8% reported a written policy. In Latin America, 78.3% of respondents used generative AI and 7.4% reported policies. These figures suggest AI reaches care without institutional rules, but no study shows a policy catches errors before they reach patients.

Interviews with 32 nursing interns, preceptors, administrators, and IT staff in China described multilevel discretionary rule-making in a policy vacuum, and stakeholders asked for institutional frameworks. This suggests that units write their own rules when no policy exists. No study measured whether a written policy is read, followed, or kept current in daily work.

One survey drew 123 emergency clinicians from 16 Latin American countries in non-English settings and found that 7.4% reported institutional AI policies. No study sampled Medicaid or safety-net organizations. None examined whether institutional policies address equitable use, language access, or health literacy for patients.

FDA draft guidance expects device manufacturers to review their quality systems at defined intervals. California AB 3030 requires disclosure of GenAI patient communications unless a licensed clinician reviews them. A written policy could record how a health system meets such duties, but these sources set obligations and do not test health-system policies.

Among 109 family medicine chairs, 56.9% reported current AI use and 37.6% reported formal written policies, strategic plans, or frameworks. In the UK sample, 11% reported institutional guidance. Many departments appear to adopt AI before governance exists. No study reports the staff time or cost of drafting, versioning, and disseminating a policy.

research_gap: No study compares organizations with and without a leadership-approved, versioned AI policy on outcomes such as the share of AI tools that pass approval review, the rate of unsanctioned tool use, staff awareness of the rules, or reported AI-related safety events. A before-and-after or stepped rollout study across several health systems, including safety-net sites, could address this gap. It would need to measure policy awareness, adherence, and whether reviews happen on schedule.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard survey sampled clinicians in non-English settings in Latin America and shows that the policy gap exists there. It offers no evidence on whether a written policy would work in under-resourced settings or protect patients with limited English or low literacy.

bottom_line: Twelve sources endorse documenting AI governance roles and decision rights, two frameworks at the must level, but no study has tested whether role mapping changes governance performance or patient outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and face validity, not on measured effect.

perspectives.view: The endorsing sources are frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries, and none reports data. No study tests the practice, and no study documents how often controls lack a responsible role or what follows. Agreement across 12 sources shows consistent expert opinion, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect.

FUTURE-AI and one auditing commentary ask that roles for risk management, auditing, incident reporting, and model updates be assigned. The reasoning is that an unowned control may go unexecuted, so errors reach patients undetected. No study has measured whether named ownership raises the rate at which safety controls are actually carried out.

One commentary proposes that clear decision rights may reduce duplicated effort and help separate model failures from workflow or governance bottlenecks. This claim is untested. Health systems adopting the practice should expect staff time to build and maintain the role map, and they have no published cost or staffing estimate to plan against.

The NIST generative AI profile adds whistleblower protections for staff who report harm, and HEAAL asks that parties responsible for managing a tool across its lifecycle be identified. A documented role map could tell patients and staff whom to contact about a problem, though no study has examined whether it does.

research_gap: No study compares health systems or AI deployments with and without documented governance role maps. Useful designs would measure whether controls such as monitoring, audits, and incident response are completed on schedule, how quickly problems are escalated and resolved, and how much staff time the mapping requires.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems with thin governance staffing may face greater difficulty assigning an owner to every control, and whether the practice works in those settings is unknown.

bottom_line: One vignette study of 513 participants in China found that a provider described as using proactive ethics practices received higher patient attitude ratings, but no study tested whether impact assessment reduces ethical, social, environmental, or workforce harms. Three hazard studies show that AI tools carry measurable energy and carbon costs, which supports the concern but does not show that the practice addresses it.

perspectives.view: A single vignette study (n=513) is the only test of the practice, and it reported attitude means of 5.67 versus 4.28. Its outcome is indirect because attitudes stand in for harms, the setting is simulated, and no replication exists. Certainty is very low, and the three environmental studies document the hazard rather than test the practice.

No study measured whether a pre-deployment assessment caught an ethical, social, or workforce harm before it reached patients. One estimate puts worldwide yearly emissions from digital pathology deep learning at up to 16 Mt. Another found a 60-fold energy increase for a 2.61 percentage-point safety gain, which suggests more compute may not yield more safety.

A simulation involving 23 clinicians estimated about 26.22 g CO2e per hour for cloud inference versus 6.84 g for edge deployment. This suggests deployment architecture is one factor an assessment could examine. The study did not test whether an assessment changed architecture choices or how much staff time such a review requires.

Across 47 model configurations, extra test-time compute did not consistently improve safety scores, which suggests smaller configurations may lower energy use with limited safety loss. No study reports the cost, staffing, or time needed to run ethical and workforce impact reviews at scale, so resourcing plans currently rest on endorsements alone.

None of the four studies enrolled or analyzed Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. The attitude study drew participants in China, and the environmental studies used slides, clinicians, or benchmarks. Whether impact assessments detect harms that fall on these populations has not been tested.

Participants rated a provider higher when it described proactive ethics practices in the vignette. This suggests openness about impact review may support trust. The study measured reactions to a written scenario, so it does not show whether patients were protected from harm or could reach a human when a tool raised concerns.

research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without structured ethical, social, environmental, and workforce impact assessment. Such studies would need to run in operating health systems and measure downstream patient harms, workforce effects such as staff burden or displacement, energy and carbon use, and the cost of conducting the reviews.
underserved_note: No test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The single attitude study used a general sample in China, so health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that impact assessment identifies or reduces harms concentrated among their patients.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether consulting an IRB or ethics committee before an AI pilot prevents unapproved research on patients, and no study documents how often that hazard occurs. The recommendation rests on 14 endorsing sources, mostly commentaries and consensus frameworks, that extend long-standing human subjects research norms to AI.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The support comes from frameworks and commentaries that state expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not count as evidence of effect, so certainty that IRB consultation reduces unapproved research through AI pilots cannot be rated.

NIST AI 600-1 directs organizations to follow applicable human subjects research requirements, including informed consent, when running feedback activities. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks whether an IRB submission is needed. These sources restate existing research obligations and do not report whether consultation changes compliance in practice.

One endorsing commentary on health equity states that IRBs must be equipped to assess algorithmic bias, data privacy, and participant protections. No supplied study examines whether IRB review of AI pilots addresses risks specific to Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often AI pilots proceed without an IRB determination, and whether a required pre-pilot consultation step changes that rate, the time to launch, or the rate of consent and oversight problems. Comparative work across health systems with and without formal AI intake review could supply direct evidence.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no evidence showing whether IRB review of AI pilots protects them or whether review processes account for consent and language barriers they face.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether defining and recording accountability for AI errors among clinicians, institutions, and developers reduces harm or clarifies recourse. Eight hazard studies report that clinicians and other stakeholders perceive accountability as unresolved, and the recommendation rests on those studies and 89 endorsing sources.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Eight hazard studies, mostly qualitative or small surveys, consistently report unclear accountability. They show that the problem exists. They cannot show whether documented accountability arrangements change liability outcomes, clinician behavior, or patient recourse.

Among 25 oncologists, 88% (70.0-95.8) expected to bear primary legal responsibility for AI errors. In 484 Reddit comments, clinicians described their signature as a legal shock absorber for institutional AI liability. If blame defaults to the signing clinician, model or institutional failures may go unreported to developers. No study tests whether documented accountability changes this.

In a deployed prescribing tool, 13 endocrinologists named accountability and liability among the themes that hindered adoption. In a UK study of 40 participants, clinicians felt ultimately liable while relying on AI-generated insights. These findings suggest that unresolved accountability may affect uptake. No study measured the burden or fidelity of documenting accountability in practice.

In a vignette study of 331 participants, physicians who followed generative AI advice drew less moral blame after an adverse outcome than those who did not (p < 0.001). This suggests that patients may shift fault toward the AI, which could complicate recourse. In a US focus group that included patient advocates, participants split on whether providers should bear full responsibility.

Of 25 physicians in Luxembourg, 64% (44.5-79.8) cited regulatory or legal uncertainty as a barrier. In a separate survey of 18 clinicians, 92% reported uncertainty about legal protection. Endorsing sources differ on how to allocate liability, and one assigns it to developers of autonomous systems. No study examines whether institutional accountability records affect liability determinations.

None of the eight hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One interview study included stakeholders in Nigeria but did not enroll patients. The evidence therefore cannot indicate how accountability gaps affect patients who have fewer means to pursue recourse after harm.

research_gap: No study compares health systems or deployments with and without documented accountability arrangements for AI. Such a study would need to measure error reporting to developers, time to resolution of AI-related incidents, clinician adoption, patient complaints and recourse, and legal outcomes. Studies would also need to record how liability is divided in vendor contracts and whether those terms match what clinicians believe.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and none of the hazard studies reports enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Most participants were clinicians, developers, or administrators rather than patients. The evidence therefore cannot indicate whether accountability arrangements would help patients who face language, literacy, or financial barriers to complaint and legal recourse.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether documenting a model's purpose, training data, limitations, and evaluation, followed by governance review, changes approval decisions or patient outcomes. Support for the practice rests on 25 endorsing sources, including one state statute, several frameworks, and multiple expert commentaries.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The endorsements are frameworks, guidance, and commentaries that express consensus but do not measure effects. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion alone does not establish certainty about whether pre-approval documentation review improves decisions.

CHAI playbooks direct organizations to make model card completion a mandatory approval step, and NIST AI 600-1 asks deployers to document how pre-trained models were adapted. The cited Utah HB 452 text addresses disclosure of AI use to chatbot users rather than internal model documentation, so it offers limited support for this specific recommendation.

The HEAAL framework asks teams to document the rationale for chosen fairness metrics, which would place subgroup performance in front of reviewers. No supplied study examines whether such documentation leads governance bodies to detect or act on performance gaps affecting underserved patients.

CHAI frames documentation as a required workflow step for internally developed AI, which implies staff time from developers and reviewers. No supplied study reports the cost, staffing demand, or review time required, so leaders cannot estimate burden at scale from this evidence.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare approval decisions, time to detection of model limitations, and downstream safety events between AI tools reviewed with standardized documentation (such as model cards) and tools approved without it. Such studies should also measure documentation completeness, reviewer comprehension, and the staff hours the process consumes.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether documentation review surfaces limitations relevant to these groups remains unknown and would depend on whether subgroup data are reported in the documentation itself.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether a centralized, retained repository of AI documentation and decision records prevents lost audit trails or improves accountability. Support for the practice rests on 24 endorsing sources, mostly frameworks, guidance, and commentaries, which agree on the aim but differ in what they ask health systems to record.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsements are expert opinion. One cited CHAI playbook excerpt defines a HIPAA business associate agreement and does not address documentation retention, which suggests some listed support is indirect.

NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to keep a document retention policy covering testing, evaluation, validation, and verification history for generative AI. One commentary asks that governance records stay accessible to notified bodies and competent authorities. These sources describe expected compliance posture, but none reports whether a repository satisfied an actual audit or inquiry.

Two commentaries list specific fields to log, such as model version, prompts, timestamps, initial and final outputs, and editing times. The AMA principles caution that disclosure should not add administrative burden. No supplied study measures the staff time, logging fidelity, or retrieval success of such records in live workflows.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without a centralized AI documentation repository on outcomes such as the ability to reconstruct a specific AI-influenced decision, time to respond to an audit or adverse-event review, completeness of retained records, and staff time spent on documentation.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One commentary on machine-assisted translation recommends logging target language and translator identity, which may help later review of care for patients with limited English proficiency, but this remains untested. Safety-net systems may have less staff capacity to maintain such repositories, and no supplied source measures that cost.

bottom_line: Seventeen sources endorse AI data governance with named stewards, a data register, and version-controlled provenance, but no supplied study tests whether these measures improve data quality or patient outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and framework language, and no study documenting the hazard was supplied either.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice and none documents the hazard. The support consists of two frameworks using mandatory language (CHAI), one NIST profile, one multi-society guidance statement, and commentaries. Consensus statements of this kind do not enter a GRADE rating, so certainty about benefit cannot be graded.

The CHAI playbooks state that organizations that only deploy vendor models must still keep data preparation procedures for data input to models, used in fine-tuning, or shared with vendors. Several commentaries tie governance to HIPAA and GDPR compliance. These are voluntary frameworks and opinion pieces, and none reports an audit or enforcement outcome.

One commentary on health equity calls for regular review of policies covering how patient data, including behavioral metadata, are collected and shared, and the SAGES statement suggests that provenance records may help detect dataset bias. Neither source reports data showing that governance reduced bias for any population.

research_gap: No supplied study compares sites with and without named data stewards, a maintained data register, or version-controlled provenance on measures such as data error rates, time to trace a model failure to its source data, or model performance drift. The staffing and cost needed to maintain these structures in a health system are also unmeasured in the supplied evidence.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether data governance helps detect or correct data problems affecting these groups remains unstudied, and safety-net systems with limited informatics staff have no evidence on the feasibility of this practice.

bottom_line: Thirty-three sources endorse version-controlled change management for AI models, configurations, prompts, and retrieval corpora, but no supplied study tests whether the practice prevents safety degradation. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and regulatory direction rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Support comes from frameworks, guidance, and commentaries whose strength ranges from "must" to "may." Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not raise certainty, so the effect of change management on patient outcomes or model safety remains unmeasured.

FDA draft lifecycle guidance asks manufacturers to describe who makes configuration decisions and what training they need. An FDA discussion paper describes postmarket oversight options for generative AI devices, ranging from quality-system documentation to authorization before changes. CHAI defines a material modification regardless of version number, which suggests the review trigger should follow the substance of a change.

No supplied study documents how often unreviewed model, prompt, or corpus changes have degraded safety. Commentaries describe logging updates so they can be reversed and running candidate models in shadow mode before release. These descriptions of intended safeguards have not been evaluated for whether they catch errors before they reach patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI deployments with and without formal change control and measure performance regressions, safety events, and time to rollback after model, prompt, configuration, or retrieval-corpus updates. Researchers could also examine what share of changes reviewers classify as material and how much reviewer effort each review requires.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence addresses Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Changes to prompts or retrieval corpora could affect translated or plain-language outputs differently from standard outputs, and without testing, health systems cannot know whether change review detects such subgroup-specific degradation.

bottom_line: Fifty-nine sources endorse identifying legal requirements, determining regulatory status, and assessing each AI tool's compliance before deployment and as rules change, but no supplied study tests whether this practice reduces noncompliant deployment or regulatory exposure. The recommendation rests on consensus and on the structure of existing law rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. All 59 endorsements come from frameworks, guidance, regulation, and commentary. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not establish certainty about effects, so the rating is no direct evidence. Agreement across sources suggests broad professional acceptance, but it does not show benefit.

The endorsements point to specific obligations. FDA draft guidance ties public summaries to 510(k), De Novo, or PMA requirements, and FUTURE-AI states that the EU AI Act classifies all health care AI tools as high risk. One set of principles states that payor automated decision-making must conform to state and federal law. These sources describe what compliance requires, and none measures whether assessment programs achieve it.

The HEAAL framework advises delivery organizations to monitor federal and local regulators, including offices of state Attorneys General and departments of health. No supplied study examines whether compliance review changes outcomes for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

CHAI playbooks state that organizations must at minimum name who is responsible for oversight, validation, monitoring, and data stewardship, and one framework offers guides for assessing legal risk before adoption. No supplied study reports the staffing, cost, or time required to conduct initial and ongoing compliance assessments at scale.

research_gap: No study measures whether structured regulatory and compliance assessment before and after AI deployment reduces enforcement actions, legal claims, or patient harm, or what such programs cost. Comparative or before-and-after studies of health systems with and without formal compliance review, including tracking of how often reassessment detects changed requirements, would address the gap.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on whether it performs for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The absence of data leaves unknown whether this recommendation is feasible or protective in settings that serve those patients.

bottom_line: The listed endorsements, one framework rated "must" and eleven sources rated "should," support written allocation of vendor and deployer lifecycle responsibilities, and no supplied study tests whether this closes responsibility gaps or improves patient outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and descriptive experience rather than comparative evidence.

perspectives.view: The listed endorsements consist of two CHAI frameworks and ten commentaries. No supplied study tests the practice or documents the hazard. The sources agree with one another, which shows consistent expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, opinion without a tested comparison cannot support a certainty rating, so the practice has no direct evidence.

One NHS implementation guide states that agreeing an IT responsibilities matrix before installation "halves deployment time." The claim comes from a single deployment described in a commentary, and the guide reports no comparison group or measurement method. It may reflect local experience, but no study has tested it as an effect of the practice.

Several commentaries name specific duties to assign, including monitoring, model updating, harm detection, incident escalation, and audit ownership. These lists describe points where failures could fall between parties. No supplied study measures whether written allocation leads to faster detection or fewer errors reaching patients.

research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without documented responsibility allocation. Useful designs would measure time to detect and correct model performance problems, incident resolution time, and disputes over accountability across sites that do and do not use a responsibilities matrix. Such studies should include deployments of open-source models, where the deployer holds most duties.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Several endorsing commentaries address equity and rural hospitals, which suggests the concern extends to under-resourced deployers. No study has examined whether such sites can carry the oversight duties assigned to them.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether executive sponsorship and dedicated budget, staff, and infrastructure for AI governance lead to safer or more effective AI deployment, so this recommendation rests on 21 endorsing frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries. Two descriptive studies suggest that the resource gap exists, with a median of 0% of family medicine departmental budgets allocated to AI and 68.4% of surveyed organizations reporting a lack of AI expertise.

perspectives.view: No study compares organizations with and without executive-sponsored, funded AI governance, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two available studies are a survey of 109 department chairs and a qualitative study of 22 leaders. They describe the hazard and do not test the practice. Endorsements are numerous but consist of expert opinion.

In one qualitative study, 52.6% of organizations reported difficulty evaluating AI effectiveness. This suggests that many sites may lack the capacity to detect a model that underperforms before it affects patients. The study does not show that added funding or executive sponsorship closes that detection gap.

Lack of AI expertise was reported by 68.4% of organizations in a study of quality and safety leaders. Validation, monitoring, and workflow design each require trained staff. Whether sponsored budgets translate into sustained monitoring with adequate fidelity in routine workflows has not been studied.

Family medicine chairs reported a median of 0% and a mean of 2.4% of departmental budget allocated to AI. The authors note that departmental figures likely undercount institutional spending. No study reports the cost, staffing levels, or return associated with funding a governance program at scale.

The HEAAL framework states that low-resource settings will need infrastructure and technical assistance investment to adopt equity practices. Neither hazard study reports results by safety-net status or payer mix. The size of the resource gap in the settings that serve Medicaid and limited English proficiency patients therefore remains unmeasured.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI safety, performance monitoring completion, and patient outcomes across organizations with differing levels of executive sponsorship and dedicated governance funding. Such studies should also report the staffing and budget levels associated with adequate validation and monitoring.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The two hazard studies surveyed department chairs and quality leaders in the United States and Canada and did not report data on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Evidence on whether governance resourcing reaches or benefits safety-net settings is absent, and those settings may face larger resource gaps than the ones described.

bottom_line: Eleven sources endorse a system-wide AI strategy that uses a structured framework to prioritize use cases and assess resources, but no study has tested whether this practice reduces adoption of low-value or infeasible AI. The only supplied study is a survey showing that formal strategies were uncommon among the institutions sampled.

perspectives.view: No study compares organizations that use a structured prioritization framework with those that do not. One cross-sectional survey of 211 emergency clinicians found that 12.0% reported a formal institutional AI strategy. This study documents that strategies are often absent. It does not show that their absence leads to low-value adoption or that a framework prevents it. Endorsements rest on expert opinion.

The survey measured whether a strategy existed and did not measure errors, harms, or failed deployments. The supplied evidence therefore cannot tell us whether a structured framework catches unsafe or poorly suited tools before they reach patients. The link between planning and patient harm remains untested.

Several endorsing frameworks ask leaders to weigh personnel, lifecycle resources, and allocation across competing AI systems. No supplied study reports the staff time, cost, or governance capacity that such a framework requires, or whether it changes which tools a system buys. The 12.0% figure suggests many institutions would be building this capacity from the start.

The hazard survey drew respondents from 14 sub-Saharan African countries, which may reflect resource-limited settings, but it did not describe patient populations and was not conducted in U.S. Medicaid or safety-net systems. The HEAAL framework names resource and personnel assessment as equity components, yet no study tests whether applying it changes outcomes for underserved patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without a structured AI prioritization framework and that measure outcomes such as the share of deployed tools later retired, total spending on AI, staff effort, clinical or operational impact, and adverse events. Such studies should also report what it costs to run the framework and whether its use differs by organization size and resources.
underserved_note: No study tests the practice, so there is no evidence on its effect in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The single hazard survey sampled emergency clinicians in sub-Saharan Africa and did not report patient characteristics. This suggests that safety-net systems, which may have the fewest resources for feasibility assessment, currently have no tested guidance on which framework to use or what it would require.

bottom_line: Two studies report findings favoring sequenced AI adoption, but neither compares staged rollout with enterprise-wide deployment, so the effect of staging itself remains unmeasured. Support for the recommendation comes mainly from 38 endorsements, most of them frameworks and commentaries.

perspectives.view: One before-after study across 26 U.S. hospitals and one German simulation both favor sequenced adoption. The hospital study has no comparison group and cannot separate the effect of staging from the effect of the decision support tools. The simulation uses stylized parameters. Certainty is very low because of risk of bias and indirectness.

In the 26-hospital rollout, postoperative acute kidney injury fell from an average of 1,031 cases per month at baseline to 400 per month after Phase 3. Intraoperative hypotension episodes fell 33% in Phase 1. These results suggest early phases may show benefit before scaling, though background trends could explain part of the decline.

The simulation found that interoperability-led sequencing reduced midtransition volatility compared with automation-first sequencing. An uncoordinated transition produced the largest variation in turnaround and throughput. This suggests the order of rollout steps and site data readiness may matter alongside pacing. No study measured site readiness criteria directly.

Staged rollout delays system-wide returns and requires staff to run pilots, collect metrics, and decide when to advance. Executives cited in one endorsing guidance asked for standardized metrics to compare sites, which suggests demonstrated value lacks shared definitions today. The 26-hospital study shows a phased model can run at multi-site scale.

Neither study reports results by payer, language, or literacy. Two endorsing commentaries, on inclusive chatbots and machine-assisted translation, call for pilots and language-specific deployment before scaling. No test examined whether staging protects underserved sites or delays their access to useful tools.

research_gap: No study compares staged rollout with simultaneous enterprise-wide deployment on patient outcomes, cost, or clinician adoption, and none tests specific site readiness criteria or value thresholds for advancing between phases. A stepped-wedge or cluster-randomized design across sites could address both questions.
underserved_note: Neither study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one was a simulation with no patients. Health systems cannot assume that readiness and value criteria developed at well-resourced sites will transfer to safety-net sites, which may also be scheduled last in a staged rollout.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether a written non-retaliation policy increases reporting of AI-related concerns, and no study documents how often fear of retaliation suppresses such reports. Support for the recommendation rests on two governance frameworks, and only one of them addresses non-retaliation directly.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements are expert framework guidance rather than empirical findings, so they do not change the rating. The size of the problem and the effect of a policy both remain unmeasured in this body of evidence.

The CHAI playbook asks whether non-retaliation appears in both the policy and the reporting interface, and whether it covers demotion, dismissal, harassment, and other adverse actions. The NIST Generative AI Profile excerpt addresses acceptable use policies and query refusal criteria. It does not mention retaliation, so it offers indirect support for this recommendation at most.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI concern reporting rates, report content, and time to resolution before and after a written non-retaliation policy is adopted, preferably with comparison sites. Surveys of staff, patients, and vendors could measure how often fear of retaliation deters reports about AI tools. Such surveys would establish whether the hazard exists at a meaningful rate.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Nothing is known about whether patients in these groups would learn of, understand, or trust a non-retaliation policy. Nothing is known about whether translated or plain-language versions would change their willingness to report AI-related concerns.

bottom_line: Five sources, three frameworks and two commentaries, endorse a centralized AI inventory with named owners, but no supplied study tests whether keeping one reduces untracked AI use or patient harm. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and regulatory expectation rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, and no study documents how often untracked AI systems operate in health systems. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The five endorsements agree on direction, but agreement among frameworks and commentaries does not substitute for comparative data on outcomes.

A commentary on the EU AI Act describes inventory and classification of all AI systems in use as a step that follows governance setup, and NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to define human oversight roles. For systems subject to these regimes, an inventory may serve as a compliance record whatever its measured effect on safety.

The CHAI playbook asks organizations to identify the tools and resources needed to build and maintain a registry, which implies ongoing staffing and software costs. No supplied study reports those costs, the effort needed to keep an inventory current, or how completeness is verified at scale.

The VIBE-HI commentary proposes recording tier, clinical purpose, owner, and review date for each tool as the minimum for audit. The logic is that a system nobody knows about cannot be monitored, but no supplied study shows that an inventory catches failures before they reach patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how many AI systems in a health system go unrecorded before and after an inventory is established, whether named ownership shortens the time to detect and correct AI malfunctions, and what staffing and tooling it takes to keep an inventory complete and current.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on whether an inventory performs differently in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Safety-net systems may have fewer resources for inventory tooling, and that possibility remains untested.

bottom_line: Twenty-one frameworks, guidelines, and commentaries endorse public transparency reporting on AI tools, but no supplied study tests whether such reports improve trust, accountability, or patient outcomes. A health system adopting this practice would be acting on expert consensus rather than on a measured effect.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests transparency reporting, and none documents the hazard of opaque AI use. The support comes from frameworks, one consensus guideline, and commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Certainty about any effect on trust or accountability cannot be rated.

One commentary on drafted portal replies proposes logging when drafting was used, how much clinicians edited, and downstream signals such as urgent visits within 24 to 72 hours. These logs could supply content for transparency reports. No supplied study shows that publishing such data catches errors before they reach patients.

A commentary on the EU AI Act proposes public reporting of algorithmic impact assessments and bias audits and compares this to financial disclosure. A regulatory discussion paper describes the argument that generative AI is too opaque for current device frameworks. Neither source reports a test of whether disclosure changes institutional behavior.

The HEAAL framework states that low-resource settings need infrastructure and technical assistance investments to adopt equity practices. The recommendation calls for reports tailored to patients, yet no supplied study examines whether such reports reach or are understood by patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

The CHAI playbook calls for trained staff assigned to defined governance roles. Producing and updating separate reports for patients, clinicians, and other stakeholders would draw on that staffing. No supplied study measures the cost, staff time, or update frequency needed to sustain such reporting.

research_gap: No study compares health systems or units that publish tailored AI transparency reports with those that do not. Useful designs would measure patient trust, clinician reliance and override behavior, complaint rates, and error detection, and would test the readability and comprehension of reports for each intended audience.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether patient-facing transparency reports are readable or useful to these groups is unknown, and translated and plain-language formats would need evaluation before a system assumes they work.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether a required intake and registration process for AI solutions reduces unreviewed use, and no supplied study documents how often AI tools enter use without review. The single endorsement quote addresses validating de-identification before training rather than intake registration, so support for R033 currently rests on expert framework guidance alone.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies of the practice and zero studies of the hazard. The one endorsing source, a CHAI playbook, is framework guidance, and its quoted text concerns de-identification of training data, which is indirect to mandatory intake registration. Under GRADE conventions, this supports no certainty rating for effect.

No supplied study measures how many AI tools reach clinical use without review or what harm follows when they do. Without that baseline, a health system cannot estimate how many errors an intake gate would intercept before they reach patients.

research_gap: Studies should first measure how often AI tools enter use in health systems without registration or review, and then compare systems with and without mandatory intake processes on unreviewed deployments, time to deployment, staff burden, and downstream safety events.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether an intake requirement is feasible for resource-limited safety-net systems, or whether it changes exposure to unreviewed tools for these patients, remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether recording minimum inventory fields improves governance or patient outcomes, and no study documents how often incomplete records cause harm. The recommendation rests on three frameworks, and only one of them names specific fields such as version and intended use.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The support comes from framework statements, which record expert agreement rather than measured effect. A GRADE assessment would treat this as an evidence gap rather than as low-certainty support.

The three sources differ in strength and fit. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide lists developer, date, version, intended use, and autonomy level at a "may" level. The CHAI playbook asks organizations to document inventory scope at a "must" level. The NIST AI 600-1 excerpt addresses safe deployment and risk tolerance but does not name inventory fields.

No supplied study links missing inventory fields, such as an absent monitoring owner or an unrecorded version, to delayed error detection or patient harm. The hazard is plausible, but its frequency and severity have not been measured in the material provided.

research_gap: Studies could compare health systems with and without required inventory fields. They could measure how often the owner and deployed version of a system can be identified, how long it takes to find affected systems after a vendor update or safety signal, and whether the field burden affects how complete and current the inventory remains.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer staff to maintain inventory records, and the frameworks offer no data on whether minimum-field requirements are feasible in those settings.

bottom_line: One voluntary framework, the CHAI governance playbooks, supports collecting AI solution information through a model card and a standardized intake questionnaire, but no study has tested a tiered intake that pairs a brief screener with a longer questionnaire for medium- and high-risk tools. Health systems that adopt this practice are relying on expert consensus rather than measured effects on review capacity or missed risks.

perspectives.view: No study tests tiered intake, and no study documents the target hazard of overwhelmed review capacity or missed high-risk details. The only support is one framework statement. Under GRADE conventions, this leaves no direct evidence on whether the practice changes review throughput, accuracy of risk classification, or downstream harm.

The CHAI endorsement recommends a model card or comparable documentation and, where applicable, a standardized intake questionnaire. The quoted text does not itself specify risk tiers or a two-step screener. Health systems should treat the tiered design as a local extension of voluntary guidance rather than as a requirement of any regulation.

A triage screener introduces a single decision point where a high-risk tool could be classified as low risk and receive only light review. No study measures how often this misclassification occurs or whether the longer questionnaire detects problems that the screener misses.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare tiered intake with uniform intake across governance committees and that measure review time, backlog, the rate at which the screener assigns tools to the wrong risk tier, and the number of safety or bias issues found before deployment.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations.
