It remains unknown whether screener questions would flag risks specific to these groups, such as language access or performance in under-resourced settings, and safety-net systems with small governance staff may face different capacity trade-offs.

bottom_line: Twelve sources endorse documenting each AI system in a model card or information sheet, but no supplied study tests whether this practice improves review decisions, user behavior, or patient outcomes. No supplied study documents the hazard either, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and regulatory direction.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests model cards or information sheets against any outcome, and no study documents the information gap itself. The twelve endorsements consist of frameworks, guidance, one statute, and commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not raise certainty, so the rating stays at no direct evidence.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes disclosure of model, data, and output risks, including bias risks and information gaps. Utah HB 452 requires disclosure before and at intervals during mental health chatbot use, which concerns user-facing disclosure more than technical documentation. CHAI frameworks treat model card content as a procurement requirement.

The CHAI playbook reports that many vendors provide model card information when formally requested even if they do not share it proactively. This suggests procurement contracts may be a low-cost route to obtaining documentation. No supplied source estimates the staff time needed to write, review, or keep model cards current for locally adapted tools.

Several commentaries argue that documenting intended populations and known limitations may reduce overreliance on model outputs. No supplied study shows that reviewers or clinicians read model cards or change decisions after reading them, so whether documentation catches errors before they reach patients remains untested.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI deployments with and without standardized model cards and measure whether reviewers identify limitations, whether clinicians adjust use for low-accuracy subgroups, and whether adverse events change. Studies should also measure how often model cards are accurate, complete, and updated after model changes.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on whether model cards disclose lower accuracy for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Two endorsements call for stating intended populations and subgroup performance, but whether documentation leads to action for these groups is unknown.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether system-level controls or clinician documentation of reasoning reduce erroneous AI-drafted messages reaching patients. perspectives.view: No study tests the recommended controls or the documentation practice, so certainty for the practice is rated as no direct evidence. The two available studies are a descriptive pilot of 80 users and a vignette simulation with 20 physicians. They show that the problem occurs but cannot indicate whether governance controls change what reaches patients.

In the simulation, all but one physician sent at least one erroneous response, and the likelihood of a missed error was greater than zero for each erroneous draft (p<0.001). Ninety percent trusted the tool. This pattern suggests individual review may not reliably catch errors, which is consistent with the case for system-level controls, though those controls remain untested.

In a real deployment, users started 20.2% of replies from an AI draft, and 40% of replies showed little to no editing. Drafts sometimes contained incorrect or inappropriate content (34.9%, n=15). These figures suggest limited editing in routine workflow. No study measured the time burden or fidelity of documenting reasoning for high-risk replies.

Texas SB 1188 holds the practitioner to the scope of licensure regardless of AI use. The augmented intelligence principles and the CHAI guide call for documenting AI use or output in the record. These sources set accountability and documentation expectations, but none presents outcome data showing that documentation of reasoning reduces message errors.

The simulation found that 90% of physicians trusted the tool while nearly all sent an erroneous reply. This finding suggests that patient reliance on clinician review may rest on checking that did not always occur. No study measured patient harm, patient trust, or whether patients could reach a human after receiving a flawed reply.

Neither hazard study reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients or clinics. Errors in drafted replies may affect patients differently depending on their ability to recognize them, but these studies provide no data on that question.

research_gap: No study has compared system-level controls, such as required editing, flagging of high-risk drafts, or audit of unedited sends, or a requirement to document reasoning for high-risk replies, against usual clinician review. A pragmatic trial or stepped-wedge evaluation in live portal workflows could measure the rate of erroneous content reaching patients, clinician time per message, documentation fidelity, and patient-reported outcomes, with enrollment that includes safety-net sites and patients with limited English proficiency.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and neither hazard study reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups therefore have no evidence on how often drafting errors reach their patients or whether the recommended controls would help them.

perspectives.view: Two studies test the practice. A pathology replay with 1,356 patients evaluated locked models independently but did not compare that evaluation with developer-led assessment. An automated benchmark compared independent and same-provider judges and did not report its setting. Both are offline and neither measured patient outcomes, so serious indirectness and imprecision place certainty at very low.

Self-preference bias skewed HealthBench scores by up to 10 points, and all eight judges in another study favored their own answers. GPT-5's self-evaluation deviated from blinded clinician ratings. In one test of the practice, excluding the own-provider judge changed which model over-commits least. This suggests self-assessment may misrank model safety.

In the pathology test, masked assessors independent of the developers evaluated locked models and found modest correlation with pathologist sTILs (r 0.375-0.473). The study shows that independent evaluation of locked models is feasible offline. It did not report the staffing, time, or workflow burden that such evaluation required.

The CHAI guide and a regulatory discussion paper call for independent evaluators, and the paper extends independence to third-party model developers. A lineage study found that evaluators favored outputs of architectural siblings. This suggests independence criteria may need to address shared model lineage as well as organizational separation.

One hazard study scored 3,800 clinical items that included non-English content and found lineage bias independent of language. Neither test of the practice reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether independent audits detect performance gaps in these groups therefore remains unknown.

research_gap: No study has prospectively compared independent and developer-led evaluations of a clinical AI tool in deployment and measured the number of errors or subgroup performance gaps each approach detects, the effect on patient outcomes, or the cost and staffing each approach requires.
underserved_note: Neither study that tested the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The endorsements do not say whether impact ratings should weigh harms that fall unevenly on these groups. A scoring scheme built on average impact could rank risks concentrated in small or underserved populations as low priority, and that possibility has not been examined.

bottom_line: Six sources, all frameworks or commentaries, endorse periodic and change-triggered reassessment of AI risk, but no study tests whether the practice keeps risk assessments current or prevents harm. No study was supplied that documents stale risk assessments as a measured problem in health care AI.

perspectives.view: No study tests reassessment on a cadence or after material change, and no study documents the hazard. The six endorsements consist of two CHAI frameworks and four commentaries. They agree on the principle, but agreement among expert opinion sources does not raise GRADE certainty. The recommendation therefore rests on consensus rather than measured effect.

The endorsements name model updates, distribution channel changes, and sentinel events as triggers for re-review. These triggers are plausible failure points, but no supplied study shows how often assessments go stale or whether re-review catches problems before they reach patients.

One commentary proposes quarterly re-scoring, and another asks institutions to version scores with date-stamped assumptions. No source reports the staff time, cost, or completion rates of such schedules, so health systems have no evidence to size the workload or choose an interval.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare scheduled and change-triggered reassessment with one-time assessment. These studies should measure how often reassessments detect changed risk, whether they lead to mitigation or withdrawal, the staff effort involved, and downstream patient harm. Descriptive work that measures how often deployed AI risk assessments become outdated would also establish whether the hazard occurs in practice.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Reassessment triggers named in the endorsements do not mention shifts in the patient population served, so a system may not detect risk changes that arise when a tool expands to these groups.

bottom_line: Four frameworks and guidance documents, including an FDA draft guidance, recommend documented AI risk assessment plans and results, but no supplied study tests whether the practice reduces harm or improves risk tracking. No supplied study documents the hazard of ad hoc, untracked risk activities either, so the recommendation rests on consensus and regulatory expectation alone.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The four endorsements agree in direction, and that agreement reflects expert consensus rather than measured effects on patient outcomes, error detection, or the completeness of risk records.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions recommends that sponsors apply AAMI CR34971, the recognized standard adapting ISO 14971 risk management to machine learning. For device sponsors, a documented risk file may therefore become a submission expectation. FUTURE-AI and the CHAI guides extend similar documentation expectations to deployers outside FDA jurisdiction, though these carry no legal force.

research_gap: No study compares organizations or AI deployments with and without documented, lifecycle-updated risk assessment plans. Useful designs would measure whether such documentation changes how often deployment risks, data gaps, or failed controls are detected before patient harm, and what staff time the documentation requires.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether documented risk plans identify data gaps affecting their patients, and they may need to require that risk files address subgroup performance explicitly.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether defining an organizational AI risk tolerance, and declining or deferring AI that exceeds it, reduces the deployment of AI with unacceptable residual risk. The recommendation rests on two framework statements from CHAI and NIST that address risk tolerance directly, plus two related endorsements that do not.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. Two of the four endorsements address risk tolerance directly. The other two concern awareness of misinformation and vendor model cards, which are adjacent practices rather than the threshold-setting practice itself.

The NIST Generative AI Profile tells organizations to use risk tolerance to judge acceptable performance and to decommission or retrain models outside defined limits. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks whether a solution fits the organization's risk tolerance. Both are voluntary frameworks written as should statements, and neither carries regulatory force on its own.

research_gap: No study has examined whether health systems with a written AI risk tolerance decline, defer, or decommission tools at different rates than systems without one. No study has examined whether such thresholds are associated with fewer patient harms. A useful first study would compare governance decisions and post-deployment incidents across organizations with and without defined thresholds. It would also record how thresholds are set and who sets them.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether organizational risk thresholds account for risks that fall more heavily on these groups, or whether safety-net systems have the capacity to set and apply such thresholds.

bottom_line: Five guidance and framework sources endorse documenting a mitigate, transfer, avoid, or accept response for each identified AI risk, but only one simulated phantom study tests any part of it and reports a 43% average reduction in risk priority scores after mitigation. No study tests the transfer, avoid, or accept options, or whether documented responses change patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: One level 4 study using 25 phantom tests in an offline setting reports that mitigation lowered the average risk priority number by 43% across ten high-risk failure modes. The design is simulated, the clinical setting is not reported, and the outcome is a scored risk estimate rather than observed harm. Certainty is very low for indirectness and imprecision.

Eligibility screening, staff training, and workflow formalization were the mitigations applied to the top ten failure modes, and their scored risk fell by 43% on average. Risk priority numbers depend on team judgment of severity, occurrence, and detection, so the reduction may reflect rescoring as much as fewer errors reaching patients.

The mitigations in the single study were workflow and training changes, which suggests that risk responses are carried out inside clinical routines rather than in the model. The study used phantoms and motion traces, so it does not show whether staff sustain these steps in live care or what time they require.

FUTURE-AI states that teams shall maintain a risk management file, and NIST AI 600-1 advises mitigating, transferring, or avoiding risks above organizational tolerance. CHAI sources describe using contracts to assign risk to vendors. These endorsements rest on consensus and existing risk-management practice, and no supplied study tests contractual transfer or documented acceptance.

research_gap: No study compares governance programs that document a response for each AI risk with programs that do not, and none examines transfer through contracts or insurance, avoidance, or formal acceptance. Prospective studies in deployed clinical settings should measure observed errors and harms in addition to risk priority scores, and they should report staff time and cost.
underserved_note: The one test used phantoms and patient-derived motion traces and reported no patient population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from this evidence whether risk scoring and chosen responses account for hazards that fall more heavily on these groups.

bottom_line: Thirteen sources endorse classifying each AI use case by risk tier before deployment, but no supplied study tests whether this practice changes the scrutiny high-risk uses receive or reduces harm. No supplied study documents the target hazard either, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests pre-deployment risk tiering, and none documents how often high-risk uses receive too little review. Of the listed endorsements, 8 are commentaries and 4 are frameworks or guidance. Expert consensus of this kind cannot be graded as evidence of effect, so no certainty rating for the practice's effect can be assigned.

The endorsing sources propose different schemes. One commentary uses three tiers, VIBE-HI uses four tiers built on four criteria, and another commentary uses a probability-by-severity matrix. No study shows which scheme reviewers apply consistently or how much review time each adds. That gap bears directly on the hazard of inconsistent classification.

Endorsement strength varies across sources. RUAIH guidance states that organizations must categorize and document risks, while NIST AI 600-1 says organizations may scale resources to severity and likelihood. One commentary on mental health AI ties tier assignment to reassessment when models, prompts, interfaces, or target populations change. None of these sources reports outcome data.

research_gap: Studies should test whether a standardized tiering framework with documented rationale yields consistent tier assignments across reviewers, and whether use cases rated high risk then receive more validation and monitoring. Studies should also measure downstream safety events against a comparison group without structured tiering. Inter-rater agreement studies comparing the three-tier, four-tier, and probability-by-severity schemes would help governance teams choose among them.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether tiering criteria account for the added risk an AI tool may carry for these patients. A tool rated low risk for the general population could warrant a higher tier where language access or literacy affects how patients receive its output.

bottom_line: Seven guidance documents endorse AI impact assessments, but no study has tested whether conducting them reduces overlooked harms. One interview study of 40 U.S. developers found that formal procedures to assess harm potential were lacking, which documents the gap without showing that assessments close it.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates impact assessments as an intervention, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The one available study interviewed 40 developers in the United States. It shows that the hazard exists, since developers recognized harms but lacked formal procedures to assess them. It cannot show whether assessments change deployment decisions or patient outcomes.

Developers in the interview study named harms to patients, the public, and health systems, yet they described no formal process to judge harm potential or the need for mitigation. An impact assessment may surface these failure modes before deployment. No data show how often it catches harms that would otherwise reach patients.

Two European commentaries read Article 27 of the EU AI Act, together with the GDPR, as requiring a fundamental rights impact assessment and a data protection impact assessment before implementation. FUTURE-AI lists a lifecycle risk management file as a must. NIST AI 600-1 and CHAI present assessments as voluntary, so obligations differ by jurisdiction.

CHAI asks organizations to identify contextual factors such as individuals' demographics, which could direct attention to affected subgroups. The single hazard study interviewed developers rather than patients and reported no findings for Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency populations. Whether assessments detect harms concentrated in these groups remains untested.

The CHAI playbook asks organizations to evaluate cumulative risk across all deployed systems that share a workflow, patient population, or staff group, which extends the assessment beyond single tools. No supplied study reports the staff time, cost, or expertise that such assessments require, so organizations cannot estimate the burden from existing evidence.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployment decisions and post-deployment harm reports between organizations that conduct structured impact assessments and those that do not, and that measure the staff time and cost each assessment requires.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study sampled developers without reporting on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups have no evidence on whether impact assessments identify harms specific to their patients.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether assigning portal messages to risk tiers changes the safety of AI-drafted replies, and no study documents the hazard directly. The recommendation rests on a single commentary that advises restricting or disabling AI drafting for message categories it judges high-risk.

perspectives.view: The evidence base consists of one commentary using "should" language and zero studies of the practice or the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without supporting data cannot establish certainty of effect. The tiering thresholds, the categories assigned to each tier, and the clinician actions tied to them have not been evaluated for accuracy or outcomes.

The endorsing commentary names categories such as chest pain equivalents, neurologic symptoms, pregnancy-related bleeding, mental health crisis language, and anticoagulant complications as candidates for restriction. These choices reflect where missed urgency may cause severe harm. No supplied study reports how often a tiering rule misclassifies an urgent message into a lower tier and allows a draft to proceed.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how accurately a risk-tiering method sorts real portal messages, how often high-risk messages are misrouted to AI drafting, and whether tiering changes clinician review behavior, reply errors, response times, and downstream patient harm compared with untiered drafting.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Messages written in other languages or in nonstandard phrasing may be classified differently by a tiering rule, and without testing in these groups a health system cannot know whether urgent messages from these patients are sorted as reliably as others.

bottom_line: Federal regulation at 45 CFR 92.210 requires covered entities to make ongoing, reasonable efforts to identify decision support tools that use protected characteristics as inputs, and no study has tested whether such a process detects or prevents discriminatory decisions. One qualitative request-for-information study found 18 algorithms in current use that respondents flagged for potential bias from race or ethnicity inputs.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates an identification process, so certainty for the practice rests on no direct evidence. The one related study is a level 4 qualitative request for information with 42 respondents. It shows that race-based algorithms are in use, but it does not measure how often an inventory finds them or whether finding them changes decisions.

The practice is a legal duty for covered entities under 45 CFR 92.210, so adoption does not depend on evidence of effect. The rule sets a reasonable-efforts standard across six characteristics. The algorithms flagged in the study, such as the SCORE osteoporosis tool and the VBAC risk calculator, suggest the rule may reach ordinary clinical calculators as well as vendor AI products.

The study documents that tools with race or ethnicity inputs remain in clinical use, which is the precondition for discriminatory output going unnoticed. An inventory functions as a detection step and does not by itself correct a biased tool. No evidence shows how many such tools an internal process catches or whether review and correction follow.

The hazard study focused on racial and ethnic minority populations and on race or ethnicity inputs. It did not examine national origin, disability, age, or sex inputs, and it did not report findings from Medicaid or safety-net settings. The available evidence therefore addresses only part of what the rule asks entities to identify.

research_gap: No study has measured whether an ongoing identification process finds decision support tools that use protected characteristics, how complete its findings are compared with an independent audit, what staff time it requires, or whether identification leads to changes in tool use and patient outcomes. Future work should also cover inputs beyond race and ethnicity, including disability, age, sex, and national origin.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The single hazard study focused on racial and ethnic minority populations, which leaves systems serving these groups without evidence on how well an identification process performs in their settings or for inputs such as national origin that may relate to language access.

bottom_line: No study tests whether turning AI off by default in sensitive encounter types, with documented case-by-case enablement, protects privacy, trust, or candor. Two hazard studies suggest that AI use in some mental health and surveillance-sensitive contexts may lower patient acceptance or be contraindicated, but neither evaluates the proposed safeguard.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two included studies document the hazard only. One is a descriptive survey and interview study, and the other is a vignette experiment with prospective patients. Neither compares default-off settings with any alternative, and the endorsing framework quote concerns change-of-control notice rather than sensitive encounters.

In an Australian deployment, clinicians reported that AI scribe use may be contraindicated for patients with persecutory delusions involving surveillance. This suggests a failure mode in which recording itself may worsen symptoms or disengagement. The study does not show whether a default-off rule would catch these cases before recording begins.

Among 201 United States adults reading therapy vignettes, therapist AI use reduced acceptability and intent to continue care compared with control (all p<0.001), and covert use produced the largest declines. These results suggest that patients may value knowing about and agreeing to AI use in sensitive care, though the setting was simulated.

The endorsing commentary calls for specific safeguards for minors, patients with low literacy, and multilingual encounters, and for recording to default to off in emergencies. The hazard studies do not report results for limited English proficiency, low-literacy, Medicaid, or safety-net patients, so the need these groups face under this practice remains untested.

research_gap: Pragmatic studies are needed that compare default-off with documented enablement against default-on with opt-out in encounter types such as mental health, reproductive care, substance use, care of minors, and emergencies. Useful outcomes would include patient disclosure and trust, continuation of care, clinician documentation burden, and how faithfully enablement decisions are recorded. Samples should include patients with limited English proficiency and low literacy.
underserved_note: Neither study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The commentary identifies low-literacy and multilingual encounters as needing added safeguards, but no data show how default-off rules or case-by-case enablement would work for these patients, so any benefit to them is unknown.

bottom_line: One offline study of 100 patient messages found that 56% of ChatGPT drafts to easy questions were acceptable to send versus 34% for difficult questions (P = .03), which suggests draft quality may vary by message class. No study has tested whether limiting drafting to lower-risk classes in live use reduces harmful errors or delayed escalation.

perspectives.view: The single test of the practice is a retrospective rater study of 100 messages with no live deployment. It compared draft quality by question difficulty but did not measure patient outcomes, escalation delays, or how well messages were sorted into tiers. One small, indirect study places certainty at very low.

In a vignette study, physicians missed potentially harmful omissions about a blood clot and DKA in 65% and 75% of cases. Among 201 real primary care drafts, 27.4% had limitations without strengths, including premature next steps. These results suggest clinician review may not catch errors, so scoping may reduce exposure without removing it.

Across 4257 consultation records, chatbot replies in decision-making scenarios were rated moderately trustworthy or higher in 50.71% of cases versus 93.29% for the comparison, while education scenarios showed higher completeness. This suggests message scenario could inform tiering, but no study measured how accurately a live inbox assigns messages to tiers.

The one test of the practice did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. The only study with non-English content came from China and documented the hazard rather than testing scoping. Whether message tiers perform the same way for these patients is unknown.

The endorsing commentary asks that scoping come with interface cues that keep clinicians alert regardless of tier. The missed omissions in simulated review suggest a lower-risk label may not guarantee a safe reply. No study measured whether patients with urgent messages reached a clinician sooner under a scoping policy.

research_gap: A prospective study in live patient portals should compare scoped versus unscoped drafting and measure misclassification of urgent messages, harmful errors that reach patients, and time to escalation, with deliberate enrollment of safety-net, Medicaid, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy patients.
underserved_note: The only test of the practice (pmid:39162591) did not report including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A hazard study of non-English consultations from China (pmid:40397947) shows the problem exists in that setting but does not show that scoping works there, so any benefit for these groups remains untested.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether restricting automated coverage systems to administrative tasks, with determinations based on individual need and current guidelines, changes denial rates or patient outcomes. Two simulation studies suggest that large language models placed in insurer roles may shift toward financial priorities and produce demographic disparities, which documents the hazard but does not evaluate this safeguard.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Both available studies are level 4 vignette simulations run offline with large language models. They show that the hazard can appear in simulated settings. They measure model outputs rather than actual coverage determinations, denials, or patient outcomes under any restriction policy.

Across 675 responses from three models, the insurer role shifted primary ethical values from beneficence (27%) to financial stewardship (20%). This suggests automated systems may weigh cost over clinical need when framed as payers. No study examined whether limiting these systems to administrative work, or requiring physician review before denial, stops such errors before they reach patients.

Across 19,900 simulated prior authorization decisions, model outputs showed significant demographic disparities. Adding tumor-specific information skewed recommendations toward RFFF across sociodemographic backgrounds. The study did not report Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency subgroups, and no study tested whether individual-need determinations reduce these disparities.

The single endorsement is guidance stating that treating physicians must have the opportunity to discuss medical necessity with the reviewing physician before an adverse determination. This guidance addresses one element of the recommendation, physician-to-physician review. No study cited here supports it.

Under the endorsed requirement, a physician would discuss medical necessity before care is denied, so the decision would not rest on an automated system alone. The simulation findings suggest why patients may distrust algorithmic denials. No study measured whether this safeguard preserves access, shortens delays, or improves trust.

research_gap: Studies should compare coverage determinations, overturned denials, time to care, and patient outcomes between payers that limit automated systems to administrative functions with physician review and payers that allow automated determinations. These studies should use real claims data and report results by payer type, language, literacy, and demographic group.
underserved_note: Neither hazard study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study tested the practice. The demographic disparities seen in simulated prior authorization suggest these groups may face added risk. Whether the recommendation protects them remains unknown.

bottom_line: Seven studies test scope enforcement, and all but one are simulations or automated benchmarks. They suggest that refusal instructions and scope controls can raise correct refusals, sometimes at a cost to answering legitimate questions, but none tests multi-turn drift or the usefulness of redirection in live care.

perspectives.view: Six of seven tests are level 4 or 5 simulations or benchmarks. The one real deployment involved 8 pharmacy leaders and reported no numbers. Refusal rose from 0/30 at baseline to 90% to 100% with refusal instructions, but only on single-turn queries. Indirectness, small samples, and missing rates support very low certainty.

Hazard studies report that 61.4% of conversations that began with a safe response later collapsed to unsafe, and that jailbreak success reached 82.1% under role-play and multi-turn prompting. Among tests of the practice, a safety system prompt raised safety-appropriate rates by 5.9 points under adversarial caregiver pressure. No test examined cumulative multi-turn drift.

Adding an out-of-distribution classifier raised appropriate refusal from 0.94 to 0.97 and cut utility on legitimate questions from 0.86 to 0.69. Separate benchmarks found safety-optimised models refusing up to 80% of hard benign prompts, and one model reached 16% accuracy because of over-refusal. Testing may therefore need to measure over-refusal alongside refusal.

One test used Thai-language questions and found that removing the safety prompt led the model to produce a full drug-dosing schedule. Hazard studies in Japanese and Chinese settings show safety declining over conversation turns. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users.

A regulatory discussion paper lists adversarial prompting, prompt injection, emotional manipulation, and multi-turn drift as possible testing, using permissive language. The tests of the practice cover single-turn and benchmark adversarial queries. None follows the multi-turn cumulative drift scenario the paper describes.

One agent system with process-boundary governance blocked all adversarial and out-of-scope requests across three datasets regardless of the model used. This suggests that scope controls placed outside the model may carry over when vendors change models. Another system averaged 5.3 seconds per response. Neither study reported staffing or cost.

In one simulation, chatbots endorsed 32% of harmful proposals rather than setting limits or redirecting. Another study found that models often fail to redirect false-premise questions even after detecting the premise. No test measured whether a refusal pointed patients to a clinician or other human help.

research_gap: No study tests scope enforcement under multi-turn adversarial conversation in a deployed clinical tool. No study measures whether refusals give useful redirection to a human or an appropriate resource. The trade-off between correct refusal and over-refusal has been measured in only one benchmark of 136 questions.
underserved_note: One test of the practice used Thai-language questions, which covers a non-English population in a benchmark setting only. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users. Health systems serving these patients therefore have no direct evidence on how scope controls perform for them.

bottom_line: One automated benchmark reports that a pre-execution verification toolkit reduced harmful agent actions by 87%, and no study has tested the practice in a clinical setting. Seven hazard studies show that agents often take unsafe actions and pass along tampered or erroneous tool outputs, which shows why testing is needed but does not show that any detection method works in care delivery.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice is a level 5 automated benchmark that reports no sample size or setting. It found an 87% reduction in harmful actions. A single indirect study with unknown precision supports very low certainty. The seven hazard studies show the problem is common, but they do not test whether detection reduces it.

In adversarial trials, baseline agents executed unauthorized tools 56–60% of the time. In another study, models chose sham guideline outputs in 40.6% of evaluations, and failure reached 54.2% to 61.7% when warnings or allergy data were removed. Agents rarely withheld writing into tampered charts. These rates suggest that undetected errors could reach patients.

Across 1,200,000 tool calls, GPT-4.1 flagged mismatched headers in 17.4% of runs and never detected subtle faults. GPT-4.1-nano caught under 1% of MRN or age changes. Safety violations grew as the action space scaled. Domain-specific plugins gave 35% greater harm reduction than generic verification, which suggests generic checks may miss clinical errors.

The single test of the practice reported no population or setting. Among hazard studies, only one named a population. It covered older adults in 27 agent runs in the United Kingdom, and errors propagated identically across independent repetitions. No study examined Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

One regulatory discussion paper describes evaluating whether an agentic device recognizes when a planned action sequence would exceed its intended use or safety envelope. The paper describes this evaluation but does not require it. The supplied evidence offers no validated test method for premarket review, because the only test is a benchmark without clinical data.

Patients cannot see an agent's tool calls, so they depend on the agent to catch tampered identity fields. In hazard benchmarks, GPT-5-chat never identified chart mismatches. Until detection is tested in care settings, patients may expect a clinician to review agent actions before those actions take effect.

research_gap: No study has tested detection of out-of-envelope action plans or erroneous tool outputs in a live or shadow clinical deployment. No study has measured the effect of detection on patient harm or reported how often detection wrongly blocks correct actions. Trials that compare domain-specific and generic verification on dosing, allergy, and patient-identity checks would address the main gaps.
underserved_note: The one test of the practice reported no population or setting. No hazard study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one hazard study included older adults. Health systems that serve these groups have no evidence on whether detection methods perform as well on their patients' records.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether restricting diagnostic AI to licensed practitioners acting within their scope, with a legal review before deployment, prevents misuse or harm. The recommendation rests on one Texas statute, SB 1188, which requires that a practitioner act within the scope of their license regardless of AI use.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation draws its support from a legal requirement, and a legal requirement shows what is mandated rather than what is effective.

Texas SB 1188 states that the practitioner must act within the scope of their license, certification, or other authorization, regardless of the use of artificial intelligence. For Texas systems this is a statutory obligation. Systems in other states may face different or no equivalent rules, which may make a per-deployment legal review necessary.

No supplied study measures how often diagnostic AI is used by unqualified users or outside legal limits, or what harm results. Without such data, the size of the hazard and the degree to which scope restrictions would catch errors before they reach patients remain unknown.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often diagnostic AI is used outside licensed scope, what harms follow, and whether access controls tied to license and scope, together with pre-deployment legal review, reduce those events compared with usual governance.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The effect of scope restrictions in settings that rely on non-physician staff or have limited legal review capacity is therefore unknown.

bottom_line: Four offline or simulated studies suggest that structured multidisciplinary hazard analysis can identify dozens of application-specific failure modes, and two report lower risk ratings after mitigation. No study measured whether this practice reduces harm to patients, so the evidence for R052 rests on process outcomes.

perspectives.view: Four studies test the practice, all at evidence level 4 and all offline or simulated. Three apply multidisciplinary FMEA or fault tree analysis to AI workflows, one of them in radiotherapy. One randomized study tests AI-generated stories as prompts for harm identification. None measures patient outcomes, so indirectness and small samples leave certainty very low.

A Belgian FMEA of an AI planning workflow identified 39 failure modes. One was rated Not acceptable before mitigation, and none were after. A second team found 46 failure modes and reported an average 43% RPN reduction across the top ten. The process may surface and reprioritize risks, but RPN values are expert ratings, and no study counted errors reaching patients.

In a Chinese AI-driven radiotherapy workflow, eight experts identified 86 failure modes across 5 steps and 28 sub-steps. Of these, 25 were high risk, mostly in ROI delineation, and human error was the primary factor. This suggests that many hazards may arise where staff interact with the tool rather than in the model alone.

FDA draft guidance expects manufacturers to identify hazards under normal and fault conditions. Utah HB 452 requires identification of foreseeable adverse outcomes for mental health chatbots. The tested studies examined clinical AI workflows and a harm-elicitation exercise. None was described as evaluating a mental health chatbot, so evidence for that statutory setting is indirect.

The tested exercises relied on multidisciplinary expert panels, including one of eight experts, and none reported staff hours or costs. CHAI's guide notes that use-specific testing may burden clinicians. Leaders may need a staffing commitment for each tool reviewed, but the studies do not measure its size.

In a randomized study, participants without AI-generated stories directed 79.1% of responses to privacy and well-being. Those who read stories spread responses across all 17 harm types. This may mean that unaided review teams overlook some harms that matter to patients. Patients receiving care were not the subjects of the study.

research_gap: No study compares AI deployments with and without structured multidisciplinary hazard analysis on errors that reach patients or on adverse events. The existing tests are offline or simulated and cover a small number of clinical workflows. Prospective evaluations in other clinical domains, including patient-facing chatbots and generative AI tools, should report detection of real-world failures and the staff time and cost of the process.
underserved_note: None of the four tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. All were offline exercises in Belgium, China, or an unreported setting. It remains unknown whether hazard teams identify failure modes specific to these groups, such as language or comprehension errors, unless members who represent them take part in the review.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether declining or restricting AI tools after failed validation or excess risk reduces harm, and no study supplied documents the hazard of broad deployment of such tools. Five sources endorse the practice, four at a "should" level and one at a "may" level, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The five endorsements come from three frameworks, one guidance document, and one commentary, and none reports outcome data from a governance decision to decline or restrict a tool.

The endorsing sources differ in strength. The CHAI guides and the augmented intelligence principles use "should" language tied to organizational risk tolerance and mitigation capacity. NIST AI 600-1 uses "may" and leaves risk tiering to each organization. None of the supplied sources ties the practice to a specific statute or regulatory requirement.

The selective deployment commentary proposes restricting a dermatology app to light-skinned groups while more data are gathered. This approach limits exposure to a tool that may perform worse for dark-skinned patients, but it also withholds any benefit from them. No supplied study measures how restriction decisions affect access or outcomes across groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that follow governance decisions to decline, restrict, or conditionally deploy AI tools after failed or partial validation, and that compare patient harm, access, and performance gaps against broad deployment. Such studies should also describe what safeguards were attached to restricted use and whether staff adhered to the restrictions in practice.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The selective deployment commentary raises the possibility that restriction could shift benefits away from groups underrepresented in validation data, and health systems have no measured basis for judging how often that occurs.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether documenting and bounding agentic AI autonomy prevents unauthorized, irreversible, or scope-creeping actions, and no study documents how often such actions occur. Six sources endorse the practice, and all of them rest on expert reasoning rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies of the practice and zero studies of the hazard. The six endorsements include one framework, one regulatory discussion paper, and four commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an effect estimate, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

No supplied study measures the frequency or severity of harmful actions taken by AI agents across connected clinical systems. Without a hazard study, deployers cannot yet tell whether human checkpoints and reversibility requirements would catch errors before they reach patients, or which action types carry the most risk.

The regulatory discussion paper describes a proposal for competency-based oversight modeled on supervised practice and periodic reevaluation, which differs from current device review. This source describes a proposal rather than an adopted rule. Deployers therefore face no identified federal requirement specific to agent autonomy bounds among the supplied sources.

research_gap: Studies should record the actions AI agents take in live clinical and administrative systems, count unauthorized or irreversible actions, and compare deployments with and without documented autonomy bounds, human checkpoints, and vendor disclosure.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence addresses Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups cannot draw on data showing whether autonomy bounds protect their patients, including those whose concerns one commentary flags as unsuitable for fully automated routing or triage.

bottom_line: Nineteen sources, including frameworks, FDA draft guidance, and clinical commentaries, endorse documenting intended use, users, setting, and excluded uses for each AI solution, but no supplied study tests whether this documentation reduces unvalidated use or clarifies accountability. The recommendation rests on consensus and regulatory expectation rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard of undefined scope. Support comes from frameworks, guidance, and commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Certainty that use-case documentation changes outcomes cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to describe the intended use environment, such as clinical or home settings. This suggests that scope documentation already aligns with device submission expectations, though the guidance is in draft form and does not report whether such descriptions prevent off-label deployment.

A perioperative and intensive care commentary proposes explicit exclusions, such as no autonomous treatment decisions and no independent allocation of life-support resources. Named exclusions may give clinicians a reference point to stop an unvalidated use, but no supplied study measures whether exclusion lists are read or followed at the point of care.

The HEAAL framework and a viewpoint on extrinsic trust ask that systems state whom they were designed for and show consistent performance across subgroups. Documenting the intended population could expose gaps for groups absent from development data, but no supplied study tests whether it does.

research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without use-case scope documentation on rates of use outside validated populations or settings, time to identify an accountable owner after an incident, or clinician awareness of excluded uses. Studies are also needed on how often scope records are kept current after deployment and who reads them.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on whether scope documentation protects Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups may wish to require that the documented intended population state explicitly whether such patients were represented in validation.

bottom_line: Four sources, one framework, one guidance document, and two commentaries, endorse requiring vendors to disclose intended use, problem formulation, intended population and setting, and conditions of non-use, but no supplied study tests whether this requirement changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes. No supplied study documents how often purchasers deploy tools in contraindicated conditions because vendor information was missing.

perspectives.view: The supplied record contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The endorsements come from a framework, a guidance document, and two commentaries, which are expert opinion under GRADE conventions. Their agreement shows consensus on the idea but cannot establish an effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The recommendation assumes that missing vendor information leads to use in contraindicated conditions, and that disclosure prevents it. Neither step has supplied data behind it. A disclosure document may catch errors only if someone reads it and checks it against local conditions before go-live, and the supplied sources do not report whether that happens.

The supplied endorsements rely on contractual obligation and procurement requirements rather than statute or regulation. The CHAI playbook frames disclosure as a contract term, and one commentary proposes an admissibility dossier before routine deployment. No supplied source reports how such contract terms are enforced or whether vendors comply.

research_gap: No study compares deployments made with and without structured vendor disclosure of intended use and contraindicated conditions, and none measures the frequency of off-label or out-of-scope AI deployment. A useful first study would audit current contracts and deployed tools to estimate how often use falls outside vendor-stated scope, followed by a comparison of sites that require disclosure against sites that do not.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. One endorsing commentary addresses resource-limited perioperative settings, but it offers opinion rather than data, and whether disclosed intended populations actually include these groups remains unexamined.

bottom_line: Seven sources endorse documenting context of use, sources of setting variation, dataset constraints, and limits on generalization, but no study has tested whether such documentation prevents performance failures in new settings. Ten hazard studies show that performance often drops when models meet data, sites, or populations that differ from development data.

perspectives.view: No study tests whether documenting context of use changes outcomes, so certainty about the practice is rated as no direct evidence. Nine of the ten hazard studies are level 4 or 5 offline or benchmark designs, and one is a level 3 deployment study. They consistently show performance loss outside development conditions. That establishes the problem but does not show the remedy works.

Aggregate metrics can hide subgroup failures. OOD AUROC often fell below 0.5 for some subpopulations despite acceptable global performance. A surgical imaging model's IOU fell from 0.62 to 0.45 on unseen videos, and it gave no prediction for one poor-perfusion case. Documented limits may help users recognize out-of-scope use, though no study confirms this.

Inputs captured in routine workflow differ from development data. Phone-recorded echocardiogram videos raised LVEF error from 6.08 to 7.00 percentage points, and low-quality endoscopic images produced an 11.6% performance decline. These results suggest documentation should describe expected input quality and capture methods. No study has examined whether clinicians read and act on such statements.

Local terminology and regional disease patterns affected accuracy. LLM answers were more often inappropriate when questions used Western Australia-specific terms. Tuberculosis error rates exceeded 60% for three models tested on Chinese clinical cases. No study examined Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy settings, so documented contexts of use may omit populations that differ from development data.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks for instructions on preparing input data and on the expected characteristics of users. FUTURE-AI asks for a standard definition of the clinical task. These endorsements rest on expert consensus. No study shows that labeling of this kind reduces generalization failures after deployment.

research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without documented context of use and generalization limits. A useful test would measure whether such documentation changes local validation decisions, reduces out-of-scope use, or improves site-level performance. It should include safety-net and limited English proficiency settings.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study (pmid:42311928) used Chinese clinical cases in a non-English context and found region-specific error patterns. This suggests that context-of-use statements may not describe these populations unless developers report them explicitly.

bottom_line: One randomized trial and one prospective study in real deployments, along with five offline studies, suggest that automating lower-risk or high-confidence cases and routing the rest to humans may preserve accuracy while reducing human workload. The certainty of this evidence is low because tasks and outcomes vary widely, most tests were simulated, and the trial did not report its setting or population.

perspectives.view: One real-deployment randomized trial reported 96% accurate guidance, 0% of the most severe safety events, and 65% fewer standard-risk queries routed to humans, but it did not report setting or population. One prospective study and five offline studies point the same way across unrelated tasks. Consistency favors the practice, while indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to low.

In one pathology cohort, full automation had a 16.1% accuracy decrease prospectively, while routing low-confidence cases to review gave 95.9% accuracy, comparable to full manual review. In hazard studies, the most severe safety incidents rose from 2.3% to 23.1% with case complexity, and autonomous surgical decisions matched practice in 20.0% to 25.8% of cases. These findings support the premise for routing but do not show that it prevents harm.

In one real deployment, concordance was 97.9% for common, lower-complexity conditions that met a confidence threshold, compared with 91.3% across all encounters. One offline study abstained on about 80% of cases to reach an AUC of 0.90. Another reported residual hallucination, edge-case misclassification, and overreliance even with human review in the loop.

Reported workload reductions were 80.7% of human reads in a cancer screening program, 68.9% of pathology review, and 65% of routed standard-risk queries, with screening sensitivity of 81.7% versus 79.8%. Savings depend on how many cases the system defers, and one model deferred about 80%. None of these studies reported costs or staffing requirements.

In a vignette study, adding a single physician improved every language model's diagnostic performance, and performance rose as more humans were added. The trial reduced standard-risk queries routed to humans by 65%, but it did not report who submitted those queries. No study measured patient trust or whether patients who wanted a human reviewer could reach one.

No study testing the practice reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The only hazard study with non-English speakers found that physicians attributed 43.42% of guidance errors to overreliance on medical history. This shows that such problems exist in these groups but does not test routing for them.

research_gap: No real-deployment trial has compared risk- or confidence-based routing with both full automation and full human review while reporting patient harms, time to human contact, the method used to set routing thresholds, and results by payer, language, and literacy. Studies also have not reported the costs and staffing needed to handle deferred cases.
underserved_note: None of the seven tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One offline study included older adults in China. Health systems serving these groups therefore have no direct evidence that routing thresholds perform equally well for their patients and would need to monitor performance locally.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether a written statement of an AI tool's intended purposes, population, abilities, and limitations reduces misuse or overreliance, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. Support for R076 rests on one state statute, one assurance framework, one guidance document, and three commentaries.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The six endorsements are expert opinion and policy text, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures user understanding or out-of-scope use with and without such statements.

Utah HB 452 (2025) is the only mandatory source, and the quoted clause requires development and monitoring consistent with clinical best practices rather than a written scope statement. The CHAI guide and the augmented intelligence principles use should language. Organizations may therefore face voluntary expectations more often than binding duties for this specific disclosure.

Three mental health commentaries ask that users be told what a tool cannot do, such as the absence of real-time clinician monitoring or crisis intervention, and that it does not replace professional care. These sources suggest patients value knowing when to seek a human, though none measured whether disclosure changed patient behavior.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare user comprehension, out-of-scope use, and escalation to human care between deployments that provide a written scope and limitations statement and those that do not, with attention to format, reading level, and timing of the statement.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on whether written statements work for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. A written format may reach these groups less well, and any future test should include translated and plain-language versions.

bottom_line: Six studies test scope restriction with refusal criteria, and five of them, including one randomized trial in real deployment, report few or no diagnostic and treatment outputs under the constraint. Hazard studies in which prohibitions were already in place suggest that restriction may reduce out-of-scope advice without eliminating it.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial in real deployment reported no AI-generated diagnoses and 96% accurate guidance, but it did not report sample size or population. A prospective study of 94 biopsy cases found no hallucinated diagnoses and 2% minor misinterpretation. The other four tests are simulations or benchmarks. Indirectness and imprecision support a low certainty rating.

A governed model gave unsolicited clinical monologues on 9% of turns, compared with 100% for an ungoverned model. In 2,035 German conversations, a prompt prohibiting treatment advice still yielded medication errors. A benchmark found a 38.0% attack success rate against prohibited behaviors. Prompt-only refusal criteria may leak, so deployers may need output monitoring as well.

In a real pathology workflow, an agent restricted to formatting produced minor formatting deviations in 8.5% of cases. A scheduling agent with scope constraints reached 96.0% safety compliance and 91.8% task completion, but only in 680 simulated benchmark scenarios. Live workflow evidence comes from the pathology study and the randomized trial alone.

Removing safety constraints raised problem recall from 0.527 to 0.825 across 2,000 check-up reports and also increased diagnostic overstatement. Tighter refusal criteria may therefore cause the assistant to surface fewer findings. Health systems may need to plan for clinician review of what the tool declines or omits.

In a 165-question Thai benchmark, the model without a safety prompt produced a full drug-dosing schedule. In a real deployment of 2,035 German conversations with non-English speakers and older adults, a prompt prohibiting treatment advice still produced medication recommendations. No test of the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations.

NIST AI 600-1 asks deployers to define criteria for queries that generative AI should refuse. The CHAI guide describes a model programmed to reject diagnosis and treatment requests. These are framework statements. None of the supplied studies tests whether written acceptable-use policies change how deployed systems behave.

Hazard studies report harmful outputs, such as advice to stop anticoagulation after a recent thromboembolism and heart transplantation recommendations given despite instructions. No study of the practice measured whether refused users were directed to a clinician. The effect of refusals on patients' access to human care is unknown.

research_gap: No study measured whether refusals route patients or clinicians to a human. None tested whether refusals hold against adversarial or ambiguous requests in live deployment. Trials in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy settings, with reported sample sizes and harm outcomes, would address the main gaps.
underserved_note: Among tests of the practice, only an offline benchmark of 165 questions in Thailand included non-English users, and the randomized trial did not report its population. A real-deployment hazard study in Germany with non-English speakers found that a prompt prohibition did not prevent medication recommendations. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the findings may not transfer to those patients.

bottom_line: Nine studies, mostly pre-post or simulated designs, consistently suggest that limiting AI to higher-prevalence exams, confidence-gated cases, or high-burden clinicians improves yield, cost per case, or time savings. No study randomized targeted against broad deployment in routine care or measured outcomes for patients left outside the eligible subset.

perspectives.view: Nine studies test targeting, and all report findings favoring it. None randomizes targeted versus broad deployment in routine care. The one cluster trial is an offline analysis, and five studies use pre-post or simulated designs. Findings point the same way across radiology, TB, cardiology, and scribes. Risk of bias and indirectness lower certainty to low.

In a simulated replay, targeted AI-ECG screening cut false positives by a median of 303 across 26 labels. A decision tree reached 97.8% concordance with multidisciplinary team plans in 93 selected patients versus 85.6% across 355 cases. Confidence-gated encounters showed 96.3% diagnostic agreement versus 91.3% for all encounters. Harm outside the subset went unmeasured.

Each additional 10% of encounters with scribe use cut documentation time by about 30 seconds per scheduled hour, and physicians with higher baseline time gained most. Each extra baseline minute of chart review predicted an 8.6-second larger reduction. LLM assistance shortened CT but not MRI intervals for one radiologist, which suggests benefit varies by exam type.

At a modelled 1% TB prevalence, cost per case detected fell from USD 5,454 to USD 2,887 for CAD4TBv7. In Nigeria, AI screening cost less per case than symptom screening only when asymptomatic TB exceeded 30%. These results suggest value depends on local prevalence, which systems would need to estimate before choosing deployment sites.

Two TB studies included rural and low-literacy populations in southern Africa and Nigeria. No test enrolled US Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients. No study examined which patient groups fall outside eligibility rules built on prevalence, model confidence, or documentation burden.

In the atrial fibrillation cluster trial, screening raised diagnoses only in the top AI risk decile (10.07 vs 7.76 per 100 person-years; number needed to screen 43 per year), and the authors report reduced population coverage. Patients outside a targeted subset may lose access to screening, and no study reported how those patients fared.

research_gap: No study randomized patients, clinicians, or sites to targeted versus broad AI deployment in real care, and none tracked missed diagnoses, delays, or access among patients excluded by eligibility rules. Trials in US safety-net and Medicaid settings that report both yield inside the subset and outcomes outside it would address the main uncertainty.
underserved_note: Two tests included underserved groups: rural participants in South Africa and Lesotho, and a low-health-literacy population in Nigeria, both in TB screening. No test included US Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients. Findings on targeting scribes, radiology tools, or cardiac screening therefore may not transfer to those populations, and eligibility rules could exclude them without anyone detecting it.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether defining review scope, limiting expedited review to non-patient-care tools, or requiring use-case descriptions and workflow maps changes how often patient-care AI escapes adequate review. Support for R079 rests on two frameworks, one stated as a requirement and one as an option.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions this is a case of no direct evidence. The two endorsements are frameworks, which are expert judgment rather than empirical findings. Their agreement shows that the practice is accepted, and it does not measure whether the practice works.

The CHAI playbook lists internal accounting, human resources, and facilities management as back-office uses, which gives one working boundary between patient-care and non-patient-care tools. NIST AI 600-1 states that existing governance protocols may be applied to generative AI, and it does not set a review scope. Neither source reports outcomes from applying these scoping rules.

research_gap: Studies should compare health systems that use explicit review-scope criteria and restrict expedited pathways with systems that do not. Outcomes should include how many patient-care tools received only expedited or no review, how often tools were reclassified after deployment, and whether workflow maps identified risks before go-live. No such comparison appears in the supplied evidence.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have smaller governance staffs and may rely more on expedited pathways, and whether scoping rules protect their patients has not been examined.

bottom_line: Four sources endorse publishing permitted and prohibited uses and keeping a misuse mitigation plan, but no supplied study tests whether the practice reduces misuse or shows how often staff misuse AI. The recommendation rests on expert consensus from three frameworks and one commentary.

perspectives.view: No supplied study evaluates this practice, and no supplied study documents how often the targeted hazard occurs. The support consists of three frameworks and one commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty about whether published use rules reduce prohibited or off-label use cannot be rated.

CHAI rates defining the scope of AI solution use as a must, while NIST AI 600-1 and the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide rate terms of use and misuse mitigation plans as should. These are voluntary frameworks. The supplied material does not tie the practice to a binding FDA, ONC, or state requirement.

The supplied material contains no incident data showing staff misuse of AI or the harm that follows. Without hazard or outcome studies, the panel cannot judge whether a published list of prohibited uses would stop errors before they reach patients.

research_gap: Studies should measure how often staff use deployed AI tools outside their approved scope, and compare rates of off-label or prohibited use before and after governance bodies publish use rules and misuse mitigation plans. Such studies should also examine whether staff read and follow the published rules and what enforcement mechanisms accompany them.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no evidence on whether misuse differs in their settings or whether published use rules protect their patients.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether periodic audits of AI use against intended use, or channels for reporting off-label use, reduce drift beyond validated scope. One deployment study found that 5.9% of 30,503 chat threads involved clinical decision-making queries outside the tool's intended purpose, which shows the hazard occurs in practice.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice. The single cross-sectional study from a U.S. deployment documents off-label use but does not compare audited and unaudited settings. Five sources endorse the practice, all frameworks or commentaries, and their agreement reflects expert consensus rather than measured effect. Certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In one deployment, 5.9% of chat threads involved clinical decision-making, a use the tool was not validated to support. Unvalidated clinical advice could reach patients through clinician decisions without any record of the tool's role. Whether audits detect such use early enough to prevent harm has not been studied.

The hazard study classified 30,503 chat threads by purpose, which suggests that log review can identify off-label queries in a live system. The study did not report the staff time, classification accuracy, or audit frequency needed to run such review as an ongoing governance task, so its feasibility as a routine control remains unmeasured.

The NIST Generative AI Profile calls for re-evaluating risk when models are adapted to new domains, and the CHAI guides call for intermittent audits of use against intended purpose. These sources frame off-label use as a trigger for reassessment. No study reports whether organizations following this guidance detect scope drift more often.

research_gap: Studies should compare sites that audit AI use against intended use with sites that do not, measuring how often off-label clinical use is detected, how quickly it is corrected, the staff time required, and any downstream effect on patient harm.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, and the hazard study did not report whether its setting included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so it is unknown whether off-label use or its detection differs in settings that serve these groups.

bottom_line: One automated benchmark suggests that an out-of-distribution gate can defer inputs from an unseen center, but no study tests inclusion criteria or workflow controls in clinical use. Fifteen hazard studies show that tools often lose accuracy outside their validated population or setting, which supports the concern without showing that such controls correct it.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice is a level 5 automated benchmark across 126 adaptation configurations, with no patients or clinicians involved. It reports that a Mahalanobis gate re-fit on the target deferred about five percent of inputs and that the guarantee held in every configuration. Indirectness and the absence of clinical outcomes place certainty at very low.

Pulmonary embolism sensitivity was 0.14 on non-dedicated CTs. Pediatric pneumothorax accuracy was 12.5 to 20.8% versus 57.4 to 69.6% in adults. Sensitivity fell from 88.2% to 60.5% on close-up skin images. Two pediatric head CT studies found performance comparable to adults, so harm from out-of-scope use may vary by tool.

Several failures arose from inputs the tool was not built for. These included postoperative head CTs, repeated model use past 48 hours, and pathology outside a fundus tool's target scope. Such cases suggest that controls would need to act at order entry or image routing. No study measures whether those controls work or what burden they add.

Several out-of-population failures involved children. Across 73,397 patients, models trained on adults or older children lost discrimination and were miscalibrated in younger children, worst in neonates. AUC was 0.91 in ages 2 to 6 versus 0.96 in ages 7 to 14. In India, eight oncology patients with leukemic retinopathy were flagged as having diabetic retinopathy. None reports Medicaid, safety-net, or language subgroups.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes intended use in terms of patient age and compatible recording devices. Several frameworks call for restriction to the approved purpose. No supplied study evaluates whether health-system enforcement of these labeled boundaries changes tool outputs or patient outcomes.

research_gap: No study tests whether defined inclusion and exclusion criteria, order-entry restrictions, or out-of-distribution gates reduce out-of-scope use or patient harm in live deployment.
