Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether pre-purchase validation review detects performance gaps for their patients.

bottom_line: Four simulated studies, three of which enrolled 5 to 20 participants, suggest that usability testing with representative users finds interface problems and comprehension gaps before deployment, but none measured whether testing reduced use errors or patient harm in live care. Frameworks, FDA draft guidance, and commentaries endorse the practice, while certainty that it prevents incorrect actions is very low.

perspectives.view: All four tests are level 4 studies in offline or simulated settings. Three enrolled 5 to 20 participants, and one did not report its sample size. Their outcomes were problems detected or usability scores, which measure correct action only indirectly. The one randomized design enrolled 20 patients. Serious imprecision and indirectness support a rating of very low certainty.

Testing surfaced use errors such as out-of-range entry and accidental value changes while scrolling, even with a mean SUS of 89.5. In a French trial of 2,727 participants, subjective comprehension rose (50.3% vs 24.0%) while objective comprehension did not change (58.3% vs 59.4%). This suggests testing should measure actual understanding rather than satisfaction.

Think-aloud testing identified most workflow implementation issues in one study, and scenario testing with 5 physical therapists found calibration and reporting barriers. In a clinician vignette study, median task completion differed (100% vs 80%) while SUS did not, which suggests task completion may detect problems that satisfaction scores miss.

One test involved non-English-speaking patients in Denmark and found that face validation corrected AI translation shortcomings, eliminating significant differences in understandability compared with human translation. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users, so the evidence does not show whether testing detects comprehension failures in those groups.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors to analyze whether a device has tasks where use errors could cause harm, and a regulator discussion paper lists communication quality and user comprehension as a topic. No supplied study tested whether this kind of human factors validation changes outcomes after deployment.

Three studies reported samples of 5 to 23 participants in simulated sessions, which suggests pre-deployment testing can surface interface problems with modest samples. None reported cost, staff time, or how often retesting was needed after model or interface updates, so the resources required at scale remain unknown.

In prototype testing with 20 patients, comprehension of an algorithm's threshold ranged from 60% to 85%. Patients who felt they understood AI reports did not understand them better on objective measures. These findings suggest that including patients in testing may reveal misunderstanding before outputs reach them in care.

research_gap: No study tested whether usability testing before deployment reduced use errors, incorrect clinical actions, or patient harm in live care. Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without structured human factors validation, measure objective comprehension of outputs and uncertainty, report the staff time and cost of testing, and enroll Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy users.
underserved_note: One test included limited English proficiency or non-English-speaking patients, in a 20-patient Danish study of AI translation. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so it is unknown whether representative-user testing detects comprehension failures among those users.

bottom_line: Twenty-five sources, including two CHAI frameworks rated as must, endorse a limited-scale pilot with phased go-live and heightened monitoring before full deployment of higher-risk AI, but no supplied study tests whether this practice reduces system-wide harm. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and analogy to general implementation practice rather than on comparative evidence.

perspectives.view: No supplied study compares piloted with unpiloted rollouts, and no study documents the hazard itself. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsements agree in direction, but agreement among commentaries and frameworks does not substitute for measured outcomes.

Several endorsing commentaries describe pilots as a way to surface integration problems and adapt tools to local workflows before scale-up. None reports pilot duration, monitoring burden, or fidelity data, so the supplied sources give teams no empirical basis for sizing a pilot or setting go-live thresholds.

The CHAI frameworks list prospective evaluation on live production data and incident monitoring as must-level controls. One commentary on FDA oversight proposes a phased introduction period in which algorithms operate alongside clinicians. These statements reflect proposed or voluntary standards, not binding regulatory requirements identified in the supplied material.

One endorsing roadmap for inclusive chatbots calls for small-scale implementation before wider use. No supplied study reports how pilots perform for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so the evidence cannot show whether pilot sites represent these groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare phased, monitored pilots against direct full-scale deployment of higher-risk AI and measure harm events, time to detection, and rollback frequency. Such studies should also report pilot size, duration, monitoring intensity, and staffing cost so that health systems can judge what a sufficient pilot requires.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems that pilot at well-resourced sites may miss failure modes that appear only when a tool reaches these patients, and pilot site selection may need to account for this.

bottom_line: Head-to-head studies on shared data often find that candidate AI tools differ widely from one another and sometimes perform no better than clinicians, simpler scores, or symptom screening, which suggests pre-selection comparison can change purchasing decisions. No study compared organizations that ran such comparisons before selection with organizations that did not, so the benefit of the practice itself is inferred.

perspectives.view: Eleven of the listed tests are randomized, and most report AI against a comparator on the same data. They show that the comparison is feasible and that it changes the picture of performance. They measure tool performance, however, and not whether comparing before selection improves outcomes. Indirectness and results that point in different directions lower certainty to low.

Several comparisons found AI performing below or equal to existing care. AI sensitivity for polyp histology was 80% versus 88% for endoscopists. A CDS screen matched human screening at 81.7% versus 80.2%. A survival model trailed both physicians and a 1995 model. Comparison before selection may catch such tools before they reach patients.

Competing products tested on the same data showed wide spread. Agreement across 21 retinal algorithms ranged from 49.4% to 92.3%. One LLM matched community health workers at 97.9% referral accuracy while another reached 47.3%. A local sepsis model had an AUROC of 81.8% versus 57.5% for the vendor model in silent testing.

A few comparisons included low-income, rural, safety-net, or low-literacy groups outside the US. In India, the specificity of three commercial algorithms ranged from 14% to 96%. In Nigeria, symptom screening dominated AI-only TB screening on cost. No test drew on US Medicaid or US safety-net data.

FDA draft guidance expects device performance to be compared with a comparator tested on the same patients or data. CDRH has also raised clinician panels as a comparator for generative AI. These expectations apply to developers. No listed study examines whether a health system's own comparison adds value beyond cleared labeling.

Comparison has a cost, but it can inform spending. In Nigeria, AI screening found 76 TB cases at US$56589, and symptom screening found 77 cases at US$48939. In Taiwan, an intrinsic screening step ranked candidate models in the same order as full fine-tuning, which suggests lighter comparisons may work. Standardized scheduling came close to an ML tool's accuracy.

Patient-facing comparisons point in mixed directions. Patients rated psychiatrist-led interviews higher than chatbot or robot interviews. An AI agent answered in 0.5 minutes versus 358 for physicians, with accuracy of 93.9% versus 98.1%. Comparing tools with human care before selection may show where patients still need a clinician.

research_gap: No study compares organizations that ran same-data comparisons before selection with organizations that did not, whether on patient outcomes, cost, or later de-adoption of tools. Few studies explain which comparator they chose and why, and few use local US health-system data.
underserved_note: Some tests included limited English proficiency or non-English-speaking, rural, low-income, safety-net, and low-health-literacy populations, mostly in China, Rwanda, India, and Nigeria. None used US Medicaid or US safety-net data. Health systems serving those patients may therefore need to run comparisons on their own populations rather than rely on published rankings.

bottom_line: No study tested whether piloting AI with structured monitoring of workflow, safety, and workforce effects prevents harm when a tool is scaled, so support for R112 rests on six endorsements from frameworks and commentaries. Four hazard studies show that workflow problems can appear or be absent during real deployments, which suggests that local pilot monitoring may be informative.

perspectives.view: Zero studies compare piloting with monitoring against scaling without it. The four hazard studies describe workflow outcomes during single deployments. Two found problems and two found none, and their designs range from one randomized trial to uncontrolled pre-post and survey data. These studies establish that the hazard varies by setting, but they cannot estimate the effect of the recommended practice.

In 45 organ donor cases in India, time from first apnoea test to retrieval rose from 1587 to 1660 minutes after an AI protocol began (p=0.04). Transfer to the operating room after legal verification rose from 125 to 384 minutes (p=0.002). This suggests that downstream delays can follow AI adoption, and monitoring may detect them before wider spread.

A US randomized trial of 536 encounters reported low accrual and workflow integration problems, including difficulty reaching the right person at the right time. By contrast, 81% of 59 staff in another deployment disagreed that their workflow was disrupted, and a four-center trauma pilot reported no disruption. Integration results appear to depend on local workflow, which supports testing at each site.

The trauma pilot enrolled 139 of 391 eligible patients over three months at four centers, and the US trial reported low accrual. These figures suggest that pilots may reach only part of the eligible population. Workflow findings from a partial pilot may therefore understate the burden that appears at full volume.

None of the four hazard studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two did not report their country. A pilot that finds no workflow disruption in the studied settings gives no information about settings with fewer staff or more interpreter-dependent encounters.

research_gap: Studies should compare sites that scale AI after a monitored pilot with sites that scale without one, measuring workflow disruption, staff burden, safety events, and downstream delays after full rollout. Pilots should also report how representative enrolled patients and staff are of the eventual deployment population.
underserved_note: No hazard study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study tested the practice itself. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume that pilot findings from other settings apply, and they may need to include these groups in their own pilot monitoring.

bottom_line: Randomized and cluster-randomized trials of AI tools in live care produce a mix of benefit, null, and harmful patient outcomes, including null results for models with high accuracy, which suggests that outcome testing detects effects that accuracy metrics miss. No study compares health systems that run such evaluations with systems that do not, so support for the practice itself rests on indirect evidence.

perspectives.view: The 25 trials summarized here evaluate specific AI tools rather than the policy of evaluating them. Their results point in different directions, with some trials showing mortality reductions, such as HR 0.83 at 90 days, and others showing no change in HbA1c, sensitivity, or deterioration events. The trials show the designs are workable, but indirectness lowers certainty about the practice.

Several trials found harms that accuracy testing would not have shown. One thromboprophylaxis support tool lowered thromboembolism (2.9% vs 4.0%), yet mortality at intervention hospitals was higher (9.1% vs 7.0%, OR 1.32). An early warning system raised unanticipated ICU transfers by 24.9%. An AI consent tool met noninferiority for anxiety but had worse recovery scores.

A graft-loss model with AUC-ROC 0.923 did not change treatment conversations (39% vs 40%). Predictive glucose alerts increased alert counts without improving time in range, and a CADe benefit weakened in the second half of its trial. Stepped-wedge and silent-mode cluster designs ran inside routine EHR workflows, which suggests these methods can fit operational deployment.

A stepped-wedge trial that included Medicaid patients reduced end-of-life systemic therapy (aOR 0.25) but did not change other end-of-life outcomes. In safety-net clinics, decision support left hypertension prescribing unchanged (34.9% vs 34.9%). A hemodialysis trial reported a larger mortality effect in primary hospitals, which suggests effects may differ by care setting.

In one English economic evaluation, no AI was always more cost-effective, with a budget impact of £16 to 35 million per year. A cluster trial of autonomous AI found 40% higher specialist productivity. A quasi-experimental screening tool lowered costs by $6,166.71 but did not meet noninferiority for service receipt. These results suggest trials can inform purchasing decisions.

In a randomized anxiety trial, patients rated AI-delivered CBT as less beneficial than peer-delivered CBT, and neither outperformed control. A genetic counseling chatbot matched counselors on knowledge and satisfaction in 37 patients. A generative AI therapy app showed no increase in adverse events. Trials of this kind may give patients outcome data on which to base trust.

research_gap: No study compares the patient outcomes or harm rates of health systems that require randomized, stepped-wedge, or A/B evaluation before scaling AI with those of systems that deploy on validation accuracy alone. The cost, duration, and staffing needed for local trials also remain unmeasured.
underserved_note: One trial included Medicaid patients and one took place in safety-net clinics, and two studies focused on racial and ethnic minority populations. No test included limited English proficiency or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether outcome trials detect, or whether AI tools produce, different effects for these groups.

bottom_line: Eight sources endorse a pre-deployment readiness gate with an evidence packet and no-go criteria, but no supplied study tests whether such a gate prevents unreviewed or unsafe activation. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and framework guidance alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests a readiness gate, and no study documents the hazard's frequency. The eight endorsements include two frameworks, two guidance documents, one descriptive framework, and three commentaries. Consensus across these sources shows agreement on the practice, but agreement among experts does not substitute for comparative evidence on outcomes.

The targeted failure is a tool that goes live without review or despite failed validation, bias, or unmitigable harm. No supplied study measures how often this happens or whether a gate with predefined no-go criteria stops such tools before they reach patients. The emergency medicine consensus describes halting advancement until criteria are met, which is a design claim that has not been tested.

Several sources describe sequential stage gates and a structured report for the decision makers. None of the supplied material reports how long a gate review takes, what staff time it consumes, or whether committees apply no-go criteria consistently in practice. Fidelity and burden therefore remain unmeasured.

research_gap: Studies should compare health systems or tool portfolios that use a formal readiness gate with those that do not. Useful outcomes include the share of tools stopped or revised before activation, post-deployment safety incidents, bias findings detected after go-live, and review time and staffing cost. Studies should also report inter-rater agreement on no-go decisions.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Several endorsements name equity and bias as review criteria, but whether gate packets capture subgroup performance for these populations, and whether safety-net systems have the resources to run such gates, has not been studied.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether scaling validation rigor, benchmark scope, and sample size to an AI tool's risk tier improves safety or reduces wasted evaluation effort. Sixteen sources endorse risk-proportionate review, but none reports outcomes from applying it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Support rests on guidance, frameworks, commentaries, and a regulatory discussion paper that agree in principle. Agreement among expert sources does not establish effect, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

One endorsing commentary on patient portal drafting warns that clinicians need interface cues to stay vigilant regardless of assigned tier. This suggests that a low-risk label may itself lower attention to errors. No study measures whether tiered review catches more errors in high-risk tools or misses errors in tools classified as lower risk.

A SAGES white paper states that pre-market evidence requirements should continue to be tiered by risk class, which mirrors existing FDA device classification. The FDA discussion paper on generative AI devices considers sponsor-proposed tests and datasets. Neither source defines how a health system's internal governance tiers should map to regulatory classes.

One commentary states that risk profiles for setting assessment level still require clearer definitions. Without tested tier criteria, each health system must write its own thresholds for full versus expedited review. No supplied source reports staff time, cost, or review turnaround under a tiered model compared with uniform review.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare tiered and uniform validation approaches within health systems and measure missed safety problems after deployment, review time, and cost. Such studies should also test whether published tier criteria classify tools consistently across reviewers.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Tier criteria that omit subgroup performance could place a tool in an expedited track even when its error rates differ for these patients, and the supplied evidence cannot show whether that occurs.

bottom_line: Among the supplied studies, twelve randomized trials and eighteen prospective or quasi-experimental studies compared clinicians with and without AI in live deployment, with results ranging from clear gains to no difference, and several found that human-AI team performance departed from standalone AI performance in both directions. No study tested whether running such evaluations changes purchasing or deployment decisions, and few measured overreliance directly.

perspectives.view: Twelve randomized trials in real deployment compared users with and without AI. Most favored AI assistance, but two found no significant difference in sensitivity or miss rate, and one cluster trial reported a 55.1% misdiagnosis rate despite AI alerts. These trials test specific tools rather than the evaluation practice, so certainty is downgraded for indirectness and inconsistency.

Standalone AI produced 381 false positives in 634 patients, yet radiologists reported one, so team performance exceeded the model alone. In other settings the reverse held. Assisted schedulers underperformed the model alone, and radiologists with discretionary AI reached 90.0% fracture sensitivity against 93.5% for standalone AI. Standalone figures may mislead in either direction.

Error profiles changed with deployment mode, as triage, safety-net, and problem-solving workflows produced different false-negative and false-positive rates from standalone AI. Automation bias degraded multi-reader but improved single-reader screening in one replay study. Clinicians followed 86% of predictions when half were wrong. Most live trials, including one ophthalmology trial, did not report overreliance.

A simulation modeled on low-income women found that as reliance on AI rose, false-negative rates moved from 27.11% versus 26.74% to 18.79% versus 33.33% for privileged and unprivileged groups. This suggests that team evaluations may need subgroup reporting. Only two live tests included limited English proficiency populations.

FDA draft guidance states that both standalone and human-device team evaluations may support a performance claim, and the radiology multi-society statement calls for evaluating the radiologist-plus-AI combination. The supplied studies show that such team evaluations can be conducted in live practice, though none tests how regulators or purchasers used the results.

The largest deployment-mode trials enrolled 105,915 and 10,476 screened patients, which suggests that adequately powered team evaluations may require substantial volume and time. One crossover trial reported 16.7 versus 14.1 daily exams on AI days. No study reported the cost or staffing needed to run the evaluation itself.

research_gap: No study compared deployment decisions or patient outcomes between organizations that conducted human-with-versus-without-AI evaluations and those that relied on standalone metrics. Few live trials measured overreliance, such as acceptance of incorrect AI outputs, and none reported the cost of conducting team evaluations.
underserved_note: Two live tests included limited English proficiency populations, a Chinese primary care diabetic retinopathy study and a United States medication identification study of 41 patients. One screening study included rural patients. No test included Medicaid or safety-net populations or reported low-literacy participants, and the only low-income evidence comes from a simulation that documented the hazard. Health systems serving these groups therefore cannot assume that team performance reported elsewhere will transfer.

bottom_line: Forty-five sources endorse screening AI tools for medical device or SaMD status before deployment, but no study tests whether such screening prevents deployment of unvalidated regulated tools. One descriptive audit found that none of 1,055 health-related GPTs held FDA, EU MDR, or TGA approval, which shows the hazard exists without showing that screening solves it.

perspectives.view: No study compares deployment outcomes with and without regulatory status screening. The one available study is a cross-sectional audit that documents the hazard, so it cannot inform the effect of the practice. The 45 endorsements reflect expert consensus and regulatory text, which GRADE treats as opinion rather than evidence of benefit.

The audit found that 624 of 1,055 health-related GPTs used healthcare professional titles in their names or descriptions, and none held regulatory approval. This suggests unvetted tools may present themselves as clinical authorities. A pre-deployment screen may intercept such tools, but no study has measured how often screening catches them or whether harm declines.

Endorsing sources cite the EU AI Act classification of health AI as high risk and FDA draft guidance expecting verification and validation data in marketing submissions. The audit shows that general-purpose model products reach users outside FDA, EU MDR, and TGA pathways. SaMD status depends on intended use, so screening requires case-by-case review of how a tool will be used.

A patient who uses a GPT bearing a clinical title may assume someone has reviewed it, yet the audit found no approved tools among 1,055. Screening by a health system may protect patients within that system's services. It would not reach tools that patients find and use on their own.

research_gap: No study has evaluated an institutional process for classifying AI tools by device status. Useful studies would measure how many tools in current use lack required clearance, how consistently reviewers classify intended use, how often screening changes deployment decisions, and whether screened portfolios show fewer safety events than unscreened ones.
underserved_note: No study tests the practice, and the hazard study did not report the populations using the GPTs it audited. The evidence therefore says nothing about Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and it cannot show whether screening works in safety-net systems that may have fewer staff available for regulatory review.

bottom_line: One prospective study in a real deployment of 88,645 examinations found that predeployment value predictions agreed with postdeployment survey respondents for 10 of 12 clinical tasks, which suggests a structured predeployment assessment may anticipate perceived benefit. No study tested whether a documented risk-benefit assessment linked to mitigation controls reduces errors or patient harm.

perspectives.view: A single prospective study with a comparator tested one component of this practice, which is predicting value before deployment. The outcome was agreement with clinician survey responses rather than harm. The risk, residual risk, and mitigation components went untested, and no second study confirms the finding. Indirectness and imprecision leave certainty very low.

The study compared predicted benefit with perceived benefit. It did not examine whether predeployment analysis of error severity and detectability identified the failures that later occurred, or whether linked controls caught errors before they reached patients. Disagreement on 2 of 12 tasks suggests that predeployment estimates may miss some effects.

The prediction step was carried out within a real deployment covering 88,645 examinations, which suggests it can be completed as part of routine governance. The study does not report staff time, the assessment method, or how consistently teams applied it, so burden and fidelity remain unknown.

The study did not report patient population characteristics. Whether predictions held for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients is unknown, and benefit and error severity may differ in these groups.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks sponsors to document and address misuse risk, and Utah HB 452 requires identification of foreseeable adverse outcomes for mental health chatbots. These provisions place risk documentation duties mainly on developers. No study measured whether health system assessments improve compliance or outcomes.

research_gap: Studies should test whether a documented predeployment risk-benefit assessment, with error severity, detectability, and residual risk tied to specific controls, predicts postdeployment errors and harms, and whether it changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes compared with deployments made without such an assessment. These studies should report staff time, patient demographics, and payer mix.
underserved_note: The one test of the practice did not report its population, so no evidence shows whether predeployment assessments were accurate for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Governance bodies cannot assume that the 10 of 12 agreement applies to these groups.

bottom_line: Eighteen sources, including CHAI frameworks, NIST AI 600-1, and several commentaries, endorse IRB consultation before evaluating research-stage or non-cleared AI in human subjects, but no supplied study tests whether this practice protects patients. The recommendation rests on established research-ethics norms and expert consensus rather than on direct empirical evidence.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests IRB consultation for AI evaluation, and no study documents the hazard. Support comes from frameworks and commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. The endorsements agree on the principle, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The endorsements tie IRB review to regulatory status. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks teams to consult the IRB when an AI solution lacks FDA clearance. The NHS guide requires MHRA no-objection and REC clearance for un-marked device investigations. These statements describe existing research-oversight rules applied to AI, and no study measures compliance or its effects.

The CHAI guide frames the first step as deciding whether a deployment counts as human subjects research. That boundary between quality improvement and research may be hard to draw for AI tools already in live workflows. No supplied study measures how often systems misclassify projects or what IRB review adds in time or burden.

research_gap: No study compares AI evaluations conducted with and without IRB review on outcomes such as participant harm, consent quality, protocol deviations, or time to deployment. Studies are also needed on how institutions classify AI projects as research versus quality improvement and how consistently IRBs review AI-specific risks.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether IRB review of AI evaluations addresses consent comprehension or risks specific to these groups. The Uganda ethics-committee guide suggests that reviewer familiarity with AI varies across settings.

bottom_line: Silent-mode evaluations on live data sometimes found drops from retrospective results, such as a white blood cell classifier falling from AUROC 0.76 to 0.69, and in other studies performance held steady. No study compared patient outcomes after activation between tools that did and did not go through a silent phase, so certainty that the practice prevents harm is low.

perspectives.view: Most tests are single-site prospective cohorts with no comparison of a silent phase against no silent phase. The two studies labeled randomized appear not to have randomized the silent phase itself. Several studies show that silent runs can reveal gaps, with one reporting F1 of 0.72 to 0.79 against 0.92 retrospectively. Indirectness to patient outcomes lowers certainty.

Silent evaluation found failures before patients were exposed. An emergency CT tool reached 84% sensitivity against 96.4% for residents. One language model reached 47.3% referral accuracy against 97.9% for health workers. A 14-day GPU outage occurred during passive deployment. These results suggest the phase may catch errors, though no study tracked harm after activation.

Silent runs showed workflow and data problems that retrospective testing may not reveal. A segmentation tool needed corrections in 8 of 10 patients, taking a median of 11 minutes. A sepsis alert tier had a PPV of 14%. A model reduced from 58 to 32 features for live EHR use had an AUROC of 0.874, compared with 0.925 retrospectively.

One test ran silently on 429 community health worker encounters in Rwanda that the study described as rural, low-income, and limited English or non-English. Another included older adults in Hong Kong. No test enrolled United States Medicaid or safety-net patients, so live performance gaps for those groups remain unmeasured.

Silent phases in these studies lasted from about one month to thirteen months. One health system ran 20,334 laboratory classifiers silently, which suggests the approach can operate at scale. No study reported the staffing, computing, or delay costs of the silent period, so administrators cannot yet weigh its cost against what it finds.

research_gap: No study compares tools activated after a silent phase with tools activated without one on post-activation errors, patient harm, or deactivation rates. No study defines how long a silent phase should last or what performance drop should block activation. No study reports the resource cost of silent deployment.
underserved_note: One silent trial included limited English proficiency, low-income, and rural populations, but it took place among community health workers in Rwanda. No test included United States Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so it is unknown whether silent-mode findings reflect performance for those patients in this country.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether dry-run evaluation of agentic AI before enabling high-impact actions reduces erroneous or irreversible actions. Five benchmark studies show that current agents often fail multi-step tool tasks and failure handling, which suggests the hazard is real but leaves the safeguard's value unmeasured.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The five supplied studies are automated benchmarks that document the hazard in simulated or offline settings. They show that agents fail, but they do not compare deployment with and without dry-run testing, so they cannot show that the safeguard prevents harm.

In emergency medicine workflows, multi-step performance fell to 1.0% and 0.0%, with safety-failure rates of 27.5% and 34.0%. GPT-4.1 withheld writes in 17.4% of tampered-identity runs and rarely detected MRN or age changes. A dry run might expose these failure modes before an action reaches a patient record, though no study confirms this.

On 100 EHR tasks averaging 27 tool calls, the best model passed 46% on first attempt and open-source models passed at most 19%. A locked benchmark found 47.08% strict task completion with unreliable failure fallback. A simulated ED shift found correct diagnoses but incomplete and late actions. No study measured the staff time a dry-run program would require.

A regulatory discussion paper describes evaluating tool use, human-oversight checkpoints before irreversible actions, and handling of tool failures. CHAI playbooks require documented risk assessment, and a Chinese consensus calls for validating surgical AI before deployment. These sources treat pre-deployment testing as expected conduct, but none cites outcome data showing that such testing reduces harm.

None of the hazard studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and two do not report a setting. Benchmark tasks may not reflect records with interpreter notes, fragmented care, or identity mismatches, which may occur more often in safety-net systems.

Agents in one benchmark rarely noticed when a patient's MRN or age had been changed, so a wrong-patient write could proceed without a person seeing it. Patients may reasonably expect that a human reviews any irreversible action taken in their record.

research_gap: No study compares agents deployed after dry-run evaluation with agents deployed without it, or measures whether dry-run findings predict erroneous or irreversible actions in live use. Studies in live or shadow-mode clinical settings should report reversal rates, near misses, and staff time.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and none of the hazard studies included or reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether agent failure rates, or any benefit of dry-run testing, differ for their patients.

bottom_line: Twenty-one studies tested explanation fidelity, stability, or clinical meaningfulness, and 14 reported favorable results, but 20 were offline or simulated and none compared decisions or patient outcomes with and without pre-release validation. Hazard studies show that explanations are often unfaithful or unstable, which suggests such testing may detect problems, though whether it prevents clinicians from being misled remains untested.

perspectives.view: Twenty of the 21 studies were level 4 or 5 and offline or simulated. The single level 3 study, the only real deployment, rated explanations on 17 patients. No study compared decisions or outcomes with and without pre-release validation. Results varied, with 14 supportive, 6 mixed, and 1 against. Certainty is very low because of indirectness and risk of bias.

In one study, SHAP explanations had 100% fidelity, yet clinicians complied with the AI in 86% of cases. This suggests faithful explanations can still foster over-trust. When AI outputs were wrong, explanations lowered trust in experienced clinicians but did so inconsistently in less experienced ones. In a hazard benchmark, 83.0% of correct chest X-ray predictions had saliency IoU below 0.1.

Expert clinicians agreed with model explanations in 74.2% of cases, and a clinician panel rated them useful in 75.0%. Another study rated 92.6% of explanations useful and linked review to changed management intent in 27.6%. A hazard survey found that physicians' preference for lesion-aligned maps may be superficial, so rater approval may not measure understanding.

FDA draft guidance states that sponsors should validate explainability metrics and visualizations for the target user group. FUTURE-AI asks evaluations to identify limitations such as sensitivity to noise. Stability appears measurable, since explanation divergence rose from 0.144 to 0.251 as sensor noise reached 20%. No study tested whether such requirements change clinical use.

Several user tests relied on panels of 6 to 28 clinicians. No study reported cost, staff time, or repeat testing after model updates. Automated fidelity and stability metrics were computed offline on existing datasets, which may require fewer resources. None of these studies measured how those metrics relate to clinician behavior.

In a vignette study of 776 participants, lay users showed more automation bias with LLM explanations than experienced primary care physicians did. This suggests that explanations shown to patients may raise trust in wrong outputs. No study tested explanations with patients as the target users.

research_gap: No study compared deployed tools whose explanations were validated before release with tools that were not. Such comparisons should measure clinician over-reliance, detection of AI errors, and patient outcomes. They should include less experienced clinicians, patient-facing explanations, and repeat validation after model updates or data drift.
underserved_note: One of the 21 tests, a fidelity analysis of logged decisions, drew on a Medicaid population. No test included safety-net settings, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users, and many did not report their setting. The findings on clinical meaningfulness therefore reflect clinicians in largely unspecified settings and may not apply to these populations.

bottom_line: Eight studies, two in real deployment, found that re-testing after updates, prompt changes, or compression detected both gains and regressions, including an 11.96% accuracy drop in a mammography model. No study compared re-testing with no re-testing or measured patient harm, so the evidence shows that re-testing detects change rather than that it prevents harm.

perspectives.view: Eight studies test re-testing after changes, and all report that it detected performance shifts. Two are prospective real-deployment studies; six are offline replays, vignettes, or benchmarks. None compares re-testing with no re-testing or measures patient harm. Certainty is low because outcomes are indirect and samples are small or simulated.

Repeat testing after a mammography model update found accuracy of 0.81 against a declared 0.92. Another software update raised AUC from 0.76 to 0.78 but cut specificity at the old threshold from 45.8% to 23.1%. A note-pipeline change raised major hallucinations from 4 to 25. Updates may improve one metric while degrading another.

In an ICU note study, a model upgrade raised accuracy from 69.12% to 80.3% while commission errors rose from 1.30% to 3.92%. Prompt edits also act as changes, and four prompt optimizations on one agent produced 18 to 28 point regressions. Re-testing may need to cover prompts, retrieval, and thresholds and to report error types.

Every compression method in an ICU prediction benchmark shifted subgroup AUROC by 1 to 4 points, which suggests re-testing should report results by subgroup. One test included older adults in Viet Nam. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so detection of regressions in these groups is untested.

FDA change control plan guidance asks whether modifications follow prespecified methods and performance specifications, and NIST AI 600-1 calls for reassessment after fine-tuning or retrieval changes. Vendor updates to general models sit outside device pathways; one study found a refusal safeguard lapsed within 12 weeks, and 21.5% of appropriate responses became inappropriate after updates.

Repeat calibration testing ran in a program covering 404,502 mammograms, though no study reported staff time or cost. Benchmark data may help set testing depth by change type, since INT8 quantization shifted accuracy by at most 1.9% while INT4 reduced one model's MedMCQA score by 19.7%. Successive call-handling iterations were evaluated across 307,000 calls.

Patients using public chatbots may not know when the underlying model changes. One model that initially refused to produce health disinformation no longer refused 12 weeks later, and fine-tuning another model on vaccination data raised safety concerns by 400%. No test of re-testing reported patient-facing outcomes such as trust or access to a human.

research_gap: No study compares deployments that re-test after changes with those that do not, and none links re-testing to patient harm, near misses, or clinician workload. Studies also do not report the cost or staffing needed to re-test at each update, do not examine vendor-pushed updates to general-purpose models under health-system re-testing, and do not test whether re-testing restores thresholds calibrated for earlier versions.
underserved_note: Only one test named a population of interest, older adults in Viet Nam, and none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that re-testing results from other settings capture regressions their patients would face, and the subgroup shifts seen after compression suggest local re-testing stratified by population may be needed.

bottom_line: No study in this evidence map tests whether assessing vendor support for local validation during procurement improves validation, monitoring, or patient outcomes, and no study documents the hazard directly. Four sources endorse the practice, including an FDA draft guidance, the RUAIH guidance, the CHAI assurance guide, and one commentary, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus.

perspectives.view: The map lists zero studies that test the practice and zero that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The four endorsements agree in direction, but agreement among guidance documents reflects shared expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative data on procurement outcomes.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions lists instructions for local site-specific acceptance testing or validation among the recommended content for marketing submissions. This suggests that some cleared devices may come with such instructions, which procurement teams could request. The guidance is in draft form and does not bind vendors of non-device tools.

research_gap: No study compares organizations that assess vendor validation support during procurement with those that do not. Useful research would measure whether such assessment increases the share of tools that receive local acceptance testing, how often vendors agree to tune or validate on representative local samples, what this costs purchasers, and whether locally validated tools show fewer performance failures after deployment.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on whether it works for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The RUAIH guidance asks vendors to validate on samples representative of the deployment context, which could include these groups, but whether safety-net systems with limited purchasing power can obtain such vendor support remains untested.

bottom_line: Nineteen studies show that missing, mismatched, or misconfigured inputs degrade AI outputs in local systems, but no study tests whether verifying input compatibility before deployment prevents these errors. Seven sources endorse the practice based on expert judgment and the documented hazard.

perspectives.view: None of the 19 supplied studies tests whether pre-deployment verification of input compatibility reduces incorrect outputs. The hazard evidence includes one randomized trial and several prospective deployments, and these studies consistently report missing or mismatched inputs. They show that the problem exists but do not show that a verification step prevents it.

Train/serve skew reduced AUROC from 0.97 to below 0.60 in one report. In another, missing two of seven features dropped AUROC from 0.74 to 0.39. Incorrect DICOM voxel dimensions accounted for 81 of 92 exams in which three imaging tools all failed. Clinicians may not see these failures unless someone checks inputs before go-live.

Mapping local data to model inputs was often incomplete. One multi-hospital study mapped 4 of 6 constructs, and a Finnish study found waist-hip ratio absent from structured records. An echocardiography model returned predictions for 578 of 1541 eligible studies (38%). In one ED study, live and completed-data outputs agreed in 97.2% of encounters, which suggests that the effect of mismatch varies by model.

One randomized deployment enrolled low-income and racial and ethnic minority patients. It found discrepancies in variable definitions and missing data during real-time scoring. In a regional HIE, only 415 of 536 facilities shared diagnoses, and 21% of those shared procedures. Input gaps may be larger where records are fragmented, but no study tested verification in those settings.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to supply instructions for ensuring that input data are compatible with the device. A commentary on the EU AI Act describes site-specific and interoperability testing by facilities. These documents divide responsibility between vendors and deployers. No supplied study evaluates whether following either approach reduces errors.

In one surgical-duration study, user-adjusted Epic settings produced a mean absolute error of 35.3 minutes. Vendor-recommended settings with standardized definitions produced 20.1 minutes. Trial coordinators in another deployment reported time-intensive manual abstraction. These results suggest that verification requires IT staff time and configuration governance, although no study has measured its cost.

In a UK community optometry study, the AI system could not process images from 48.5% of 396 participants. Patients whose inputs fail may receive no result or a delayed result, and they may not know that a human review is needed. The supplied studies do not report how patients were informed or routed when inputs failed.

research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without a structured input-compatibility check before go-live. Stepped rollouts across sites with differing EHR and imaging configurations could measure unprocessable input rates, silent performance loss, and staff time required for verification.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Among the hazard studies, one trial enrolled low-income and racial and ethnic minority patients, one audit covered older adults, and one benchmark included people with disability. Whether verification helps in settings with fragmented or sparse records remains unknown.

bottom_line: Nine sources endorse comparing development and local populations, and four offline or benchmark studies show that such comparisons can surface differences and, in one case, flag a shifted cohort with lower accuracy. No study tested whether the comparison changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes, and one found that performance held despite large population differences.

perspectives.view: Four studies examined the practice, all at level 4 or 5 and none in live deployment. Each described differences between development and local data, and one found that a cohort applicability score of 48% matched the lowest accuracy of 53%. No study measured effects on decisions or outcomes, so certainty is very low.

In one hazard study, local prevalence was 4.1% against 45.0-62.2% in the manufacturer's populations, and local PPV was 33% against 95-98% reported. A comparison may reveal such gaps before go-live. One test found large population differences with stable performance, which suggests the comparison flags risk but does not replace local performance testing.

The ward study compared 52 features and found that missingness differed by more than 5% in 9 of them, with deterioration rates of 4.5% versus 2.5%. Hazard studies tie performance drops to documentation and service setting, such as a coding F-score falling from 0.754 to 0.620 and theme accuracy of 57% in community and mental health services.

The Finnish psychosis study found that 100% versus 55.3% of patients were White European or not reported across samples, and the ward study found 20% versus 49% non-White patients. Neither reported insurance, language, or literacy. A Kenyan hazard study found a younger population with more diabetes and hypertension than the UK Biobank development cohort.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors who use data from outside the United States to explain how disease presentation, prevalence, and demographics compare with American patients and medical practice. This assigns part of the comparison to manufacturers. Local teams still depend on vendors disclosing development populations, and none of the studies assessed how often that disclosure occurs.

research_gap: No study measured whether a structured comparison of development and local populations before go-live changed adoption decisions, prompted recalibration, or reduced harm in live use. No study reported what the comparison costs in staff time or data access. Studies that pair the comparison with local performance testing could show which differences, such as missingness, prevalence, or scanner type, predict degradation and which do not.
underserved_note: None of the four tests reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The ward study reported race only, with 49% non-White patients at the external site. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether the comparison detects the shifts most likely to affect their patients, such as differences in documentation, language, or access to follow-up care.

bottom_line: One multi-site study of six U.S. hospitals suggests that local validation infrastructure can be stood up, with a median of 66 days for IRB approval and 157 days for local installation, but no study shows that such capacity improves model performance or patient outcomes. Three hazard studies show that monitoring resources and local sample sizes often fall short, especially at smaller and rural sites.

perspectives.view: Only one study tests the practice, and it reports implementation timelines from six hospitals in an offline setting rather than clinical effects. The design is prospective with a comparator but small, indirect, and unreplicated. Certainty that building local validation capacity changes outcomes is very low. The hazard studies establish the problem but do not test the remedy.

The six-hospital study reports a median of 66 days for IRB approval and 157 days for local installation. These figures suggest that local validation carries months of setup work before any model is evaluated. Radiologists interviewed across the U.S. and Europe said they were unsure how to build a scalable monitoring process, which points to workflow design as an open problem.

When a site cannot recalibrate or monitor a model, miscalibration may reach patients undetected. One benchmark found that two smaller sites needed 16,461 and 15,299 admissions for recalibration but had 3,187 and 905. No study shows that added tools or partnerships catch errors before harm, so the safety benefit remains an inference.

Two hazard studies found that rural sites lacked the sample sizes needed for local recalibration. This suggests that a local-only validation model may leave smaller hospitals unable to check the tools they deploy. The single test of the practice does not report whether it included rural, safety-net, or Medicaid-serving hospitals.

Radiologists named lack of resources as the largest barrier to AI monitoring. The six-hospital study suggests that a leader should plan for roughly five months to install validation infrastructure after about two months of IRB review. No study reports staffing levels or costs, so budgeting must rely on local estimates.

CHAI's playbook states that validation tools must be available whether or not a vendor assists. An NHS roundtable and an evaluation-principles commentary propose national or public test platforms for sites that lack local resources. No study has evaluated these shared-infrastructure models, so their effect on small sites is untested.

research_gap: No study measures whether securing validation tools, infrastructure, or partnerships leads to detection of model failures, better calibration, or fewer patient harms. The one test reports only setup timelines at six hospitals. Studies are needed that compare local, pooled, and vendor-supported validation arrangements, report cost and staffing, and include small, rural, and safety-net sites where sample sizes fall short.
underserved_note: The single study that tests the practice does not report inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two hazard studies involve rural sites and show sample shortfalls for recalibration. This suggests that the hospitals facing the largest capacity gaps are the least represented in tests of the practice, and that shared or external infrastructure may be needed for them.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether risk-tiered validation requirements and review routes lead to better-validated high-risk tools or less burden on low-risk ones. The recommendation currently rests on a single framework endorsement from the CHAI governance playbooks.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single supporting source is a framework statement, which reflects expert consensus and does not measure whether tiering changes validation quality, deployment decisions, or patient outcomes.

The CHAI governance playbooks carry this as a must-level item and direct committees to flag validation gaps in high-risk clinical AI as priority remediation. That endorsement gives committees a reference for their policy language. It does not establish which risk thresholds should trigger mandatory local validation, and no supplied study addresses that question.

research_gap: No supplied study compares risk-tiered validation routes with uniform validation or with no formal requirement. Useful designs would track, across health systems, how often high-risk tools reach deployment without local validation, how many performance problems local validation detects that vendor attestation missed, and how much reviewer time each tier consumes. A related question is how accurately committees assign tools to risk tiers in the first place.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Vendor attestation and prior evidence may come from populations that differ from a safety-net system's patients, and the existing record gives no information on whether tiering rules account for that mismatch.

bottom_line: One governance framework (CHAI) recommends meaningful human review of agentic AI actions during initial deployment before oversight is reduced, but no supplied study tests this practice or documents the hazard it targets. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and no empirical evidence.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests staged human review of agentic AI, and no study documents harm from relaxing oversight too early. Under GRADE conventions, a single framework statement counts as expert opinion and cannot support a certainty rating. The effect of this practice on error rates or patient outcomes is unknown.

The only endorsement comes from CHAI governance playbooks, which use "should" language and carry no legal force. The supplied materials cite no FDA, ONC, or state statute that requires a staged oversight period for agentic AI. Adoption therefore depends on each organization's internal governance choices.

research_gap: No study has compared staged human review during early agentic AI deployment with immediate reduced oversight. Studies are needed that measure how often reviewers catch erroneous agent actions, how long review must last before error rates stabilize, what staffing burden review imposes, and what performance thresholds should trigger a reduction in oversight.
underserved_note: No study tests this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from current evidence whether an early review period would detect agent errors that fall unevenly on these patients, or how long such review would need to last in settings with fewer staff.

bottom_line: Two sources, the HEAAL framework and the AIPI meeting proceedings, endorse prospective equity assessment with diagnostic outreach to all high-risk patients, but no supplied study tests this practice or documents the hazard it targets. The recommendation currently rests on expert reasoning alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests prospective outreach-based equity assessment, and no study documents how often biased historical labels hide underperformance. Both endorsements are a framework and a meeting commentary. Under GRADE conventions, expert statements without supporting data cannot establish certainty, so the effect of the practice on detecting missed underperformance remains unknown.

The practice aims to correct underdiagnosis in disadvantaged groups. No supplied study measures whether outreach to all high-risk patients reveals performance gaps in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The groups the recommendation intends to protect therefore have no direct evidence showing that the approach works for them.

research_gap: Prospective studies are needed that deploy a model, conduct diagnostic workup on all high-risk patients regardless of prior diagnosis, and compare subgroup performance estimates from that confirmed-diagnosis cohort against estimates from historical labels. Such studies should also report outreach completion rates, workup costs, and staffing requirements by patient group.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems adopting the practice for these groups would be acting on expert judgment and should plan to collect subgroup outcome data from the start.

bottom_line: Four studies report that pre-go-live testing found integration, processing, coding, or monitoring-data faults that were then corrected, and a fifth reports that two computational pipelines met predefined acceptance criteria. None compared go-live failures or patient harm between tested and untested deployments, and none tested acceptance checks of load capacity or provenance mechanisms.

perspectives.view: Before deployment, functional testing found incomplete processing in one of four mammography studies. In another study, testing found that the monitoring log recorded overwritten values instead of the data the tool used. A camera mounting-angle error left 49% of PET/CT studies off-centered until recalibration cut this to 27%, which suggests installation faults can reach patients.

Component-level checks of population capture, risk calculation, thresholds, and CDS coding found small coding errors and a monitoring data-capture fault in live EHR settings. Across nine NHS trusts, common deployment script errors involved file paths and SQL column mismatches. One offline burst-load test reached 86.8% completion, but no study tested load acceptance as a go-live gate.

One rural safety-net deployment used a two-week integration test of hardware, connectivity, and workflow. The test led to improved connectivity, mandatory clinical variables, faster turnaround, and local data storage. No study reported the staff time or cost of acceptance testing, so leaders cannot yet weigh its burden against avoided failures.

CHAI states that installation qualification must come before assessment of a third-party AI system, and NIST advises testing data and content flows. FDA draft guidance describes manufacturer verification and validation, which does not replace local acceptance testing. An FDA discussion paper notes that input-output testing may be impractical for generative AI devices.

The one study set in safety-net and rural sites found connectivity and workflow bottlenecks during pre-implementation testing. The echocardiography position statement warns that bandwidth and data-transfer requirements may strain centres with limited digital capacity. Evidence from low-resource sites therefore rests on a single deployment in India.

research_gap: No study compared go-live failure rates, downtime, or patient harm between deployments that did and did not undergo acceptance testing. No study tested acceptance checks for load capacity, provenance mechanisms, or monitoring alert logic, and none reported the cost or staff time of testing.
underserved_note: Only one test (pmid:40925861) included safety-net and rural populations, and it took place in India. No test reported Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The results may therefore not transfer to U.S. safety-net systems or to interfaces used by patients with language or literacy barriers.

bottom_line: Thirteen observational studies suggest that running a tool silently on live data can reveal performance drops, data feed failures, coding errors, and false triggers before outputs reach clinicians. No study compared go-live with and without a silent phase, so the effect on patient harm has not been measured.

perspectives.view: All 13 tests are observational, and eight used a prospective comparator. None compared deployments with and without a silent phase. The studies measure whether silent mode detects problems, which is an indirect outcome for patient harm. Findings point the same way, but small samples limit precision, such as 100 encounters with a sensitivity confidence interval of 66% to 99%.

Silent runs surfaced failures that may otherwise have reached care. One run exposed an EHR data feed outage, another found coding errors, and a third logged 73 false triggers. In one screening program, AI missed 8 cancers that human readers recalled. Across 12 laboratory models, prospective AUROC fell below retrospective estimates.

Live performance often matched testing. Sensitivity was 81.7% versus 82.0% in one study, 91% versus 92% in another, and 85.29% in a third with similar testing values. A shadow AUC of 0.78 fell within the original 0.75 to 0.81. Local predeployment evaluation agreed with postdeployment value for 10 of 12 tasks. CT angiography shadow testing found setting-specific metrics.

Silent phases took time and reviewer effort. Reported runs lasted from 1 month to 77 days. One screening program reviewed 1,135 discordant cases and found 1 additional recall. None of the studies reported staffing hours or costs, so the resources needed for a silent phase remain unknown.

One ICU deployment judged 1 month of silent-mode results (AUC 0.908) against a 0.85 threshold in a predetermined change control plan and concluded that no fine-tuning was needed. This suggests that silent-mode data can feed formal change-control decisions. The regulatory discussion paper frames prospective scenario testing as something developers may do, not as a requirement.

No test reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Sites were in the United States, United Kingdom, the Netherlands, and Singapore, and several studies did not report a setting. The endorsement for resource-limited hospitals rests on commentary, not on a test.

research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without a silent phase on patient harm, time to detecting failures, or cost. Evidence is also lacking on how long a silent phase should run, how many cases it needs, and which thresholds should trigger a decision not to go live.
underserved_note: None of the 13 tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A silent run in one population may therefore miss performance gaps that appear only in those groups. Health systems serving them would need to check subgroup results in their own silent phase.

bottom_line: Studies of local tuning mostly report better accuracy, recall, or calibration on local data, but the one randomized trial found that fine-tuning a model on local dialogues lowered referral quality. Health systems may plan for local tuning while treating each retuned model as a new version that must be tested against the original before clinical use.

perspectives.view: Of 207 studies testing local tuning, the one randomized trial found that fine-tuning on local dialogues lowered referral quality. Most prospective comparisons report gains in accuracy, recall, or calibration, and one federated study found AUROC gains under 0.01. Outcomes are technical, many designs lack comparators, and interventions vary, so certainty is low.

Tuning can introduce new errors. In the trial, the locally tuned model failed to provide diagnoses in 30.0% of cases. Elsewhere, calibration on local data cut false positives by 72.7% while preserving sensitivity, and a threshold change raised sensitivity to 100% at the cost of more false positives. These results suggest retuned models need retesting before release.

Some studies suggest modest local data can suffice. Fine-tuning with 10% of local data raised recall from 0.67 to 0.77 at one site, and 25% or more of local data gave acceptable ICU performance. Fundus AUC reached 0.82 at about 500 images, with smaller gains beyond that. Clinician-led prompt refinement ran over 12 weeks.

The only trial, in rural, low-income, low-literacy Chinese populations, found that local fine-tuning lowered quality. In Medicaid, a population-adapted model outperformed Medicare coefficients applied unchanged, and prompt refinement raised actionable alerts above 95%. Rural sites in the United States failed sample size requirements for local recalibration, which may leave small sites unable to tune.

Retraining after onboarding new clinics raised document classification accuracy by 10.2%, and mammography AUC rose from 0.73 to 0.91 after adjustments based on local testing. Adding local predictors to a commercial model raised AUC from 0.81 to 0.87 offline. Budgets may need to cover local labeling, retraining, and repeat validation for each update.

Patient preference for the tone and quality of AI message replies rose from under 15% to 62% after local prompt tuning. In the trial of patient-facing referral dialogues, the locally tuned model lowered history-taking, diagnosis, and test-ordering scores. Patients may benefit from tuning only when each retuned tool is checked against its prior version.

research_gap: No study linked local tuning to patient outcomes such as missed diagnoses or alarm burden, and few compared tuned and untuned models concurrently in the same population. Controlled studies are needed that define minimum local sample sizes, test retuned versions against the originals before release, and report results separately for small and safety-net sites.
underserved_note: The one randomized trial enrolled limited English proficiency, low-literacy, low-income, and rural patients in China and found that local fine-tuning lowered quality, while two lower-level studies in the United States that included Medicaid populations reported gains. No study tested tuning in safety-net hospitals in the United States serving limited English proficiency patients, and a rural hazard study suggests small sites may lack enough data to recalibrate at all.

bottom_line: Local validation studies produced site-specific performance estimates, several of them below vendor or published figures, and in two studies local testing stopped deployment of algorithms that underperformed, one of them against a predefined 0.80 threshold. No supplied study compared patient outcomes between deployments with and without local validation, so the evidence that the practice prevents harm is indirect.

perspectives.view: Most supplied studies are single-site accuracy studies that show local validation is feasible and yields site-specific estimates. In two, local testing stopped deployment, once for an FDA-approved algorithm with low specificity and once until another passed a 0.80 threshold on its third test. No study compares outcomes with and without validation, and two entries appear to report one study.

Local testing exposed failure modes that summary accuracy can hide. In one stroke study, e-ASPECTS sensitivity was 58.6% and hyperdense thrombus PPV was 22.9%. A murmur algorithm missed heart defects when no murmur was audible, and agreement on blast cells reached kappa 0.08. A vendor mortality model had a local AUC of 0.73 against a stated 0.86.

Local results depended on workflow and case mix. AI contours differed from clinical contours partly because of local protocol differences, with median VDSC ranging from 0.23 to 0.88. One tool fell from 94% retrospective to 88% prospective accuracy, and a genetic risk model showed 2.92% precision locally versus 33.3% earlier, which the authors attributed to prevalence.

Three tests included rural, safety-net, or low-income patients in India and Australia. In one, commercial retinopathy algorithms ranged from 68.3% sensitivity to flagging disease in 89.2% of eyes against 27.48% by reference. Hazard studies in South African and Kenyan settings found moderate or shifted discrimination. No test addressed limited English proficiency, low literacy, or US Medicaid patients.

FDA draft guidance allows sites to supply historical data to assess expected performance, and a Swiss pathology commentary recommends internal validation even for certified systems. The supplied evidence is consistent with that view, since an FDA-approved algorithm showed unacceptably low local specificity and a mammography algorithm reached a specificity of 0.70 against a declared 0.88.

No supplied study reports the cost or staff time of local validation. Among studies testing the practice, samples ranged from 60 patients to 404,502 mammograms, which suggests the effort varies widely by product. In one laboratory study, local testing also showed that 30.5% of urine cultures met auto-release or batch-review thresholds, which may inform staffing plans.

research_gap: No supplied study compares patient outcomes, missed diagnoses, or false alarms between sites that gate deployment on local validation and sites that do not. The evidence also does not establish how to set acceptance criteria when positive predictive value shifts with local prevalence, how many local cases are sufficient, or how well retrospective historical results predict prospective performance. Studies that report the cost and staff time of validation are also absent.
underserved_note: Three tests of the practice included rural, safety-net, or low-income patients (India and Australia), and one of them found that local validation prevented deployment of an FDA-approved algorithm in a safety-net setting. Hazard studies in Chilean public hospitals, South Africa, and Kenya add context. No test included limited English proficiency, low-literacy, or US Medicaid populations, so the evidence cannot show whether local validation detects performance gaps specific to those groups.

bottom_line: Thirteen sources endorse multi-site validation, and studies that broke results out by site or device found performance gaps that pooled figures hid. No study compared this practice with pooled validation or measured patient outcomes, so certainty is low.

perspectives.view: Of 44 studies listed as testing the practice, most applied a model at several sites or on several devices. None compared per-site reporting with pooled reporting or tracked patient outcomes, and some reported only pooled accuracy. Per-site and per-device breakdowns exposed gaps in several studies, which suggests the practice detects variation. Indirectness and inconsistent reporting lower certainty to low.

Per-device reporting surfaced weaknesses that combined figures concealed. One retinal tool had 97.1% combined sensitivity but 83.3% on ZEISS images, and a pathology model's grading agreement fell to 0.44 on one scanner. In hazard studies, sepsis AUROC fell from 0.92 at development to 0.77 externally, and coding precision fell from 0.875 to 0.137.

A qualitative study of 39 interviews linked site variation to workflow integration, technical configuration, and infrastructure, which a one-time validation may not capture. In a smartphone study, image capture succeeded in 28.9% of attempts in users' hands, and diagnostic performance differed by phone model. Device-level validation may need to use the equipment that staff and patients actually use.

In a tuberculosis screening trial in South Africa and Lesotho, staff had to re-determine site thresholds because score distributions depended on each site's X-ray equipment. Per-hospital fine-tuning of a terminology mapping model produced top-1 accuracy from 25.0% to 96.3%. These findings suggest per-site validation may bring recurring recalibration work that budgets should anticipate.

Device-dependent gaps appeared in low-resource settings. In rural India, one diabetic retinopathy tool had 97.5% sensitivity on one camera and 81.7% on another. Among the testing studies, one used an Iraqi cohort, and none enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software says multiple collection sites, such as academic and community hospitals, may assure a more representative sample. FUTURE-AI advises selecting multiple evaluation sites. The quoted regulatory and consensus passages do not address separate reporting by site or device, so that element rests mainly on commentaries.

Patients usually cannot learn whether a tool was checked on the scanner or phone used in their care. A gestational age study reported error separately for Chicago (4.1 days) and Nairobi (4.3 days). Its reporting shows that site-level results can be stated in terms a clinician could explain to a patient.

research_gap: No study compared validation with separate site and device reporting against pooled validation for detecting failures before deployment, or linked either approach to patient outcomes. The evidence also does not show how many sites or devices are enough, or what response after a detected gap, such as recalibration or local thresholds, restores performance.
underserved_note: None of the 44 studies testing the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One testing study used an Iraqi cohort and one studied older adults. Hazard studies from rural India, South Africa and Lesotho, and a rural China trial that enrolled limited English proficiency and low-literacy participants documented site- and setting-dependent problems, including consultation completion that fell to 40% in mountainous regions (pmid:41659358). Health systems serving these populations probably cannot assume that validation at other sites will transfer, and local validation may be needed.

bottom_line: Three offline replay studies found that re-testing after a software update, over time, or in a new trial setting detected performance losses that recalibration or brief adaptation then recovered. No study tested local reassessment in a live deployment, measured patient outcomes, or evaluated the equity reassessment the recommendation calls for.

perspectives.view: All three tests of the practice are level 4 retrospective replays in offline settings. They agree in direction, with performance falling after change and recovering after local adjustment. Certainty is very low because the designs are observational and simulated, and no study measured whether revalidation changed clinical decisions or patient harm.

An updated software version used at the old threshold had specificity of 23.1% versus 45.8% and produced 36.4% more diagnostic testing, and it matched its predecessor only after recalibration.
