In a separate benchmark, naive quantization dropped AUROC to 0.500, which a plausibility filter raised to 0.699. These results suggest that routine updates can silently break validated performance.

In a real deployment in India, sensitivity rose from 68.4% to 99.6% and specificity fell from 96% to 64.7% between validation and implementation. Expanding a fax model to new clinics coincided with lower performance. One adaptation study needed 20 events per end point to transfer a trial-derived tool, which suggests local retesting may be feasible with modest labeled data.

No test of the practice reported subgroup or equity metrics. Hazard studies show that performance shifted in a rural safety-net setting in India, and that three language models followed explicit non-US guidelines 30.0-36.7% of the time versus 76.7-86.7% for US guidelines. These findings may indicate that populations far from the development setting carry more risk.

In a Canadian simulation of 319,012 patients, AUROC fell from 0.807 to between 0.670 and 0.677 by 2022-23, and updating on the full data restored it. This suggests revalidation is a recurring cost rather than a single event. The adaptation study suggests the labeling effort per new context may be small, though no study reported staff time or cost.

When an updated tool ran at an unrevalidated threshold, specificity fell by about half and diagnostic testing rose by 36.4%. For patients, this may mean more follow-up tests, more false alarms, and more worry. Recalibration before release brought performance back to the prior level in that study.

research_gap: The evidence lacks a prospective study in live care that compares deployments with and without pre-release local revalidation and measures clinical decisions, patient harm, and subgroup performance. No study tested revalidation of large language model updates, fine-tuning, or retrieval changes, and none reported the staff time and cost of repeated validation.
underserved_note: The three tests of the practice included older adults in Viet Nam and a racial and ethnic minority focus in Canada, but none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The safety-net and non-English contexts appear only in hazard studies, so health systems serving these groups have evidence that performance can shift for their patients but no evidence on how well local revalidation corrects it.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether showcasing clinically impressive cases during local evaluation improves stakeholder buy-in or adoption of beneficial AI tools. The recommendation rests on expert guidance from a single multi-society radiology statement, which appears twice in the source list.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard of low buy-in. The two endorsements quote identical text from one ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR and RSNA statement, so they count as a single expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without supporting data does not raise certainty above no direct evidence.

No study measures whether presenting selected impressive cases changes how clinicians weigh AI output. The supplied evidence therefore cannot show whether the practice affects the rate of errors that reach patients, in either direction.

research_gap: Studies should compare local evaluations that present selected impressive cases with evaluations that report only aggregate performance. Outcomes should include clinician adoption, stakeholder approval decisions, and whether users' trust matches the tool's measured accuracy. No such study appears in the supplied evidence, and no study documents how often low buy-in blocks adoption of beneficial tools.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether impressive cases drawn from local data would represent their patients or would influence adoption decisions for them.

bottom_line: Five offline studies measured how well AI screening or human review caught AI errors, and three of them routed review by model agreement, confidence, or flag tier and reported lower residual error rates after targeted review. All five used retrospective or simulated designs outside live care, so the evidence suggests that tier-level measurement is feasible but offers little certainty about how review tiers perform in deployment.

perspectives.view: All five studies are level 4, retrospective or descriptive, and run offline. Samples range from 20 CT scans to 1,166 records. Tasks span contouring, pharmacogenomics, pathology, and clinical records, and only three assigned review by risk tier. None tested tiered review prospectively or in live care. Indirectness and risk of bias lower certainty to very low.

In the Korean records study, 62.4% of cosine-flagged and 78.6% of RAG-fallback records had errors, compared with 3.8% of randomly sampled unflagged records. That residual rate suggests the low-risk tier may need its own random audit. The contouring study reported that overestimation bias could let inadequate cases pass LLM screening.

Error measurement in these studies depended on expert ground-truth labels assembled for research. In the pathology study, adjudicated review restored ACIS calls from 13 of 20 to 18 of 20 and reduced SCC calls from 4 to 1. No study tested whether teams can sustain this kind of labeling within routine clinical workflows.

In the pharmacogenomics study, model agreement cut manual review by 88.6%, and a threshold strategy sent 11 of 385 items (2.9%) to priority review with a 0.5% error rate in the remainder. In the French study, reviewing the 30% of outputs with lowest confidence lowered error rates to 4.4%. No study reported staffing time or cost.

One study used clinical records from South Korea, which the map tags as non-English. No study drew on Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, and none reported error-detection rates by patient subgroup. Tier thresholds validated on these datasets may not hold for records from under-resourced settings.

research_gap: No study measured error-detection rates by review tier in a live clinical deployment, tracked how those rates change over time, or tested whether adjusting tiers based on measured rates reduced the number of errors reaching patients. Prospective studies that include random audits of low-risk tiers, report results by patient subgroup, and record reviewer time and cost would address these gaps.
underserved_note: The South Korean clinical records study used non-English records, and it is the only test tagged for a language population. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, or patients with limited English proficiency in US care settings. Health systems serving these groups will need to measure tier-level detection rates in their own patient populations rather than rely on published thresholds.

bottom_line: One simulated study suggests that a structured red-teaming protocol can surface chatbot errors in a defined use context, finding errors in 12 of 80 BA probes and in 0 of 60 KA probes. No study shows that such protocols reduce patient harm in deployment, and a qualitative study reports barriers that may limit independent external evaluation.

perspectives.view: A single level 4 study tested the practice offline, using 160 probes rather than patients or clinical encounters. It measured whether the protocol detects errors and did not measure downstream outcomes. Indirectness, reliance on one study, and small counts such as 4 of 19 in the high-severity category support very low certainty.

The protocol found no errors in 60 KA probes and found errors in 12 of 80 (15%) BA probes. The study also reports 4 of 19 (21%) as high-severity, though the summary does not state what the 19 refers to. Error rates may differ by probe type. The study does not show whether detected failures were fixed before reaching users.

The qualitative study reported five linked barriers to independent context-specific testing of consumer health LLMs, including rate limits, interfaces that cannot be reset between probes, and unsuitable accuracy criteria. These barriers may reduce the fidelity and repeatability of red-teaming conducted outside a vendor's own environment.

NIST AI 600-1 calls for regular reassessment of risk measurement approaches but does not specify a protocol. The qualitative study found that terms of service can restrict independent testing and that no reliable independent evaluation framework exists. Contract terms that allow external evaluation may therefore be a precondition for carrying out this recommendation.

The tested protocol used 160 designed probes, including 20 multi-turn scenarios, for one chatbot. The study reports no staffing time or cost. Rate limits and non-resettable interfaces reported in the hazard study suggest that repeated testing at a regular cadence may require more effort than a single pilot in one department.

research_gap: No study compares organizations or deployments with and without a standardized context-specific risk measurement protocol on patient-level outcomes, error rates after deployment, or the rate at which detected errors are corrected. Studies are also needed on the staff time and cost of repeated red-teaming and on contract terms that permit independent evaluation.
underserved_note: Neither the testing study nor the hazard study reports probes or participants drawn from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A protocol checked only on probes of unstated language and literacy level may not detect errors that arise when those patients use the tool, so local protocols would likely need probes written for those groups.

bottom_line: Four studies, three of them offline, suggest that subgroup analysis on local data can reveal performance gaps that aggregate metrics and population-level validation miss. No study compared patient outcomes between deployments that did and did not include local subgroup validation.

perspectives.view: One prospective deployment tested 50 of 256 eligible patients after an AI flag, and three offline or benchmark studies applied subgroup analysis. All four support the practice, but they measure gap detection rather than patient outcomes. Hazard studies are split, and several found no subgroup differences. This suggests that gaps vary by tool and site, which argues for checking locally.

In one local analysis of 58,464 encounters, c-statistic, ICI, and Brier score showed no consistent differences, yet false negative rates were higher for Black, Hispanic, younger, Medicaid, and low-SES patients. A benchmark of 33 models found that population-level validation concealed subgroup disparities. A hazard study reported aggregate accuracy of 88.7% to 94.3% alongside poorer performance in older patients.

In a Canadian cohort of 319,012 patients, local model AUROC was lowest for Black patients (0.612). After provincial updating, the ethnic range narrowed to 0.749-0.790. This suggests that subgroup findings can inform model updating before use. None of the four studies reported the analyst time, data preparation burden, or sample sizes needed for stable subgroup estimates.

The one test that included Medicaid and low-income patients found higher false negative rates in those groups. A separate hazard study found false positive rates 1.36 to 1.39 times higher for non-White patients and bias by area deprivation and insurance type. That study included limited English proficiency and low health literacy patients, but it did not test the practice.

A survey of US hospitals found that 44 percent of those using predictive models evaluated them locally for bias, compared with 61 percent that evaluated accuracy. This suggests many systems would need new capacity to adopt the practice. No study reported the cost, staffing, or time required to run subgroup fairness analyses before deployment.

Subgroup analysis in the Canadian angiography study found that benefit skewed to females, with 42 of 50 procedures avoided compared with 18 of 32 for males. Findings like this may show patients and clinicians which groups a tool serves less well. None of the four tests of the practice measured patient trust or patients' access to a human reviewer.

research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without local subgroup validation on patient outcomes, missed diagnoses, or disparity trends after go-live. Studies are also needed on the minimum local sample sizes for reliable subgroup estimates, on the resources the analysis requires, and on how often vendor bias reports disagree with local results.
underserved_note: One offline test (pmid:37001995) included Medicaid, low-income, and racial and ethnic minority patients and found higher false negative rates in those groups, and the Canadian test analyzed marginalization subgroups. No test of the practice included limited English proficiency, low-literacy, or explicitly safety-net populations. Whether local subgroup validation detects gaps for these groups therefore rests on hazard studies rather than on tests of the practice.

bottom_line: No study in this map tests whether phased rollout of AI tools catches problems before they spread system-wide, and no study documents the hazard itself. Nine sources endorse or describe phased deployment, and their support rests on reasoning and single-organization accounts rather than comparative data.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test phased rollout against system-wide launch, and zero studies measure how often AI problems spread before detection. The nine endorsements include one framework, two guidance documents, and six commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion and descriptive accounts do not yield a certainty rating for the practice's effect.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes a one-month deployment on a subset of patients to find integration issues and measure performance before use across a site's full population. This is an illustrative example in draft guidance and does not create a binding requirement for phased rollout.

The CHAI playbook reports that a pilot revealed variation in rapid response team staffing, training, and documentation across hospitals, and that standard infrastructure had to be built before expansion. Another account describes scaling department by department after a 60-physician pilot. These accounts suggest pilots may surface local differences, but neither reports cost, delay, or outcomes compared with other approaches.

The logic of limiting exposure is plausible, since an error found at one site affects fewer patients than an error found everywhere. No study here measures how many problems pilots actually detect, how many escape detection until after expansion, or whether pilot sites resemble the sites that follow.

research_gap: Health systems need studies that compare staged and system-wide AI rollouts and count the issues detected at each stage, the patients exposed before detection, and the harms that appeared only after expansion. Studies should also report which pilot site characteristics predicted problems at later sites.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Commentaries on pediatric imaging equity, glaucoma care, and low-resource settings in Somalia endorse phased pilots, but if early pilots take place at well-resourced sites, problems specific to underserved patients may first appear after expansion.

bottom_line: Clinician review of real inputs and outputs before full deployment repeatedly found errors, including tail-risk outputs that aggregate scores missed, but no supplied study compares deployments with and without such review. One pre-post study suggests tiered review may reduce potentially harmful advice, and the certainty of the evidence is very low.

perspectives.view: The record lists 67 studies as testing the practice. The 25 supplied are mostly level 3 or 4 single-arm reviews, and none compares deployments with and without pre-deployment review. One pre-post study reported advice with potential minor harm falling from 1.32% to 0.13% and 0.07% after tiered review. Design, indirectness, and differing criteria keep certainty very low.

Clinician review found problems that summary scores missed. In 50 neurology cases, aggregate ratings did not differ, yet 10% of LLM responses scored as concerning versus 0% of human responses. Other reviews found 5 misleading answers in 588 and one hallucination in 60 reports. Samples of 100 outputs may be too small to detect rare severe errors.

The choice of reviewer may change what review finds. Primary care physicians identified more omissions with greater harm likelihood than hospitalists did. Senior consultants graded more conservatively than an automated grader that otherwise agreed with ophthalmologists (Spearman rho 0.80). Three fetal radiologists reached an ICC of 0.93, which suggests predefined scoring criteria can yield consistent ratings.

Review at scale carries staffing cost. One program used 6,234 licensed clinicians to review more than 307,000 calls. In two studies, automated grading tracked clinician grading (rho 0.80, and P=.55 between clinician and LLM scores). This suggests a hybrid design could lower reviewer hours, though no study measured cost or time.

Two tests involved limited English proficiency settings. An offline review of 200 translated discharge instructions found variable translation quality. In a Nigerian vignette study, 17% of outputs were acceptable only with human review. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. A safety-net hazard study reported diabetic macular edema sensitivity of 26.5%.

A regulatory discussion paper suggests that reviewers consider whether a device performs consistently across clinically relevant subgroups. None of the supplied tests reported sampling reviewed outputs by subgroup. The evidence therefore does not show whether pre-deployment review meets that expectation.

In one hazard study, rheumatologists rated AI answer accuracy at 6.48 versus 9.08 for physician answers. Patients scored 0.49 on identifying AI answers versus 0.97 for physician answers. This suggests patients may not be able to screen outputs themselves, which leaves clinician review as a check made on their behalf.

research_gap: No supplied study compares harm reaching patients in deployments with and without pre-deployment clinician review. Such comparative studies are needed. They should also report how sample size was chosen to detect rare severe errors, how reviewer qualifications and criteria were set, and whether sampling covered clinically relevant subgroups. Studies should report reviewer time and cost as well.
underserved_note: Two tests of the practice involved limited English proficiency settings. One was an offline translation review and the other a vignette study. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, and hazard studies in rural, safety-net, and low-literacy groups do not test the review itself. Whether sampled review catches errors specific to these populations therefore remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether predefined pilot thresholds and a formal decision gate change scaling decisions or patient outcomes, and no study documents how often tools scale without evidence of pilot success. Eight sources endorse the practice, mostly commentaries and two frameworks, so the recommendation currently rests on expert agreement.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Of eight endorsements, two are frameworks, one is guidance, and five are commentaries. Agreement across sources reflects expert opinion, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

Several endorsers ask for prespecified stop rules, safety thresholds, and real-time adverse event monitoring during pilots, which would give a committee a defined point to halt a tool before wider exposure. Without studies, it remains unknown whether such gates catch failures that informal review would miss, or how often thresholds are set too loosely to trigger.

Two endorsers call for subgroup calibration and equity-stratified performance audits as part of pilot criteria, and one addresses low-resource community settings. These sources describe what thresholds should contain, but no study shows that stratified gates detect or prevent performance gaps in Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups.

One guidance source states that some functional areas lack standard metrics and will need focused measurement approaches before enterprise scaling. This suggests that defining thresholds may require local analytic work for each tool. No study reports the staff time, cost, or delay that a formal decision gate adds to deployment.

research_gap: No study compares deployments governed by predefined success, failure, and responsible AI thresholds with deployments scaled through informal judgment. Useful studies would measure how often gates lead to halting or remediation, whether halted tools would have caused harm, the time and staff cost of the gate, and whether subgroup-stratified thresholds change decisions.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two endorsements recommend equity-stratified audits and one addresses low-resource settings, but whether decision gates protect these groups remains untested.

bottom_line: Four small offline studies suggest that clinical expert review before deployment can find and correct AI content that conflicts with local guidelines, clinical relevance, or clinician interpretation, but none measured effects on patient outcomes in live use. Eleven hazard studies show that AI outputs often diverge from local guidelines and practice, which supports the need for the safeguard without showing how well it works.

perspectives.view: All four tests of the practice are level 4 retrospective replays with raters in offline settings, with samples from 15 to 1000 patients plus one cohort of 55,303 deliveries. Results point in the same direction, but the outcomes are process measures, one contouring effect was not statistically significant, and no study used a concurrent control. Certainty is very low.

Clinician review removed 18% of LLM-matched codes as not clinically relevant, and five neurologists rated two AI-linked pathways below the appropriateness threshold (medians 6 and 5). These results suggest that review catches some errors before use. Hazard studies report omitted diagnoses in 30.0% of simulated cases and physician rejection of 7 of 15 recommendations for deviating from national TB guidelines.

Adjusting AI seminal vesicle contours to the institutional guideline brought dose distributions closer to manual contouring (g=0.53-0.63 versus 0.67-0.78), though no difference reached significance. Hazard studies found that operational workflow problems made up most LLM errors and that only 19% of AI order set suggestions were useful. No test reported reviewer time or burden.

Multidisciplinary review in a 55,303-delivery obstetric cohort raised concern that clinicians would read race as a predictor, and the team moved to a race-blind model. In non-English settings, LLMs followed non-US imaging guidelines in 30.0% to 36.7% of vignettes versus 76.7% to 86.7% for US guidelines, which suggests local validation may matter more outside US contexts.

Six sources endorse expert validation, and three of them, including the CHAI assurance guide, state it as a requirement. One guidance document calls for human examination of patient records before a care denial. None of the supplied studies tests whether meeting these expectations changes compliance or outcomes.

Vendor defaults conflicted with local practice in several radiation oncology studies. Vendor-recommended plans exceeded local maximum-dose tolerance in three of 12 cases, 9 of 10 radiation oncologists said auto-segmented targets differed from their routine practice, and vendor breast contours departed from institutional conventions. No study reported the staffing or cost needed to perform expert validation.

Patient-facing content showed local mismatches, with one model citing US resources in 57.1% of responses to Caribbean patients and faculty judging 40% of AI-generated consent forms unfit for Indian use. No test of expert validation examined patient-facing content, so its effect on what patients read and whom they can contact is unknown.

research_gap: No prospective or real-deployment study has compared AI tools with and without pre-deployment expert validation on the rate of guideline-discordant outputs reaching clinicians or patients, on downstream patient outcomes, or on the reviewer time and cost involved. Studies of patient-facing tools and administrative uses such as care denials are also absent.
underserved_note: The four tests of the practice included a racial and ethnic minority focus in one study and older adults in another, but none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Hazard studies documented local mismatches in limited English proficiency, low-literacy, low-income, and rural populations, so the practice remains untested where the hazard has been shown to occur.

bottom_line: Twenty-one studies suggest that local or simulated testing often reveals performance gaps that benchmarks miss; for example, a skin-lesion algorithm that outperformed specialists in experimental reader studies scored 11.6% lower than specialists in clinic. No study compares deployments that did and did not undergo local testing, so the evidence shows that the practice detects problems but not that it prevents patient harm.

perspectives.view: Four of 21 studies are prospective comparisons in real deployment, and the rest use descriptive, replay, or benchmark designs. Most studies measure whether local testing detected a gap, not whether testing changed patient outcomes. Indirectness and inconsistency, including four null or mixed results, lead me to rate certainty as low.

Low serious-error rates in single components (3.4%) coexisted with end-to-end note risk of up to 24%. In a stepwise simulation, GPT-4o reached 45.2% specificity, and 10% of LLM advice responses had concerning safety scores compared with 0% of specialist responses. These findings suggest that system-level local testing may catch failure modes before they reach patients.

Local configuration changed model behavior. Embedded system instructions raised persistent structured-output failure from 0.3% to 5.0% in the same environment. A simulated deployment found batch runtimes from 19.54 to 383.77 minutes, and scenario-based validation in Sokoto identified three fixes before pilot. Phantom-based testing appeared feasible for site-specific imaging checks.

A field test in rural Mexico reported 94% sensitivity for two retinal screening tools. In hazard studies, an Indian safety-net site saw specificity fall from 96% to 64.7%, and U.S. community screenings found 38.9% of eyes ungradable by AI compared with 2.6% by humans. These results suggest that performance may shift in lower-resource settings.

FDA design controls already require device testing under actual or simulated use conditions, and CDRH is considering clinical confirmation beyond benchmarking for generative AI devices. One simulated test against prespecified criteria found that a locked triage configuration failed its undertriage criteria. This finding suggests how deployer-side testing could apply the same logic before go-live.

In one trial, AI prioritized 29% of cases in deployment against 14% expected from retrospective testing, which increased immediate reads. In one simulated pipeline, data extraction took 13.30 hours. One site ran a 300-case pre-implementation test in a program covering 37,529 surgeries. These figures suggest that local testing carries staff time costs but may prevent workload surprises.

In one five-site clinic study, 86% of patients reported being highly satisfied under real-world use. Feedback from 13,000 consented users led to targeted improvements. NIST advises informed consent and compensation when people take part in feedback activities, which bears on trust when local testing involves real patients.

research_gap: No study compares sites that performed pre-deployment local testing with sites that did not. None reports whether problems found in testing were corrected and whether patient outcomes then changed. Studies also offer no standard for local test sample size or for performance thresholds that should halt go-live.
underserved_note: Several tests of the practice included non-English-speaking populations, including in China and Nigeria, and one included rural and disabled patients in Mexico. No test enrolled Medicaid, U.S. safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The only safety-net study is a hazard study from India, which found specificity falling from 96% to 64.7% at an implementation site. This result suggests that local testing may matter in settings where direct evidence is sparse.

bottom_line: Ten studies, most of them offline analyses, consistently show that predictive values and clinician-plus-AI performance change substantially when measured at local prevalence, and one deployment study found that local augmentation metrics matched later radiologist-perceived value for 10 of 12 tasks. No study tests whether reporting these metrics leads to better adoption decisions or patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Of 10 studies, 6 are level 4 offline analyses and none is randomized. Results consistently show predictive values shifting with prevalence, for example NPV rising from 48% to 92% (39425597) and PPV of 19.9% in routine EEGs (41615503). Most studies demonstrate the arithmetic rather than effects on decisions, so indirectness keeps certainty low.

In Spain, AI support raised cancer detection by 3.2 per 1,000 and PPV by 4%, with recall up 0.7% (37975920). That tradeoff became visible only through comparison with local readers. At 0.4% prevalence, suicide-risk PPVs were 0.012 to 0.050 (42114005), which suggests local reporting may reveal false-alarm burdens before deployment.

Local metrics appear feasible to produce from routine data. One site computed calibrated false discovery rates across 130,712 local mammograms (PPR985282). Augmentation metrics from 88,645 examinations agreed with radiologist-perceived value for 10 of 12 tasks, though the survey response rate was 43.2% (41779377). Net benefit analysis showed subgroup threshold shifts that AUROC did not show (41036091).

One emergency department found a local PPV of 33% against a manufacturer-reported 95% to 98% (39741216). Elsewhere, a specificity of 0.93 yielded a PPV of 0.5 at 9% stroke prevalence (39878893). These findings suggest that performance figures supplied at purchase may not transfer, which is consistent with the multi-society radiology statement on reporting predictive values at local prevalence.

The emergency department tool with a local PPV of 33% was removed from practice (39741216). Local evaluation before purchase might have avoided that sunk cost. The augmentation-metric approach (41779377) suggests systems may be able to forecast perceived value before full rollout. None of the supplied studies reports the staff time or data costs of producing local estimates.

A three-year pathology deployment in Puerto Rico found that pathologist-plus-AI review revised 1.8% of diagnoses, with rates of 0.75% to 3.5% per pathologist (38868487). A Chinese simulation found that rural and urban settings required different sensitivity, 94.7% versus 96.9% (38383738). Both suggest that site-level metrics differ, but neither study examined Medicaid or safety-net populations.

In one surveillance program in the United States, 57 of 255 inflammatory breast cancer cases (22.4%) were identified only by the AI pipeline (40493814). Comparisons with local clinicians may show patients what a tool adds to their own care team. Low local PPVs indicate how often patients may face false alarms and follow-up testing.

research_gap: No study compares health systems that report local metrics with systems that rely on vendor or published metrics. The effect of local reporting on purchasing decisions, clinician trust, and patient outcomes therefore remains untested. Studies also do not report the case volume, staff time, or cost needed to generate stable local estimates, particularly at low prevalence where confidence intervals widen.
underserved_note: The Puerto Rico pathology deployment focused on a racial and ethnic minority population, and one Chinese simulation modeled rural settings. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Prevalence and case mix may differ in these settings, so metrics reported at the tested sites may not reflect local utility there, and the practice itself has not been evaluated in them.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether recording local validation status and flagging unvalidated high-risk AI systems reduces the number of such systems left in clinical use, and no study supplied here measures how often that hazard occurs. The recommendation rests on two CHAI framework documents, one rated must and one rated should.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The support consists of expert framework guidance, which reflects consensus rather than measured effect.

No study supplied here reports how many unvalidated high-risk systems remain in use or what harm follows from them. Without such data, the size of the safety gain from a validation registry and a remediation flag cannot be estimated.

The CHAI governance playbook states the practice as a must and asks committees to note which systems have and have not been validated. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide rates it should and assigns validation to developer and implementer teams. Both sources are voluntary frameworks and do not carry regulatory force.

research_gap: Studies should first measure how many AI systems in use at health systems lack local validation and how many of those are high risk. Studies should then compare the share of unvalidated high-risk systems that are remediated or withdrawn, and the time that takes, in systems that keep a validation registry with priority flags against systems that do not.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from this evidence whether validation records capture performance in these groups, and a system marked as validated may not have been checked in the patients it serves.

bottom_line: Two randomized head-to-head trials and several smaller local comparisons found that ambient scribe products differed on documentation time, satisfaction, and note errors, which suggests side-by-side pilots can surface differences that a single-product pilot would miss. No study tested whether choosing a product through such a pilot leads to better outcomes than choosing without one, and vendor rankings shifted with the measurement method used.

perspectives.view: Two randomized trials compared products directly. One found Nabla reduced time-in-note by 7.8% versus DAX, and the other found Product B reduced minutes-in-notes by 3.19 more than Product A. Both show that pilots detect differences, which is an indirect outcome. Small samples, order effects, and method-dependent rankings lower certainty further.

Error audits of identical recordings found 3 errors for one vendor and 8 and 9 for the others, yet Likert ratings ranked a different vendor first. One product had fewer omissions but more irrelevant or misplaced text. Pilots that rely on clinician ratings alone may miss error patterns, so error audits may need to be part of the comparison.

In an 18-physician crossover, DAX was favored on unadjusted burden, note quality, and satisfaction, but adjusted models showed order effects and no overall preference. A 97-clinician pilot found higher utilization for one vendor. These results suggest pilot design, including randomized order and adequate sample size, shapes which product appears better.

One system narrowed 4 vendors to 2 and then 1 through simulations and workflow demonstrations, and it reported reduced vendor influence in selection, but it measured no comparative outcome. None of the studies reported the cost or staff time of running parallel pilots. Leaders may need to budget for these without published estimates.

In one emergency department study, AI scribe notes were similar to or lower in quality than human scribe notes, and in a standardized comparison all 11 AI tools scored below human notes. Patients depend on accurate notes, and these findings suggest the product chosen, and whether it is compared at all, may affect what enters the record.

No comparison study reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, and none reported whether product rankings held across languages or patient groups. A product that performs better in an academic English-speaking clinic may not perform better with interpreted or multilingual visits.

research_gap: No study compared outcomes after pilot-based selection with outcomes after selection by other means, such as vendor demonstrations or reference checks. Trials are needed that measure downstream note accuracy, patient harm, and sustained use after selection, and that report the cost of running parallel pilots. Studies should also test whether rankings stay stable across specialties, measurement methods, and patient language groups.
underserved_note: None of the nine tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one did not report its country. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume that a product ranked higher in these pilots will rank higher in their own settings, so their local pilots may need to include encounters with interpreters and multilingual patients.

bottom_line: Two retrospective imaging studies suggest that validation by a party independent of the developer may produce lower performance estimates than developer-reported results, which fits the concern that developer testing overstates accuracy. Neither study tested a governance committee requirement or measured patient outcomes, so certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: Both studies are level 4 retrospective replays in offline settings. In the European CT study, independent validation gave a kappa of 0.62 against 0.78 from developer testing, and an opacity DSC of 0.59 against 0.76. The Cyprus dental study reported 73.1% sensitivity and 64.7% PPV without a direct developer comparator. Indirectness and small samples lower certainty to very low.

The gap between internal and independent results in the CT study suggests that a tool approved on developer figures may perform worse than expected. A PPV of 64.7% in the dental study implies that about one in three positive flags may be false, which could prompt unneeded treatment. Neither study followed errors through to patient harm.

Both validations used archived images outside live workflows. They show what independent testing can detect, but they do not show how a governance committee would staff, schedule, or enforce it. Neither study reports the time, expertise, or data access the independent validators needed, so the burden of routine adoption remains unmeasured.

Neither study reported patient insurance, income, language, or literacy. The samples came from hospitals in the Netherlands, Belgium, and Italy and from a dental setting in Cyprus. Independent validation might expose larger performance gaps in groups underrepresented in developer data, but these studies did not examine that question.

research_gap: No study has compared governance processes that require an independent validator with processes that accept developer validation, and none has measured effects on deployment decisions, post-deployment error rates, patient outcomes, or validation cost. The existing tests cover two imaging tools in European settings. Prospective studies of non-imaging tools in U.S. health systems, including safety-net hospitals, would address the main gaps.
underserved_note: Neither study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The findings therefore offer no direct information on whether independent validation detects performance shortfalls that affect these groups, and health systems serving them cannot assume the reported discrepancies apply to their patients.

bottom_line: Seven deployment studies quantified local outcomes after AI rollout and all reported favorable changes, but five used before-after designs without comparison groups, and none tested whether documenting and measuring outcomes changes decisions to deploy or retain tools. Two quasi-experimental studies found no benefit and, in one, higher mortality after deployment, which suggests local outcome measurement may reveal results that model performance alone would not.

perspectives.view: Five of seven studies are pre-post designs without comparators. One is a quasi-experimental study of 352 patients that reported a hazard ratio of 0.56 for 30-day mortality, and one compared screening costs. All seven evaluated the tools rather than the evaluation practice, so the evidence is indirect. Uniformly favorable findings may reflect selective publication. Certainty is very low.

Two larger quasi-experimental deployments found that a fall-prediction tool raised nurse interventions without lowering falls, and that a drug-induced long QT tool was followed by higher mortality. These studies show that tools can fail or cause harm locally. They do not show that outcome documentation prevents harm, although both findings came from post-deployment measurement.

The studies suggest that outcome, safety, and cost data can be collected in real deployments across varied settings, including 3,966 colonoscopies and 4,231 alarm events. None reported the staff time, data infrastructure, or observation period the measurement required. The burden and fidelity of sustained local evaluation therefore remain unknown.

Two studies quantified costs. One reported lower total and medication costs and a median stay of 7 days after an AI-assisted prescription service. Another reported US$773 per case detected with AI plus symptom screening, compared with US$1198 for cough-only screening. Neither study reported what the evaluation itself cost.

One study screened 5,297 people in Nigeria with low health literacy. Another, in a US safety-net setting, found adenoma detection rose by 7.6% (95% CI 4.6-10.6) from a 31.5% baseline. No study reported results for Medicaid or limited English proficiency groups, and none reported outcomes stratified by population subgroup.

Two studies measured mortality. One reported lower 30-day mortality after deployment, and the other reported higher mortality. The remaining studies tracked process or safety measures such as evaluation rates, alarm counts, and contraindication rates. No study measured patient experience, trust, or access to a clinician, so patients have little evidence on how local evaluation affects their care.

research_gap: No study compared tool deployments with and without structured local outcome evaluation to learn whether measurement leads to earlier retirement of ineffective tools, fewer harms, or better cost decisions. Controlled or interrupted time-series designs would address this question if they used prespecified outcomes and reported both evaluation costs and subgroup results.
underserved_note: Two tests included underserved groups. One was a Nigerian screening program with participants of low health literacy (pmid:40498780), and the other was a US safety-net colonoscopy program (pmid:40858859). No test included Medicaid-identified or limited English proficiency populations, so it is unknown whether local evaluation captures benefits and harms for those patients.

bottom_line: Twenty-one studies report on pilot usability testing and feedback-driven revision, and most show that feedback changed tool design or raised acceptance and usability scores. None compares tools refined through structured end-user feedback against tools deployed without it on patient outcomes, and the one comparative study found no change in pathway adherence.

perspectives.view: The two randomized trials measure clinician acceptance or interface preference inside an AI trial rather than comparing feedback-informed with uninformed deployment. The only comparative test of a human-centred tool found adherence of 0.63 versus 0.60 (p=0.18). The remaining studies are uncontrolled pre-post, qualitative, or simulated designs with user-reported outcomes, so certainty is very low.

Hazard studies show that burdensome multistage workflows led to ignored alerts and unplaced orders, and that monthly clinician use of one tool fell from 88.7% to 66.2%. In one pilot, end-user interviews led designers to exclude certain patients and allow clinicians to refuse recommendations. This suggests feedback may catch fit problems early, though no study links such changes to fewer harms.

Iterative feedback raised usability from 47.9 to 69.3 on the System Usability Scale in one study, and 93% of clinicians adopted a search tool after a user-centered rollout. Another team used human-centered design and still saw 3% utilization in the first three months. These results suggest that feedback processes improve ratings but do not reliably produce use.

One trial that enrolled older, rural, low-literacy, and limited English proficiency participants found a 60% preference for voice interfaces among older or low-literacy users. In a Danish study of 20 patients, preference for human translation fell from 90% to 50% after patient face validation. These findings suggest that testing with representative users may surface needs that clinician-only testing would miss.

Clinicians used 17.5% of AI-drafted patient messages in one system, and a later prompt revision informed by feedback raised patient preference for drafts from under 15% to 62%. A Dutch rollout lost 9% of practices in eight weeks and reported that assistants were under-involved in design. These studies suggest that omitting some user groups may carry retention costs.

Few studies asked patients directly. In South Africa, 100 community members gave a simulated HIV tool a mean usability score of 81.6, and 94.9% said they would use it again. Patient preference for message drafts rose after revision. These results suggest that patients can give usable feedback, but none of the studies measured trust or patients' access to a human.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to show that users can operate the device and interpret its output in the actual context of clinical decision-making. CHAI guidance asks whether user acceptance testing is both qualitative and quantitative. No supplied study tests whether meeting these expectations changes outcomes.

research_gap: No study randomizes or otherwise compares deployments that did and did not use structured end-user feedback before full rollout while measuring sustained use, errors, or patient outcomes, and few studies report how representative the tested users were.
underserved_note: Three tests included limited English proficiency or non-English users, and one of these also included low-literacy, rural, and older adults, but all three took place in China or Denmark, and two used offline or simulated settings. No test enrolled Medicaid or U.S. safety-net populations, so the evidence does not show whether pilot feedback processes capture the needs of those users.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring clinicians to edit a clinically meaningful element of moderate-risk AI drafts improves review quality or reduces errors reaching patients. Two hazard studies give conflicting signals, with 2.6% of drafts sent nearly unedited in one real deployment and 35-45% of erroneous drafts submitted unedited in one simulation.

perspectives.view: No study compares a mandatory-edit rule against usual review, so certainty for the practice cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two hazard studies differ in design, setting, and outcome. One is an uncontrolled pre-post deployment and one is a 20-physician vignette study, and their results point in different directions.

In a simulation, 35-45% of drafts containing errors were submitted without any edit, which suggests that automation bias may let errors reach patients. Whether a forced edit catches those errors is untested. A clinician could change one element and still miss an error elsewhere in the draft, so the safeguard may prove weaker than it appears.

In a real deployment of 7,605 messages, only 2.6% of drafts went out identical or nearly identical, which suggests clinicians in that setting already edited most drafts. A mandatory-edit rule would add steps to every moderate-risk message. No study reports the time cost, the fidelity of edits, or whether clinicians would satisfy the rule with token changes.

Neither hazard study reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Both were conducted in the United States with no stratification by patient population. The evidence cannot show whether rubber-stamp approval or its remedy differs for messages sent to these groups.

research_gap: A controlled study is needed that randomizes clinicians or clinics to a mandatory-edit rule versus standard review for moderate-risk drafts and measures detection of seeded or naturally occurring errors, the substance of edits made, clinician time per message, and patient-facing harm. Such a study would also need to show whether clinicians meet the rule with token edits.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, and neither hazard study reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no evidence on whether the rule works for them, including for translated or plain-language messages where review errors may carry different risks.

bottom_line: Local evaluations of ambient scribes, including four randomized trials, show that such assessment can be done and that time savings, accuracy, and adoption differ across sites, products, and clinicians. No study tested whether local assessment itself changes deployment decisions or reduces documentation errors reaching patients.

perspectives.view: Four randomized trials and many pre-post studies evaluated ambient scribes within local deployments, which shows that local assessment can be done. No study compared organizations that evaluated locally with those that did not. Time-in-note results were inconsistent across trials, and well-being measures improved more consistently. Indirectness limits certainty for the practice to low.

Few studies measured accuracy, and one pre-post study of 210 providers did not assess it. Physician review of 356 local notes found 94.7% free of significant errors, while a Japanese deployment found 81.8% of 11 summaries had at least one error. Simulated ICU rounds showed omissions averaging 15.5%. Error rates appear to vary by setting.

At two Canadian public health units, scribe use was associated with a 12.9-minute reduction at one and a 10.4-minute increase at the other. In one trial Nabla cut time-in-note 9.5% while DAX did not change it. Among 310 physicians, perceived and actual time savings were not associated, which suggests evaluations may need objective EHR measures alongside surveys.

One study of 100 clinicians found benefit varied by sex and specialty, and a two-resident study found gains for one resident only. A safety-net study included nine pharmacists, and Swedish and Spanish studies evaluated non-English documentation. No test reported outcomes for Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

Uptake varied, which affects the return on any evaluation effort. Oncology providers used the scribe in 13.9% of 4,449 visits, fewer than one-third of trained clinicians adopted it in a Spanish study, and individual use ranged from 30% to 89%. In one emergency department, AI scribes were associated with more EHR note time than human scribes (4.3 vs 1.8 minutes for adults).

One pilot reported improved patient satisfaction across domains after deployment, but most studies measured clinician outcomes only. One endorsing source asks that benefits not accrue mainly to well-resourced, dominant-language settings. Patient experience and patient-detected errors are largely absent from the evaluation measures tested so far.

research_gap: No study tests whether conducting a local assessment leads to different adoption decisions, earlier detection of documentation errors, or fewer errors reaching patients, compared with deploying without one. Standardized accuracy audits, patient-reported outcomes, and subgroup analyses by clinician type and patient population are rarely included in the local evaluations published to date.
underserved_note: One test included a safety-net setting (nine pharmacists), and studies from Sweden, Spain, and Japan evaluated non-English documentation. No test reported results for Medicaid patients, patients with limited English proficiency in English-dominant settings, or low-literacy patients, so current local evaluation methods may not detect accuracy problems or uneven benefit in these groups.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether disabling one-click sending or AI drafting for high-risk patient messages reduces erroneous replies, and no supplied study documents how often such errors occur. The recommendation rests on a single commentary that treats disabling drafting as one of two acceptable options for high-risk messages.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies of the practice and zero studies of the hazard. The only support is one commentary rated as a must, which is expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, this yields no direct evidence, and the size and direction of any effect on reply errors or patient outcomes remain unknown.

The endorsing commentary allows either disabled drafting or a mandatory second check with documented reasoning for high-risk messages. These two safeguards act at different points. One removes the AI draft, and the other adds a human check before sending. No supplied data show which, if either, catches errors before they reach patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare high-risk message tiers with AI drafting disabled, with one-click sending removed, and with a mandatory second check. These studies should measure how often erroneous replies reach patients, time to clinician response for urgent messages, and how accurately messages are assigned to the high-risk tier.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether tiering rules classify messages from these patients accurately or whether restrictions change response times for them.

bottom_line: One offline study of 1,200 LLM-generated answers to simulated patient questions found that adding a second reader cut the average miss rate for deficiencies from 12.4% to 0.6%. No study has tested a documented second check on real high-risk portal messages or measured its effect on patients.

perspectives.view: The only test is a single retrospective replay with raters, in simulated conditions, on 1,200 answers to invented patient questions. It measured detection of deficiencies rather than patient outcomes, and it did not limit analysis to high-risk message tiers. Indirectness and reliance on one study place certainty at very low, even though the effect favored dual review.

A single reader missed an average of 12.4% of deficiencies, and a second reader lowered that to 0.6%, with triple review detecting all of them. These figures suggest that one reviewer may let a meaningful share of errors through. The study did not grade miss severity, so the harm that the second check prevents remains unmeasured.

The study took place offline, so it did not capture time pressure, inbox volume, or how reviewers would record their reasoning in the portal. It also did not compare a second clinician with the structured checklist option that the endorsing guidance allows. Fidelity and burden of the check in live workflows have not been tested.

The study reported miss rates but no reviewer time, staffing, or cost data. Health systems therefore cannot estimate from this evidence what a second check would cost per high-risk message. The endorsing guidance lets systems disable drafting in the high-risk tier instead, which may cost less where message volume is high.

research_gap: Prospective studies should compare single review, second clinician review, and structured checklist review on real high-risk portal messages, and measure severity of missed errors, reviewer time, reply delay, and patient harm.
underserved_note: The single study used simulated patient questions and reported no information on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether second checks catch errors at the same rate in translated or plain-language replies to these patients is unknown.

bottom_line: One guidance document states that AI tools must not generate records, communications, or other content on a physician's behalf without that physician's consent and final review, but no supplied study tests whether obtaining consent prevents unauthorized attribution. The recommendation currently rests on professional consensus rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests physician consent as a safeguard, and no study documents how often unauthorized attribution occurs. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated for an untested practice. The single endorsement is a guidance statement, which reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative data.

The endorsing source is a set of professional principles that uses mandatory language and pairs consent with final physician review. This wording treats consent and review as a joint condition. The supplied materials do not tie the requirement to any federal rule or state statute, so its force comes from professional guidance rather than law.

research_gap: No study has measured how often AI tools produce content attributed to physicians without authorization, or whether consent processes, final-review requirements, or both reduce that rate. Studies could compare signed-note error rates, patient message attribution, and physician awareness of AI-drafted content under different consent models, and could record the time burden each model places on clinicians.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Patients in these groups may rely more on written messages and translated materials, and whether consent requirements protect them equally remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether individualized human clinical review with override ability reduces wrongful AI-assisted denials of care, claims, or prior authorization. One simulation study found that large language models assigned an insurer role denied guideline-endorsed treatments more often, which suggests the hazard exists, and two guidance documents endorse human review.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, so certainty about its effect cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study used 675 simulated model responses to 25 vignettes. It shows that role framing shifted model outputs toward denial. It does not measure whether a human reviewer would catch or reverse those denials.

When prompted as an insurer, models showed alignment with endorsed treatments falling 50% for GPT-5.4, 45% for Gemini 3.1 Pro, and 10.5% for Opus 4.6. This suggests an unreviewed output could deny appropriate care. Whether human review intercepts these errors, or whether reviewers defer to the model, has not been studied.

Two sources endorse the practice. The augmented intelligence principles state it as a requirement that reviewers examine patient records before a denial, and the CHAI guide describes human oversight as necessary for fairness in prior authorization. These endorsements reflect expert consensus rather than tested outcomes.

The hazard study indicates that the same model can reach different conclusions depending on whose interests it is told to represent. Patients facing a denial may reasonably expect a clinician to have read their record, and the endorsing guidance supports that expectation, though no study shows how often review changes the decision.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI-assisted denial workflows with and without individualized clinician review, measuring overturn rates, appeal outcomes, time to care, reviewer agreement with model outputs, and reviewer workload in live payer operations.
underserved_note: The only study was an offline vignette simulation that did not report patient population characteristics, and no study tested the practice in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether human review would reduce wrongful denials for these groups, who may have fewer resources to pursue appeals.

bottom_line: Four of six hazard studies found that model discrimination, calibration, or segmentation accuracy declined over time or after protocol changes, but only two offline benchmarks tested monitoring or revalidation itself, and neither measured patient outcomes. Health systems may reasonably schedule local revalidation on the basis of the hazard evidence and 27 endorsements, while treating the method, interval, and sample size as unsettled.

perspectives.view: Two studies tested the practice, and both were level 5 offline automated benchmarks. One reported that forecasting performance improved by 38% with MLOps. The other found control-chart monitoring feasible, but in many cases it needed more than 18 validation cases. Neither was randomized or measured clinical outcomes, so indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

Across four deployed systems, calibration slope fell by a mean of 0.14 by nine months while AUROC declined by 0.01 to 0.03. This suggests that checks limited to discrimination may miss drift. In another study, whole gland Dice fell from 99.46% to 91.24% after an acquisition protocol change, which periodic local checks may detect.

Declines were uneven across settings. One model's AUROC fell from 0.84 to 0.73 in a U.S. dataset of 851,499 discharges, while a CT phantom study found stable results over fifteen months. Adding recent training data did not necessarily raise performance, which suggests that revalidation triggered by workflow changes may matter as much as fixed schedules.

The Duke commentary proposes performance assessment at least twice a year, but no study reports staffing or cost. The control-chart study found that 18 validation cases were often too few to accept or reject a hypothesis. This suggests that local revalidation may require case volumes that smaller sites cannot readily assemble.

Neither test of the practice reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A Canadian hazard study with a racial and ethnic minority focus found that AUROC fell from 0.737 in 2021 to 0.670 in 2022. That study did not examine whether revalidation corrected the decline for any subgroup.

research_gap: No study compared deployed models with and without scheduled local revalidation on patient outcomes, rates of undetected drift, or cost. Prospective studies should test revalidation intervals, minimum sample sizes, and triggers such as acquisition protocol changes. They should report calibration alongside discrimination and include subgroup results for underserved populations.
underserved_note: Neither of the two studies testing the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. They drew on a Turkish pediatric emergency department dataset and a UK sample of 318 patients. Whether local revalidation detects drift that affects these groups remains untested, and small subgroup sizes may make such detection harder at a single site.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether assigning AI-assisted denial reviews to licensed specialty physicians without denial incentives changes denial accuracy or patient outcomes, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The one endorsing source addresses transparency for end users and does not speak directly to reviewer licensure or financial incentives.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation currently rests on one guidance document whose quoted language concerns tailoring transparency, which offers only indirect support.

The single endorsing source is a principles document that uses "should" language about tailoring transparency to end users. It does not state requirements for reviewer specialty, licensure, or compensation structure. Payers that adopt this recommendation would therefore be relying on the panel's reasoning rather than on a cited standard that addresses conflicted or unqualified reviewers.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI-assisted denial reviews conducted by matched-specialty physicians without denial-linked incentives against reviews by other reviewer types, measuring overturn rates on appeal, time to care, and patient harm. Studies documenting how often AI denials are upheld without substantive reviewer engagement would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Payers cannot tell from this record whether the safeguard would work equally well for groups who may be less able to file appeals after a denial.

bottom_line: Fourteen prospective pilots with real users reported tool performance, safety events, and usability during limited deployment, and several surfaced problems such as falling adoption or unanalyzable exams. No study compared piloting with direct full rollout, so whether piloting prevents population-wide harm has not been tested.

perspectives.view: Two RCTs and nine prospective comparator studies evaluated AI tools inside limited real deployments, and most reported favorable results. These designs compare the tool with usual care rather than comparing a pilot strategy with immediate full rollout. Certainty for the practice is low because of this indirectness, single-site designs, and the possibility that successful pilots are published more often.

Several pilots measured error rates before full rollout. The surgical triage tool had specificity of 0.74, and LLM misclassification accounted for 2 of 19 false-negative cases. iAorta identified 21 of 22 aortic syndrome cases. In one 100-patient pilot, real-time supervisors did not need to stop any consultation, which suggests supervision during a pilot may help contain harm.

Pilots reported workflow findings that earlier testing did not show. In an Israeli emergency department, adoption fell from 68% to 30% and length of stay was 4.9 h in both wings. A staged deployment with over 13,000 consented users identified challenges not apparent in initial testing. In a handheld echo pilot, 71.8% of attempts were analyzable.

One pilot enrolled 50 non-English-speaking patients in China, and another enrolled 120 older adults. A Thai community hospital pilot of 1,375 patients reported no system failure. No pilot reported Medicaid, U.S. safety-net, or low-literacy participants, so pilots conducted elsewhere may miss failures specific to those groups.

FDA draft lifecycle guidance describes a one-month deployment on a patient subset before site-wide use, and CHAI playbooks treat piloting as a requirement for high-risk tools. Both are recommendations rather than binding rules. Only one pilot in this set took place in the United States.

The supplied summaries report no pilot cost, staffing, or time needed to reach a rollout decision. Pilot sizes ranged from 50 to 13,846 patients, which suggests there is no shared standard for scope. The adoption decline in the Israeli pilot suggests pilots may need to run long enough to observe sustained use.

In a 100-patient pilot, safety supervisors watched every AI interaction in real time and patients reported high satisfaction. This design kept a human available during each consultation. The staged deployment enrolled over 13,000 consented users, which indicates participants in that pilot agreed to take part.

research_gap: No study compared sites or units that piloted a tool with those that deployed at full scale, so the effect of piloting on harm, rework, or tool abandonment is unknown. Future studies should also report pilot duration, sample size, stop criteria, the problems found, and the changes made before rollout.
underserved_note: One pilot included 50 non-English-speaking patients in China, and one Thai community hospital pilot reported no system failure. No pilot reported Medicaid, U.S. safety-net, or low-literacy participants. Health systems serving those groups have no direct evidence that pilots at other sites will surface the problems their patients may face, which suggests the pilot itself should include them.

bottom_line: Clinician review changed AI drafts and caught some errors before release across notes, reports, and image contours, but in one trial 15% of summaries still contained errors after editing and over-read, and in one simulation unaided reviewers found about 12% of errors. The studies suggest that review is necessary, while its reliability as a standalone safeguard remains uncertain.

perspectives.view: Four randomized trials and several comparator studies report that review changed AI outputs. Most compare the same draft before and after editing rather than randomizing review itself. Outcomes are error counts or quality scores, not patient harm, and many studies test image contours or teaching feedback. These limits in directness and design suggest low certainty.

Review catches some errors but misses others. In one trial, 26% of plain language summaries had errors on ophthalmologist review and 15% on independent over-read after editing, though none carried severe harm risk. In a simulation, unaided clinicians found about 12% of errors. In one deployment, 5.3% of drafts had serious-risk errors and 14.9% of notes went unedited.

Review effort varies by task. Clinicians corrected 8 of 10 kidney tumor segmentations, with a median correction time of 11 minutes. In a Japanese trial, reviewing drafts shortened summary writing by 59.4 seconds but lengthened referral letters by 94.8 seconds. Among 23,760 ambient notes, edit rates differed by section, specialty, and clinician, which may reflect uneven review fidelity.

Four tests involved non-English documentation and one involved low-literacy leaflets, all in offline or simulated settings. Physician edit burden was 59.0% for Thai-pivot records versus 50.7% for English-pivot records, which suggests review demands may rise for non-English encounters. Clinician revision restored the quality of simplified Chinese consent forms. No test included Medicaid or safety-net settings.

Texas SB 1188 requires practitioners to review all AI-created records, and professional guidance calls for physician approval. No study tests whether such mandates change error rates. Deployment data show that 14.9% and 15.6% of AI notes were signed without edits. This suggests that a signature alone may not document meaningful review, which bears on how compliance is audited.

Review burden may concentrate on abnormal findings. Radiologists accepted 91.7% and 83.2% of AI reports on normal chest films without changes, compared with 52.4% and 37.0% on abnormal films. In a German deployment covering 15,615 discharge letters, senior physician revision counts held at about 1.3 per document, which suggests existing supervision structures may absorb AI drafts.

Radiologist review found that 3 of 50 simplified reports needed correction before patients received them. When five urologists reviewed AI-written biopsy explanations, all five were comfortable sharing only 40% of the reports, and at least one flagged severe harm concern in 20%. These findings suggest that patients may be protected when a clinician checks content before release.

research_gap: No trial randomizes clinical documents to clinician review versus no review and measures downstream patient harm. Studies have not measured how review accuracy changes with reviewer experience, fatigue, or document volume at scale. None tests aids that direct reviewer attention to likely errors, or audits that separate a signature from actual review.
underserved_note: Four tests included non-English documentation (Thai, Chinese, and European languages), and one included low-literacy patient leaflets. All five were offline or simulated. No test reported Medicaid or safety-net populations, and most real-deployment studies did not report patient demographics. The effectiveness and burden of review in these settings, where edit demands may be higher, remain untested.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether documenting autonomy level, oversight roles, intervention points, and the human-AI interface changes oversight or patient outcomes, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. Support for R165 rests on 23 endorsing sources, mostly guidance, frameworks, and commentary, that agree the practice is expected.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsements show consistent expert agreement, but agreement among guidance documents and editorials is not an estimate of effect.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions asks sponsors to explain the intended degree of automation, and one principles document states that AI-influenced clinical decisions must include specified qualified human intervention points. These sources suggest documentation may already be expected for regulated devices, though the supplied sources do not show that documentation improves oversight.

No supplied study measures how often undefined intervention points lead to missed errors or harm. The size of the problem, and whether written oversight roles catch errors before they reach patients, remain unmeasured in this evidence set.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI deployments with and without documented autonomy levels and intervention points, measuring whether clinicians intervene at the specified points, how often errors are caught before reaching patients, and how much staff time the documentation and inventory upkeep require.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether documented oversight roles work in settings with thinner staffing or where patients rely more on AI-mediated communication.

bottom_line: Two studies support parts of this practice: in a real deployment, a specialist interpreted 88.1% of encounters the AI could not grade, and in a vignette survey, clinician presence raised the probability of choosing an AI visit by 18.4%. No study tested review requested by a patient or caregiver, so the evidence for the recommendation as written is indirect.

perspectives.view: Neither study tests the recommendation as worded. The screening study sent AI-ungradable encounters to a human reader automatically rather than at patient request. The survey measured stated choices in hypothetical vignettes. Both designs start at low certainty, and indirectness lowers certainty to very low.

AI returned ungradable results in 36.5% of 1,222 screening encounters, and a specialist interpreted 88.1% of those. This suggests a human fallback can resolve results that AI alone leaves open. The study did not report whether human review caught AI outputs that were wrong, which is the hazard this recommendation targets.

The screening study built fallback into a live workflow. Adjudicated consensus found 77.7% of AI-ungradable encounters interpretable, lower than the 88.1% reported by a single reader, and this gap may reflect variation between readers. No study described how patients would request review through portals, phone lines, or other channels.

The AI could not grade about one in three encounters in the screening deployment. At that rate, a health system would need specialist reading capacity for a large share of volume. The study did not report reader time or cost. No study estimated how many review requests patients would make.

Among 3,000 survey respondents, clinician presence raised the probability of choosing an AI visit by 18.4% (95% CI, 17.3%-19.5%). This suggests patients may value human involvement when AI is part of their care. The result reflects hypothetical choices, and no study asked patients whether they could actually reach a clinician when they wanted one.

research_gap: No study compared offering patient- or caregiver-requested clinician review with not offering it. Such a study would need to measure how often patients use the option, time to human contact, AI errors detected and corrected, patient trust, and staffing cost in real deployments across several care settings.
underserved_note: Neither study reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and both were conducted in the United States. Patients facing language or literacy barriers may have more difficulty finding and using a request channel. The current evidence cannot show whether human fallback works for these groups.

bottom_line: Six simulated studies tested clinician review of AI-drafted patient messages, and their results conflict: review raised rated validity and empathy in some, while physicians missed most embedded errors in another. No study measured patient harm in live use, so single-clinician review may not reliably stop unsafe messages.
