perspectives.view: All six tests are level 4 vignette or replay studies in offline settings. Sample sizes ranged from 8 presentations to 1200 answers. Two studies support the practice, one points against it, and three are mixed. Certainty starts low and drops to very low because the settings are indirect, the findings are inconsistent, and most samples are small.

Each erroneous draft was missed by 13 to 15 of 20 physicians, and only one physician caught all four errors. Expert-edited drafts carried 2% high-risk incorrect content versus 0% for expert-written replies. A single reader missed 12.4% of deficiencies, and a second reader reduced misses to 0.6%. Single review may let errors reach patients.

Between 35% and 45% of physicians submitted erroneous drafts unedited, which suggests that reviewers may accept what the draft says. In a separate test, physicians judged 72.50% of drafts acceptable without changes, and 22 of 80 needed edits before they were safe to send. No study measured review fidelity in real workflows.

Physician edits to discharge instructions improved accuracy but lowered objective readability scores. This trade-off may matter for patients with low literacy. A Japanese study found that physician-revised drafts scored higher on validity and empathy. That study covers non-English communication, but it does not include U.S. patients with limited English proficiency.

California AB 3030 states that the requirements of its subdivision (a) do not apply when a licensed or certified provider reads and reviews an AI-generated communication. The supplied excerpt does not say how thorough that review must be. The CHAI excerpt concerns model escrow rather than clinician review, so it offers no direct support for this recommendation.

Dual-reader review reduced the average miss rate from 12.4% to 0.6%, and triple review detected every deficiency. Each added reader would add clinician time per message. None of the six studies reported review time or staffing cost, so the burden at scale cannot be estimated from this evidence.

In one test, expert-edited drafts were rated higher on quality and empathy than expert-written replies but performed worse on most safety metrics. This suggests that warmer wording and accurate content may not travel together. A message that reads well after clinician approval may still contain errors that a patient cannot detect.

research_gap: No study tested clinician review in a live portal deployment with patient harm, near misses, or clinician time as outcomes. No study compared single review with dual review, or with tiered edit requirements, inside real workflows. Training interventions for reviewers also remain untested.
underserved_note: One test included non-English communication (Japan), and none included Medicaid, safety-net, U.S. limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The finding that physician edits reduced readability suggests that review could make messages harder for low-literacy patients to use, and that possibility has not been studied in those groups.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether risk-proportional human oversight, or routing tools without human-in-the-loop design to full review, reduces harm from AI use in health care. The recommendation rests on 32 endorsing sources; the 12 quoted here are frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries, and no hazard studies were supplied.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about effect cannot be rated when no comparative or observational data exist. The endorsements reflect expert agreement, which may guide priorities but does not estimate benefit, harm, or the size of either.

The endorsing sources include NIST AI 600-1, which states that generative AI use may warrant added human review, and a commentary on the EU AI Act proposing oversight proportionate to potential patient harm. Among the 12 endorsements quoted here, the one rated "must", from CHAI playbooks, addresses a data acquisition register rather than oversight tiers.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks organizations to weigh fairness and bias when setting the balance of human judgment and AI decisions. The Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use call for culturally and linguistically appropriate disclosure. No supplied study examines whether oversight tiers perform differently across patient groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare risk-tiered oversight with uniform review or no structured review, measuring caught errors, patient harm, reviewer workload, and time to deployment. Evaluations should also test how governance committees assign risk tiers and how consistently tools lacking human-in-the-loop design are identified and routed.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether risk tiers set elsewhere would capture harms specific to their patients.

bottom_line: Two offline simulation studies suggest that restricting an agent to permitted tools may sharply reduce unauthorized actions, with one reporting a drop from 56–60% of adversarial trials to 0%. No study tested isolated execution environments, dry-run previews, or per-action audit logs, and none measured effects in live clinical use.

perspectives.view: Both studies are level 4 simulations with no patient outcomes, so directness is low. Each tests only the allow-list or curated-tool component of the bundle. The 0% rate (95% CI 0.00 to 0.07) rests on 50 trials per condition, which limits precision. Consistency in direction is favorable, but certainty remains very low.

Deterministic middleware blocked every unauthorized tool call in adversarial trials across two models, which suggests enforcement outside the model may catch errors that prompting alone misses. A curated 20-tool agent also scored higher on a safety rubric. Neither study shows whether audit logs or dry-run previews help staff detect or reverse harmful actions.

The curated-tool agent answered 375 clinician-authored questions across 41 cases with embedding recall of 0.877 and 0.803, outperforming broader-tool agents (p<0.05). This suggests tool restriction may not cost answer quality. Both tests ran offline, so workflow burden, latency, and fidelity of the controls in production systems are unmeasured.

Neither study reported testing with Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One study did not report its setting, and the other drew on international adversarial scenarios. The evidence therefore cannot show whether these controls perform equally across patient groups.

research_gap: No study has tested isolated execution environments, dry-run previews of high-impact actions, or per-action audit logs, and no study has evaluated any part of the bundle in live clinical deployment. Prospective studies should measure unauthorized-action rates, time to detect and trace errors from logs, staff burden of reviewing previews, and patient-level harms.
underserved_note: Neither test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that the controls work as intended for their patients.

bottom_line: Seven small offline or simulated studies suggest that letting clinicians edit, reject, or reweight AI outputs may improve output accuracy and catch some model errors, but no study tested a defined override rule or a logged disagreement process in live care. The certainty that the full practice improves patient outcomes is very low.

perspectives.view: All seven tests are level 4 or 5 and offline or simulated. Patient-level samples ranged from 12 plans to 29 patients, one vignette study enrolled 22 physicians, one benchmark used 11,748 images, and one study did not report sample size. Each favored human correction, but imprecision, indirectness, and no test of required-override rules or logging support a very low rating.

Surgeons rejected AI suggestions in 9 of 13 false-positive cases, which means 4 errors passed through review. The contestable interface caught only a portion of model errors. These results suggest override access intercepts some errors but not all, and no study measured whether corrected outputs changed harm reaching patients.

Manual editing raised Dice agreement to 0.84 from 0.60 and 0.55, and raised prostate contours to 0.86 from 0.82. Adjustable weights were rated 4.18 versus 3.41 for static weights. One hazard study found readers had difficulty correcting slice-level annotations, which suggests interface design affects whether override is usable. No study reported editing time or workload.

A European pathology society paper reads the EU AI Act as requiring manual override mechanisms, and the CHAI guide lists user override as a must. These endorsements set expectations for vendors and purchasers, but none of the supplied studies tests whether meeting them changes outcomes.

Five tests were run in the United Kingdom, Italy, Russia, Japan, and a mixed Israel, USA, and Canada physician sample, and two did not report setting. None described patient insurance, language, or literacy, so the evidence cannot show whether override tools perform equally across populations.

Every test gave the correction power to clinicians or experts. No study examined whether patients could contest an AI output or learn that a clinician had overridden one, so the evidence says nothing about patient trust or access to a human reviewer.

research_gap: No study has tested a defined threshold for when override is required, a logged disagreement workflow, or the downstream use of override logs, and none has measured patient outcomes, clinician time burden, or override rates in live clinical deployment.
underserved_note: No test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so whether override and contest mechanisms work for these patients and the clinicians serving them remains unknown.

bottom_line: Studies comparing AI output alone with AI output after clinician review, mostly in imaging, radiotherapy contouring, and screening, report fewer false positives and better agreement after review, but most measure surrogate outcomes and none tests a verification requirement as a policy. In a real-deployment study of generative AI in Kenya, clinicians did not modify 62% of AI-drafted documentation and 67 harmful recommendations reached the final record, which suggests that requiring verification may not ensure it occurs.

perspectives.view: Of 25 listed tests, one is an RCT, and it reports that clinicians disagreed with 20.7% of electronic AKI diagnoses rather than reporting patient outcomes. Most other studies are descriptive or replay designs that measure PPV or contour overlap. Results agree for imaging and contouring but diverge for generative AI and teledermatology, and indirectness lowers certainty to low.

Specialist overread raised PPV from 47.7% to 95.5% with sensitivity unchanged, and radiologists reported only one of 381 AI false positives. Review can also remove true findings, as teledermatology review lowered sensitivity from 82.5% to 75.3%. In Kenya, 67 harmful LLM recommendations reached final documentation, and residents detected hallucinations with 55% accuracy.

Verification fidelity varied in real workflows, as clinicians did not modify LLM-drafted documentation in 62% of encounters, and interviewed staff endorsed verification but enacted it unevenly. A simulated co-pilot mode reported better detection of drug-related problems than an autonomous LLM, which suggests that the design of the review step may matter as much as the rule requiring it.

Readers rejected 16.8 false CAD markings per scan, expert chart review removed 208 of 388 model-flagged patients from outreach, and pathologists reviewed 1733 alerted benign cases, of which 128 changed, so review adds workload. Editing AI contours took 12.3 minutes versus 25.0 minutes for manual contouring, which suggests review may still save time compared with working without AI.

One deployment in Puerto Rico served a racial and ethnic minority population, and pathologist review resolved all 17 false-positive validation alerts. The Kenyan study, set in a lower-resource health system, found that verification often did not happen. No test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

One case report describes a team that judged an AI pneumothorax alert inconsistent with the clinical picture, excluded it by CT, and avoided an unneeded procedure. In a simulation, most of 38 intensivists rejected unsafe AI advice and many sought senior help. A hazard report notes that erroneous AI care plans can look reasonable, so cursory review may leave patients exposed.

research_gap: No study compares units with and without a formal verification requirement, and few measure patient outcomes such as treatment errors or harm. Studies of generative AI workflows could measure how often clinicians catch seeded errors, the time review adds, and whether review design, such as source links, checklists, or attestation prompts, changes detection rates.
underserved_note: No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One test took place in Puerto Rico with a racial and ethnic minority focus, and one took place in Kenya, where verification frequently failed. Health systems serving these populations therefore cannot assume that verification performs as reported in the imaging and contouring studies.

bottom_line: Twenty-one studies tested interface cues, prompts, or presentation choices meant to promote clinician scrutiny of AI outputs, and results varied by design, with most studies favorable, five null or mixed, and one trial in which explanations failed to reduce and sometimes worsened the effect of misleading AI. Twenty of the studies were offline or simulated, and the one real-deployment study bundled missing-information cues with other workflow changes, so the effect of any specific cue in live care remains uncertain.

perspectives.view: Twenty of 21 tests ran offline or in simulation, many with fewer than 25 clinicians, and the one real deployment used a pre-post design without a comparator. Results were inconsistent across cue types. A behavioral nudge raised reasoning scores by 7.6 points, while a prompt to judge the AI list showed no accuracy gain. These features suggest low certainty.

A box outlining the suspicious region lowered false negatives from incorrect AI from 33.0% to 20.7%, and heatmaps lowered automation bias (aOR 0.56) without eliminating it. With explanations, only 52% of clinicians overrode a wrong recommendation, and in one trial explanations did not blunt misleading AI. The effect of a cue on harm appears to depend on its design.

Disagreeing with the model took a median 84 seconds versus 38 seconds for agreeing, and an interactive coding interface lengthened coding time slightly. A disagreement-guided display cut simulated burden by 4.8% but raised it 12.04% when the false-positive rate reached 0.10. Highlighting error-prone spans reached a positive predictive value of 56.3% and was never tested with clinicians.

The only test tagged as involving a limited English or non-English population enrolled nine clinical coders in China, who showed higher recall and precision with an interactive interface than with black-box predictions. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence says little about how these cues perform in under-resourced settings.

FDA draft guidance asks manufacturers to describe how configurable elements affect user decisions. In one trial, chain-of-thought output produced more selective adherence than a differential diagnosis list, and in another, suppressing outputs in high-risk zones was estimated to cut automation bias by 41.7%. These findings suggest that presentation settings may warrant documentation and validation.

In the single real deployment, report completeness rose (adjusted difference 1.95 points), but adopters volunteered and the cues were one part of a bundle. Concurrent AI reading saved 33.6 seconds per case with no loss in diagnostic performance compared with second reading. Neither study reports the cost or staffing figures needed to plan adoption across a health system.

In a simulation with a standard editable draft interface, physicians submitted 35% to 45% of erroneous drafts without edits. No supplied study tested whether cues in patient-portal reply drafts reduce the number of errors that reach patients. Patients therefore have little direct evidence that these designs protect the messages they receive.

research_gap: Health systems need prospective trials in live clinical workflows that test single, well-defined cues against usual interfaces. These trials should measure patient-level errors and harms, clinician time, and whether effects persist as clinicians become familiar with the cues. They should also compare cue designs directly, since some explanation formats appear to help and others appear to hurt.
underserved_note: One test was tagged as involving a limited English or non-English population, but it was a small vignette simulation with nine clinical coders in China rather than a test with patients. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore cannot show whether these cues work for clinicians in under-resourced settings or protect the patients those settings serve.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring vendors to disclose unconfirmed agent actions, or to acknowledge the deployer's oversight authority in contract, reduces hidden autonomous functionality or preserves deployer control. The recommendation currently rests on a single governance framework that uses "should" language.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains no studies that test the practice and no studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no comparative or observational data exist. The recommendation therefore reflects expert consensus from one source rather than measured effects on vendor behavior, deployer control, or patient outcomes.

The only endorsement comes from the CHAI governance playbooks, which advise that vendors should disclose which actions an agent can take without confirmation and which require human approval. This is voluntary framework guidance and carries no enforcement mechanism. The contractual acknowledgment of oversight authority does not appear in the quoted endorsement text and has no cited source of its own.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare contracts with and without autonomy-scope disclosure and oversight clauses. Such studies would measure whether disclosed action lists match observed agent behavior in production, how often undisclosed autonomous actions occur, and whether deployers use the contractual authority to pause or modify agents. Descriptive audits of current vendor disclosures would also establish whether the hazard occurs and how often.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no data on whether disclosure requirements change vendor practices in their settings, where bargaining power in contract negotiations and staff capacity to review disclosures may differ from larger systems.

bottom_line: Two small offline or simulated studies suggest that human checkpoints may reduce quality and safety problems compared with fully autonomous AI workflows, and in one study the checkpointed workflow took 245 minutes versus about 68 minutes. No study tested stepwise reduction of oversight after demonstrated performance, and no study took place in live clinical care.

perspectives.view: Both tests are level 4 and offline or simulated. One reports no numbers. The other involved a single expert, a single clinical topic, and one development run. Imprecision, indirectness, and risk of bias each lower certainty to very low. Neither study examined the stepwise reduction of oversight that the recommendation proposes.

In the comparative test, critics within the autonomous 14-agent system flagged 17 issues, 9 of them high severity. The checkpointed version had 19 human interventions, and external review found none of the most serious class of safety errors. In a separate benchmark, browser agents submitted deficient forms, although this shows the hazard exists rather than that checkpoints fix it.

In one study the fully autonomous workflow finished in about 68 minutes and the checkpointed workflow took 245 minutes, which suggests checkpoints may add reviewer time. A second study reported gains in coding precision, turnaround time, and audit readiness over manual and fully automated pipelines, but it gave no figures that would allow the burden to be estimated.

A single run in which one expert made 19 interventions and took roughly 3.6 times the autonomous run time gives a rough sense of staffing cost. It cannot support a projection of labor needs at scale. The studies did not measure how often checkpoints would fire in routine operations or who would staff them.

Neither test reported patient populations, languages, or literacy levels. A regulatory discussion paper asks whether escalation and refusal behaviors hold across dialects and lower health literacy, but no study examined whether checkpoints perform equally across these groups.

research_gap: No study has tested checkpoints in live clinical deployment, measured harm reaching patients, or evaluated criteria for reducing human oversight after an agent shows sustained performance. Comparative studies with adequate sample sizes, defined lists of high-consequence actions, and reported reviewer burden would address these gaps.
underserved_note: Neither test included or reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence cannot show whether checkpoint designs protect these patients as well as others.

bottom_line: Sixteen studies test whether clinicians should read every case regardless of AI triage, and their results split: real-deployment studies show human readers catching AI misses, while several simulations report that skipping low-priority cases kept sensitivity similar and cut workload. The evidence supports human review of AI-negative cases as a way to catch misses, but it does not show that reviewing every case outperforms well-validated partial review in patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Of 16 studies, 9 favor the practice, 4 oppose it, and 3 are mixed. Three prospective real-deployment studies favor it, but none randomized readers or measured patient outcomes. Eleven studies are offline or simulated, and five come from real deployment. One study defined false negatives by the over-read itself. Inconsistency and indirectness lower certainty to low.

Radiologists diagnosed all 45 hemorrhages the AI missed, and review of lesions the AI deemed benign found four cancers. Review does not guarantee a catch. Readers who kept AI results missed 33.0% of AI-false-negative cases versus 2.7% without AI, and reviewers corrected 3% to 30% of AI misses for macular degeneration.

Simulations report that prescreening cut workload by 85.2% with higher specificity. A 50% worklist cut kept sensitivity noninferior (difference 0.8%). Reading time fell from 164 to 143 seconds. In a fracture study, AI triage raised false negatives for every reader subgroup except trainees, so the effect may depend on who reads.

The authors of an Australian band-pass study, where AI made final calls on high and low scores, reported that the lack of a human decision-maker poses adoption challenges. This suggests that current oversight expectations favor human review, even where simulated accuracy was similar to standard reading.

In Thailand, specialist over-reading found 5 missed referrals among 444 AI-negative cases, and 4 of those 5 patients attended tertiary care after being contacted. In Norway, one prematurely discharged patient was recalled for treatment after the radiologist's report. These cases suggest that human review gives patients a route back to care.

No test of the practice reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies include a Puerto Rico pathology deployment, where AI called nine cancer slides benign, and a Medicaid message-triage study, where no autonomous benchmark was met. These studies show the hazard exists in these groups but do not test the safeguard.

research_gap: No study randomized sites or readers to universal review versus AI-triaged partial review with patient outcomes such as delayed diagnosis or harm as endpoints. Studies are also needed that measure automation bias during universal review and that report results by reader experience.
underserved_note: None of the 16 studies testing the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Only hazard studies touched these groups, so it is unknown whether universal review catches AI misses at the same rate in safety-net settings.

bottom_line: Seven studies suggest that keeping clinicians in charge of AI-supported decisions may improve diagnostic accuracy and plan stability, but only one was a prospective comparison in real care, and none measured patient outcomes such as harm or mortality. Many sources, including FDA draft guidance, endorse the recommendation, while the evidence from tests of the practice is of very low certainty.

perspectives.view: One prospective study in Ukraine (n=728) found 6-month diagnosis and treatment-plan changes of 14.73% with tumor board plus AI, 24.3% with AI alone, and 28.08% with tumor board alone. The other tests are simulations, record replays, or one case report. Plan change is a surrogate outcome, so certainty is very low.

In a neurosurgical replay of 86 scans, clinician-controlled review reached 94% accuracy and 98% sensitivity, above model-only baselines. A case report describes clinicians overriding a false-positive alert. A hazard study found 46.3% of AI contours needed major revision, which shows the failure mode exists but does not show that retained authority catches it.

A replay of 250,000 decision records found care teams better addressed patient needs in 77% of divergent overrides. In a vignette study of 276 clinicians, physicians who used AI to verify their work received higher peer skill ratings (4.99 vs 3.79) than those who relied on it primarily, but their ratings stayed below the control condition.

The 250,000-record replay drew on a Medicaid population, and the Ukrainian deployment included rural patients. No test enrolled safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Two hazard studies involving limited English or non-English populations found LLM errors in imaging cases and kidney diet plans, but neither tested whether clinician authority prevents those errors.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software states that a tool should not replace standard-of-care diagnosis and should be applied jointly with clinician judgment. In a vignette study of 331 participants, following AI advice reduced blame directed at the physician (p < 0.001), which suggests that perceived accountability may shift away from clinicians who defer to AI.

In a vignette study of 2,790 participants in China, care-seeking intention fell as AI involvement rose, from β=-0.682 at low intensity to β=-1.267 at high intensity, with the largest drop when the doctor deferred fully to AI. Visible clinician authority may matter to patient trust, although vignettes may not predict real behavior.

research_gap: No randomized or controlled deployment study has compared retained clinician authority with more autonomous AI use on patient outcomes such as diagnostic error, harm, or mortality. No study has tested whether labeling AI tools as adjuncts changes clinician behavior or patient understanding. No study has measured the time, staffing, or cost burden of clinician review at scale.
underserved_note: One test, a retrospective replay of 250,000 decision records, drew on a Medicaid population, and the Ukrainian deployment included rural patients. No test of the practice included safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore cannot show whether clinician override works as well in settings where language barriers or thin staffing may limit review.

bottom_line: No study tests whether verifying licensure, role, or expertise before allowing use of AI outputs reduces misinterpretation or harm. Three offline hazard studies found that less experienced users deferred more to AI or performed worse with it than senior clinicians or coders, which suggests the hazard is real but does not show that credential restrictions correct it.

perspectives.view: No study compares restricted and unrestricted user access, so certainty for the practice is rated as no direct evidence. The three hazard studies are simulations or retrospective replays from three countries. Two used 9 coders and 10 readers, and one enrolled 1,096 participants. Their findings on expertise point the same way, but they describe the problem rather than test the safeguard.

After misleading LLM output, residents switched to an incorrect diagnosis in 60.6% of cases, compared with 32.4% for thoracic radiologists (p = .009). Medical students also deferred to AI more than primary care physicians did. These findings suggest that automation bias may be larger among trainees, although none of the studies measured patient outcomes.

In a coding simulation, intern coders working with AI stayed below AI-only performance, while senior coders working with AI reached 0.95 recall and 0.95 precision. This suggests that the value of human review may depend on reviewer skill. No study examined how role-based access controls perform in live workflows or how often users bypass them.

FDA draft guidance asks manufacturers to list the qualifications or clinical role of intended output interpreters, and a European pathology society paper reads the EU AI Act as requiring qualified supervision. These sources set labeling and deployer expectations. They do not supply evidence that enforcing those expectations changes outcomes.

In the coding study, intern coders working with AI stayed below AI-only performance, while senior coders working with AI reached 0.95 recall and 0.95 precision. If that pattern holds, restricting interpretation to senior personnel may shift workload toward a smaller and costlier group. No study reports staffing, cost, or throughput effects of such restrictions.

One hazard study was conducted with coders in China in a non-English setting. No study tested the practice in Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy settings. Restricting AI use to specialists could affect who receives AI-supported care in settings with few specialists, but no study has measured this.

research_gap: Prospective studies should compare outcomes when AI output interpretation is restricted by credential or role with outcomes when it is open to all clinicians, measuring diagnostic errors, patient harm, and access delays. Studies should also test whether training or competency checks for non-specialists can close the performance gap seen in the hazard studies.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. One hazard study involved a non-English coding setting in China, and none included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The effect of credential restrictions on care access in resource-limited settings therefore remains unknown.

bottom_line: Four simulation or replay studies show that pre-deployment tests of whether clinicians catch incorrect AI outputs can be run and produce usable detection rates, but none tests whether doing such an assessment reduces harm after deployment. Certainty for the practice itself is very low, while 82 hazard studies document that users sometimes accept incorrect outputs.

perspectives.view: All four tests are level 4 offline studies in single countries, covering 38 intensivists, 99 biopsies, 1142 reader-case pairs, and 86 OCT scans. Three support the practice and one is mixed. They measure detection during the assessment, not the effect of assessing on later patient outcomes, so indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

In one replay study, surgeons rejected 9 of 13 AI false positives, yet 4 errors were still confirmed. Hazard studies show accuracy falling from 84.9% to 73.3% with flawed LLM advice, and resistance to incorrect answers falling from 92% to 34.8% when citations appeared. Assessments that inject known errors may reveal these failure modes before patients are exposed.

Detection varies with user experience. In one simulation, trainees reached 0% accuracy when the AI was wrong versus 66.67% for trained clinicians, and confidence stayed high regardless. Readers were persuaded by correct AI output in only 30% to 45% of cases, which suggests assessments may need to measure algorithm aversion as well as overreliance across the intended users.

None of the four tests reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. One trial in China that enrolled non-English-speaking, low-literacy, low-income, and rural patients found no direct adoption of LLM content in notes (F1 0.57), but that trial examines the hazard and does not test the assessment practice.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes overreliance arising from information gaps, and the CHAI and FUTURE-AI frameworks call for evaluating automation bias and uncertainty aversion during usability testing. These sources recommend assessment without citing a trial showing that pre-deployment assessment changes outcomes, so the recommendation rests on consensus.

The tests used small rater panels, such as 5 neurosurgeons scoring 86 scans and 38 intensivists in simulation, which suggests a pre-deployment detection study can be run with modest staffing. None of the studies reported cost, staff time, or how often the assessment should be repeated after model updates.

In the intensivist simulation, many clinicians who rejected unsafe recommendations sought senior assistance, while a few accepted them after nurse influence. In Kenya, a minority of frontline workers reported deferring diagnosis to the AI. These findings suggest assessments may need to examine team dynamics and escalation paths, because patients depend on a person who questions the output.

research_gap: No study compares deployments that underwent a pre-deployment assessment of automation bias with deployments that did not, and none follows whether detection rates measured in simulation predict acceptance of AI errors in live care. Prospective studies with patient outcomes, across settings and levels of user experience, would address this gap.
underserved_note: None of the four tests of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and all were offline studies with clinician raters in the United Kingdom, Norway, the United States, and Russia. Detection rates from these settings may not transfer to under-resourced sites where staffing, training, and time pressure differ.

bottom_line: One small simulated trial in 72 surgical residents found that structured training on how to query and check a large language model raised decision quality scores (16.2 vs 13.5), and a pre-post study of 139 medical students found higher self-rated evaluation skill that was not objectively measured. No study tested training on override, escalation, or intervention points in agentic workflows, and none measured patient outcomes in practice.

perspectives.view: Two studies test training. The randomized trial is small, simulated, and uses a decision-quality score rather than patient outcomes. The pre-post study has no comparator and measures self-perception. Indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low. Neither study addresses override, escalation, or agentic workflows, which make up much of the recommendation.

Two hazard studies show that the skill gap exists. Medical students scored 0.41 of 3 on verifying AI outputs. A failure mode analysis of 86 modes ranked human error first and inadequate training second among high-risk modes. In the trial, trained residents solicited more evidence per case (3.0 vs 0.7), which may reflect checking behavior that intercepts errors.

Both tests took place offline with trainees, so fidelity and retention in live clinical workflows remain unmeasured. The trial attributes 88% of the improvement to changes in how residents interacted with the model. This suggests that training on the interaction process may carry the effect. Neither study reported training time or burden.

Both tests used trainees and simulated tasks, one in Taiwan and one in an unreported setting, and neither described the patient populations represented. No study examined whether trained clinicians detect AI errors in documentation or advice for patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

research_gap: Trials in practicing clinicians within live workflows should test whether training on verification, override, escalation, and agentic intervention points reduces errors that reach patients. These trials should use objective verification measures, follow users long enough to assess retention, and report training time and cost.
underserved_note: Neither test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and both used simulated tasks with trainees. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume the reported gains will transfer and would need to evaluate training effects locally.

bottom_line: Workflow studies of AI in clinical use often report results that differ from standalone model metrics, and human-AI teams sometimes perform better and sometimes worse than the model alone. No study tests whether requiring in-workflow evaluation before deployment changes purchasing decisions or patient outcomes, so the evidence supports the reasoning behind the practice more than the practice itself.

perspectives.view: Three randomized trials and many comparative deployment studies measured clinician performance with AI in routine work. Swedish screening sensitivity rose from 73.8% to 80.5%, while chest radiograph readers showed no accuracy gain. Certainty is low because these studies measure AI effects rather than the evaluation practice, and their designs and outcomes differ.

Standalone AI detected 95.8% of micrometastases, but AI-assisted pathologists reached 80.0%. Standalone fracture sensitivity was 93.5%, compared with 90.0% for AI-assisted radiologists. A wrong-eye injection occurred despite correct AI warnings. These cases suggest that failures can arise at the handoff between AI and clinician, which standalone testing may not reveal.

Geometric segmentation metrics correlated weakly with physician correction times for most organs, and silent alert simulations predicted postimplementation performance poorly. AI raised cancer detection among generalist radiologists but not specialists, and CADe gains shrank later in the day. These findings suggest that local workflow and user mix shape results.

AI shortened sonography exams and coding time, and cut musculoskeletal reading time from 34 seconds to about 21 to 25 seconds without changing accuracy. AI-assisted mammography added 4-6% reading workload, and an AI triage tool did not shorten transfer decisions. No study measured the staffing cost of conducting local workflow evaluation.

One pathology deployment in Puerto Rico reported a 1.8% diagnostic revision rate after AI second review, and one Hungarian screening study included rural sites. No workflow evaluation reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. As a result, the effect of AI on clinicians who serve these patients has not been measured.

In simulated studies, physicians using large language models scored 11.5 to 21.3 percentage points lower than the model alone and often left out useful AI recommendations. For patients, this suggests that a tool's published accuracy may not describe the care they receive from a clinician using it.

research_gap: No study compares deployment decisions or patient outcomes between sites that evaluated AI in their own workflow and sites that relied on vendor standalone metrics. Future studies should report how in-workflow results vary with user experience, fatigue, and patient population, and should measure what local evaluation costs.
underserved_note: One test focused on a racial and ethnic minority population in Puerto Rico and one included rural sites, but none reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no direct evidence that published human-AI team results apply to their clinicians and workflows.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether written non-retaliation commitments increase reporting of AI concerns or reduce coerced use of unsafe AI, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on one governance framework and one clinical commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The two endorsements, a CHAI governance playbook and an emergency medicine commentary, are expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply a certainty rating for an effect, so the effect of this practice on reporting or harm remains unmeasured.

The recommendation assumes that fear of retaliation suppresses reports of AI errors and that some staff feel pressed to use tools they judge unsafe. No supplied study measures how often either occurs, and none shows that a written commitment changes staff behavior or brings errors to light before they reach patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that first measure how often staff withhold AI safety concerns or use AI they consider unsafe, and then compare reporting volume, report quality, and downstream patient harm between organizations or units with and without written non-retaliation commitments. Such studies should also record whether the commitments are enforced when staff invoke them.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these populations cannot tell from this evidence whether the commitment affects the safety of AI used in their care.

bottom_line: One uncontrolled before-and-after study in Tanzania and Rwanda logged clinician rejections of algorithm diagnoses, used the stated reasons to adapt the algorithm, and saw acceptance improve for some diagnoses. The evidence that monitoring overrides and reliance prevents unsafe drift is of very low certainty, and no study measured patient outcomes from the practice.

perspectives.view: Only one study tests the practice, and it used a pre-post design without a comparator across 27,593 consultations. For children aged 2 months to 14 years, acceptance was 94.1% in Tanzania and 67.2% in Rwanda, and adaptations improved acceptance for some diagnoses. Acceptance is a surrogate outcome, and the lack of a control group keeps certainty very low.

The hazard studies suggest that reliance problems can persist after deployment. In a cluster trial, clinicians engaged with 29.8% of ECG alerts, and high engagement was associated with higher diagnostic yield (22.3% vs 5.0%). In Brazil, near-miss potassium prescriptions stayed at a median of 27.4%. These studies show the problem exists but do not show that logging catches it.

The Tanzania and Rwanda deployment suggests that rejection logging combined with clinician interviews can feed back into algorithm changes during routine care. The study does not report the staff time spent reviewing logs or how often anomalies were flagged. The fidelity and burden of this approach in other workflows therefore remain unknown.

The single test ran in Tanzania and Rwanda, and its study populations were not coded as low-literacy or limited English proficiency. A trial in China that did enroll low-income, rural, low-literacy, and non-English-speaking patients found no direct copying of LLM text into notes (F1 score 0.57). That trial describes reliance but does not test monitoring.

The endorsements come from frameworks and commentaries. They include NIST AI 600-1, CHAI, FUTURE-AI, and an analysis of EU AI Act and MDR post-market duties that calls for recording each confirmation or override. CHAI also warns that vendor model updates may occur silently. None of these sources reports tested outcomes of a logging requirement.

The one test captured rejections across 27,593 consultations in two countries, which suggests that logging at this volume is possible within a deployed tool. No study reports the cost, the staffing needed to review logs, or the rate of false alarms. One commentary warns that false alarms could prompt unnecessary interventions.

research_gap: No controlled study has tested whether monitoring overrides, reliance patterns, and workarounds detects drift earlier or reduces patient harm compared with usual oversight. Controlled trials or interrupted time series should measure anomaly detection rates, false alarms, reviewer workload, and downstream clinical outcomes, and they should include safety-net settings in the United States.
underserved_note: The single test of the practice, conducted in Tanzania and Rwanda, did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Only a hazard study in China enrolled low-literacy, non-English-speaking, low-income, and rural patients. Whether override monitoring works for these groups in health systems in the United States has not been tested.

bottom_line: Nine studies, all offline or simulated and most with small samples, suggest that expert feedback during development may improve the concordance, relevance, and safety review of specialized AI tools. No study measured patient outcomes in live care, so the recommendation rests mainly on professional consensus and one Utah statute.

perspectives.view: Seven level 4 and two level 5 studies all favor expert involvement, so the direction of findings is consistent. Every study was offline or simulated. Samples ranged from one development run to 516 social media posts, and none compared patient outcomes. Indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

A fully automated algorithm build produced 17 issues, 9 high priority, while an expert-governed build needed no mandatory safety corrections. Human judgment remained necessary to detect subtle reasoning failures, and expert oversight identified data bias and leakage. A trial in which a data-tuned model omitted diagnoses in 30.0% of cases shows the hazard but did not test expert review.

Pathologist-in-loop fine-tuning raised agreement from 81.8% to 96.4% (κ 0.62 to 0.91), and tumor board feedback raised semantic similarity from 0.71 to 0.76. Expert-authored prompt framing reached 0.562 macro F1 versus 0.395 for moderation APIs. These gains were measured offline, and fidelity in routine development workflows remains unknown.

Expert time is the main cost. The fully automated algorithm build ran 3.6 times faster than the expert-governed build, and automated screening reduced but did not replace expert review burden. No study reported staff hours, cost, or the number of experts needed per tool, so budgeting will depend on local estimates.

Two tests took place in non-English settings, a Korean chatbot pilot with 15 graduate students and an Italian extraction study. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users. The trial documenting the hazard included rural, low-income, and low-literacy patients in China, which suggests these groups face the problem the practice targets.

In the only test with end users, 13 of 15 participants preferred a mental health chatbot after expert-guided enhancement, and ratings rose from 5.40 to 7.63. Participants were graduate students rather than patients, so the result says little about whether people in distress would trust such tools or could reach a human when needed.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbots to be developed and monitored consistent with clinical best practices, and NIST AI 600-1 recommends human moderation of generated content. Neither source defines who qualifies as an expert or what a review must document. None of the supplied studies tests compliance with these provisions.

research_gap: No study compared expert involvement with its absence in a live clinical deployment that measured patient outcomes. Prospective comparisons, ideally randomized, of expert-reviewed and unreviewed specialized tools, including mental health chatbots, would address this gap if they reported safety events, clinical accuracy, expert hours, and results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy users.
underserved_note: Two tests included non-English-speaking populations in South Korea and Italy, but neither enrolled patients, and no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The hazard trial in China enrolled low-income, rural, and low-literacy patients, so the problem is documented in these groups while the safeguard remains untested there.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring care-management staff to assess patients beyond the AI risk score and refer missed high-risk patients improves program eligibility decisions or outcomes. One qualitative study from Australia found that a risk algorithm missed suitable community patients at increasing risk and that staff saw clinician referrals as an important additional way to select patients.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single supporting study is a level 3 qualitative account of staff views in one Australian deployment. It shows that the hazard exists but does not measure whether added staff assessment changes who enrolls or how patients fare.

Staff reported that the algorithm identified previously hospitalised patients but missed community patients whose risk was rising. This suggests a failure mode in which patients without a prior admission may be excluded before deterioration. Whether a staff review step catches these patients reliably, and how often, has not been measured.

In the one deployment studied, clinician referrals already worked alongside the algorithm as a second selection route, which suggests the practice may fit existing care-coordination workflows. The study did not report staff time, referral volume, or how consistently clinicians applied the referral step.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide rates this practice as a must and states that factors beyond the model output should be considered when determining eligibility. This is a voluntary industry framework rather than a regulatory requirement, and its statement rests on a cited reference rather than on a test of the practice supplied here.

research_gap: Studies should compare eligibility decisions made with and without a required staff assessment and referral step, and report how many high-need patients the step adds, the staff time it takes, and downstream outcomes such as admissions and emergency visits for patients the algorithm missed.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems therefore have no evidence on whether staff review recovers missed high-need patients in these groups, who may be more likely to lack the prior hospital records that the algorithm relied on.

bottom_line: One descriptive study from a Swiss hospital found that clinical pharmacists screening 10,556 alerts passed 2,231 to physicians after review, and physicians accepted 68.4% of those reviewed alerts. No study tested remote nurses as the intermediary, and the one test does not state whether its alerts came from an AI system.

perspectives.view: The only test is a cross-sectional study. It examined clinical pharmacist review rather than remote nurses, and its summary does not state whether the alerts came from an AI system, which limits directness. Four hazard studies show alert fatigue exists but do not test intermediary review. The CHAI endorsement describes pre-go-live shadowing, not an intermediary team. Certainty is very low.

In the pharmacist study, physicians accepted 89.8% of direct alerts and 68.4% of reviewed alerts. The summary does not report whether filtered-out alerts included true risks or whether patient harm changed. The hazard is documented. In one AI deployment, 6 of 17 practitioners tended to ignore advisories and 10 could not recall their content.

Pharmacists received 17.2 alerts per day, compared with 7.8 notifications per day for all physicians. This suggests that the burden moves to the reviewing team rather than disappearing. Adenoma detection with computer-aided detection fell from 49.9% to 39.9% in later procedures. That finding suggests a reviewing team may also be exposed to fatigue.

The one deployment relied on pharmacists handling 17.2 alerts per day. A health system would need dedicated reviewer time and a way to hand off urgent findings. No study reported costs, staffing models, or results for remote nurse teams, so feasibility at scale has not been tested.

The single test took place in Switzerland, and its summary does not describe the payer mix, language, or literacy of the patients. The summaries of the hazard studies from the United States, Canada, and South Korea also report no subgroup data. Evidence on which patients benefit or lose when alerts are filtered is absent.

research_gap: Comparative studies are needed that place remote nurses or other intermediary teams between confirmed AI alerts and frontline clinicians. These studies should measure missed true-positive alerts, time to clinical response, reviewer fatigue, patient outcomes, staffing costs, and results by patient subgroup.
underserved_note: No test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only test came from a Swiss hospital and did not report patient characteristics in its summary. Health systems serving these populations cannot tell from current evidence whether intermediary review helps or harms their patients.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether an institution-level disclosure performs better than per-message disclaimers for patient understanding or trust. One simulated qualitative study of 30 adult portal users found that per-message disclosure statements raised concerns about error, authorship, and depersonalization, which shows the problem exists but does not show that the proposed alternative solves it.

perspectives.view: No study compares institution-level disclosure with per-message disclaimers, so certainty cannot be rated for the practice. The one hazard study is qualitative, uses a simulated setting, and enrolled 30 patients. It suggests per-message statements may provoke concern. It is indirect for the recommendation and too small to estimate how often the concern occurs.

Participants reading draft-reply disclosure statements voiced worries about errors, about who wrote the message, and about losing a personal connection. These reactions suggest per-message wording can unsettle patients. No study shows whether a single institutional notice leaves patients better informed, keeps their trust, or helps them know how to reach a human clinician.

The endorsing commentary cites California Health and Safety Code section 1339.75 (AB 3030), which requires disclosure for AI-generated clinical communications unless a licensed clinician reviews them. An institution-level notice fits that exemption only if licensed clinician review actually occurs for each message. Systems in California would need to confirm that review is documented and consistent.

The hazard study reports that patients linked disclosure statements to fears of error. An institutional notice that states the clinical team reviews drafts places the safety burden on that review step. No study measures whether review catches draft errors before they reach patients, so the notice's accuracy depends on review fidelity that has not been tested here.

research_gap: Trials or controlled comparisons are needed that test institution-level disclosure against per-message disclaimers in live portal use, with outcomes that include patient comprehension of AI involvement, trust, message follow-up behavior, and requests to reach a clinician. Studies should also verify how often clinician review occurs as the notice states.
underserved_note: The single hazard study enrolled 30 adult portal users in the United States and did not report inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. No test of the practice exists in any population, so it is unknown whether an institutional notice reaches or is understood by patients who read portal messages in another language or with limited literacy.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether labeling advertisements or disclosing sponsorships in chatbot conversations changes how users interpret or act on health advice. One automated benchmark found that embedded pharmaceutical ads shifted model drug selection by 12.7 percentage points and that models rarely disclosed the ad, which shows the hazard exists but not that labeling addresses it.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single hazard study is an automated benchmark of 258,660 API calls with no human users. It measures model outputs, not whether users notice labels or change decisions, so its findings are indirect for this recommendation.

In the benchmark, ads shifted selection of the advertised drug by 12.7 percentage points even when both drugs were guideline-appropriate, and models repeated ad claims at 2.7 times the baseline rate. This suggests the failure may go unseen. A label may help users discount promotion, but no study shows it reduces harm from the shifted recommendation itself.

Utah HB 452 (2025) requires suppliers of mental health chatbots to clearly and conspicuously identify any advertisement shown to a Utah user within a conversation. The statute applies to mental health chatbots in one state. The recommendation's call to disclose sponsorships and business affiliations extends beyond the quoted statutory text.

The benchmark found that models rarely disclosed embedded ads, so a patient reading the response would have no way to tell that a drug suggestion reflected paid promotion. Labeling would give patients information they currently lack, though no study has measured whether patients read, understand, or act on such labels.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare labeled and unlabeled chatbot responses in real or simulated patient interactions and measure whether ad labels and sponsorship disclosures change user recognition of promotion, trust, and drug choices. Such studies should also test whether disclosure alone offsets the shift in model recommendations or whether operators also need to keep advertising out of clinical content.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the only hazard study was an automated benchmark with no human participants, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Whether these users would notice or understand an advertisement label, including labels in languages other than English, remains unknown.

bottom_line: In two offline studies, experts corrected 28.99% of AI-generated term definitions and flagged 12 of 41 (29.3%) revised articles for edits, but eight of the nine tests were offline and mostly concerned educational content, and the one real genomic deployment (39 patients) gave mixed results. No study compared errors reaching patients with and without expert review.

perspectives.view: Nine studies test expert review, but eight are offline evaluations without a comparison group. Most concern patient education or training material rather than specialized outputs such as variant calls. The single real deployment, a molecular tumour board reviewing genomic outputs for 39 patients, returned mixed findings. No study measured errors reaching patients, so certainty is very low.

Automated somatic variant classification agreed with the expert reference for 56 of 70 variants, and automatic contours shifted dose by more than 5% in most cases. Experts found reasoning failures in synthetic cases that automated screening had passed. One tumour board excluded no drugs, and 8 patients received targeted therapy without benefit, which suggests review may miss weak actionability evidence.

Reviewer seniority appears to matter. Attending radiologists identified more errors than residents (OR 4.52, 95% CI 2.38-8.57), though the gap narrowed when workload was matched. Clinicians endorsed 421 of 514 (82%) LLM-suggested ICD-10 matches, which suggests review often confirms output rather than correcting it. No study reported reviewer time or how review fit into daily workflow.

Three studies included non-English speakers and one included low health literacy readers, all in China or Spain and all on consent or education text. Clinician review raised consent risk scores from 3.28 to 3.69, and expert revision raised accuracy from 3.23 to 4.49. Traditional Chinese medicine topics scored lowest in every group, which the authors linked to limited LLM depth.

Experts corrected 28.99% of ChatGPT term definitions and flagged 12 of 41 (29.3%) revised articles for edits, so in these two studies about three in ten outputs returned to a specialist. None of the studies measured reviewer hours, cost, or turnaround time, and staffing needs for genomic review therefore remain unestimated.

In the consent study, four laypersons joined four surgeons as raters, and overall quality scores rose from 2.86 to 3.64 after clinician review (p = 0.004). No study asked patients whether expert sign-off affected their trust or whether they could reach the reviewing specialist.

research_gap: No study compares genomic or other specialized AI outputs with and without expert review in live care and counts the errors that reach patients. Prospective studies should also record reviewer time, reviewer qualifications, and results in safety-net laboratories and clinics.
underserved_note: Three tests included limited English proficiency or non-English populations and one included low health literacy readers, but all were offline studies of educational or consent text in China and Spain. No test included U.S. Medicaid or safety-net settings, so the evidence says little about expert review of genomic outputs for those patients, where specialist access may be more limited.

bottom_line: Forty-two sources endorse telling patients when AI contributes to their care, and six simulated studies suggest disclosure may modestly raise or preserve trust, although one study found that disclosing AI that disagreed with the clinician raised anxiety and second-opinion intent. No study has tested disclosure in routine care or measured its effect on patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Six studies test disclosure, and all used simulated or offline settings with trust, acceptability, or intent as outcomes rather than care outcomes. Two randomized trials found a 5% trust difference in Denmark and no agreement penalty for disclosed AI in the United States. An Italian vignette study found harms when AI and clinician disagreed, so results are inconsistent and indirect.

In the Italian mammography vignette, disclosing AI that disagreed with the clinician lowered trust from 90.1 to 73.0, raised anxiety from 16.0% to 58.0%, and raised second-opinion intent from 8.7% to 50.0%. In a US trial, agreement fell to 4.01 when the radiologist undercalled AI. Disclosure may change how patients respond to discordant findings.

Almost all German ophthalmology patients interviewed expected to be told about AI decision support, but they differed on how much information they wanted and in what format. Among 226 imaging patients, 67.4% reported minimal or no AI knowledge. No study tested a disclosure script or workflow in routine care, so fidelity and clinician burden remain unmeasured.

No test of disclosure enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A qualitative study of five US safety-net organizations found that limited guidance on communicating with patients about AI was a key barrier. A request-for-information analysis found that clinicians and patients are often unaware of algorithm use and its potential for bias.

Texas SB 1188 requires practitioners who use AI for diagnostic purposes to disclose it to patients, and HB 149 requires disclosure when consumers interact with AI. Among 114 consent documents from AI clinical trials, 58% did not disclose the AI type or intended use and 18.4% omitted risks. These findings show a disclosure gap, not the effect of closing it.

No study reported the staff time, cost, or training needed to disclose AI use at scale. The safety-net study identified missing communication guidance as a barrier, which suggests that systems adopting this practice may need to develop their own scripts and patient materials.

In a survey of 226 imaging patients, 90.3% believed they should be informed about AI use. In a US vignette study of 201 adults, covert AI use in therapy produced the largest declines in acceptability and continuation intent, and transparency reduced but did not remove negative reactions. A Korean survey of 1,000 respondents rated AI-use information as important.

research_gap: No study has tested AI disclosure in a live clinical deployment. A pragmatic trial comparing disclosure formats in routine care would need to measure patient comprehension, trust, second-opinion seeking, and downstream care decisions, with particular attention to how clinicians explain cases where AI output and clinical judgment disagree.
underserved_note: None of the six tests of disclosure included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only safety-net evidence is a hazard study reporting that organizations lacked guidance on how to talk with patients about AI, and with 67.4% of imaging patients reporting minimal AI knowledge, the effect of disclosure on comprehension and trust in these groups is unknown.

bottom_line: Studies suggest that confidence-based deferral may raise accuracy on the cases an AI tool keeps while reducing human review burden. Nearly all tests are offline replays, and few measure how often high-risk cases are missed or answerable questions are needlessly deferred.

perspectives.view: Three studies tested the practice in real deployment: one randomized trial, one prospective comparison, and one quasi-experimental study. The remaining studies were offline replays, simulations, or benchmarks. The trial reported a 65% drop in standard-risk queries routed to humans but did not quantify missed high-risk deferrals. Results point one way, but indirectness and sparse over-deferral data support low certainty.

In replays, deferral raised accuracy from 0.847 for AI alone to 0.869, and cleared decisions carried 1.22% harm versus 6.67% among flagged ones. Hazard benchmarks show models selecting an answer in 53-82% of items lacking a correct option. This suggests a tool's deferral behavior should be tested before use rather than assumed.

Consistency-based deferral raised F1 to 0.62-0.73 on a harder step, but the gains were marginal because confidence was poorly calibrated. In one benchmark, safety-aware prompting reduced premature commitment only by shifting errors toward excessive abstention. These results suggest deferral thresholds may need local tuning and ongoing monitoring of both under-deferral and over-deferral.

Replays reported 66% less clinician workload in breast screening, a 68.9% workload reduction in pathology, and a 75% cut in manual review. One Vietnamese study found that sending every clinically significant disagreement for a second read would raise burden by 6.67%. These figures suggest staffing effects depend on where the deferral threshold is set.

One simulation found that an automated filter reduced errors but did not penalize false deferrals. Its authors judged it likely counterproductive if patients were redirected on answerable questions, and harmful errors remained. In another study, models flagged text-assessable items as not assessable more often than clinicians did (19.4% vs. 11.4%).

One replay used 250,000 Medicaid intervention records, and one used Finnish-language patient records. Both were offline analyses, and no test reported low-literacy populations. Hazard studies in Turkish and Italian found concordance on specialist-referral coding as low as 37.5% and a model answering when it should not.

A regulatory discussion paper describes checking whether a device defers when information is insufficient without over-deferring when information is adequate. One prospective offline study reported 12.4% of colonoscopy cases flagged for manual review and 97.5% accuracy on automated cases. Few tests report a rate of unnecessary deferral of the kind the paper describes.

research_gap: No study measures, in live clinical use, both the rate of missed deferrals on high-risk or complex cases and the rate of unnecessary deferrals on answerable questions. No study links deferral behavior to patient outcomes and clinician workload. Prospective deployment studies that report these paired measures are lacking, as are live studies in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy settings.
underserved_note: Two tests included underserved or language-diverse populations: one offline replay of Medicaid decision records (pmid:41667212) and one offline replay of Finnish-language records (epmc:PPR1276359). No test reported low-literacy populations, and none of the real-deployment studies reported underserved populations. Evidence for these groups therefore rests on retrospective data and may not reflect how deferral performs in live care for them.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this recommendation tests whether tracking ambient scribe opt-out rates detects patient discomfort or consent problems, and no study documents the hazard itself. One guidance document offers permissive support, and its quoted text describes documentation quality metrics rather than opt-out rates.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero that document the hazard. The single endorsement is guidance worded as "may," and its quoted passage names draft retention, incorrect content, and quality analyses, which do not include opt-out percentage. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure ambient scribe opt-out rates across clinics and compare them with direct measures of patient discomfort and consent quality, such as post-visit surveys or consent audits. Such studies would show whether opt-out rates are a valid signal, what baseline and threshold values mean, and whether low opt-out rates reflect comfort or patients' reluctance to decline.
underserved_note: No supplied study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, because no study was supplied. Opt-out rates may understate discomfort in groups who face language or literacy barriers to understanding or refusing recording, so any monitoring program would need its own validation in those populations.

bottom_line: Five simulated studies suggest that AI labels may slightly lower patient ratings of reliability, satisfaction, or willingness to return without changing intention to follow advice, and one qualitative study found that written labels often did not tell patients that AI wrote the draft. No study tested labeling in live clinical messaging, so whether labels correct patients' assumptions about authorship remains unshown.

perspectives.view: All five tests used simulated or offline settings, and none measured whether labels corrected misattribution in real patient messages. Satisfaction effects were small (0.13 and 0.09 points), a labeled-ad trial of 614 found no effect, and a vignette study of 2,280 found lower reliability and empathy ratings. Indirectness and inconsistency support low certainty.

In one trial 7.3% of participants identified LLM-written material, and in another, patients generally missed that clinician avatars were AI-generated. In the only test of comprehension, nearly half of 30 portal users still could not identify AI as the draft's writer after reading a written disclosure, which suggests label wording may determine whether it works.

No study measured labeling inside a live portal or messaging workflow, so fidelity, placement, and clinician burden are unknown. The qualitative study of 30 portal users suggests that a generic statement attached to a draft reply may be misread, and that label design would need testing with patients before rollout.

None of the five tests reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The one non-English population appears in a hazard study from China, where 32% overall correctly identified authorship. Written disclosures that confused portal users may be harder for low-literacy readers, but no study examined this.

California AB 3030 requires disclaimers, including verbal ones at the start and end of audio interactions, and Texas statutes require AI disclosure in some settings. These mandates rest on transparency principles, and the available study does not show that a compliant written label improves patient understanding of authorship.

Most patients in the qualitative study preferred disclosure even when they could not interpret it, and over 75% of 1,455 respondents were satisfied regardless of disclosure. Disclosure reduced willingness to return to the same dentist (d=0.35 to 0.37), which suggests labels may affect trust while honoring patients' stated wish to know.

research_gap: No study has tested labeling of AI-generated messages in a live patient portal or phone line with a measure of whether patients correctly understand who wrote the message and whether a clinician reviewed it. Trials comparing label wording, placement, and audio formats, with outcomes that include comprehension, trust, and follow-up contact with a human, would address this gap.
underserved_note: None of the five studies testing labels reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. The only non-English population appears in a hazard study, so the effect of labels for patients who most need plain-language or translated disclosures is unknown.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring formal consent for higher-risk AI uses changes patient understanding, trust, or outcomes compared with passive notice, and no study documents how often such uses proceed on notice alone. Six sources endorse the practice, one as a framework requirement tied to existing state or specialty consent rules and five as commentary or guidance.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The six endorsements consist of one framework, one guidance document, and four commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not raise certainty, so no effect estimate exists for consent versus notice on any patient or system outcome.

The CHAI playbook ties explicit consent to cases where state or specialty regulation already requires it, such as certain genomic or behavioral health uses. A commentary on the EU AI Act describes updating consent forms and patient leaflets to reflect AI. These sources suggest that some consent duties may already apply, though no source maps which ones.

No study measured the time, staff effort, or workflow changes needed to classify AI uses into the five triggering categories and obtain consent. One dental commentary proposes that consent explain the level of autonomy an AI tool exercises, which would require health systems to document that attribute for each tool before the process could run.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare formal consent with passive notice for AI uses meeting the five criteria, measuring patient comprehension, opt-out rates, trust, staff burden, and whether consent processes identify uses that should not proceed. Baseline audits of how often higher-risk AI uses currently run on notice alone would establish whether the hazard occurs at meaningful frequency.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Consent processes that rely on written forms may perform differently for patients with limited literacy or English proficiency, and health systems adopting this practice would be doing so without data on comprehension in those groups.

bottom_line: Endorsing sources, including Utah HB 452, which makes disclosure mandatory for mental health chatbots, support AI-identity disclosure, but only one simulated trial has tested disclosure, and it did not measure whether disclosure reduces over-trust. In that trial, disclosure left intention to follow instructions unchanged and lowered intention to return to the same dentist.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial (n=906) tested disclosure using simulated dental scenarios. Its outcomes were intentions to comply and to return, not misidentification of the agent or over-trust, so directness is poor. A single study cannot establish consistency or precision. Downgrading for indirectness and imprecision leaves the certainty of benefit for the targeted hazard very low.

The hazard study found that ChatGPT disclosed its AI identity less often than Bard when answering caregiver questions. This suggests that a model's own statements may not reliably disclose what it is. In the trial, disclosure did not change intention to follow instructions, so disclosure may not reduce reliance on advice that is wrong.

The model-to-model variation in self-disclosure suggests that deployers should not depend on the language model to announce itself. A fixed disclosure at the interface, set outside model output, may be more consistent. No study tested how disclosures should be timed, repeated after inactivity, or worded in real patient-facing workflows.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbots to disclose clearly and conspicuously that they are AI and not human.
