Only one hazard study included limited English proficiency content, and it tested emergency sensitivity rather than the practice. The evidence therefore cannot show whether multi-turn escalation testing works for these groups, who may express minimization in ways current scenario sets do not capture.

bottom_line: Fourteen studies test automated blocking or filtering of generative AI queries and outputs, and most report fewer unsafe outputs, but 13 are benchmarks or simulations and four found that filters missed harmful content or blocked benign queries. No study measured whether alerting humans to deviations changed patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Of 14 studies, 13 are level 4 or 5 benchmarks or simulations. Only one, with 207 screening queries, comes from a real deployment. Four report null or mixed results, and several abstracts give no numbers. Indirect outcomes, inconsistent findings, and imprecision suggest very low certainty that the practice reduces harm to patients.

A safety filter applied to 1,250 synthetic coaching dialogues lowered error rates but did not remove harmful responses. A safety cue cut harmful decisions from 16.6% to 10.1% without eliminating them. Top models in a validation agent test failed on one category of harmful materials. These results suggest blocking layers reduce harm but leave gaps.

An input classifier cut unsafe responses by 52 percentage points but flagged 45% of benign queries. External guardrails produced brittle blocking and weak safe helpfulness. A hybrid middleware reported full interception at baseline cost and latency, but only on synthetic tests. False rejections at these rates may lead clinicians and patients to work around the tool.

No study measured the staffing cost of human alerts. A rule-based sentinel with handoff kept deploy violation rates at or below 6%, while strict violation rates ranged from 1.5% to 49.5%. A 45% false alarm rate on benign queries would generate review volume that may exceed what staff can absorb.

Two benchmarks used non-English content. A classifier reached 88.8% accuracy and 90.6% unsafe recall on 2,537 Turkish health queries. In a Qatar study, the Jais and Fanar models scored 0.40 and blocked no harmful materials. An older-adult benchmark reported up to 96.2% detection. Performance appears to vary by language and model.

In about 500 simulated scenarios, an AI supervisor corrected each harmful chatbot response, but the correction came from software rather than a person. No study reported how patients experienced rejection notices or whether they reached a human after a block. Frequent refusals of benign questions may erode patient trust.

research_gap: No study tested the full practice in live clinical use, with rejection notices paired with human alerts. None measured patient harm, false rejection burden, staff response time, or patient access to a human after a block. Prospective deployment studies that report these outcomes with numbers would address the gap.
underserved_note: Two benchmarks tested non-English health content, one with Turkish queries and one with patient education materials in Qatar. The one real deployment ran in Caribbean jurisdictions. No study included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving those populations cannot assume that the reported detection and false alarm rates apply to their patients' queries.

bottom_line: Six sources, three frameworks and three commentaries, recommend that health systems set and periodically revisit predefined triggers for escalating, re-reviewing, suspending, or deactivating AI tools, but no supplied study tests whether doing so leads to faster or more reliable action on degraded performance. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and conceptual reasoning.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests predefined thresholds or triggers, and no study documents the hazard of unacted-upon degradation. All six endorsements are frameworks or commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, this leaves no body of evidence to rate. The agreement across sources reflects shared expert judgment, which should not be read as evidence of effect.

The endorsing sources describe graduated responses, ranging from ending a single session to suspending an entire application, and they tie those responses to the scope and severity of an event. This logic mirrors other safety escalation schemes. No supplied study shows whether predefined triggers catch degradation before it reaches patients, or which threshold levels balance missed signals against alert overload.

NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to set and review deactivation criteria tied to their stated risk tolerances. The CHAI guides frame thresholds as part of assurance and governance practice. These documents are voluntary guidance. In the supplied material they do not create a binding requirement, and they leave the specific threshold values to each organization.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without predefined escalation and deactivation thresholds. Useful outcomes would include time from detected performance drift to governance action, the number of harmful outputs reaching patients, and the volume of reviews committees receive. Separate work should examine how threshold levels are chosen and whether scheduled review of those thresholds changes decisions.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Because performance degradation can differ across subgroups, thresholds set only on aggregate metrics may fail to trigger when a tool degrades for these groups. No supplied study has examined this question.

bottom_line: Two cluster randomized trials suggest that human outreach after AI risk flagging may raise follow-up completion and reduce preventable admissions, but a trial in a low-income population found no benefit and several descriptive studies report low uptake. No study tests care coordination for patients who lack the data needed for risk categorization.

perspectives.view: Three randomized trials test outreach after flagging. Two cluster trials favored outreach: a 27% drop in preventable admissions (95% CI -44% to -6%), and follow-up of 38.2% vs 23.5% and 25.4% vs 19.7%. A 220-patient trial found hospital use of 20.0% vs 16.4% (RR 1.2). Inconsistency and the untested coordination component lower certainty.

Hazard studies show that flagged patients often go unseen. Only 15% of referred patients scheduled a falls visit, 44.7% completed a confirmatory eye exam, and 29.8% missed an ophthalmology visit. Uncontrolled studies suggest that outreach workflows may close part of this gap, with nodule follow-up rising from 53.5% to 67.9% and scheduled aneurysm monitoring reaching 99% vs 65%.

In one cluster trial, decision support alone did not raise follow-up, while decision support paired with patient outreach did. This suggests that a risk flag may need a human contact step to change care. Direct outreach for familial hypercholesterolemia yielded 19% visits and 15% new diagnoses, and the authors described the process as labor intensive.

Uptake after outreach was low in several deployments. In one study, 8.2% of eligible high-risk patients enrolled in workup, 8.7% of invited older adults attended a follow-up clinic, and 4 of 62 contacted patients returned for testing. None of these studies reported staffing hours or cost per patient reached.

The only randomized trial focused on low-income and racial or ethnic minority patients found no reduction in postpartum hospital use after navigation and education. In American Samoa, 1 of 62 contacted high-risk patients agreed to colonoscopy. These results suggest that outreach alone may not overcome access barriers in these groups.

Outreach gives flagged patients a human contact. Patients who engaged with a follow-up clinic gave positive feedback, but 91.3% of invited patients did not attend. An interdisciplinary review of 13 very high-risk opioid patients was followed by more treatment engagement, from 3 to 6 patients. That study had no comparator group.

research_gap: No study tests how to identify or coordinate care for patients whose records lack the data needed for risk categorization. Trials comparing outreach intensities, reporting staffing cost, and measuring diagnostic and health outcomes by subgroup are also absent.
underserved_note: One trial enrolled low-income and racial or ethnic minority patients and found no benefit, and one descriptive study in American Samoa found very low return rates. The only safety-net population appears in a hazard study. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups as defined populations, so the benefit seen in the two positive trials may not carry over to these patients.

bottom_line: Nine sources endorse incident response plans for AI failures, drift, or nonconforming outputs, and one FDA draft guidance frames nonconforming-product control as a manufacturer requirement. No supplied study tests whether such plans shorten harm or improve outcomes, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself.

perspectives.view: The evidence base consists of nine endorsements: one draft guidance, three frameworks, one multi-society statement, and four commentaries. No comparative, observational, or case-series study was supplied. Under GRADE conventions, the effect of incident response plans on time to detection, harm duration, or patient outcomes cannot be rated, and agreement among sources reflects expert opinion rather than tested effect.

The FDA draft guidance ties AI device oversight to existing quality-system duties to control nonconforming product, which gives manufacturers a regulatory basis for procedures. For health systems, the radiology multi-society statement, CHAI, NIST AI 600-1, and HEAAL use should-level language. A Korean legal commentary proposes postevent review by a designated safety officer with reporting to authorities.

The sources name the elements they expect in a plan: notification, a defined mode of operation while the model is under assessment, severity classification, auditable escalation records, and a designated lead. No supplied study shows which of these elements catches errors before they reach patients or how quickly a plan contains harm once drift is detected.

research_gap: No supplied study tests incident response plans for clinical AI, and no supplied study measures how often uncoordinated responses prolong harm. Useful designs would include before-and-after or interrupted time-series studies across sites that adopt plans. These could measure time from drift detection to containment, the number of patients exposed to nonconforming outputs during the interval, and the fidelity of interim operation such as fallback to manual workflows. Simulation or tabletop exercises could also report which plan elements fail under realistic conditions.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. HEAAL and the Arabic-language triage commentary raise equity-relevant settings but offer no data. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence on whether incident plans reach patients who may be less likely to report problems or to receive notifications in their language.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether contractual disclosure of escalation triggers, halt conditions, and reversibility makes agentic AI safer, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement whose wording addresses vendor-applied model constraints in general rather than these three specific terms.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the opaque-agent hazard. Under GRADE conventions this is a case of no direct evidence. The single endorsement is expert opinion, and its text asks for disclosure of vendor constraints on the foundation model, which only indirectly covers escalation triggers, halt conditions, or reversibility.

The CHAI governance playbook states that health systems should obtain disclosure of vendor-applied constraints on model behavior specific to the health care deployment. This supports disclosure as a contracting norm. The playbook language does not name escalation triggers, automatic halts, or reversal of agent actions, so the recommendation extends the endorsed text rather than restating it.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without contractually documented escalation, halt, and reversibility terms and measure outcomes such as time to detect and reverse erroneous agent actions, the rate of agent errors reaching patients, and the share of vendor-disclosed triggers that function as described when audited. Descriptive work documenting how often opaque agent behavior has impeded oversight or reversal would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Health systems serving these patients cannot tell from this evidence whether escalation triggers route patients to human staff who speak their language, or whether halt conditions account for the documentation gaps and resource limits common in safety-net settings.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether training frontline staff to escalate, halt, or roll back agentic AI actions reduces harm, and no supplied study documents how often staff fail to stop erroneous agent actions. The only endorsing source, a CHAI governance playbook, addresses pre-contract vendor subgroup performance data and does not speak to user training for stopping or reversing agent actions.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for R256 contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement comes from a framework rather than empirical work. Its quoted text concerns vendor subgroup data before contract execution, so it offers indirect support at most for a training recommendation.

The supplied material does not show how often staff are unable to stop or reverse agent actions, how severe the resulting harms are, or whether trained users intercept errors before they reach patients. Without hazard or intervention data, the size of the safety benefit from halt and rollback training remains unknown.

The CHAI playbook language supplied here sets an expectation that vendors disclose subgroup performance data before contracting. That expectation applies to procurement and does not establish a standard for frontline escalation, halt, or rollback training. Health systems adopting R256 would be acting without a directly matching endorsement in this evidence map.

research_gap: No study has measured whether trained frontline users halt or reverse erroneous agentic AI actions more often or more quickly than untrained users, or whether such training changes patient harm. Studies are also needed that document how often agent actions go unstopped in clinical workflows and whether systems provide working halt and rollback controls for training to build on.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. This means health systems serving these groups have no data on whether halt and rollback training works under their staffing levels and workflows.

bottom_line: One simulated study reports that an agentic system abstained more often when it could not support a safe recommendation, but it gives no numbers, and no study has tested pause or escalation rules in live clinical use. A separate benchmark shows that larger models rarely withheld action on deficient cases, which suggests the hazard is real and that escalation conditions may need to be defined and tested rather than assumed.

perspectives.view: One level 4 offline study tests the practice and reports that ETHOS increased abstention when safe recommendations could not be supported. The abstract gives no numbers, sample size, or comparator. Serious risk of bias, indirectness from simulation, and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

In 836 synthetic prior authorization records, Gemini 3 Pro and Claude Opus 4.5 completed 95.45% and 93.67% of tasks yet nearly always submitted deficient profiles. Gemini 3 Flash withheld 17.33%. High task completion therefore may coexist with failure to stop, so pause conditions likely need direct testing.

Both studies ran offline, and neither reports how escalations reach a human reviewer, how often reviewers act, or what workload results. Commentary sources ask health systems to measure what happens after escalation, and no study here has measured that.

The CHAI playbook rates documentation of the systems, APIs, and data sources an agent may query as a must. That inventory defines the limits of authorized action, but no supplied study tests whether documenting those limits changes agent behavior.

One commentary argues that escalation triggers belong in system logic because patients may not recognize when a question exceeds safe self-care. The benchmark finding that larger models rarely withheld action suggests patients cannot count on an agent to stop on its own and route them to a person.

research_gap: No study has measured escalation or abstention rules in live clinical workflows. Such studies would need to report how often agents pause or escalate appropriately, the rate of missed escalations, reviewer response time and burden, and patient outcomes after escalation, compared with agents that run without defined stop conditions.
underserved_note: Neither study reports the populations represented, and both used simulated or synthetic data, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Whether escalation triggers work for patients who describe symptoms in other languages or with limited health literacy remains untested.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether documented, vendor-independent means to disable, halt, or roll back AI shorten the time that a malfunctioning tool affects patients, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on three endorsements, one of which is a multi-society radiology statement written as a requirement.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsing sources are guidance documents and frameworks. They express expert consensus, and they do not supply effect estimates, comparison groups, or measured outcomes that GRADE could weigh.

The radiology multi-society statement frames a simple disable mechanism as a requirement for autonomous AI. The CHAI playbooks address a related case, vendor sunset, through notice periods and data export. NIST AI 600-1 calls for an inventory of generative AI systems, which a health system would need before it could locate and halt embedded tools.

The radiology statement links training in failure modes with a disable mechanism as a way to keep errors from reaching patients. No supplied study measures how often AI malfunctions persist, how long they persist, or whether a halt procedure intercepts them. The safety benefit therefore remains a stated rationale rather than an observed effect.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure time from detection of an AI malfunction to its disablement, with and without documented vendor-independent procedures, and that record patient exposure during that interval. Simulation drills or post-incident reviews could test whether staff can execute rollback procedures as written, and whether compensating controls such as manual workflows or feature toggles work for AI embedded in electronic health records and devices where the health system lacks direct control.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer technical staff to maintain and rehearse disable procedures, and whether the practice performs the same way in those settings remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether allow-lists, environment isolation, dry-run modes, or per-action audit logs prevent irreversible or untraceable harm from autonomous AI agents in health care. The recommendation currently rests on one governance framework (CHAI) that lists these controls as a must.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement reflects expert consensus within a framework and does not supply effect estimates for any of the four controls.

The only support comes from the CHAI governance playbooks, which classify agent-specific guardrails as a must. This is a voluntary framework and not a statute or FDA requirement. Deployers adopting these controls would be following consensus guidance whose effect on patient harm has not been measured in the studies supplied here.

research_gap: Studies are needed that deploy autonomous agents in clinical or administrative health care workflows with and without reversibility bounds, and that measure rates of irreversible erroneous actions, time to detect and reverse errors, and completeness of audit trails. No study in this map documents how often agent actions cause irreversible or untraceable harm, so the baseline size of the hazard is also unknown.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Whether these controls work equally well in under-resourced settings, where staff may have less capacity to review dry-run outputs or audit logs, remains untested.

bottom_line: Six frameworks and guidance documents endorse a process for deciding whether underperforming AI continues, is remediated or retrained, or is decommissioned, but no supplied study tests such a process or measures how often the hazard occurs. Health systems that adopt this recommendation would be acting on expert consensus rather than on outcome evidence.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The six sources are frameworks, guidance, and one commentary, which express consensus rather than measured effects. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about whether a disposition process improves safety or outcomes cannot be rated, because no study informs it.

Endorsement strength varies across sources. One CHAI playbook states the practice as a must, CHAI's assurance guide, NIST AI 600-1, and the TRUST commentary use should, FUTURE-AI uses may, and HEAAL describes it. NIST ties decommissioning or retraining to performance outside defined organizational risk limits, which gives administrators a documented threshold approach to cite.

research_gap: No study compares health systems or AI deployments with and without a structured continue, remediate, or decommission process. Studies are needed that measure how long underperforming tools stay in use, how often disposition decisions are made, what thresholds trigger them, and whether patient harm or performance changes after remediation or retirement.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on whether a disposition process works for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The HEAAL framework frames decommissioning around equity objectives, but that is guidance, and whether disposition decisions account for subgroup performance remains untested.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether rehearsing AI fallback, backup, recovery, or incident response procedures, or keeping records of those tests, changes outcomes, and no supplied study documents the hazard of untested fallback. The recommendation rests on three voluntary frameworks that use "should" language.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsements are expert frameworks, and they reflect consensus judgment rather than measured effects on downtime, recovery time, or patient harm.

All three endorsing sources are voluntary frameworks. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks whether records show the contingency plan was tested, NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to practice incident response plans for harmful generated content, and the CHAI playbooks ask whether AI systems can be restored after ransomware and what the recovery time objective is. None of these sources creates a binding legal requirement.

No supplied study reports how often AI fallback procedures fail during real outages or what harm follows when they do. The hazard therefore remains a plausible failure mode that the frameworks describe, and its frequency and severity in clinical settings have not been measured in the material provided.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units that run scheduled AI failover drills, restore tests, and incident response exercises against those that do not. Such studies should measure time to safe manual workflow, recovery time relative to stated objectives, missed or delayed care during AI outages, and the staff time the drills require. Descriptive studies of how often untested AI fallback plans fail during real incidents would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. This leaves unknown whether fallback testing protects these patients during AI outages, and whether safety-net systems with smaller IT staffs can sustain the testing the frameworks describe.

bottom_line: Four sources, three of them frameworks from CHAI and NIST, recommend that health systems keep backup workflows for times when AI tools are down or reject requests, but no supplied study tests whether such workflows prevent care disruption. No supplied study documents the size of the hazard either, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests backup workflows, and no study measures how often or how badly care processes fail during AI downtime. The four endorsements are frameworks and one commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks for alternative workflows for downtime and sunsetting, and NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to document third-party dependencies and identify fallbacks. Both use should language and are voluntary. The supplied sources do not cite any federal or state rule that requires AI downtime procedures.

The CHAI playbook extends outage planning to upstream cloud and foundation model vendors that the AI vendor does not control. This suggests that contracts may need notification timelines covering those parties. The supplied sources give no data on the staffing or cost of keeping manual fallback workflows current and rehearsed.

research_gap: No supplied study measures how often AI outages or request rejections disrupt care, or compares sites with and without defined backup workflows on delays, errors, or missed tasks during downtime. Simulation or downtime-drill studies and analyses of real outage events could supply the first direct evidence, including whether staff retain manual skills after long periods of AI use.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net sites with thin staffing, and services such as AI-supported interpretation or patient messaging, may depend more heavily on AI tools, but the supplied evidence cannot confirm or size that risk.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether contract terms for wind-down use, limits on remote disablement, or transition assistance protect care when an AI vendor withdraws, and no study documents how often such withdrawals disrupt care. The recommendation rests on a single governance framework, which addresses transition assistance only in the context of termination for cause.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The only support is one framework endorsement, which reflects expert judgment rather than observed outcomes. Neither the size of the problem nor the effect of the contract terms can be estimated from the supplied record.

The CHAI playbook names transition assistance, data return or destruction, and continued cooperation on open incidents, but it ties these to termination for cause. It does not address vendor-initiated discontinuation, continued wind-down use, or limits on remote disablement. The recommendation therefore extends beyond what its one endorsing source states.

research_gap: Studies are needed that count how often AI vendors discontinue products or disable them remotely, measure what happens to dependent clinical workflows and patients when they do, and compare outcomes at health systems whose contracts include wind-down, disablement, and transition clauses with those whose contracts do not.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may hold less negotiating power with vendors, and whether they can secure these contract terms, or what happens to their patients when they cannot, remains unmeasured.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether prohibiting deployment above a residual-risk tolerance, or limiting post-failure deployment to bounded pilots with halt criteria, reduces harm from AI in health care. The recommendation rests on two CHAI framework documents that use "should" language, and no study documenting the hazard was supplied either.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no body of evidence exists to rate for design, consistency, directness, or precision. Under GRADE conventions the certainty is no direct evidence. The two endorsements are expert consensus statements, and consensus does not substitute for outcome data.

Both endorsing sources are voluntary CHAI frameworks rather than statutes or agency rules. One asks health systems to define explicit no-go conditions for unmitigated high-severity harm. The other asks whether safety concerns that trigger a pilot delay should be shared with developers and regulators. Neither source sets a numeric tolerance or specifies halt criteria.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without predefined residual-risk tolerances and pilot halt criteria. Such studies would measure how often deployments are stopped or delayed, whether halted tools would have caused harm, and how often bounded pilots reach their halt criteria. Descriptive work documenting how often AI is deployed with unmitigated high-severity risk would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from the supplied evidence whether risk tolerances set by governance bodies account for harms that fall disproportionately on these groups.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether AI retirement plans reduce care disruption when a tool is withdrawn, although four frameworks recommend such planning. Two reports, which appear to describe the same UK survey of 40 radiology staff, found that some staff had relied on a withdrawn triage tool and that 35% recalled logistical burden afterward.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The two hazard reports share a setting, a sample of 40, and their findings, and they likely represent one survey reported twice. The reliance figures rest on 5 reporting staff, which makes them imprecise. The descriptive design cannot link withdrawal to patient outcomes.

One of 5 reporting staff had grown reliant on the tool, and 35% of 40 respondents recalled logistical issues after withdrawal. This suggests that removing a tool can disturb workflow. Neither report measured missed findings, delays, or patient harm during the transition. The severity of harm is therefore unknown, and no study shows that backup arrangements catch errors.

Free-text responses described both a loss of clinical value and operational relief after decommissioning. This suggests that reliance varies across users, so a retirement plan may need to assess it by role. No study reports the workload of assessing reliance, activating backups, or communicating with staff, so how these steps perform in real workflows is untested.

The four endorsing sources are voluntary frameworks from NIST and CHAI plus a decision-point guide. They use "should" or descriptive language and create no legal duties. The CHAI guide asks whether organizations have a plan for end-of-life processes driven by the developer. That question places part of retirement planning in vendor contracts.

Thirty-five percent of 40 respondents recalled logistical burden after withdrawal, while some free text described operational relief. This mix suggests that decommissioning carries staffing and workflow costs that planning may anticipate. No study reports the cost or staff time needed to maintain retirement plans, so this evidence cannot show whether the practice is feasible at scale.

Both reports surveyed staff only. Seventy percent of respondents still believed the AI had improved patient care. No study asked patients whether they noticed the withdrawal, knew whom to contact, or experienced delays. The evidence does not show whether retirement communication reaches patients or preserves their access to a human.

research_gap: No study compares AI withdrawals that followed a structured retirement plan with withdrawals that did not. Such a study could measure turnaround times, missed or delayed findings, staff workload during the transition, and whether patients received information about alternatives and contacts.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice. The two hazard reports surveyed UK radiology staff and did not describe any Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The evidence therefore cannot show whether harms from withdrawal, or the benefits of retirement plans, differ for these populations, whose backup capacity and communication needs may differ.

bottom_line: Six sources, three frameworks and three commentaries, endorse including AI in continuity and disaster recovery plans, but no supplied study tests the practice or measures how often AI outages disrupt care. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and on reasoning by analogy from general IT continuity planning.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests whether mapping AI dependencies or documenting lost functionality changes outage duration, recovery time, or patient outcomes. No study documents the hazard either. The support consists of three frameworks and three commentaries, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The commentaries describe loss of availability as a predictable failure mode and propose fallbacks such as locally cached models and redundant components. These proposals are design reasoning. No supplied data show how often AI failures reach patients or whether documented contingency plans shorten the period of exposure to harm.

The CHAI playbook lists a computing resource inventory, including cloud dependencies, as a must. The CHAI assurance guide and NIST AI 600-1 frame contingency planning and data redundancy as should. These are voluntary frameworks, and the supplied sources cite no statute or rule that requires AI-specific continuity planning.

research_gap: Studies are needed that document the frequency and clinical consequences of AI outages and dependency failures in health systems. Studies are also needed that compare recovery time, workaround use, and adverse events between sites with and without AI-specific continuity plans and staff training.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may have fewer redundant resources, and it is unknown whether outage effects or the value of planning differ in those settings.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether multilingual, multi-format training for AI users reduces misuse or misunderstanding, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on one international consensus guideline and one commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Support comes from a consensus guideline (FUTURE-AI) and a commentary on AI translation tools, both of which rank as expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures user errors by training language or format.

The hazard concerns users who do not speak the training language, yet no supplied study measures how often this occurs or whom it affects. Without data, a health system cannot tell whether staff with limited English proficiency, or patients using patient-facing tools, face higher misuse rates than other users.

FUTURE-AI states that developers should use formats and languages accessible to intended end users. The translation-tools commentary calls provider training key. Both sources use advisory language and describe no enforcement mechanism. The supplied materials cite no FDA, ONC, civil-rights, or state statutory requirement for multilingual AI training.

research_gap: No study compares multilingual or multi-format AI training with single-language training on outcomes such as user error rates, override accuracy, or patient harm. The field also lacks baseline data on how often language mismatch between training materials and users leads to AI misuse in clinical settings.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The recommendation targets a language barrier directly, but its value for these groups remains unmeasured, and health systems serving them have no outcome data to guide what formats or languages to prioritize.

bottom_line: Three offline or simulated studies suggest that structured failure-mode analysis with quality assurance, or a built-in safety floor, may lower estimated risk from AI errors. No study measured whether these fail-safes kept errors from reaching real patients, so certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: Two failure mode analyses and one synthetic benchmark tested the practice. Mean risk priority number fell from 55.80 to 16.17 with quality management, and lack-of-detectability fell from 8.17 to 3.51 with case-specific QA. These are team-rated scores or synthetic outcomes without patient data, so indirectness and risk of bias are serious.

The hazard study found premature diagnosis in up to 9.3% of LLM sessions and futile invasive procedures in 3.7% to 18.1% of failed cases, which shows errors can proceed without a stop. A safety floor held guideline compliance at 1.00 across all shift conditions in synthetic patients, which suggests fail-safe design may contain such errors.

Both failure mode analyses were done offline by review teams rating hypothetical failures. Neither reports the time, staffing, or workflow changes that case-specific QA required in routine use, and neither measured whether errors were actually detected and corrected at the rated rates after go-live.

Seven sources endorse the practice. NIST AI 600-1 asks that systems fail safely when operating beyond their knowledge limits, and the CHAI playbook asks health systems to document the approach used and any remaining gaps. The supplied sources are voluntary frameworks, professional statements, and commentaries rather than binding requirements.

None of the three tests reports patient demographics, payer mix, language, or literacy, and one used only synthetic patients. The studies therefore cannot show whether error detection and fail-safes perform equally for the patients a safety-net system serves.

FUTURE-AI lists fallback measures that include warnings to users, system shutdown, and reliance on human judgment only. No supplied study measured whether patients reached a clinician when an AI system failed, or how patients viewed those fallbacks.

research_gap: Prospective studies in live clinical settings should measure how often AI errors are detected and corrected before they reach patients, compare fail-safe designs with usual practice, and report staffing cost and patient outcomes, including results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy populations.
underserved_note: No test included or reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; two studies analyzed failure modes rather than patients, and one used synthetic patients. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that the reported risk reductions apply to their patients.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether assessing language barriers in AI feedback channels changes who gives feedback or which problems get reported, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on two endorsements, a framework and a commentary, so it reflects expert judgment rather than tested effect.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Support comes from one framework (CHAI) and one commentary on machine-assisted translation, both using "should" language. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without supporting data cannot be rated, so certainty in any effect of this assessment is not estimable.

The hazard concerns patients with limited English proficiency, yet no supplied study measures whether these patients are underrepresented in AI feedback data. The translation commentary proposes patient advisory boards to gather feedback on translation clarity, but it reports no data on whether such boards reach patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

research_gap: Studies should first measure the size of the gap by comparing feedback submission rates and complaint content for AI tools between patients with and without limited English proficiency. Later studies could test whether translated feedback channels, interpreter-assisted outreach, or advisory boards change participation rates and surface safety problems that English-only channels miss.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Health systems that adopt this recommendation would be acting on expert consensus alone and would need to collect their own data to learn whether their assessment reaches the patients it targets.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether offering multiple accessible channels for AI feedback and incident reporting increases reports from people with disabilities or access barriers, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from CHAI, which uses permissive language ("may").

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is a governance playbook, which reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative data on reporting rates or harm detection.

The CHAI playbook proposes embedding AI reporting in existing structures, such as adding AI categories to compliance hotline intake forms and updating non-retaliation language in HR policies. This approach suggests the added cost may be modest, but no supplied study measures cost, staffing needs, or whether added channels receive any use.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI incident reporting volume, reporter characteristics, and time to harm detection before and after health systems add accessible channels such as phone, text, sign language video, screen-reader-compatible web forms, and multilingual options. Such studies should also establish whether people with disabilities or access barriers currently underreport AI problems relative to other patients.
underserved_note: No supplied study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, low-literacy, or disability populations, because no study was supplied at all. Health systems adopting this practice therefore have no evidence on which channels reach these groups and should track channel use by patient population to generate that evidence locally.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether evaluating feedback and incident-reporting channels for ability, language, or access barriers improves detection of AI harms in excluded groups, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from the CHAI Responsible AI Guide.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The support comes from one framework source, which reflects expert consensus rather than measured effect.

The CHAI Responsible AI Guide lists this evaluation as a must, directing systems to check whether some individuals or groups are systematically excluded from giving feedback. This is a voluntary industry framework. The supplied material cites no FDA, ONC, civil-rights, or state statutory requirement that mandates it.

No supplied study examines who uses AI feedback or incident-reporting channels, so the evidence does not show whether patients with limited English proficiency, disabilities, low literacy, or limited digital access are underrepresented in these reports. The size of any gap remains unmeasured.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare the demographic and language profile of AI feedback and incident reports against the population served by the tool. Such studies would also need to test whether barrier audits, followed by changes such as interpreter-supported or non-digital reporting options, increase reporting from excluded groups and lead to earlier detection of harms.
underserved_note: No supplied study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, because no study was supplied at all. Health systems therefore have no empirical estimate of how often these groups are missed by current feedback channels or whether an evaluation would change that.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether presenting screening AI performance as expected true- and false-positive patient counts at intended-population prevalence, compared with standard care, changes how users judge the tool or act on its output. One emergency department study of 48 patients reported sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 92% alongside a positive predictive value of 33%, and the gap between these figures may have contributed to users' removal of the tool.

perspectives.view: No included study compares count-based presentation at local prevalence with relative metrics or any other format. The single available study is a descriptive, cross-sectional report of 48 patients, and it documents the hazard rather than testing the practice. Certainty that the practice improves interpretation cannot be rated, so it is classed as no direct evidence.

The emergency department study found a false discovery rate of 67%, meaning two of every three positive flags were wrong at that site's prevalence. Users who expected accuracy near the reported 92% specificity perceived the tool as unreliable. The study suggests that misreading metrics can cause abandonment as well as overtrust, but it does not show that counts would prevent either.

In a real deployment, clinicians discontinued a tool whose headline sensitivity and specificity did not match the positive predictive value they experienced. This observation suggests that performance summaries not matched to local prevalence may set expectations that the workflow then contradicts. Whether count-based displays would be read correctly at the point of care has not been studied.

FDA's draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions describes this format and gives a worked example of 0.8 false positives per true positive, compared with standard care and with a worst case of 4. The guidance is a draft and describes the approach rather than requiring it, and no cited study evaluates its effect.

The one deployment study ended with removal of the tool after users judged it inaccurate at a 33% positive predictive value. This suggests that a purchase and implementation effort may be lost when expected local performance is not set out before go-live. The cost and staff time needed to produce prevalence-specific counts for each site have not been measured.

research_gap: Studies are needed that randomize clinicians or patients to count-based presentation at intended-population prevalence versus sensitivity and specificity alone, and that measure accuracy of interpretation, trust calibration, tool retention, and downstream testing. These studies should also examine how developers and deployers obtain reliable local prevalence estimates and how often the counts must be updated as prevalence shifts.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the single hazard study of 48 emergency department patients in the United States did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or literacy characteristics. Prevalence often differs in safety-net populations, so counts calculated for one population may misstate expected false positives in another. The effect of count-based formats on low-literacy or limited English proficiency users is unknown.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether checking language support before adopting an ambient scribe improves documentation quality for patients who speak languages other than English. Six hazard studies suggest that scribe and speech tools perform worse in non-English and mixed-language encounters, which gives the recommendation a plausible rationale but no evidence of effect.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates pre-adoption language verification, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Six studies document the hazard. The largest, with 54,160 encounters, found non-English encounters were 21% to 25% less likely to reach the performance threshold. The others are small qualitative or offline studies, and their findings agree in direction but are indirect for the practice.

In 24 reenacted Mandarin–English and Spanish–English visits, overall error rates were low, but Mandarin–English transcripts often dropped words at language switch points. Whisper's word error rate rose from 18.4% on standard Persian clinical speech to 28.7% in heavy code-switching. Such deletions may omit clinical details from notes, and no study shows whether pre-adoption checks catch them.

Clinicians in Singapore (n=28) and U.S. physicians (n=22) described limited multilingual function as a barrier during real deployments. These reports suggest that language gaps appear in daily workflow after rollout. Neither study examined whether vendor testing or local validation before purchase would have predicted the problem.

The 54,160-encounter study included safety-net and non-English populations and found lower performance for non-English encounters. A separate test found ChatGPT answers in English more accurate and practical than answers in Chinese (all Ps<.001), though that study concerns chatbot responses rather than scribes. No study reports results for low-literacy patients or tests whether verification narrows the gap.

Physicians reported limited function with non-English speaking patients as a barrier to use. This may mean these patients are less likely to benefit from scribe tools or more likely to receive notes with errors. No study asked patients with limited English proficiency about their experience or measured their trust in scribe-generated notes.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare scribe deployments with and without pre-adoption language validation and that measure note accuracy, omissions, and clinician editing time by patient language. These studies should include low-literacy patients and languages beyond Mandarin, Spanish, and Persian.
underserved_note: One real-deployment study included safety-net and non-English encounters, and three offline studies included non-English or mixed-language speech, but none tested the verification practice. Medicaid and low-literacy populations were not reported. The hazard evidence therefore covers some limited English proficiency groups, yet it cannot show whether verification protects them.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether delivering AI-use disclosures in culturally and linguistically appropriate formats improves patient understanding or decisions. Five sources endorse the practice, and two offline studies suggest that machine translation of patient documents, one way a system might produce such disclosures, can introduce errors.

perspectives.view: No study in this set tests the practice. Support rests on one guidance document and four commentaries. The two available studies are offline, level 4 designs that examine the translation quality of discharge instructions and consent forms rather than the disclosure of AI use. They are indirect to the recommendation and cannot establish benefit.

In one offline study, Microsoft Copilot and Google Translate produced five potentially harmful errors in translated discharge instructions, and ChatGPT-4 produced none. In another, AI-translated Spanish consent forms scored 3.32 to 4.89 on equivalence, compared with 4.99 for certified translations. If disclosures are machine translated without review, the disclosure itself may carry errors.

The consent-form study rated three documents with two physician raters, and its authors judged AI translation unsuitable for clinical deployment without human review. This suggests that producing disclosures in many languages may require certified translators or bilingual reviewers. No study here has measured the staffing cost of that work.

Both hazard studies examined documents intended for patients with limited English proficiency, and one was set in a safety-net context. Neither measured whether patients understood AI-use disclosures. The studies show that translation quality varies by tool, but they do not address low-literacy formats, cultural adaptation beyond word-for-word translation, or the full range of languages patients speak.

Patients with limited English proficiency depend on translated text to learn that AI shaped their care. One endorsing commentary also calls for interpreter-accessible digital supports and staff-assisted intake, which would give patients a person to ask. No study reports how patients received or trusted a translated disclosure.

research_gap: No study has compared translated or culturally adapted AI-use disclosures with English-only or standard disclosures on patient comprehension, trust, or decision outcomes. Studies should test disclosure formats with limited English proficiency and low-literacy patients in real clinical settings. They should also measure translation error rates with and without human review and report the costs of each approach.
underserved_note: Neither study tested the practice. The two hazard studies addressed limited English proficiency populations, one in a safety-net setting and one with a racial and ethnic minority focus, but both were offline and examined document translation rather than disclosure. No study included low-literacy or Medicaid-specific samples, so effects for those groups remain unknown.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether expandable digital formats, visualizations, or user-centered research make model cards and labeling easier for nontechnical users to understand. The recommendation currently rests on one FDA draft guidance that encourages dynamic labeling and one NIST framework whose quoted text addresses error tracking rather than labeling design.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The claim that dense documentation confuses nontechnical users is plausible, but the supplied material does not measure comprehension under any labeling format.

The FDA draft guidance states that sponsors should consider dynamic labeling when possible, which lends partial support to expandable digital formats. The NIST Generative AI Profile passage concerns recording errors, near-misses, and negative impacts, and it does not speak to visualization or audience-centered design. Neither source is binding, since one is draft guidance and the other is a voluntary framework.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare static technical model cards with expandable, visual, or co-designed formats and measure whether clinicians, administrators, and patients correctly identify intended use, performance limits, and known failure conditions. Such studies should also test whether better comprehension changes decisions about when to rely on or override a model.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that labeling designed for a general audience will be understood by their staff or patients, and they would need to conduct their own usability testing.

bottom_line: Eight sources endorse accessible AI interfaces and reasonable accommodations, but no supplied study tests whether these practices improve use or reduce harm for people with disabilities or diverse needs. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and framework guidance rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard. Six of the eight endorsements are commentaries, and the two frameworks use permissive "may" language. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without comparative data does not support a certainty rating, so the evidence base for this recommendation is empty.

NIST AI 600-1 lists accessibility and reasonable accommodations among governance actions that carry over from other AI systems to generative AI. The CHAI guide frames user-friendly interfaces as something a system may develop. Neither source reports data on whether these measures change access or outcomes for users with disabilities.

Several commentaries name lower literacy, disability, and multilingual needs as design targets for chatbots and patient-facing tools. Because no study was supplied, there is no evidence on whether accessible designs reach Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients or improve their experience.

research_gap: No supplied study compares accessible or accommodated AI interfaces with standard interfaces on task completion, comprehension, errors, or harm among patients with disabilities, limited literacy, or limited English proficiency. No study documents how often current AI tools exclude or harm these users. Evaluations that measure both the size of the hazard and the effect of specific features such as text-to-speech, captioning, plain-language output, and non-AI alternatives would give health systems a basis for setting priorities.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The endorsements name these groups as intended beneficiaries, but whether accessible AI interfaces serve them remains unmeasured.

bottom_line: One offline automated benchmark found that an AI interface passed WCAG 2.2 AA text criteria and that its met requirements rose from 14 to 38 after revision, but no study has tested whether pre-deployment accessibility verification changes access or outcomes for patients with disabilities. Two deployed chatbots received high usability ratings while still showing accessibility gaps, which suggests that satisfaction scores alone may not detect the problem.

perspectives.view: A single level 5 automated benchmark in a simulated setting tests the practice, and it measures interface conformance rather than patient outcomes. Certainty is very low because of indirectness, the absence of real users with disabilities, no comparison group, and no replication. The two hazard studies show that gaps exist but do not test verification itself.

One deployed tool used 10-px text and a 2.56:1 contrast ratio while averaging a SUS near 92. Another fall-risk chatbot rated highly for usability still left gaps for users with impairments. These findings suggest that inaccessible features can pass routine user acceptance checks and reach patients unless someone measures them against a standard.

The benchmark shows that automated conformance checks can be run and repeated during development, with unmet requirements falling from 18 to 7. The study does not report the staff time, tooling, or manual review required, and automated checks covered text criteria only. How well this process fits a health system's procurement workflow remains untested.

The only study testing verification did not report enrolling limited English proficiency, Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users. The fall-risk chatbot study included limited English proficiency patients and older adults and found remaining accessibility gaps, which indicates that the populations at greatest risk of exclusion are absent from the test of the safeguard.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks deployers to confirm adherence to accessibility standards, and one commentary names WCAG 2.2 as the reference. These endorsements rest on expert consensus. The benchmark used WCAG 2.2 AA as its measure, which suggests that this standard can serve as a practical verification target, though no study links conformance to patient benefit.

Patients in the fall-risk chatbot study described accessibility gaps even though they found the QR interface easy to use. For patients with visual or motor impairments, a tool that others rate as usable may still be one they cannot operate. The evidence does not show whether verification restores their access or their path to a human.

research_gap: No study has compared AI tools that underwent pre-deployment accessibility verification with tools that did not, using outcomes such as task completion, error rates, or abandonment among patients with visual, motor, cognitive, or hearing impairments in real deployments. Studies should also measure how much automated checks miss relative to manual testing with disabled users, and what verification costs a health system.
underserved_note: The single study that tested the practice did not report including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study included limited English proficiency patients and older adults and found accessibility gaps, so the populations most likely to be excluded are documented as affected but are not represented in any test of whether verification helps them.

bottom_line: Four sources endorse plain-language explanations of an AI model's development, purpose, limitations, safety risks, and underrepresented subpopulations, but no supplied study tests whether such explanations reduce over-reliance or misuse. The recommendation currently rests on one framework and three commentaries.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard. The four endorsements include one assurance framework and three commentaries, and none reports outcome data. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement of this kind does not establish certainty that the practice changes user behavior or patient outcomes.

One commentary proposes a layered facts label written at a 6th-grade reading level to account for varying health and technical literacy. This design choice addresses low-literacy users on paper, but no supplied study measures comprehension or behavior among low-literacy, limited English proficiency, or Medicaid populations.

research_gap: No supplied study compares plain-language model explanations against technical documentation or no documentation. Needed tests would measure whether clinicians and patients understand the stated limitations, whether their reliance on AI output changes appropriately, and whether errors tied to misapplication decline. Such studies should also test reading-level targets and translated versions.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. One commentary targets a 6th-grade reading level and another addresses low- and middle-income settings, but whether plain-language explanations work for these groups remains unmeasured.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether language-stratified evaluation of ambient documentation detects or reduces errors, and the one study classed as testing the practice measured chatbot engagement rather than note quality. Hazard studies, including one of 54,160 outpatient encounters, suggest that ambient scribe performance can be lower in non-English encounters, which gives the recommendation a plausible rationale.

perspectives.view: The only study linked to the practice compared chatbot engagement in 1,282 limited English proficiency and English-primary patients and found 12.3 vs 12.2 text responses (P = .959). It stratified by language but did not assess ambient documentation, so indirectness is serious. With one study and no outcome on note accuracy, certainty is very low.

In a scripted study of 2,302 sessions, serious note errors rose from 7% to 10% to 15% as language resources became scarcer, while note generation alone showed no gradient. This suggests errors may enter at transcription, a stage that aggregate metrics can hide. No study shows that stratified monitoring catches these errors before they reach the chart.

A study of 54,160 outpatient encounters linked language to the share of unedited AI-generated words and found non-English encounters 21% to 25% less likely to meet the performance threshold. This suggests stratified analysis can run on routine deployment data. Results elsewhere vary, with Arabic notes scoring 4.53 vs 4.77 (P=.06) and simulated AI notes outscoring clinician notes in five languages.

The 54,160-encounter study included safety-net and non-English patients and found no difference between interpreter-mediated and bilingual provider encounters. In reenacted conversations, median mixed error rate was 9% for Mandarin-English, with outliers at 67%. In a UK survey of 141 GP scribe users, 31% named non-English encounters as an error setting. Language-specific reporting may reveal gaps a binary split hides.

The largest hazard study used an outcome, the share of unedited AI-generated words, that health systems may be able to compute from existing logs once encounter language is recorded. No study reports the cost or staff time of capturing language metadata or running stratified reviews, so the resource burden remains unmeasured.

When 400 machine translations of medical text were checked, 4% contained potentially harmful errors, and 9% of Russian translations did. Patients who speak less common languages may bear more of the error burden. Stratified evaluation could make that burden visible, but no study measures whether it improves patient safety or trust.

research_gap: No study has compared ambient documentation deployments with and without language-stratified monitoring to see whether stratification leads to detection and correction of errors in non-English notes. Studies are needed that capture encounter language, report error rates by specific language and interpreter use, track whether findings change vendor configuration, clinician review, or patient outcomes, and report the cost of doing so.
underserved_note: The one study classed as testing the practice included limited English proficiency patients but measured chatbot engagement, not documentation accuracy. Safety-net data appear only in a hazard study, and no test included Medicaid or low-literacy populations, so health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that stratified evaluation works for them.

bottom_line: One industry framework, the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, recommends that deployment risk assessments account for end users who lack the background to understand AI output accuracy, risks, and limitations. No study supplied here tests this practice or documents the hazard it targets, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus alone.

perspectives.view: No study tests whether adding user-understanding risk to deployment assessments changes how outputs are interpreted or used, and no study documents the size of the hazard. Under GRADE conventions the certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation reflects a single framework's judgment rather than tested effect.

The sole endorsement comes from the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide, a voluntary industry framework that uses "should" language. The supplied material contains no statute, FDA guidance, or ONC rule that requires this item in a risk assessment. Health systems that adopt it would do so as a voluntary practice.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without a documented assessment of user background and literacy, measuring misinterpretation of AI outputs, override errors, and downstream patient harm. Baseline studies that measure how often clinicians and patients misread AI accuracy and limitation statements would also establish whether the hazard is common enough to warrant routine assessment.
underserved_note: No study was supplied, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The recommendation's concern with users who lack background knowledge may apply with particular force to these groups, but the evidence base offers no information on how the practice performs for them.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether culturally adapted AI disclosures improve patient understanding or trust, and no study documents how often current disclosures fail culturally diverse patients. The recommendation rests on one professional guidance document and one regional commentary.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The two endorsements are a guidance statement and a commentary focused on cosmetic surgery in the Middle East and North Africa. Neither reports data, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the size of any benefit remains unknown.

The recommendation targets culturally and linguistically diverse patients, yet no supplied study measured disclosure comprehension in any population. Health systems therefore lack evidence on which adaptations, such as translation, plain-language rewriting, or community review, change understanding for the groups most likely to be misserved.

research_gap: Trials or controlled comparisons are needed that test culturally and linguistically adapted AI disclosures against standard disclosures, measuring patient comprehension, trust, and decisions about care. Descriptive studies are also needed to establish how often current AI disclosures are misunderstood across cultural and language groups.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Systems serving these groups would be adopting the practice on the strength of expert opinion alone and may wish to evaluate their own disclosures locally.

bottom_line: One randomized trial of 2,113 participants in China found that early user-needs work identified a need among older adults for explicit guidance to start interactions with the tool, which supports the practice. Four sources endorse the practice, including FDA draft guidance, but the evidence rests on a single study conducted outside the United States.

perspectives.view: A single randomized trial (n=2113) in a real deployment supports the practice. Certainty is low for three reasons. One study cannot show consistency. The report describes a needs-identification finding rather than a measured effect on outcomes. The Chinese setting limits directness for US health systems. No study documenting the hazard was supplied.

The trial found that older adults required explicit guidance to begin interactions, and design reviews without user input may miss needs of this kind. The supplied evidence does not show whether acting on the finding reduced errors, automation bias, or harm. The safety benefit therefore remains an inference.

The needs assessment took place within a real deployment, which suggests it can run alongside routine use. The report does not describe how often needs were reassessed during design, how much staff time the work required, or how the findings changed the tool. Fidelity and burden therefore cannot be judged.

The trial enrolled older, rural, low health literacy, non-English-speaking, and minority participants, who are the groups the recommendation aims to protect. It was conducted in China and included no US Medicaid or safety-net setting. How well the findings transfer to those US populations is uncertain.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software states that understanding users' needs and limitations should occur early in development and may be repeated. CHAI treats the practice as a must for patient-facing tools. These sources are endorsements, and the single supplied trial gives limited empirical support for their specific requirements.

Older adults in the trial needed explicit prompts to start using the tool. This suggests that some patients may be unable to begin an interaction without that help. The trial does not report whether patients could reach a human when the tool did not meet their needs.

research_gap: No study compared tools built with and without human factors methods on usability, error rates, automation bias, or patient harm. No study tested whether reassessing users' needs repeatedly across the design cycle adds value beyond a single early assessment. Trials in US Medicaid, safety-net, and limited English proficiency populations have not been reported.
underserved_note: The one trial included participants with low health literacy, non-English language, rural residence, minority status, and older age. It was conducted in China and did not involve US Medicaid or safety-net settings. The finding may inform design for similar groups, but US health systems serving these populations lack direct evidence.

bottom_line: No study tests whether evaluating AI on non-standard dialects, accents, colloquialisms, or low-literacy inputs improves accuracy or safety once a tool is deployed. Twenty-two hazard studies, most of them simulations or benchmarks, report performance gaps for these inputs in many settings, while several report small or no gaps.

perspectives.view: No included study compares deployments with and without this kind of subgroup testing. The 22 hazard studies are mostly level 4 and 5 simulations and benchmarks with inconsistent results. One UK scribe study found no accent differences, and one Indian benchmark found gaps of up to 24 points. These studies show the problem exists but not that testing fixes it.

Triage accuracy fell by up to 24 points for romanized queries, with an estimated nearly 2 million excess triage errors at one organization. Nepali-to-English translation distorted meaning in 17.1% of utterances. Swiss German raised word error rate to 17.66%, yet triage accuracy stayed at 90-100%. This suggests testing may need to measure downstream clinical outputs as well as transcription error.

Results differed by model even within the same language. On Kinyarwanda encounters, o3 reached 97.9% accuracy and Gemini 2.5-Flash reached 47.3%. The 8-billion-parameter Llama 3.1 model scored 67.8% in English and 31.4% in Chinese, while qwen2.5 models scored similarly in both. These results suggest that a test of one model or version may not carry over to another.

Whisper showed a word error rate disparity of 11.0 for non-native English speakers. ChatGPT gave more accurate answers to questions phrased at high language proficiency, which may serve as a proxy for literacy. A youth slang benchmark found a 10-14 point comprehension gap. None of these studies enrolled low-health-literacy patients directly.

A regulatory discussion paper lists consistency across dialects, accents, colloquialisms, and literacy levels as an element to consider, including escalation and refusal behavior. It is a discussion paper and does not set a binding requirement. None of the supplied studies measures compliance with it or its effect.

In Kinyarwanda, LLM responses degraded slightly but cost over 500 times less per response than local clinicians. In Korean nursing notes, 70.83% of sentences contained code-switched terms that required normalization. Building test sets may therefore require locally sourced language samples. No study reports the staff time or cost of doing this testing.

Phonological speech impairment markedly reduced scribe word recognition. An English keyword search returned zero results for Pashto queries. Patients whose speech or language falls outside the training data may receive incomplete or empty outputs without knowing it. One commentary recommends that community health workers and cultural mediators take part in validation.

research_gap: Studies should compare AI deployments that did and did not receive pre-deployment testing on dialect, accent, colloquial, and low-literacy inputs. They should measure whether testing detected failures, whether it changed model selection or configuration, and whether patient-level errors fell afterward. They should also report the cost and staffing needed to build and maintain local test sets.
