underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Several hazard studies involved limited English proficiency, rural, or low-income groups, mostly in Rwanda, Nepal, India, and Pakistan. Only one examined low-proficiency phrasing, and it did not enroll patients. The evidence therefore does not show whether testing protects US Medicaid, safety-net, or low-health-literacy patients.

bottom_line: Two sources endorse delivering AI training in multiple formats and languages, but no supplied study tests whether doing so improves user understanding, safe use, or patient outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and commentary alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests accessible training formats, and no study documents the hazard of inaccessible formats. The support consists of one consensus guideline and one commentary. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an effect estimate, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The FUTURE-AI guideline names English, Chinese, and Swahili as example languages, and the radiation therapy commentary suggests modules tailored to regional needs. Neither source reports data on whether users with limited English proficiency or low literacy were reached or whether their use of AI changed as a result.

research_gap: No supplied study measures whether multi-format or multilingual AI training changes clinician or staff comprehension, appropriate reliance on AI output, error rates, or patient outcomes compared with single-format training. Studies are also needed that document how often current training formats exclude intended users and which user groups are affected.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these populations have no direct evidence on which training formats work for their staff or for patient-facing users, and any adoption would proceed on consensus alone.

bottom_line: Three randomized trials suggest that user instruction may improve how people use AI tools, but they measured response quality and health awareness rather than safe-use outcomes, and none tested instructions for mental health chatbots. The case for this recommendation rests mainly on FDA labeling expectations, a Utah statute, and expert commentary.

perspectives.view: Three randomized trials test forms of user instruction. A deployed trial of 2,113 participants in China reported awareness scores of 2.95 with e-learning versus 2.34 without. Two simulated trials of 300 participants each found that prompting boosts improved response quality, and one reported quality still below optimal. Indirect outcomes and settings lower certainty to low.

The two simulated trials measured the quality of chatbot answers after users received prompting guidance. They did not measure harms, crisis recognition, or whether users stayed within safe-use limits. Better answers may lower some risk. No supplied study shows that instructions or disclaimers stop misuse before it reaches a patient.

Only the China trial took place in a real deployment, and it delivered structured e-learning rather than brief on-screen directions. The simulated trials used short prompting boosts, which suggests that light-touch guidance can shift user behavior. They did not report how often users read or retained the instructions in routine use.

The China trial enrolled rural, older, low-literacy, and non-English-speaking participants and found higher awareness scores with e-learning. This suggests that instruction can reach groups with fewer resources. The results may not carry over to American Medicaid or safety-net patients, who differ in language, health system, and access to technology.

FDA draft guidance says device manufacturers are required to provide labeling with adequate directions for use. Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbots to put user safety ahead of engagement metrics. These sources create obligations for AI tools that qualify as devices and for chatbots in Utah. Neither source cites trial evidence on whether instructions work.

Commentators ask that users understand what a chatbot can and cannot do and be told to seek human help when in distress. The supplied trials did not test disclaimers or referral to a human. Whether instructions help a distressed person reach care remains untested.

research_gap: No supplied trial tested safe-use instructions or disclaimers for mental health chatbots, and none measured misuse, missed crises, harm, or contact with a human clinician. No study documenting the hazard was supplied. Trials in clinical deployments in the United States should compare instruction formats against safety outcomes rather than response quality alone.
underserved_note: The China trial included limited English or non-English, low health literacy, rural, older adult, and racial or ethnic minority participants. No trial included Medicaid or safety-net populations in the United States. The UK and German trials reported no underserved subgroups, so there is little basis for judging whether instructions work for low-literacy or limited English proficiency users in American care settings.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether writing AI disclosures, consent records, or privacy notices in plain language improves patient understanding. One review found that 14% of 114 AI trial consent documents met brevity and readability thresholds, while a simulation found most patients rated AI labels easy to read.

perspectives.view: No study compares plain-language disclosures with standard versions, so the practice itself has no direct evidence. The two available studies describe the hazard and point in different directions. One is a descriptive review of documents, and the other relies on self-reported comprehension in a vignette, which may overstate actual understanding.

Of 114 consent documents from AI trials, 16 (14%) were both under 15,000 characters and had a SMOG score under 13. Higher-risk trials were no more readable (P>.05). This suggests that patients in riskier AI studies may receive consent material they cannot follow. No study has tested whether shorter documents reduce misunderstanding.

A vignette study of 340 patients focused on racial and ethnic minority participants. In that study, 86.7% said the labels were easy to read and 84.2% said they were easy to understand. Self-report may miss comprehension gaps among patients with low literacy or limited English proficiency. Neither study specifically enrolled those groups or Medicaid or safety-net patients.

The CHAI playbook observes that the HIPAA Privacy Rule already requires covered entities to distribute a clear, user-friendly notice of privacy practices. The recommendation extends that expectation to AI disclosures and consent records. The supplied studies do not assess compliance. They also do not assess whether plain-language notices change what patients know or do.

Endorsing commentaries call for brief, just-in-time disclosures adapted to cognitive and digital literacy. They also ask for explicit explanations of withdrawal options and human oversight. The supplied evidence shows that lengthy consent documents are common in AI trials. It does not show that simpler versions help patients understand their rights or reach a human.

research_gap: Trials are needed that compare plain-language AI disclosures and consent forms with standard versions. Outcomes should include objective comprehension, recall of opt-out and withdrawal rights, and staff time required. These trials should enroll patients with limited English proficiency or low health literacy.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The one hazard study with a stated population focus enrolled racial and ethnic minority patients. Neither study included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups, so the effect of plain-language disclosures for patients most likely to struggle with technical text remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether accessible-format AI transparency materials improve understanding or access for patients with disabilities, and no study documents the hazard. The single endorsing source addresses documentation of patient opt-outs rather than accessible formats, so support for this recommendation rests on inference rather than direct evidence.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated without direct tests. The one endorsement, a CHAI framework, states that opt-out requests should be documented and flagged for the care team. That statement does not speak to material formats or disability access.

The only supplied source is a voluntary governance framework using "should" language, and its quoted text concerns opt-out documentation. The supplied material contains no endorsement that directly addresses accessible formats for AI disclosures. Administrators may therefore find that this recommendation lacks a source-specific basis in the evidence map and must justify it on other grounds.

research_gap: No study has measured whether patients with visual, hearing, cognitive, or motor disabilities can locate, read, and understand AI transparency materials, or whether providing alternative formats such as screen-reader-compatible text, large print, audio, sign language video, or plain-language versions changes comprehension, opt-out rates, or trust. Studies are also needed to document how often current AI disclosures fail basic accessibility checks.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Patients with disabilities who also have limited English proficiency or low literacy may face compounded barriers, and the absence of data means health systems cannot yet judge which formats reach these groups.

bottom_line: One simulated randomized trial in Denmark with 992 patients found that an explanatory intervention raised trust by 4 to 5 percentage points and lowered distrust by 3 to 4 points compared with controls. No study measured whether plain-language materials improve patients' understanding of AI use or AI-generated information in real care.

perspectives.view: The only test is a randomized trial with 992 participants, which starts as strong evidence. Certainty falls to low because the setting was simulated, the outcomes were trust and distrust rather than comprehension, and a single study cannot show consistency. The effects were small (mean differences of 3% to 5%), with p-values between 0.0096 and 0.022.

The trial ran offline, so it does not show how explainers perform when delivered through patient portals, visit summaries, or clinic staff. Uptake, reading rates, and the effort needed to keep materials current as AI tools change remain unmeasured.

The trial suggests patients who received explanations trusted AI-supported decisions slightly more and distrusted them slightly less. Trust is a different outcome from understanding, and the study did not report whether patients could explain what the AI did or knew how to reach a clinician with questions.

Both endorsements come from voluntary CHAI frameworks. One lists plain-language explainers as an example a system may use, and the other describes educational resources without setting a requirement. Neither source ties the practice to a federal or state mandate.

research_gap: Trials in live clinical settings should test whether plain-language explainers and FAQs improve patients' comprehension of AI use and AI-generated information, and should measure trust calibration, question-asking, and requests to speak with a clinician alongside trust scores.
underserved_note: The single trial enrolled Danish patients in a simulated setting and did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Whether plain-language materials work for the patients most likely to struggle with technical content therefore remains untested.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether designing AI device communications around information load, user familiarity, interaction frequency, and information placement improves user understanding. One vignette study of 340 patients found that 63.9% reported that reading AI labels was not too mentally demanding, which suggests the hazard may not affect most readers in that setting.

perspectives.view: No study compares communications designed with these four considerations against usual designs, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study used simulated vignettes in the United States with 340 patients. It measured perceived mental demand rather than comprehension, which limits its directness to the recommendation.

In the vignette study, 63.9% of patients reported that reading AI labels was not too mentally demanding. The study did not test whether patients understood key content or acted on it correctly. Perceived ease may not show whether important warnings are missed, so the safety effect of information placement and volume remains unmeasured.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions states that additional information may detract from understanding, and FUTURE-AI calls for adjusting explanations for each end-user subgroup. Both are guidance documents using should language. The FDA text is a draft and does not create binding requirements, and neither source cites outcome data for this design approach.

The one hazard study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients and found that 63.9% did not find AI labels too mentally demanding. It did not report results for patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy, who may be the users most affected by dense or poorly placed information.

research_gap: Trials or usability studies are needed that compare AI device labels and interface text designed around information load, prior familiarity, interaction frequency, and placement against standard designs. These studies should measure comprehension and correct use in real clinical settings rather than self-reported mental demand in vignettes.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice. The single hazard study included a racial and ethnic minority focus but did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence does not show whether these groups experience information overload from AI device communications or whether design changes would help them.

bottom_line: Three randomized trials suggest that structured AI or eHealth literacy education may raise literacy scores and knowledge and reduce overconfidence and intended risky chatbot use, though all measured short-term surrogate outcomes. Whether this education prevents harm from AI or online misinformation has not been tested.

perspectives.view: Three trials tested education, two in real deployment in China and one simulated in Australia, and all favored it. Certainty is low because outcomes were surrogates and the interventions differed. In the Chinese caregiver trial, the eHEALS difference was 1.73 at T1 and 2.40 at T2, but the group-by-time interaction was nonsignificant (P=.26).

In the Australian trial, brief animation or image interventions lowered intention to ask ChatGPT higher-risk questions (M=2.42 and 2.69 vs 3.12 for control) and left lower-risk intentions unchanged. A survey in Northern Cyprus found that AI delayed doctor visits for 22.5% of users. No trial measured delayed care or harm, so the safety benefit remains inferred.

The largest trial enrolled 2113 participants in a real deployment and found that e-learning narrowed the gap between self-rated and objective health awareness (0.83 vs 1.37, P<0.001). None of the trials reported staff time, delivery cost, or how education fit into clinical workflows, so fidelity and burden at scale are unknown.

The 2113-participant trial in China included rural, older, low health literacy, racial or ethnic minority, and non-English-speaking participants. No trial enrolled Medicaid or US safety-net patients. The results may not transfer to US populations whose language access, device access, and trust in institutions differ.

In the Northern Cyprus survey, 73.7% of 2825 patients and companions used AI for health questions and 47.5% were unsure whether to trust it. The Australian trial found that education lowered trust in ChatGPT. Lower trust may protect patients if it prompts them to contact a clinician, but no trial tested whether they did.

research_gap: No trial has tested whether AI literacy education reduces patient harm or delayed care, or whether it increases contact with clinicians. None was conducted in a US health system or measured delivery cost and staff burden. Trials with longer follow-up and behavioral or clinical outcomes would address these gaps.
underserved_note: One trial of 2113 participants in China included limited or non-English-speaking, low health literacy, rural, older, and minority participants and found reduced overconfidence. No test included Medicaid or safety-net populations. The finding suggests education may reach low-literacy groups, but its effect in US safety-net settings is untested.

bottom_line: No study tests whether preparing physicians to counsel patients about consumer generative AI changes what patients do or reduces harm from inaccurate AI advice. The only supplied study documents the hazard: a simulation of five stroke questions found that most chatbot answers scored below a competency threshold of 60.

perspectives.view: Five sources endorse the practice. One is a guidance document and four are commentaries, and none reports outcome data. No study tests counseling or physician preparation. The single hazard study is a level 4 offline simulation of five questions in Taiwan. It shows that a problem exists and cannot show that counseling solves it, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence.

In the hazard study, most chatbot scores for patient-facing stroke advice fell below 60, and scores above that threshold typically reached only 60 to 65. Stroke care is time-sensitive, so poor advice may delay treatment. Counseling acts only when a patient reaches a clinician, and no data show whether it catches errors before patients act on them.

The one hazard study used five questions in an offline setting and reported no patient population. It gives no information on how Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients use chatbots or respond to physician counseling.

research_gap: Trials or controlled implementation studies should test whether physician training in AI counseling changes patient reliance on chatbot advice, time to appropriate care, and harm events. They should also measure the effect on visit time and clinician workload.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the hazard study did not include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems therefore have no evidence on whether counseling reaches or helps these patients.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether measuring user satisfaction with the clarity of AI information improves clarity, use, or patient outcomes, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on one federal framework and one commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements express expert opinion and do not supply comparative data on whether clarity measurement changes design decisions or user outcomes.

NIST AI 600-1 advises verifying the adequacy of generative AI user instructions through user testing. This is voluntary guidance rather than a binding FDA or ONC requirement. A second source, a commentary, calls for regular usability audits with validated instruments. Neither source specifies a satisfaction metric or a threshold for action.

No supplied study measured clarity satisfaction among patients or clinicians in any population. Satisfaction surveys that are offered only in English or at a high reading level may miss the users most likely to find AI output unclear. The current evidence cannot show whether this measurement reaches those groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without structured clarity feedback and that track whether the feedback leads to interface or content changes, higher comprehension, fewer errors, or lower rates of users abandoning the tool. Such studies should also test which validated instruments detect clarity problems in clinical settings.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether clarity measurement captures their experience, and any measurement they adopt would need translated, plain-language instruments to avoid excluding those users.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether separate patient- and caregiver-facing labeling for AI tools improves understanding, safe use, or decisions, and no study documents the hazard directly. The recommendation currently rests on an FDA draft guidance and the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide, both of which use 'should' language.

perspectives.view: No studies test the practice and no studies document the hazard, so the certainty rating is no direct evidence. The two endorsements reflect expert and regulatory judgment rather than measured outcomes. A claim that tailored labeling improves comprehension or safe use of AI tools would require comparative testing against clinician-oriented documentation.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions asks sponsors either to provide patient- and caregiver-specific material or to explain how patients will understand device use and output. The document is a draft and does not bind sponsors. The CHAI guide asks deployers to decide whether patients and clinicians receive the same documentation.

The CHAI guide names health literacy as a reason to consider separate materials, while the FDA draft text supplied here does not mention it. No supplied study measures comprehension among low-literacy, limited English proficiency, Medicaid, or safety-net patients, so health systems lack evidence on which formats, reading levels, or languages would serve these groups.

research_gap: Studies should compare patient-tailored AI labeling with clinician-oriented documentation, measuring comprehension, correct use of device output, and decision quality, and should report how often patients currently receive documentation they cannot understand.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The health-literacy rationale stated in the CHAI guide remains untested in the groups it is meant to protect.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether evaluating user understanding of AI provenance labels, with feedback analyzed by literacy level, improves understanding or reduces misattribution of AI-generated content. One small simulated study found that nearly half of 30 adult portal users could not identify AI as the writer of a draft, which shows the hazard exists but does not show that this evaluation practice corrects it.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is qualitative, simulated, and small (n=30). It documents misunderstanding of AI origin disclosure but provides no comparison of deployers who evaluate label comprehension against those who do not.

In a simulated portal setting, nearly half of 30 participants did not recognize that AI wrote the draft. Patients who believe a clinician wrote a message may give it more weight than they would give machine text. Comprehension testing could surface this failure before deployment, though no study shows that it prevents harm.

The hazard study does not report participant literacy, language, or insurance status, so it cannot show whether misunderstanding differs by literacy level. The recommendation's call to stratify feedback by literacy addresses a plausible gap, but no data yet describe how low-literacy or limited English proficiency patients read provenance labels.

The only endorsement, NIST AI 600-1, asks deployers to evaluate vulnerabilities to circumvention of safety measures. That language supports periodic evaluation in general but does not name provenance label comprehension or literacy stratification. The link between the endorsement and this specific practice is indirect.

Nearly half of participants in one study could not tell that AI had written a portal draft. Patients have a stake in knowing who wrote what they read. Asking patients whether labels make sense is a direct way to check this, though its effect on trust and understanding has not been measured.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare label designs or comprehension-testing programs against usual practice in live patient portals, measure correct identification of AI authorship as the outcome, and report results stratified by health literacy and preferred language.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study of 30 United States adult portal users did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or literacy characteristics. As a result, there is no evidence on how these populations interpret AI provenance labels or whether literacy-stratified evaluation would detect differences.

bottom_line: Three simulated studies with 20 to 340 participants suggest that testing AI outputs with intended users can surface comprehension problems that clinician proxies and self-rated clarity may miss, but none stratified results by health literacy or measured escalation. Certainty that the practice prevents misunderstanding or missed escalation is very low.

perspectives.view: Three level 4 studies tested user comprehension, all in offline or simulated settings, with 20 to 340 participants. None stratified results by health literacy, and none measured whether users knew when to escalate. The designs, sample sizes, and indirect outcomes lead to a very low certainty rating that comprehension testing across literacy levels reduces misunderstanding.

In one hazard study, 89.5% to 95.7% of lay raters called summaries clear, yet 63.0% to 87.4% answered comprehension questions correctly. A French trial of 2,727 participants found lay summaries did not raise comprehension (58.3% vs 59.4%). Self-rated ease, as used in the 340-patient label study, may therefore overstate understanding, and objective checks may catch more errors.

In the UK study, 119 women and 29 clinicians rated the same chatbot responses differently in postpartum care. Comprehensibility favored women (p=0.012) and readability favored clinicians (p=0.008). In Denmark, revising a questionnaire after face validation with 20 patients raised ChatGPT-4 understandability from 4 to 5. Both findings suggest clinician proxies may not substitute for intended users.

A Chinese study of 320 reports found an age by education interaction on comprehension of simplified reports, and lower education was linked to lower comprehension (P<0.05). The practice tests included non-English speakers in Denmark and a racial and ethnic minority focus in the United States. None reported results by literacy or enrolled Medicaid or safety-net patients.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks developers to validate that intended users can functionally understand key information. NIST AI 600-1 calls for verifying user instructions through user testing, and a regulatory discussion paper names health literacy and escalation explicitly. The supplied studies do not show whether meeting these expectations changes patient outcomes.

No supplied study asked patients whether they knew when to contact a clinician or how to reach one after reading an AI output. In the French trial, comprehension of normal reports was lower with lay summaries (72.5% vs 76.6%, P = .001). This result suggests patients may misread results without anyone detecting the error.

research_gap: No study compared tested and untested AI outputs on downstream errors or escalation behavior. No study stratified comprehension by measured health literacy, and none was conducted in live deployment. Future work should use objective comprehension and escalation measures, enroll users across literacy levels, and report results by subgroup.
underserved_note: One practice test included non-English-speaking patients (Denmark, n=20), and one focused on racial and ethnic minority patients (United States, n=340). No test enrolled Medicaid or safety-net populations, and none stratified by literacy. A hazard study found lower comprehension among less-educated and older users, so it remains unknown whether comprehension testing detects failures in the groups most likely to experience them.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether pre-specifying equity objectives, fairness metrics, and priority subgroups improves the detection of disparities, and no supplied study documents the hazard directly. Support for R302 rests on seven endorsements from frameworks, guidance, and commentary, two of which rate it as a must.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The seven endorsements reflect expert agreement, and agreement among frameworks is a different thing from empirical findings on whether pre-specification changes which disparities evaluators find.

Two frameworks, the CHAI Responsible AI Guide and HEAAL, state the practice as a must, and five sources rate it as a should. All seven are voluntary frameworks, guidance, or commentary. None of the supplied sources is a statute or regulation that requires documented fairness metric selection.

The NHS stroke imaging commentary calls for groups of interest that extend beyond one protected characteristic and allow for intersectionality and local context. No supplied study examines whether governance teams that pre-specify subgroups include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, or whether data for those groups are available to evaluate.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare fairness evaluations with and without pre-specified objectives, metrics, and subgroups, and that measure whether pre-specification changes which disparities are detected and acted on. Studies should also report how often governance teams find that evaluable subgroup data are missing and what they do in response.
underserved_note: No supplied study tests the practice in any population, so no evidence includes Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems cannot yet tell from evidence whether pre-specified subgroup lists capture these groups or whether the data needed to evaluate them exist.

bottom_line: Two offline studies that evaluated generative AI output aimed at lower-literacy readers both found that simplification lowered content quality or accuracy, which suggests such evaluation can detect a real performance gap. No study has tested whether developer evaluation of this kind leads to safer products for actual lower-literacy patients.

perspectives.view: Two studies evaluated performance for lower-literacy targets. A Chinese study of 360 texts found C-DISCERN quality fell in all 6 models (Qwen 57.0 to 40.5), and a US benchmark of 67 terms found accuracy fell from 4.56 to 3.99. Both were offline, rater-scored, and indirect for patient outcomes, so certainty is very low.

Hazard studies suggest the failures carry clinical weight. At a 7th-grade level, 20% of simplified radiology reports had potential management changes, and 21% of AI-simplified education materials fully preserved clinical content. Fourth-grade prompts omitted safety information. Under-triage near 100% across all literacy strata in one study suggests that comparing strata alone may miss a uniformly unsafe model.

Studies used different ways to represent lower literacy, including simplification prompts, simulated personas, and real lay users writing their own prompts. One simulation found that aggregate scores concealed variation across personas. Developers may need persona and paraphrase testing in addition to a single simplification prompt, because each method probes a different failure.

Both tests used simulated or target-level text rather than real lower-literacy patients. One test framed prompts for older adults in Chinese. Hazard studies in Turkish and French found lower performance than in English, which suggests literacy and language effects may compound for patients with limited English proficiency.

The sole endorsement is a regulatory discussion paper that describes paraphrase consistency across health literacy levels as a relevant consideration. It does not set a requirement, and no cited source establishes a testing standard or acceptance threshold for lower-literacy performance.

In a randomized study of 300 laypeople, higher education and more LLM experience were associated with better information quality, so patients with less schooling may receive weaker answers. Lower-literacy personas in another study preferred expert-written responses over chatbot responses. Patients may need a route to human-written material when AI output falls short.

research_gap: No study has tested whether developer evaluation for lower-literacy users changes model design or reduces harm, and no evaluation has enrolled actual lower-literacy patients, measured their comprehension and actions, or compared evaluation methods such as persona testing, paraphrase testing, and simplification prompts.
underserved_note: Both tests targeted low health literacy, and one also framed prompts for older adults in Chinese, but neither involved real patients, Medicaid enrollees, or safety-net settings. The findings therefore rest on expert-rated text and may not reflect how lower-literacy patients in underserved settings phrase questions or act on answers.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether a structured equity impact assessment before AI adoption reduces differential harm to subgroups, although several endorsing sources, including a multi-society radiology statement and a primary care commentary that describes a prospective health equity impact assessment tool, call for attention to disparities before deployment. One qualitative study of 13 academic medical centers found that only a minority of governance leaders reported considering inequity, racism, or bias.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single supplied study documents the hazard and does not evaluate an assessment. It is qualitative, with 17 interview participants from 13 academic medical centers, which limits directness and precision. The endorsements rest on expert consensus and commentary, not outcome data.

Interviews with 17 informatics leaders at 13 academic medical centers found that a minority reported weighing inequity, racism, or bias during AI governance. This suggests the gap the recommendation targets exists in practice. The study cannot show whether a pre-adoption assessment would change which tools are adopted or whether subgroup outcomes would improve.

The interview study found no consistent approach to equity review among academic centers building governance for predictive tools. That finding suggests assessments are not yet embedded in routine intake workflows. No supplied study measures the staff time, data requirements, or fidelity of a structured equity assessment when governance committees apply one to each tool.

The HEAAL framework advises organizations to track federal regulators, state attorneys general, and health departments, which may signal that oversight of AI in health care is evolving. The supplied sources do not cite a specific statute that requires pre-adoption equity assessment, and no study examines whether such assessments reduce legal or civil-rights exposure.

research_gap: No supplied study compares health systems or AI tools with and without a structured pre-adoption equity impact assessment. Future work could measure whether assessments change adoption decisions, alter tool configuration, or reduce performance gaps and outcome differences across racial, language, insurance, and literacy subgroups after deployment. It could also record the staff time and data such assessments require.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The one hazard study drew only on leaders at academic medical centers, did not include safety-net hospitals, and did not report on Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. How equity review functions in settings that serve these groups remains unmeasured, and those settings may have fewer resources to conduct it.

bottom_line: Fourteen frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries endorse documenting dataset provenance, metadata, and demographic attributes, and three studies show that missing race, ethnicity, or socioeconomic data prevented subgroup bias analysis. No study has tested whether documentation practices lead health systems or developers to detect or correct bias.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Three hazard studies consistently report that missing demographics limited fairness analysis. These are a descriptive deployment study, a retrospective replay, and an automated benchmark. They show that the problem occurs. They do not show that documentation or case-by-case missing-attribute handling solves it.

In one real deployment with 254 patients, race/ethnicity and socioeconomic status were not collected during routine device use. As a result, no one could check whether the device performed worse for any subgroup. A performance gap that is never measured cannot be caught before it reaches patients. Documentation may make such gaps visible, but that effect has not been tested.

In a Canadian cohort of 319,012 angiography outpatients, ethnicity was unknown for 57%. This suggests that routine data capture does not reliably record these fields. The endorsing guidance proposes datasheets and plain-language dataset factsheets. No supplied study reports the staff time, completeness, or fidelity of such documentation in real workflows.

An automated audit across 7 cohorts could not assess 30% of studies because race was never recorded. Two of the hazard studies focused on racial and ethnic minority populations. None reported Medicaid status, safety-net setting, language preference, or literacy. The attributes most relevant to those groups may therefore be absent even where race is captured.

The endorsements come from an assurance framework, consensus guidance including a multi-society radiology statement, and commentaries, all phrased at the should level. None of the supplied sources is a binding rule. No supplied study examines whether documentation expectations change developer or health-system behavior.

research_gap: No study compares settings that adopt structured dataset documentation with settings that do not. Such studies should measure demographic field completeness, the share of models that receive subgroup performance audits, and whether those audits detect performance gaps that are then corrected. Studies should also evaluate methods for handling missing attributes, such as record linkage or imputation, and report the workload these methods add for data and registration staff.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two hazard studies focused on racial and ethnic minority groups, but none reported insurance type, safety-net status, language, or literacy. Health systems serving these populations therefore have no evidence on whether documentation captures the attributes needed to assess bias for their patients.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether identifying data-poor subgroups and managing their AI-supported care changes model performance or patient outcomes. Two of three hazard studies found that missing data concentrated in disadvantaged groups and was linked to worse calibration or to audit blind spots, while the third found that discrimination held despite more missingness.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates the recommended practice, so the rating is no direct evidence. The three supplied studies document the hazard using offline designs at evidence levels 4 and 5. Their findings are inconsistent, with two reporting the hazard present and one reporting it absent. These studies describe the problem and do not test the remedy.

In a cohort of 406,230 patients, missingness was greater among underserved groups, with one laboratory measure (TC) missing in 52.2% of cases. Calibration was worse in the relaxed cohort, most of all in disadvantaged subgroups. Miscalibration may place patients in the wrong risk tier. No study shows whether a subgroup process catches these errors before they reach patients.

One offline study found that patients with moderate or low comorbidity burden had more missing laboratory data, yet missingness patterns within event cohorts were similar and discrimination held. Read alongside the calibration findings, this suggests that the amount of missing data alone may not flag affected subgroups. Checking calibration as well as discrimination may be needed. No study reports workflow burden.

A benchmark across 7 cohorts found that harm reached patients whose race was never recorded. An audit based on recorded demographics was blind to 30% of studies. A subgroup identification process that relies on recorded race or ethnicity may therefore miss the patients whose data are least complete.

The recommendation rests on a single endorsement, the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, which states it at the must level. No regulatory or statutory source was supplied that requires health systems to identify data-poor subgroups or to coordinate their care.

research_gap: No study compares health systems or units that identify subgroups with missing or poor-quality data and set up care-management processes for them against those that do not. Such studies should measure calibration by subgroup, rates of incorrect risk categorization, time to appropriate care, and staff burden. They should also test methods for finding affected patients when demographic fields such as race are unrecorded.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Among the hazard studies, one reported greater missingness in underserved and disadvantaged groups and one focused on racial and ethnic minority populations, but none reported results specific to Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether the recommended process works for their patients.

bottom_line: Randomized trials in real deployments suggest that plain-language AI versions of radiology and other reports improve patient comprehension, though a large simulated trial found no gain in tested comprehension. Simplified outputs often miss sixth-grade reading targets and sometimes drop content, so review for accuracy and completeness may be needed.

perspectives.view: Three randomized trials in real deployments, with 64 to 120 patients each, found that simplified reports raised patient comprehension; one reported quiz scores of 74.7% vs 54.7%. A fourth trial found clinician diagnostic understanding rose 9.0 points. A simulated trial of 2727 participants found no difference in objective comprehension (58.3% vs 59.4%). Small samples and inconsistency limit certainty to moderate.

Simplification may drop content. In one offline study a plain-language prompt lowered DISCERN treatment-information scores by 11.58 and 11.00 points and reduced completeness, and in another comprehensiveness ratings fell from 3.91 to 3.68. Tested comprehension of normal MRI reports fell from 76.6% to 72.5% with lay summaries. A cardiologist found none of 143 revised materials less accurate.

Automated simplification often misses target reading levels. Only 14 of 86 revised education materials and 2 of 25 simplified answers reached sixth-grade level. In routine use, 4 of 982 AI visit summaries met a sixth-grade benchmark, which documents the problem rather than testing a fix. One chatbot study found technical language produced larger knowledge gains (OR 2.73).

In a pre-post study of 698 pathology reports, doctor-patient communication time fell from 35 to 10 minutes with plain-language interpretations. A quasi-experimental study found median patient reading time fell from 7 to 2 minutes. Neither study reports cost, and no study measures the staff time needed to review simplified outputs before release.

A study in China with non-English-speaking patients found that simplified language and standardized formatting improved clarity (adjusted P=.02). An offline study of heart failure materials for low health literacy readers found median grade level fell from 10th to 7th. In a minority-focused survey, 35.0% of chatbot users reported they could not fully understand responses.

Patients favored plain-language versions, and 87.5% preferred an AI translation of their MRI report. In the large simulated trial, satisfaction and self-rated comprehension rose while tested comprehension did not change. In a hazard study, 83-90% of patients rated chatbot text as clear although it exceeded recommended reading levels. Self-reported clarity may overstate understanding.

research_gap: No trial measured downstream outcomes such as medication errors, follow-up adherence, or treatment decisions after patients read simplified outputs, and only one randomized trial tested clinician-facing summaries. Most trials examined radiology reports, so evidence for patient education materials and chatbot outputs rests on offline readability studies. Trials that pair objective comprehension with content-omission endpoints, and that compare clinician-reviewed with unreviewed simplification, are needed.
underserved_note: None of the randomized trials that tested plain-language simplification reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Among tests of the practice, three smaller or offline studies involved non-English or low health literacy contexts (pmid:42464799, epmc:PPR1312893, epmc:PPR937748), and two of them measured readability or rated clarity rather than tested comprehension. Two randomized studies that enrolled limited English or non-English patients (pmid:40162329, pmid:42425711) documented hard-to-read chatbot output but did not test simplification as a remedy. The comprehension gains seen in trials may therefore not carry over to patients with limited literacy or limited English.

bottom_line: One offline benchmark study suggests that tracing a subgroup performance gap to a specific bias source, here a self-reported outcome label, may account for most of that gap, but no study tested whether governance teams that systematically document bias sources produce safer or fairer tools. Seven hazard studies show that bias from labels, data composition, and historical practice exists and can shift who receives care.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice is a single automated benchmark using 642,205 BRFSS 2015 respondents. It attributed 89% of the sex true positive rate gap (95% CI 0.65 to 0.99) to the self-reported survey outcome. Certainty is very low because the design is offline, the result is unreplicated, and the method studied is an analytic attribution technique rather than a governance documentation process.

Hazard studies describe the failure modes this practice aims to surface. Changing the cost label shifted predicted eligibility for Black (RRR 4.31) and Asian (RRR 0.24) Medicare beneficiaries. Flipped labels cost 30.6 missed pleural effusions per 1,000 imaged patients in the targeted group. No study shows that documenting these sources caught them before they reached patients.

Most hazard studies focused on racial and ethnic minority patients, and one covered older Medicare beneficiaries. Registry-trained models recommended surgery less often for Black patients, and minority stroke patients needed higher NIHSS scores to receive thrombolysis. The single test examined a sex gap only and did not examine race, income, language, or literacy.

No study measured how long bias documentation takes, who performs it, or how consistently teams complete it in real development or purchasing workflows. The single test ran offline on survey data, so it offers no information on fidelity or burden when a governance committee applies the practice to vendor tools with limited data access.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software states that characterizing bias sources is necessary to assess AI bias, and the CHAI governance framework lists bias identification as a requirement. These positions rest on expert consensus. None of the supplied studies evaluates whether meeting these expectations changes device performance across subgroups.

research_gap: No study compares governance teams that use structured bias documentation, such as a Team Card or bias-source checklist, with teams using usual review. Needed studies would measure how many bias sources are found before deployment, subgroup performance after deployment, staff time required, and whether findings lead to model changes, in real health-system settings including safety-net hospitals.
underserved_note: The one test of the practice used BRFSS survey respondents and examined a sex-based gap; it did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies involved racial and ethnic minority and Medicare populations, so the evidence shows bias affects these groups but gives no indication whether bias documentation helps the underserved populations most exposed to it.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether inventorying decision support tools that use protected-characteristic inputs, followed by efforts to find and reduce discrimination, changes outcomes for patients. The practice rests on a federal regulation (45 CFR 92.210), a Utah statute, and four professional guidance documents or frameworks, so covered entities face a legal duty that the evidence base does not yet inform.

perspectives.view: The evidence map contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no study addresses the question. The six endorsements reflect expert and regulatory consensus, and consensus does not substitute for measured effects on detection of bias or on patient outcomes.

45 CFR 92.210 places an ongoing duty on covered entities to make reasonable efforts to identify tools that use race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability as inputs. Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbots to implement measures against discriminatory treatment. Compliance is therefore required regardless of the evidence gap, though "reasonable efforts" remains undefined by outcome data.

No supplied study measures algorithmic discrimination or its mitigation in any population, including Medicaid enrollees, safety-net patients, people with limited English proficiency, or people with low literacy. The groups the regulation aims to protect therefore have no evidence showing which inventory or audit methods reduce unequal treatment for them.

No supplied study documents how often protected-characteristic inputs produce harmful decisions or how severe those harms are. Without hazard data, a health system cannot estimate how many errors an inventory would catch before they reach patients. The radiology multi-society statement acknowledges that no straightforward process exists for identifying these biases.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units that conduct structured inventories and bias audits of decision support tools with those that do not, measuring the number of discriminatory tools detected, the changes made, and subsequent differences in care decisions and outcomes across race, sex, age, disability, and national origin groups. Studies should also report the staff time and cost of meeting the reasonable-efforts standard.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on which identification and mitigation methods work for them and may need to collect their own subgroup performance data during use.

bottom_line: Sixteen sources endorse documenting dataset demographics and comparing them with served populations, but no study has tested whether doing so improves model performance or patient outcomes. One offline glaucoma benchmark shows that training and external validation populations can differ sharply by race and ethnicity.

perspectives.view: No study evaluates the practice itself. The single supplied study documents the hazard in an offline benchmark of 39,090 patients and does not measure whether documenting or comparing demographics changes decisions or outcomes. Under GRADE conventions, the endorsements reflect expert consensus rather than tested effect, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In the glaucoma benchmark, Black patients made up 20.7% of training data, 76.3% of one external set, and 8.7% of another, and Hispanic patients ranged from 2.3% to 12.0%. Gaps of this size suggest that a model can be validated on populations quite unlike a given local service area, which may matter most for minority-serving systems.

The benchmark shows that demographic mismatch between development and deployment sites exists, which is a precondition for performance loss in underrepresented groups. Whether recording these gaps leads staff to catch degraded performance before it reaches patients has not been tested, so the safeguard's error-catching value remains an assumption.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks sponsors to describe demographic characteristics of training and validation data alongside those of the intended-use population. This creates a documentation expectation for cleared devices, but the guidance is a draft and does not by itself require health systems to compare vendor data with their own patients.

research_gap: No study tests whether documenting dataset demographics and comparing them with local populations changes procurement choices, triggers local validation, or reduces subgroup performance gaps; prospective or comparative implementation studies across health systems are needed, including measures of staff time and the thresholds used to define a significant gap.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The one hazard study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients and did not report insurance, language, or literacy, which suggests that demographic documentation may omit the variables most relevant to safety-net populations unless systems add them deliberately.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether stopping or redirecting AI proposals at intake, when vendors cannot disclose or meet training-data demographic thresholds, changes which tools are adopted or how they perform for patients. The recommendation rests on one governance framework and one commentary, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard in this entry. The two endorsements are a framework playbook and a commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the effect of an intake gate on adoption or outcomes is unknown.

The commentary proposes pausing procurement until adequate geriatric data exist, and the CHAI playbook suggests a mitigation plan for risks listed on the model card. Neither source reports whether an intake gate catches unrepresentative tools before they reach patients, or how often a disclosed threshold predicts subgroup performance after deployment.

The CHAI language asks reviewers to consider a mitigation and monitoring plan, which is softer than a hard stop at intake. The recommendation goes further than its framework source by making nondisclosure a reason to halt review. No supplied study shows how vendors respond to such a requirement.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or procurement cycles with and without a demographic-representation gate at intake, measuring the share of proposals stopped, vendor disclosure rates, reviewer time, and subgroup model performance after deployment. Work is also needed to set threshold values and to test whether reported training-data composition predicts local performance for underrepresented groups.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only population named in the endorsements is older adults. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether an intake threshold protects them or on which demographic categories and cutoffs a threshold should use.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether prespecifying subgroup analyses and enrolling enough patients per subgroup produces more accurate fairness findings; eight sources endorse the practice on reasoning and consensus. Three hazard studies show that small subgroups, sometimes with fewer than 10 cases or a minimum size of 1, yield unstable subgroup estimates.

perspectives.view: No study compares prespecified, adequately powered subgroup analyses with post hoc or underpowered ones, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three hazard studies are level 4 and 5 offline evaluations. They are consistent in showing imprecise subgroup estimates when counts are small, but they do not test the remedy.

In one tuberculosis chest X-ray evaluation, 58 cases in total left some subgroups with fewer than 10 cases. That pattern suggests a model could underperform in a group without the evaluation detecting it, and the failure would then surface only after deployment.

In an ICU cohort of 10,038 older adults, estimates for Black, Asian, and Hispanic patients were highly unstable because samples were small. In another benchmark, intersectional subgroups fell to 1 or 2 patients. Groups that are already underrepresented may be the ones whose disparities go unmeasured.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks for a subgroup analysis plan in marketing submissions. The CHAI playbooks ask for minimum sample sizes and subgroup requirements in validation documents. Both are recommendations drawn from consensus and do not rest on outcome evidence for the practice.

The hazard studies suggest that total sample size does not guarantee subgroup adequacy. One benchmark drew on 7,168 records and still had intersectional cells of 1 or 2 patients. Meeting per-subgroup targets may require targeted enrollment or multisite data, and the cost of that effort has not been measured.

research_gap: No study has compared prespecified, adequately powered subgroup analyses with post hoc or underpowered analyses. Such a study would ask whether prespecification changes the detection or accuracy of disparities, and what enrollment it would take to power intersectional subgroups.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard studies did not report these populations either, although one covered older adults and flagged small racial and ethnic subgroups. Evidence on whether the practice protects these groups is absent.

bottom_line: The listed tests, all level 4 studies in offline or simulated settings, suggest that asking a language model for a target grade level often lowers readability scores, though outputs frequently remain above the target and some simplifications lose accuracy. No listed test measured whether patients or caregivers in care settings found, understood, or acted on information more reliably, and the one test reporting a knowledge outcome found technical wording associated with better scores among 71 college students.

perspectives.view: All listed tests are level 4 studies in offline or simulated settings, and most use readability formulas as a surrogate for comprehension. Some added clinician or lay raters, but none tested patients in care. In one study of 71 college students, technical responses were more likely in the high knowledge-gain group (OR 2.73, 95% CI 1.05-7.41). Indirectness and inconsistency support very low certainty.

Simplification may trade accuracy for readability. In one study, the lowest-grade prompt reduced accuracy scores from a median of 5.0 to 4.0. Another reported expert-rated inaccuracy of 19.0% versus 28.6%, a difference that was not statistically significant (p=0.47). A third study found that eighth-grade translations gave the best balance of accuracy and readability.

Prompted Spanish materials scored better than standard handouts on seven readability measures, but no patients read them. In real deployments, 982 AI-generated visit summaries had a mean FKGL of 9.3, and chatbot responses in a trial including patients with limited English proficiency averaged an 11th-12th grade level. These hazard studies did not test a fix.

The FDA draft guidance says materials should suit the intended audience's reading level but names no metric or grade. The listed studies used sixth-, seventh-, and eighth-grade targets and several different formulas. This variation may make it hard to show that a product meets the guidance.

research_gap: No listed study tested reading-level-matched materials with intended users in real workflows. Such studies would need to measure comprehension, time to find key information, correct action, and errors, with accuracy checked against the original text. Studies also need to establish which readability metric and target grade best predict understanding for each user group and task.
underserved_note: Two tests targeted materials toward low health literacy and one assessed Spanish-language materials, but these were text analyses with no patient readers. A hazard study included patients with limited English proficiency, but it did not test the practice. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users, so benefit for these groups remains unverified.

bottom_line: Seven small offline studies ran the kind of paraphrase testing this recommendation describes, and they found that consistency held for some models and phrasings but broke down for others, most clearly when prompts requested simpler language or used informal or vague wording. No study examined whether performing such testing before deployment reduces harm to patients, so the case for the practice rests on the documented hazard rather than on a demonstrated benefit.

perspectives.view: All seven tests are small level 4 offline studies of 15 to 240 items, and they measure consistency rather than any effect of testing on outcomes. The results diverge across studies, with one finding stable appropriateness across phrasings, two finding declines for some models or prompts, and four reporting mixed results. Indirectness, imprecision, and inconsistency support a very low certainty rating.

When prompts asked for simple language, DouBao accuracy fell from 57.5% to 7.5% and Kimi fell from 70.0% to 48.8%. In a hazard study, urgent or demanding framing raised same-day care advice from 14% to between 37% and 63%. These results suggest that paraphrase testing may detect failures that standard-phrasing evaluations would miss.

Some tests found little inconsistency. Clinically reliable ratings were 89.3% for clinician language and 91.3% for patient language (OR 0.78, 95% CI 0.57-1.06). Emotional framing changed tone but not completeness on 43 features, and safety scores did not differ across four phrasings (p=0.334). The size of the risk may vary by model and task.

Consistency on rephrased questions ranged from 23% to 92% across chatbots, and flip rates on meaning-preserving paraphrases ranged from 3% to 37% across nine vision-language models. These spreads suggest that a paraphrase test result for one model may not carry over to another, so testing may need to be repeated with each model or version change.

One test addressed low health literacy. It found a borderline accuracy gradient across prompt styles (2.53, 2.67, 2.80; p=0.050), all below the clinician score of 4.00. Separately, simplification prompts lowered accuracy in a Chinese-language study. Patients who need plain language may receive less accurate answers, and these studies suggest that testing could reveal that gap.

A regulatory discussion paper asks whether safety and clinical proficiency hold across populations that may be underrepresented or face barriers to care. Paraphrase testing by literacy level and emotional framing is one way to generate that evidence. The paper describes the consideration but does not set a test method or threshold.

In one test, diagnostic accuracy was 92% and did not change when patients offered their own diagnosis, but it was lower when symptoms were described vaguely. Patients rarely describe symptoms in textbook terms, so a tool that performs well only on precise wording may give weaker answers to the people who have the least clinical vocabulary.

research_gap: No study has tested whether developers who run literacy-level and emotional-framing paraphrase tests before release produce tools with fewer harmful responses in live use. The field also lacks a shared paraphrase test set, agreed thresholds for acceptable variation, and evaluations conducted with real patient messages from US Medicaid, safety-net, and limited English proficiency populations.
underserved_note: No test included Medicaid or safety-net populations. Four tests were conducted in non-English-language settings (China, Poland, Turkey), and one Chinese study included material for low health literacy readers. None tested limited English proficiency patients in US care settings. The findings therefore may not describe how these tools respond to the phrasing patterns of underserved US patients, who are the group this recommendation most directly aims to protect.

bottom_line: Nine offline studies suggest that structured evaluation can detect and help raise empathy and tone scores in AI-generated patient communications, but none measured whether this evaluation changes patient harm or outcomes in real use. Hazard studies show that warmth can coexist with unsafe or therapeutically inappropriate content, so evaluations that score empathy alone may miss failures tied to clinical risk.

perspectives.view: All nine tests are level 4 and offline or simulated. Only one is randomized, with 300 patients rating texts. Outcomes are rater or model scores of empathy, tone, and clarity rather than patient outcomes. Findings point the same way, but they use different instruments and small samples, and three report no numbers. Indirectness and imprecision lower certainty.

Single-objective tuning reached 93.6% empathy but 47.8% safety in one study. In another, surface acknowledgment scored about 0.91 to 1.00 while therapeutic appropriateness fell to 0.22 to 0.33 at the highest severity. Lay raters detected 60% of expert-confirmed instances of the Endorse response style. These results suggest evaluations may need expert review of appropriateness by risk level.

An AI grader agreed with reference grades at κ=0.44, close to lay raters at κ=0.43. Distribution decisions based on AI grades matched reference decisions 88.1% of the time. Automated screening may make routine tone evaluation feasible, though agreement was moderate. In one live deployment, patients preferred human replies for tone 68% of the time over initial-prompt AI drafts.

Two tests involved non-English communication, one with Chinese-language consultations and one with 60 radiology impressions translated to Spanish. In a hazard trial that included low-literacy, low-income, and rural patients, a model tuned on local data reproduced an unfriendly clinician-like tone. This finding suggests evaluation criteria may need to reflect the intended population rather than local clinician habits.

research_gap: No study tested whether evaluating communications before or during deployment reduces patient harm, distress, or disengagement in real clinical use. Prospective studies should pair empathy and tone scoring with safety and therapeutic-appropriateness outcomes stratified by risk level. They should also validate automated graders against expert judgment and enroll low-literacy and limited English proficiency patients.
underserved_note: Two tests included non-English communication, one with Chinese-language consultations and one with 60 Spanish-translated radiology impressions. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Evaluation methods and thresholds therefore remain unvalidated for patients whose literacy and trust needs may differ most from those of the raters who set the scores.

bottom_line: Seven studies test representation or remediation of training data, and six report better subgroup performance, but all were offline benchmarks or a survey, and none tested representative validation cohorts or human evaluators in deployment. Health systems can reasonably require representation reporting and subgroup validation from vendors, with the understanding that representation reduced but did not always close performance gaps.

perspectives.view: Six of seven tests are level 5 automated benchmarks, and one is a survey experiment. Five benchmarks report gains after adding underrepresented data, while one reports that balanced sex sampling reduced but did not remove gaps. No study measured patient outcomes or ran in live care. Indirectness, unreported populations, and one mixed result lower certainty to very low.

Adult-only segmentation models scored mean Dice below 0.5 for bladder and spleen in children aged 0 to 2, and adding pediatric data raised Dice above 0.85 for all organs. A deployed model showed a 77% false negative rate in an underrepresented subgroup. These results suggest subgroup validation may catch errors before release.

Balanced 50/50 sex sampling narrowed accuracy gaps, yet sampling scenario explained only 0.2% of gap variance, which suggests representation alone may not correct disparities. Synthetic augmentation improved F1 by up to 21% in one benchmark, but no study examined how remediation works within real procurement, retraining, or local validation workflows.

One validation cohort reported no American Indian and Alaska Native patients and another reported 1.1%, although the target sample was 94.0% AIAN. Triage tools missed benchmarks in Medicaid messages, and models performed worse in Korean and Haitian Creole. None of the remediation tests enrolled these populations, so benefit for them remains untested.

FDORA section 3601(b) requires sponsors to submit diversity action plans for studies of certain devices, and FDA draft guidance cites this requirement for AI-enabled devices. This obligation covers clinical studies for regulated devices and does not reach many non-device tools such as general-purpose language models used by health systems.

No study reported the cost or staff time of assembling representative data or auditing vendor cohorts. The HEAAL framework states that implementation requires expertise, infrastructure, and personnel effort. Synthetic data pretraining improved fairness across five institutions in one benchmark, which may offer a lower-cost path, but its costs were not measured.

In a survey of 3,000 US respondents, information that a tool used representative US training data increased preference for a visit (AMCE 0.119; 95% CI 0.106 to 0.131). This suggests disclosure of representation may affect patient trust, although stated preference in a vignette may differ from behavior in care.

research_gap: No study tested whether representative validation cohorts or representative human evaluators change detection of subgroup errors or patient outcomes in deployment. Prospective studies that compare locally validated and unvalidated tools in live settings, with subgroup results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, and low-literacy patients, would address this gap.
underserved_note: Two remediation tests focused on racial and ethnic minority groups, but none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Hazard studies documented failures in Medicaid, safety-net, and non-English settings, so the populations with documented harm are those for which remediation has not been tested.

bottom_line: Nine sources, including CHAI playbooks, FDA draft lifecycle guidance, and the HEAAL framework, endorse naming an owner and running a recurring, resourced process for AI bias evaluation, but no supplied study tests whether doing so reduces biased outputs or disparate outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and regulatory direction rather than measured effect.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests an assigned owner or recurring lifecycle process for bias management, and no study documents the hazard itself. The endorsements come from frameworks, guidance, and commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not establish certainty of effect, so the size and direction of any benefit remain unknown.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks that bias control be built in from the earliest design stage through decommission across the total product lifecycle. This is a draft and applies to device manufacturers, so it may shape vendor expectations more directly than hospital governance duties. No supplied study measures compliance or its effects.

The HEAAL framework and the related action guide organize equity review across adoption stages and five domains, including accountability and fairness. These documents describe procedures but report no evaluation of whether they change outcomes for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

The recommendation calls for defined roles and resources, yet no supplied source reports staffing levels, cost, or time needed to sustain recurring bias reviews. Health systems would need to estimate these burdens locally until implementation data become available.

research_gap: Studies should compare health systems or deployments with and without a designated bias owner and scheduled lifecycle reviews, measuring detection of performance gaps across patient subgroups, time to remediation, and changes in disparate outcomes, along with the staffing and cost of maintaining the process.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Whether a governance owner and recurring review detect or correct bias affecting these groups is currently unmeasured.

bottom_line: Seventeen sources endorse documenting bias assessment methods, subgroup performance, underrepresented populations, and residual bias in model cards, but no supplied study tests whether this documentation changes how users apply AI or reduces harm to patients in low-accuracy groups. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and draft regulatory guidance, and no study was supplied that documents the hazard itself.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests the practice, and none documents how often users are unaware of low-accuracy populations. The endorsements come from frameworks, draft guidance, and commentaries. Under GRADE conventions this gives no direct evidence, so any benefit from model-card bias reporting is assumed rather than measured.

A model card can only prevent harm if a clinician reads it and changes a decision for a patient in an affected subgroup. No supplied study measures whether disclosure changes user behavior at the point of care. The safeguard's ability to intercept errors before they reach patients therefore remains untested.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks sponsors to explain missing demographic data and how the resulting risks are controlled. CHAI, NIST AI 600-1, and FUTURE-AI make similar documentation recommendations. These sources set expectations for disclosure. They do not provide outcome data showing that disclosure works.

Several commentaries propose subgroup reporting and calibration by sex, ethnicity, and age as a check on inequitable performance. No supplied study reports subgroup results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. It is also unknown whether documentation leads deployers to act on gaps affecting these groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without subgroup performance and residual-bias disclosures. These studies should measure whether clinicians read the disclosures, whether they adjust their reliance on AI output for affected subgroups, and whether error rates or patient outcomes differ in those subgroups. Baseline studies that measure how often users are unaware of low-accuracy populations would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Health systems serving these patients have no evidence that model-card disclosures identify or reduce performance gaps affecting them. They may need to run their own local subgroup evaluations rather than rely on developer documentation.

bottom_line: Twenty-two sources endorse staffing AI bias review with demographically and professionally diverse teams, but no supplied study tests whether such teams find more bias or reduce harm than homogeneous teams. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and a federal framework rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the evidence base tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard of blind spots from homogeneous teams. The endorsements come from one federal framework, one international consensus guideline, and commentaries.
