Under GRADE conventions, agreement among expert opinions does not raise certainty, so the rating is no direct evidence.

NIST AI 600-1 calls for interdisciplinary teams that reflect a range of demographic groups, professions, and lived experiences to conduct risk measurement and management. The framework is voluntary, and the supplied sources do not cite any binding FDA, ONC, or state requirement for team composition.

Several endorsing commentaries argue that diverse teams may expose assumptions that disadvantage specific groups, and FUTURE-AI names representative citizens as team members. No supplied study measures whether including community representatives changes bias findings for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

Some endorsing sources ask organizations to invite patients and caregivers into all levels of the process and onto review boards. No supplied study reports whether patient participation on these teams affects patient safety, trust, or access to human review.

research_gap: Studies should compare the bias findings, missed disparities, and downstream patient outcomes of AI review teams that differ in demographic, professional, and community composition, ideally using the same models and audit tasks. Research should also define which forms of diversity matter and how much representation is needed for a measurable effect.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether diverse or community-inclusive review teams improve bias detection for their patients.

bottom_line: Four offline studies compared models with and without race or other sensitive inputs and found mixed effects on accuracy and fairness, which suggests the effect of an input has to be measured model by model rather than assumed. No study tested a governance review process that applies an inclusion policy, so evidence for the review step itself is indirect.

perspectives.view: Four offline or simulated studies compared models with and without race or sensitive attributes. Race added a discrimination gain of 0.022 in one cohort only when polygenic scores were present, and exclusion preserved AUROC (0.834 vs. 0.836) in another. Fairness shifted in different directions across sites. Inconsistency and indirectness lower certainty to very low.

In the glaucoma study, removing sex, race, and ethnicity did not eliminate bias. In survival models, disparate impact persisted after race was excluded. A proxy study found subgroup signals carried by age group, glucose, and BMI. These findings suggest that dropping an input may not prevent discriminatory outputs, and they support measuring effects directly.

One benchmark found that language models relied on proxies in ways uncalibrated to predictive evidence, and accuracy-based evaluation detected none of it. Another found that including all metadata may harm subgroup fairness. Reviewers who quantify justified effects would likely need subgroup fairness testing with and without each input across sites, as the glaucoma study did.

Three of the four tests focused on racial and ethnic minority patients, but none reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. A hazard study of 164,041 patients, including safety-net and low-income patients, found Race_Black was the third most important feature (OR 1.94). No study has tested review policies in those settings.

The endorsements point in different directions. Texas SB 1188 requires EHR decision tools to include recorded biological sex. The CHAI guide calls for anti-classification, meaning protected characteristics are not explicitly used to make decisions. An explicit inclusion policy that documents the clinical justification for each input may help reconcile these duties. No study examined compliance with either requirement.

research_gap: No study evaluated a governance review that applies an inclusion policy to protected or proxy inputs and then tracked patient outcomes or disparities after deployment. Prospective evaluations in live clinical settings would show whether the review changes model choices and reduces discriminatory outputs. These evaluations would need prespecified fairness metrics and would need to include patients covered by Medicaid or served by safety-net systems.
underserved_note: None of the four tests reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and three focused on racial and ethnic minority groups. The only safety-net and low-income data come from a hazard study. The effect of this practice in those populations is therefore unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether adding population sensitivity and disparity risk as modifiers in AI risk tiering changes fairness validation or patient outcomes, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on two voluntary frameworks, NIST AI 600-1 and the CHAI governance playbooks, which both use "should" language.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies describing the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements reflect expert consensus from framework authors, and consensus of this kind does not substitute for comparative data on whether risk modifiers change validation rigor or harm rates.

Both endorsing sources are voluntary frameworks. CHAI names population sensitivity and disparity risk directly as risk modifiers. NIST AI 600-1 addresses the topic less directly, asking organizations to obtain stakeholder community input on unacceptable use. Neither source is a binding regulation, so adoption depends on each health system's governance choices.

The recommendation is aimed at tools that affect vulnerable groups, yet no supplied study measures whether tiering by population sensitivity leads to more fairness testing for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Without such data, a health system cannot yet estimate how much added scrutiny this approach produces for those groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare governance programs using population sensitivity and disparity risk modifiers with programs that do not. These studies should measure how often tools are assigned higher tiers, whether subgroup fairness validation is performed and reported, and whether disparities in performance or outcomes detected after deployment differ between the two approaches.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Whether the practice protects these populations, which it is meant to serve, remains unmeasured.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring vendors to disclose sensitive and social-determinant inputs, bias assessment methods, and mitigation evidence during procurement changes which tools health systems buy or reduces biased performance after deployment. Ten sources endorse the practice, two at the "must" level, but the support rests on guidance, frameworks, and commentary rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The ten endorsements consist of two frameworks, two guidance documents, and six commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement does not substitute for comparative data, so certainty about the effect of procurement disclosure on purchasing decisions or patient outcomes cannot be rated.

One endorsing source states that, starting in 2025, EHR developers supplying Predictive DSIs must disclose specific attributes and inform users whether demographic, social-determinant, or health assessment data are used. That requirement applies to tools supplied within an EHR offering. Procurement contract terms may be the main route for obtaining similar disclosure from other vendors.

Several endorsing commentaries frame procurement disclosure as an equity safeguard and ask for subgroup performance and dataset representativeness. No study shows whether vendors' disclosed subgroup results reflect performance in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Disclosure of this kind may reveal gaps without closing them.

No study in this set measures how often tools bought without bias information later produce harmful subgroup errors. The size of the hazard this safeguard targets is therefore undocumented here. The CHAI guide's suggestion of third-party bias evaluation implies that endorsers do not regard vendor self-report alone as a sufficient check.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or purchasing cycles with and without structured bias-disclosure requirements. Such studies should measure whether disclosures change which tools are selected, whether disclosed subgroup results match local validation, and whether post-deployment subgroup performance differs. Research should also assess how complete and accurate vendor disclosures are when checked against independent evaluation.
underserved_note: No test of this practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that vendor-disclosed bias results apply to their patients and may need to request subgroup data matching their own population or run local validation.

bottom_line: Across 30 studies, subgroup and site analyses repeatedly found performance gaps that aggregate metrics concealed, including a 9% higher false-negative rate in female adolescents and site-level AUROCs ranging from 0.608 to 0.851. No study tested whether evaluating subgroups before deployment changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes, so certainty is low.

perspectives.view: Of 30 studies, two were prospective in real deployment (108 visits and 8,493 patients), and most were offline retrospective analyses. They consistently show that subgroup analysis is feasible and often finds gaps that aggregate metrics hide. No study compared deployments with and without such evaluation, so certainty that the practice improves outcomes is low.

In pediatric anxiety prediction, female adolescents had 4% lower accuracy and 9% higher false-negative rates than males, and aggregate results did not show this gap. A deployed suicide risk model had a 77% false-negative rate in transgender patients. These findings suggest subgroup review may catch missed-diagnosis risks early, though no study showed that it prevented harm.

Performance varied by site in several studies. Local AUROC ranged from 0.608 to 0.851 across sites for coronary angiography decisions, error rates differed by cancer registry and by geography, and fairness metrics passed in one dataset and failed in another. This pattern suggests vendor or single-site results may not transfer to a new setting.

Three tests included safety-net or Medicaid patients, and none included limited English proficiency or low-literacy groups. In a Brazilian cohort, AUC was 0.57 for mixed-race participants versus 0.77 overall. An intersectional analysis found a sex-by-age gap 5.2 times the single-attribute gap, which suggests single-attribute checks may miss disparities.

FDA draft guidance asks developers to report subgroup analysis by sex, age, race, ethnicity, disease severity, site, and equipment. A review found subgroup analyses reported for 11 of 26 authorized devices with change-control plans, and none of these analyses included patient outcomes. This finding suggests health systems may not be able to rely on submission data for subgroup assurance.

Subgroup testing requires enough cases per group. A GPT-4 evaluation on 539 notes found error-rate differences with overlapping confidence intervals, and some groups had fewer than five patients. One triage study set a prespecified F1 gap threshold of 0.05 and found a 0.020 gender gap, which shows one way to make subgroup review a pass-fail step.

research_gap: No study compared AI deployments that underwent pre-deployment subgroup and site evaluation with deployments that did not, measuring either the deployment decisions made or patient outcomes. Methods for evaluating small subgroups and intersectional groups with adequate precision remain untested in real deployment. Language and literacy subgroups have not been examined in tests of the practice.
underserved_note: Three tests included Medicaid, low-income, or safety-net patients. One was a real-deployment study of 225 patients, 69.0% of whom were African American, and two were offline analyses. No test included limited English proficiency or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore says nothing about how subgroup evaluation performs for language and literacy groups, and systems serving those patients would need to define and test those subgroups locally.

bottom_line: Nine sources, two CHAI governance documents and seven commentaries, advise health systems to set documented quantitative criteria for subgroup performance shifts and parity gaps, but no supplied study tests whether doing so changes decisions or patient outcomes. The recommendation currently rests on expert agreement rather than measured effect.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The support consists of two framework documents and seven commentaries. Consensus among these sources is consistent in direction, but under GRADE conventions expert opinion does not establish an effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

No supplied study measures how often subgroup disparities go unaddressed without prespecified criteria, or whether criteria lead to earlier review. One commentary offers a sensitivity gap of 5% or less between groups as an example trigger, but that figure is illustrative and has not been evaluated for missed harms or false alarms.

Several endorsing commentaries frame thresholds as protection for underserved populations. No supplied study examines whether prespecified thresholds detect disparities affecting Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, whose small sample sizes may produce wide estimation error.

research_gap: No study compares deployments that use prespecified, sample-size-adjusted subgroup criteria with deployments that do not. Useful studies would measure consistency of escalation decisions across reviewers, time to detect a subgroup performance shift, false alarm rates in small subgroups, the burden of maintaining criteria, and downstream patient outcomes by subgroup.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. These groups are often small within a single health system's data, and it remains unknown whether criteria that account for estimation error would flag or miss disparities affecting them.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether assessing the fairness of AI agent actions, as distinct from their outputs, reduces discriminatory actions toward patients. Two studies of the hazard point in different directions, and both used simulated or benchmark settings rather than live care.

perspectives.view: No study compares action-level fairness assessment with output-only assessment or with no assessment. The two hazard studies are a vignette simulation and an automated benchmark, both offline, and they disagree. One found demographic favoritism under adversarial prompting. The other found no disparity for a single model. Certainty about the practice cannot be rated.

In a triage simulation, an adversarially prompted agent allocated resources by demographic group rather than clinical need, and neither agent's allocation was ethically adequate alone. This suggests that harm may arise at the point of action, where an output review would not detect it. Joint allocations could meet fairness criteria, which may indicate that layered agent checks catch some errors.

A benchmark measured disparity across 864 agent decisions and tool invocations, including medical triage, and found 0 of 120 pairwise and 0 of 9 omnibus contrasts significant after correction for one model. This suggests action-level fairness can be measured across scaffolds. Whether such measurement holds up in production workflows, and at what burden, remains untested.

Neither hazard study reported the populations represented in its scenarios. The null finding applies to one model on a benchmark and may not generalize to other models, prompts, or patient groups such as people with limited English proficiency. The absence of disparity in one test does not establish equitable actions in safety-net settings.

research_gap: Prospective studies are needed that compare action-level fairness audits with output-only audits in deployed AI agents, measure whether audits detect and reduce disparities in resource allocation, triage, and tool use, and stratify results by payer, language, literacy, and safety-net status across multiple models and adversarial conditions.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and neither hazard study reported whether Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations were represented. One endorsing source addresses Arabic-speaking post-conflict populations, but it is a theoretical proposition rather than a test, so health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on how action-level fairness assessment performs for them.

bottom_line: One large randomized trial in a real deployment found that supportive automated phone outreach to patients flagged as high risk raised appointment completion, with the largest gain among Black patients and a smaller preexisting gap by race. No study compared supportive outreach directly with punitive responses such as overbooking or exclusion, and none measured punitive harms.

perspectives.view: A single randomized trial of 59,994 patients supports the practice. Certainty begins high for randomized designs and is lowered here for indirectness. The trial tested one outreach mode, interactive voice response, on one outcome, appointment completion. The summary does not show that the comparison arm involved punitive actions. With no replication in other settings, the certainty is rated low.

The trial reported results by race and found that completion rose most among Black patients, which narrowed an existing gap. This suggests that supportive use of a risk flag may reduce rather than widen disparities on this outcome. The summary gives no results by insurance type, language, or literacy.

The trial measured whether patients completed appointments. It did not count denied or overbooked visits, dismissals, or other exclusionary events. It therefore shows a benefit of outreach but does not show that pairing flags with outreach prevents punitive use of the same flags elsewhere in the organization.

The outreach in the trial was automated interactive voice response delivered in a real deployment at large scale. This suggests that a supportive response can run in routine workflows without adding staff contact for every flagged patient. The trial did not test the medical workup or social support outreach that the HEAAL framework describes.

In the trial, a high-risk flag led to a reminder and support rather than a penalty, and more patients kept their visits. The outreach was automated, however, and the summary does not report whether patients could reach a person or how they viewed the calls.

research_gap: Trials are needed that compare supportive outreach with punitive responses such as overbooking or discharge from a practice. These trials should measure exclusionary events, access, and clinical outcomes, and they should test human-delivered medical and social support alongside automated calls.
underserved_note: The one trial reported effects by race but did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Automated voice outreach may perform differently for patients with limited English or low literacy, so the benefit for these groups remains untested.

bottom_line: Of 74 studies testing bias mitigation, most report reduced subgroup disparities with small or no loss of accuracy, but nearly all are offline analyses and several show mitigation shifting bias to other groups or lowering performance for everyone. The evidence supports the recommendation's requirement to check fairness and accuracy together after any mitigation, across more than one subgroup axis.

perspectives.view: Only one study measured mitigation in a real deployment, where recalibration reduced miscalibration across subgroups in 49,282 patients. The remaining shown studies are offline or simulated. Results are inconsistent across methods and settings, and outcomes are model metrics rather than patient outcomes. Indirectness and inconsistency lead to low certainty.

In a simulation, error-rate parity methods cut the mortality rate ratio from 3.77 to about 3.05 by raising mortality in the privileged group. In one obstetric study, reweighing lowered sensitivity by about 0.25. Two benchmark studies also found fairness gains that came with accuracy or calibration loss. These results suggest that checking accuracy after mitigation may catch leveling down before deployment.

Prompt-based mitigation for language models gave variable results. One study found bias gaps falling from 45 to 27 points while accuracy rose, but one model got worse. In another, a ZIP-code income gap fell from 11.4 to 5.8 points and was not eliminated. These findings suggest each model and prompt needs re-testing after changes.

When reweighing targeted area deprivation, it introduced language bias. The equal opportunity ratio moved from 0.91 to 1.35 and predictive equality from 0.84 to 0.29, and race bias also worsened. This suggests mitigation on one axis can harm limited English proficiency patients unless all relevant subgroups are re-audited.

research_gap: No study shown links bias mitigation to patient outcomes in a live clinical deployment, and only one measured mitigation effects in real use. Prospective studies are needed that track fairness, accuracy, and harm across several subgroup axes at once after mitigation, including in safety-net settings.
underserved_note: Several offline tests included underserved groups. Two involved Medicaid populations, one included limited English proficiency and low health literacy patients, and a few involved low-income populations. The LEP study found that mitigation aimed at one group worsened bias against non-English speakers. No test was set in a safety-net system, so effects in those settings remain unmeasured.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether assessing demographic representation in the trial evidence behind genomic AI recommendations, or the socioeconomic accessibility of AI-identified trials, changes patient outcomes or access. The recommendation rests on one framework endorsement from the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single support is a framework statement that uses the word should, and this reflects expert judgment rather than measured effect.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide states that an essential consideration is whether trial options are accessible to patients from various socioeconomic backgrounds. This is voluntary framework guidance. None of the supplied materials identify a binding federal or state requirement that deployers perform this assessment.

The recommendation addresses representation and access for disadvantaged patients, but no supplied study measured trial representation or trial accessibility for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients receiving genomic AI recommendations. The size of any gap for these groups is therefore unmeasured in this evidence map.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare genomic AI deployments with and without a structured review of trial-population demographics and trial accessibility, measuring trial referral, enrollment, travel and cost barriers, and treatment outcomes by insurance type, language, and income. Descriptive studies quantifying how often AI-identified trials are geographically or financially out of reach would also establish whether the hazard occurs at a meaningful rate.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups have no local or published evidence here on whether the assessment improves their patients' access to trials.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether requiring payers to show nondiscrimination evidence or publish coverage-decision statistics by demographics reduces discriminatory automated decisions. One descriptive Medicare study suggests that the choice of cost target in an algorithm may shift eligibility by race and ethnicity, which shows the hazard exists but not that this practice addresses it.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is a level 4 cross-sectional simulation in Medicare fee-for-service data. It examines eligibility under cost-based targeting schemes rather than payer coverage denials, so it is indirect even as evidence of the specific hazard.

Among 1,848,654 Medicare beneficiaries, a hospitalization and emergency department cost target raised inclusion for Black (RRR=4.31) and Hispanic (RRR=2.28) beneficiaries and lowered it for Asian (RRR=0.24) and Other (RRR=0.43) beneficiaries relative to total costs. This suggests that demographic reporting may reveal target-driven disparities that aggregate statistics would hide.

The one endorsing guidance calls for automatic physician referral of any automated recommendation to limit or deny care at initial review and appeal. It does not address nondiscrimination evidence or publication of demographic statistics, so the recommendation as written rests on no direct endorsement or test in the supplied material.

The hazard study shows that small design choices, such as which cost measure an algorithm predicts, can change who is selected by large ratios across groups. Public demographic reporting could surface such patterns after deployment, but no supplied study measures whether reporting leads payers to correct them before patients are denied care.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare payers who publish coverage-decision statistics by demographic group, or who submit nondiscrimination evidence, with payers who do not, and that measure changes in denial rates, appeal outcomes, and disparities over time. Such work should use actual coverage and prior authorization decisions rather than simulated eligibility schemes.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice. The only supplied study, a hazard study, focused on racial and ethnic minority groups and older adults within Medicare fee-for-service and did not include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The effect of demographic reporting on coverage decisions for these groups, who may face higher rates of automated denial, remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether educating end-users, disadvantaged patient groups, or other stakeholders about inequities and user bias changes how AI is used or improves outcomes. Three sources endorse the practice, a framework and two commentaries, and none of them reports trial or observational data on it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The three endorsements are one framework and two commentaries, which represent expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion does not supply an effect estimate, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The HEAAL framework asks that solution design draw on input from disadvantaged patient subgroups, and one commentary asks physicians to consider patients' educational, socioeconomic, and cultural background. Neither source reports whether education reached or helped Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare bias and inequity education for clinicians and patients against usual practice, with outcomes such as clinicians' reliance on AI outputs, detection of biased recommendations, patient understanding, and differences in care across patient groups. Studies should also measure whether the hazard itself, low awareness of AI bias among users and patients, occurs and how often.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on what form of education works, in what languages or reading levels, or whether it changes care.

bottom_line: Studies that evaluated deployed AI by patient subgroup mostly found similar or larger benefits for Medicaid, non-English-speaking, and homeless patients, and one analysis suggests that prediction-based fairness checks can miss differences in outcomes. No study tests whether conducting such evaluations improves outcomes, and evidence on clinician-driven differential treatment comes only from a 50-physician simulation.

perspectives.view: Six studies report subgroup outcomes of AI tools, but none compares health systems that conduct subgroup evaluation with systems that do not. The largest, a cluster RCT of 20,506 patients, found a greater effect among Medicaid beneficiaries (aOR 2.19, interaction P = .03). Subgroup results are secondary analyses with limited precision and indirect relevance, so certainty is low.

The UTICalc analysis found that a revision improved true positive rate parity across racial groups but did not improve expected utility parity. This suggests that model-level fairness checks may miss outcome differences, which favors measuring outcomes directly. In a simulation, fairness constraints reduced the mortality disparity by about 12 per 100k, and better screening access reduced it by about 57 per 100k.

Evidence on clinician-mediated differential treatment comes from one simulated trial of 50 physicians. In that trial, AI assistance improved decisions by 18% for patients in each race and sex group. No real-deployment study measured whether clinicians acted on AI output differently by patient group. A Portuguese study found no differences in urgency advice appropriateness by sex or age.

Three real-deployment studies reported larger benefits in disadvantaged groups. Medicaid beneficiaries had an aOR of 2.19. Spanish-speaking patients had FIT opt-in of 18.2% versus 7.1%. Non-English speakers had an adjusted mortality HR of 0.419. A Canadian study found more code status documentation for patients experiencing homelessness. These results show that subgroup evaluation is feasible, though they may be specific to each tool and setting.

None of the six studies reported the staff time, data infrastructure, or cost needed to run subgroup outcome evaluations. The two controlled real-deployment studies used large samples of 20,506 and 12,877 patients to examine subgroups. This suggests that smaller systems may lack the statistical power to detect subgroup differences with local data alone.

research_gap: No study compares patient outcomes between health systems that routinely evaluate deployed AI by subgroup and systems that do not, so the benefit of the practice itself is untested. Real-world measurement of whether clinicians act on AI output differently by patient race, language, insurance, or literacy has not been reported. Studies powered in advance for subgroup interactions, and studies that report the cost of running these evaluations, are also absent.
underserved_note: Tests included Medicaid beneficiaries in one cluster RCT, Spanish-speaking or non-English-speaking patients in two US studies, and patients experiencing homelessness in one Canadian study. No test reported low-literacy populations or identified safety-net settings. This implies that subgroup evaluation has been carried out in some underserved groups, but the findings may not transfer to other tools, to low-literacy patients, or to safety-net institutions with fewer analytic resources.

bottom_line: One randomized trial of an AI tool in 59,994 US patients reported subgroup results and found that appointment completion rose most among Black patients, but it did not report subgroup effect sizes and did not test equity assessment itself as an intervention. Hazard studies show that the reach and benefit of AI tools can differ by race, insurance, income, and rurality in either direction, which suggests these gaps become visible only when a system measures them.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial (n=59,994) tests the practice. It reported that appointment completion increased most among Black patients. The trial did not report subgroup effect sizes, and it evaluated an AI tool with subgroup analysis rather than the effect of a health system's equity assessment. Certainty is low because of indirectness, imprecision, and reliance on a single study.

Subgroup gaps appear in both directions. Postpartum chatbot reach was lower for Black patients (OR 0.73) and publicly insured patients (OR 0.72), and newborn reach was lower for patients who received prenatal care at an FQHC (OR 0.50). At AI eye screening sites, the Asian-Black adherence gap shrank from 15.6% to 3.5%. No study shows that assessment itself prevented harm.

Deployment studies suggest that subgroup analysis is feasible with routine data. In England, a chatbot self-referral study (n=129,400) compared demographic subgroups against matched services and found that ethnic minority referrals rose 31%. A pediatric chat study linked engagement to insurance and Social Vulnerability Index scores. None of these studies measured the staff time or data work that such assessments require.

The trial that tests the practice reported no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups. Hazard studies that included such groups found lower engagement among Medicaid patients (OR 0.68) and smaller gains for rural participants in a Chinese trial that enrolled low-literacy and non-native-language participants, with listenability gains of 0.27 versus 0.47.

A simulation of 500,000 women per run found that access barriers affected disparities more than algorithm fairness did. Enforcing equalized odds reduced disparity by about 12 per 100,000, compared with about 57 per 100,000 with 93% screening access. This result suggests that assessments may need to cover access and uptake as well as model metrics. The finding comes from simulation.

Uptake varies before any benefit can occur. In a Spanish telemonitoring program, 40.2% of patients refused an AI virtual assistant, and refusal was associated with lower sociocultural level and fewer devices. In a US dermatology survey, Black race and darker skin tone predicted lower acceptance of AI-assisted care. Assessments that count only tool users may miss patients who declined.

research_gap: No study has tested whether a health system that routinely assesses AI access, benefit, and harm by subgroup achieves smaller disparities or fewer concentrated harms than one that does not. Trials of AI tools should report subgroup effect sizes with confidence intervals by insurance type, language, literacy, and safety-net site, and studies should measure the cost and staffing needed for ongoing equity monitoring.
underserved_note: The one study that tests the practice did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups, so its findings do not extend to these groups. Several hazard studies did include them and found lower chatbot reach among publicly insured and FQHC patients and lower engagement among Medicaid patients, which suggests that assessment is least tested in the populations where gaps have been observed.

bottom_line: One offline study of 104 simulated Brazilian e-prescription scenarios found that reviewing generated medication instructions detected gender bias in anywhere from 0/104 to 104/104 texts depending on the prompt, which suggests output evaluation can surface population-specific problems. No study has tested field testing of subgroup exposure, and the 78 hazard studies show that the problem exists without showing that evaluation prevents harm.

perspectives.view: A single level 4 simulation of 104 scenarios tests the practice. GPT-4 showed gender bias in 6/104, 104/104, and 0/104 texts across three prompts, and Llama 3 showed none. The study is offline, small, limited to one bias type, and does not test field testing. Certainty is very low because of indirectness and imprecision.

Hazard studies report race-based medicine content from all four models tested, validation of harmful statements and stigmatizing language across 20 models in psychiatric scenarios, and omission of erectile dysfunction in 4 of 7 male-tailored handouts. An evaluation could target these failure modes, but no study shows that evaluation catches them before patients see them.

Output quality may differ by language within one model. ChatGPT F1 fell 6.45% with Chinese prompts, and physicians rated substance lower in Hebrew than English. One audit located differences in rationale tone and structure rather than in the recommendation, which suggests evaluations that score only final answers may miss this bias.

The only test used simulated scenarios from Brazil, tagged as involving a non-English population, and measured gender bias alone. Hazard studies document stereotyping of racial and ethnic minority, LGBTQIA+, older, and disabled groups. No test evaluated these groups, and none included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients.

A regulatory discussion paper describes checking population-specific clinical knowledge for pregnant, pediatric, and geriatric patients, and the NIST Generative AI Profile calls for domain expertise when modeling hateful content. These documents state expectations rather than tested methods, and no supplied study shows that meeting them reduces biased output.

Patients may encounter stereotyped content in material generated about them. One study found anal sex in 100% of generated cases for gay men versus 3% for heterosexual men. A Kenyan study rated LLMs similar to clinicians on avoiding demographic bias, so the size of the problem may vary by task and setting.

research_gap: No study has tested live monitoring of subgroup exposure to generated content, and none has compared evaluated with unevaluated deployments on error rates, patient trust, or outcomes across populations. Studies are needed that span several languages, low-literacy readers, and safety-net settings, and that measure whether detected bias is corrected before content reaches patients.
underserved_note: The one test used simulated e-prescription scenarios from Brazil and is tagged as involving a non-English population, but it was offline and included no Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients. Evidence that evaluation works for these groups is therefore absent, and hazard studies in Chinese and Hebrew suggest that an evaluation run only in English may miss language-specific gaps.

bottom_line: Offline studies that swapped patient demographics in otherwise identical inputs often detected output changes by sex, race, income, language, or housing status, which suggests the method can surface this hazard before deployment. No study tested whether running these tests reduced biased outputs reaching patients, and one study found that run-to-run model instability can mask or mimic demographic effects.

perspectives.view: All listed tests are level 4 offline simulations. Many reported demographic shifts, such as lower triage severity for female sex swaps (1.1% and 2.2%), while several found no meaningful change. The studies show that the method detects differences. None measured whether acting on findings changed care, and the inconsistency and indirectness suggest low certainty.

The tests surfaced failure modes that could reach patients. These included less guideline-recommended ACS management for female, African American, and Hispanic patients, and mental-health flags for unhoused cases at 78-87% versus 9% in controls. An 8.7% run-to-run instability floor suggests single-run flips may produce false alarms, and majority voting over five draws removed 39% of that floor.

Results varied by model, so a test of one model may not transfer to another. A ZIP code alone shifted one model's ER referrals by 11.4 points, compared with -0.1 and 2.0 for two others. Audio inputs changed surgical recommendations by up to 35% versus identical text, which suggests text-only tests may miss voice-driven shifts.

Homelessness produced the largest eligibility shift across 5.3 million trial-screening evaluations. Low-income profiles were less likely to receive environmental adjustment in nursing plans (aRR 0.90). Language often did not alter pain recommendations in a study of 60 prompts, while a hazard study found that non-English prompts with a US location raised ER recommendations by up to 76.7 points.

The tests ran at large scale offline, up to 5.3 million evaluations across nine models. Reliable results required repeated sampling, such as 20 runs per vignette or five draws per case, which adds compute and analyst time. No study reported costs or staffing, so the resources needed for routine testing remain unknown.

When race was stated or implied, models often proposed inferior treatments. In another study, models were 16.8 times more likely to add unprompted cost warnings for a patient named Lakisha than for one named Emily. In a randomized study of 50 physicians, GPT-4 advice improved decision accuracy without adding race or gender bias, though the text gave no numbers.

research_gap: No study tested whether counterfactual testing before or during deployment reduced biased outputs or harm to patients in live care. Studies are needed that pair testing with remediation and measure downstream clinical outcomes. They should also report run-to-run instability floors, cover audio and multilingual inputs, and include data from Medicaid and safety-net settings.
underserved_note: Some tests varied low-income, homelessness, rural, and language attributes in synthetic vignettes, and one used Finnish-language queries. No test used Medicaid or safety-net patient data or examined low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore shows that swapping these attributes can reveal output changes, but it does not show how testing performs for these patients in real care settings.

bottom_line: Eight sources endorse verifying and documenting the legal basis, consent, or data use agreement for each AI data use, but no supplied study tests whether this practice reduces unlawful use or disclosure of PHI. The recommendation rests on professional consensus and legal obligation rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice, and no supplied study documents the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The eight endorsements include two frameworks, two guidance documents, and four commentaries. They agree on direction, but agreement among expert sources does not show that documentation and approval steps prevent improper disclosure.

The endorsing sources frame the practice as meeting existing legal duties. CHAI playbooks limit permitted uses to defined functions, RUAIH guidance asks that data use agreements prohibit re-identification, and the Uganda ethics guide calls for sharing agreements that bind both parties. These statements describe expected compliance, but no supplied study measures whether it reduces violations.

The ILAE roadmap states that people with epilepsy should know how their data will be used, shared, and protected. The practice may support that expectation by making each data flow traceable to a documented basis. No supplied study measures patient awareness, trust, or complaints before and after such a process.

research_gap: No study evaluates whether per-use legal basis documentation and privacy officer or data steward sign-off reduce unauthorized PHI disclosure, secondary reuse, or feedback-loop reuse in AI projects. Useful designs would compare audit findings, breach reports, or data use agreement exceptions across sites or periods with and without the approval step, and would record the review time and backlog it adds.
underserved_note: No supplied study tests the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Consent and notice processes may reach these groups differently, and whether documented consent reflects their understanding remains untested.

bottom_line: Two offline studies found that analytics and federated model training ran without row-level patient data leaving the local environment, but neither tested export review, small-cell suppression, or the handling of embeddings. A separate simulation found that 79.9% of LLM conversations reached k < 5, which shows the disclosure risk exists but does not show that suppression prevents it.

perspectives.view: Two level 4 studies without comparators test only the data-locality part of the recommendation. One replicated a single published study, and the other trained a model across 12 hospitals. Both ran offline or in simulation. No study measured disclosure events, export review, or suppression thresholds, so certainty for the full practice is very low.

A simulation of 5,000 patients found that 79.9% of LLM conversations reached k < 5 and 86.2% reached k < 11. This suggests small-cell exposure may occur routinely in conversational AI outputs. No study tested whether a suppression rule or export review catches these outputs before release.

In one study, an external LLM received zero row-level patient data while core analyses ran through local R execution. In another, federated training across 12 hospitals in 8 nations shared no data outside each hospital. These results suggest that local execution is technically workable. Neither study reported staff burden, workflow fidelity, or how long export review took.

CHAI sets a minimum of 10 patients for exported metrics and bars proportions that could derive smaller values. FDA draft guidance asks sponsors to exclude patient identifiers from submissions. RUAIH guidance requires protection against unauthorized release. The endorsements agree on the principle, but no study tested whether meeting these thresholds prevents re-identification.

The multinational federated study ran across 12 hospitals using a secure aggregation server for model averaging. This suggests that keeping data local can work across sites. The study did not report costs, staffing, or infrastructure requirements, so the resources needed at scale remain unknown.

research_gap: No study compared export review or small-cell suppression against no review and measured disclosure or re-identification events. No study tested whether embeddings kept inside or exported from the secure environment can be inverted to recover patient data. Studies in live deployments that report staff time and false-positive suppression rates are also missing.
underserved_note: Neither test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and the multinational study did not describe patient characteristics. Small subgroups produce small cells more often, so suppression rules may disproportionately hide results for these populations. That trade-off between privacy and visibility for these groups has not been measured.

bottom_line: Two post-deployment studies found that subgroup monitoring of deployed tools detected performance differences by age, and hazard studies found that subgroup gaps can emerge or widen after launch. No study tested whether monitoring at set intervals led to correction or better patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: One quasi-experimental study (n=12877) and one cross-sectional study (n=254) tested the practice in real deployments. The first found sensitivity of 70.1% with no subgroup variation, while specificity fell from 93% under age 60 to 84% over age 80 (P<.001). The second found higher positive predictive value under 48 months. Neither measured correction or patient outcomes, so certainty is low.

Hazard studies suggest that subgroup failures can appear after launch. In one, Hispanic/Latino AUC fell from 0.81 to 0.71 in production. In another, race and sex gaps grew over time (P<.01 for trend). A deployed malnutrition model underestimated malnutrition in females. These studies show the problem exists. They do not show that monitoring prevents harm.

The fairness drift study found gaps widening over time after deployment. This suggests that a single validation at launch may miss them and that repeated checks may be needed. The supplied studies do not report monitoring frequency, staff time, or how intervals were matched to tool risk. The proportionate-interval element of this recommendation therefore has no tested basis.

The Canadian study focused on racial and ethnic minority patients and older adults, and the age signal appeared there. The tested and hazard studies stratified by age, sex, and race only. Monitoring designs that omit payer, language, or literacy may miss disparities affecting those groups, and the current evidence cannot say whether they do.

One test was framed as post-market monitoring of a device by sex and age. FUTURE-AI calls for periodic auditing to identify drift and newly occurring biases, and the RUAIH guidance calls for regular monitoring to identify biases. The supplied evidence does not show how such guidance becomes a binding requirement or whether the vendor or the health system holds the monitoring duty.

research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without scheduled subgroup monitoring, tested which intervals suit which risk tiers, or followed detected disparities through recalibration to patient outcomes. No study measured the staff time or cost of monitoring, and none stratified results by insurance, language, or literacy.
underserved_note: The Canadian quasi-experimental test focused on racial and ethnic minority patients and older adults. Neither test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether subgroup monitoring detects disparities along payer, language, or literacy lines.

bottom_line: Nine sources endorse an AI data register, including two CHAI frameworks at the must level and an FDA draft guidance at the should level, but no supplied study tests whether a register reduces use of untracked or unknown-origin data. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and commentary rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard's frequency or consequences. The nine endorsements include frameworks, guidance, and commentaries, and none of these designs yields an effect estimate. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. Agreement across sources shows consistent expert opinion, not demonstrated benefit.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks sponsors to describe storage of training and test data, and NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to track dependencies between upstream and downstream data and systems. A register may help organizations answer these requests. Neither document is final binding law for local deployers, and the draft status may change.

No supplied study examines the register in any population. Commentaries on prenatal and pediatric image data raise consent and secondary-use concerns for groups who cannot consent for themselves. These concerns suggest that sensitivity classes may need to capture consent status, but no evidence shows whether a register protects these groups.

research_gap: No study has compared organizations with and without an AI data register on outcomes such as unauthorized dataset use, time to trace data behind a model error, completeness of provenance records, consent-violation incidents, or staff burden to keep the register current. Studies of the hazard itself, including how often AI projects use data of unknown origin or rights, are also absent.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups have no evidence on whether a register affects data rights or harms for their patients, or on the cost of maintaining one with limited staff.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether limiting AI data collection, vendor sharing, or logging to the minimum necessary, with documented justification for each element, reduces patient data exposure. One simulation study shows that re-identification risk can build up across multi-turn AI prompts even when no single prompt contains a direct identifier.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single available study documents the hazard in 5,000 simulated patients drawn from synthetic records and does not evaluate a minimization policy. Twenty-two sources endorse the practice, but most are guidance or commentary, and the number of endorsements does not substitute for outcome data.

In the simulation, 79.9% of patients reached k<5 within a disclosure sequence, with a median of 7 steps under progressive disclosure, although no turn contained direct identifiers. This suggests that element-by-element review may miss harm that arises from combinations of individually harmless fields. A safeguard that justifies each element separately may leave cumulative exposure unchecked.

The hazard study concerns multi-turn prompts to a language model rather than structured vendor data feeds. Justification lists for each data element fit structured exports more easily than free-text chat. No study reports how organizations apply minimum-necessary review to prompts, logs, or agent tool calls, or how much staff time that review requires.

The endorsements vary in scope and force. Texas SB 1188 bars collecting, storing, or sharing credit score or voter registration status in the electronic health record, which is narrower than a general minimum-necessary rule. The CHAI playbook statement listed concerns validating tool-call outputs rather than data minimization. Most remaining sources are guidance or commentary using should.

research_gap: No study compares AI deployments with and without per-element minimum-necessary review. Such studies should measure re-identification risk, the volume of data shared with vendors or retained in logs, effects on model performance, and staff time. They should also test whether per-element justification detects cumulative disclosure across prompts and conversation turns.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study used synthetic patients and reported no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups. Organizations serving these populations therefore have no evidence on whether minimization reduces exposure for their patients. Patients from small communities or less common language groups may carry more distinctive quasi-identifiers, but this has not been studied.

bottom_line: Twelve sources endorse data management plans, standardized preparation, and recurring data-quality checks for each AI solution, but no study has tested whether these practices improve AI performance or protect personal data. One offline benchmark suggests that model discrimination holds up at data error rates below 10% and declines at 10% or higher, which shows the hazard exists without testing the safeguard.

perspectives.view: No study tests the recommended practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is a level 5 automated benchmark in an offline setting with 42,110 older-adult patients. It reports that ROC-AUC deteriorated at error rates of 10% or more, which is indirect evidence about data quality and says nothing about management plans.

The benchmark suggests a possible threshold: errors below 10% were tolerated, and performance dropped at 10% or higher. If that pattern holds in live settings, recurring quality evaluation might catch degradation before it affects predictions. No study shows that such evaluation detects errors in time or prevents harm, and the privacy exposure named in the hazard was not examined.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software lists explicit term definitions as a may-level practice and gives the example of a sex field that one party codes as sex at birth and another as self-reported. NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to document data accuracy and representativeness across the life cycle. Both documents rest on expert consensus rather than on trial data.

The only study drew on older adults in the United States and Australia and did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Data errors and missing fields may cluster in records for these patients, so an overall error-rate threshold could hide higher error rates in subgroups. No evidence addresses this question.

research_gap: No study compares AI performance, data-quality drift, or privacy incidents between deployments with and without a documented data management plan, standardized preprocessing, or scheduled quality audits. Prospective evaluations in live clinical settings should measure how often recurring checks detect errors near the 10% level reported in the benchmark, what the checks cost in staff time, and whether they reduce downstream harm or data exposure.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, and the one hazard study included older adults without reporting Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether data-quality procedures perform equally well for their patients or whether error rates in their records exceed the tolerated range.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether mapping AI data flows, third parties, and legal agreements reduces data exposure. One deployment audit found an undocumented third-party analytics tag that contradicted an app's local-only privacy claim, so the hazard is documented but the practice has not been evaluated.

perspectives.view: Six sources endorse the practice, all frameworks or commentaries, and no comparative or observational study measures its effect on exposure or breach rates. The single supplied study is a hazard report of level 3 evidence with sample size not reported. Under GRADE conventions, certainty for the practice itself cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

A code audit in a real deployment found a third-party analytics tag sending data despite a local-only privacy claim. This suggests vendor statements alone may miss exposures. Whether a data flow map made before deployment would have caught this tag is untested, since the finding came from a code audit rather than from documentation review.

The audited tag surfaced only through inspection of code, which suggests that maps built from vendor questionnaires or contracts may not reflect runtime behavior. No study reports how long mapping takes, how often maps drift from actual traffic, or whether plugins added after go-live are captured.

CHAI playbooks tie data governance to breach notification within 10 to 15 days, and NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to inventory third parties with access to content. A current map may help an organization determine what was disclosed and to whom when a notification deadline applies, though no study has measured this.

The audited app told users their data stayed on the device while a third-party tag operated in the background. Patients generally cannot inspect code, so they depend on the organization to confirm privacy claims. An unverified claim of this kind may reduce trust once it is discovered.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations or AI deployments with and without structured data flow mapping, measuring undocumented third-party transmissions found at audit, breach incidents, time to breach notification, and staff effort. Such studies should also test whether maps built from documentation match network or code-level observation over time.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The one hazard study involved older adults and did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, so there is no evidence on whether mapping protects these groups or whether their apps and vendors differ in third-party exposure.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether logging AI queries, outputs, and data access, or auditing those logs, detects or reduces inappropriate access to patient data. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus from frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Of the 12 endorsements listed, two come from frameworks, two from guidance, and eight from commentaries. One CHAI playbook statement addresses subgroup performance reporting rather than logging. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements cannot substitute for tested outcomes.

No supplied study measures how often inappropriate access to patient data through AI systems occurs, or whether audit logs catch it before harm. Without hazard data, the size of the problem and the yield of log review remain unknown, so the expected safety benefit cannot be estimated from this evidence.

No study reports the storage, review workload, or audit fidelity of logging LLM interactions in live clinical workflows. The endorsements describe what to capture, such as inputs, outputs, timestamps, and source references. They do not describe how often reviewers can examine those records or how accurately they flag policy violations.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI deployments with and without interaction logging and scheduled audits. These studies should measure detection rates of inappropriate access, time to detection, false-positive audit flags, and reviewer staffing hours. Baseline studies are also needed on the frequency of inappropriate patient-data access through AI tools.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether logging and audit protect their patients' data equally, or whether safety-net systems can staff the audit workload.

bottom_line: Two CHAI frameworks endorse role- and context-based screening of EHR-connected LLM queries and retrieval corpora, but no supplied study tests the practice or measures how often LLMs expose patient data to unauthorized users. Adoption currently rests on framework guidance and on existing access-control principles rather than on outcome data.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests query or corpus screening, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements are expert frameworks, which carry the weight of consensus opinion rather than empirical findings on effectiveness or error rates.

Without hazard studies, the frequency and severity of unauthorized disclosure through LLM interfaces remain unmeasured. No study reports whether an intermediary screening layer, such as the Safeguard LLM that CHAI describes, catches inappropriate retrievals before they reach users, or how often it blocks appropriate access that clinicians need.

The CHAI playbook states access controls for the retrieval corpus as a must, and the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide frames an intermediary safeguard as a should. Both are voluntary frameworks. The supplied material contains no regulatory requirement or enforcement data specific to LLM access screening.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often EHR-connected LLMs return patient information outside a user's role or encounter context, and that compare disclosure rates, false blocks, and clinician workflow burden with and without query and corpus screening.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Organizations therefore have no evidence on whether screening performs differently for these patients, for example in shared-device, proxy-access, or interpreter-mediated encounters.

bottom_line: Thirty-four sources endorse encrypting patient data used by AI at rest and in transit, but no study tests whether this practice reduces interception or exposure of patient data in AI systems. The only supplied study documents the hazard, finding no encryption in any of three student-built dementia app prototypes.

perspectives.view: No supplied study compares AI deployments with and without encryption on any outcome, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single hazard study is a level 4 offline assessment of three student prototypes. It shows that encryption can be omitted in practice, but it does not measure whether adding encryption prevents exposure.

None of three vibe-coded dementia mHealth prototypes implemented data encryption, which suggests that rapidly built AI tools may reach users without basic data protection. Encryption would address one failure mode, interception of stored or transmitted data, but the supplied evidence does not show how often exposure occurs in deployed clinical AI or how much encryption reduces it.

The endorsements tie encryption to existing HIPAA security practice, and the FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to address dataset security under its cybersecurity section. Several frameworks use mandatory language. These sources establish an expectation that regulators and assessors may apply, although none reports data on compliance or effect.

research_gap: No study measures whether encrypting AI training data, inference logs, backups, and vendor API channels reduces breaches or unauthorized access compared with partial or absent encryption. Studies are needed that audit encryption coverage across deployed clinical AI systems and vendor integrations and that link coverage to breach incidents, along with estimates of implementation cost and performance effects on inference.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study did not report participant populations, so no evidence addresses Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. Safety-net organizations with smaller security budgets may face greater difficulty verifying encryption across vendor channels, but the supplied evidence cannot confirm or quantify that risk.

bottom_line: One simulated benchmark found that least-privilege, defence-in-depth agent workflows lowered attack success from 31% to 10% and from 42% to 25% and raised accuracy from 72.5% to 86.5%, but no study tested isolated environments or governance of persistent memory and retention in clinical settings. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement and indirect, offline evidence.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice (arxiv:2606.28666) is a level 5 automated benchmark with 800 report generations and 500 attack scenarios run offline. Its results favor least privilege, but indirectness, a single study, and no patient or clinical outcomes lower certainty to very low. The memory retention and access-control component has no test at all.

Attack success fell from 31% to 10% and from 42% to 25% under restricted workflows, which suggests fewer paths for an agent to reach data outside its task. A separate benchmark (arxiv:2609.29341) observed no cross-user leakage in 240 cases, but finite test suites cannot show that leakage never occurs, and that study did not test the safeguard.

Both studies ran in simulated environments, so they say nothing about how least-privilege scoping, sandboxing, or memory retention rules perform inside live EHR integrations. The accuracy gain from 72.5% to 86.5% may not carry over once agents face real permission models, credential management, and clinician workflows.

The CHAI playbook gives a must-level expectation to define which records are eligible for a retrieval corpus, such as defined date ranges. That guidance addresses data scope for retrieval and only partly covers agent system privileges, isolation, or memory retention, so the endorsement supports the recommendation indirectly.

Neither study reported the patient population behind its test data, and both used synthetic or benchmark cases. No evidence shows whether access restrictions perform the same way for records of Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients, whose data may be spread across more systems.

research_gap: No study has tested least-privilege access, environment isolation, or persistent-memory access controls and retention limits for agents operating on real clinical data. Prospective evaluations in live health system deployments should measure unauthorized data access, aggregation, and retention events, along with the operational cost of maintaining permission scopes.
underserved_note: Neither the test study nor the hazard study reported population characteristics, and both used offline benchmark cases, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups have no evidence on whether the safeguard performs equally for their patients' records.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this recommendation tests whether baseline security controls on AI infrastructure reduce compromise of AI systems, models, or data stores, and no study documents the hazard in AI settings. The recommendation rests on endorsement by frameworks, federal guidance, and commentaries that extend general information-security practice to AI.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Support comes from frameworks, guidance, and commentaries, several of which state the need for security in general terms. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about the effect of these controls on AI-specific compromise cannot be rated.

FDA draft guidance asks device sponsors to describe access controls, encryption, and de-identification, and one playbook notes that the annual HIPAA Security Risk Assessment is a condition of federal funding for community health centers. These sources suggest that existing legal obligations may already require much of this practice, although none shows its effect on outcomes.

The endorsements point to established external standards, including ISO/IEC 27001, the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and the Cloud Security Alliance controls matrix. Organizations may be able to fold AI infrastructure into security programs they already run, but no supplied source reports the staffing, cost, or time needed to extend segregation, patching, and integrity checks to AI systems.

No supplied study describes an incident in which weak infrastructure security led to a compromised model or data store that affected patient care. The failure mode the recommendation targets is plausible, but its frequency and severity in health care AI remain undocumented in this evidence set.

research_gap: Studies are needed that document how often AI infrastructure in health care is compromised and by what route, and that compare organizations with and without segregated environments, configuration baselines, patching schedules, and integrity verification on outcomes such as intrusion rates, model tampering, data exposure, and time to detection.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One endorsing playbook addresses community health centers and treats the HIPAA Security Risk Assessment as their de facto security baseline, which suggests that safety-net organizations may rely on a minimum compliance standard and could lack capacity to add AI-specific controls; this possibility has not been examined.

bottom_line: Two studies test parts of this practice, and neither measures whether review, correction, deletion, or opt-out controls reduce privacy harm in a deployed clinical AI system. One simulated study links greater data autonomy to more self-disclosure, and one benchmark suggests patient-level data deletion from deployed models may be technically feasible at small accuracy cost.

perspectives.view: The two tests are a level 4 simulated VR study (n=90, plus a survey of 152 patients) and a level 5 automated benchmark, and both provide indirect evidence. One measures self-disclosure and trust rather than privacy harm, and the other measures deletion speed and accuracy. Neither evaluates the full set of controls in real use, so certainty is very low.

The hazard studies show that the failure mode exists. Only 2 of 12 chatbot apps let users disable data sharing at sign-up. LLM outputs disclosed sensitive information in 722 of 2,113 documents (34.2%) despite do-not-share requests. These findings suggest that preference settings alone may not stop disclosure unless the model reliably honors them.

On 1,646,139 EHR records, sharded retraining (SISA) removed individual patient data 8.9 times faster than full retraining (7.5 s vs 66.7 s), with a 0.024% accuracy cost. On a genomic dataset it was 9.8 times faster, with a 0.048% cost. This suggests deletion requests may be workable for some model types, although the benchmark did not test live clinical workflows.

The benchmark reports deletion times measured in seconds for antimicrobial resistance models. This may indicate that honoring deletion requests need not require costly full retraining for similar models. The study did not examine staffing, request-handling procedures, or costs for larger generative models.

In the German study, mental health participants given more control over their data disclosed more to an AI therapist, but their trust did not change. This result suggests patients may share more when they hold control. The chatbot app review found that most apps offered users little control over their personal data.

The two tests were conducted in a German laboratory sample and on a benchmark dataset without reported demographics. Neither reports inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether these groups can find and use data-control interfaces.

research_gap: No study has evaluated review, correction, deletion, opt-out, and preference controls together in a deployed clinical AI system with privacy-harm outcomes. It is also unknown whether models enforce stated preferences in their outputs, given 34.2% disclosure despite requests, and whether deletion methods work for large generative models.
underserved_note: Neither test included or reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, so the evidence cannot show whether data-control interfaces are usable or effective for these populations. Controls that depend on reading privacy dashboards or English-language consent text may be less accessible to them, and no study has tested this.

bottom_line: Thirteen sources endorse telling patients through the Notice of Privacy Practices and published notices how AI uses their data, but no study tests whether such notices improve patient awareness or reduce privacy harm. The one related study documents disclosure gaps in custom medical GPTs and does not evaluate the recommended practice.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so the certainty rating is no direct evidence. The single hazard study is an automated benchmark of custom medical GPTs rather than health system notices, and it is indirect to the question. The endorsements come mostly from commentaries and frameworks, which reflect expert agreement rather than measured effects on patients.

An automated review sampled 1,500 of 6,233 custom medical GPTs and found that 57.06% of the Action-enabled models lacked adequate privacy disclosures. This suggests that people may use some AI tools without knowing how their data are handled. The study does not show whether an updated notice would prevent that exposure.

The CHAI playbook points out that the HIPAA Privacy Rule already requires covered providers and health plans to distribute a notice explaining privacy rights and practices. Adding AI content to that notice would build on an existing legal duty. No study reports whether regulators or patients find such AI language adequate or understandable.

The benchmark found that 57.06% of Action-enabled models in a sample of custom medical GPTs lacked adequate privacy disclosures, which suggests that some patients may not be able to learn how AI tools use their information. No study has measured whether a revised notice gives patients usable knowledge of their rights or a way to reach a person with questions.

research_gap: Studies should compare AI-specific language in the Notice of Privacy Practices and public web notices against the standard notice and measure patient comprehension, trust, opt-out use, and complaint rates. They should also measure how many patients read these notices at all.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, and the hazard study did not report patient populations, so there is no evidence for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Notices written only in English or at high reading levels may reach these groups less well, but no study has tested this.

bottom_line: One uncontrolled 90-day study of nine autonomous AI agents found that an automated security audit agent surfaced four high-severity vulnerabilities, all of which were remediated, which suggests recurring scanning can find real flaws. No study has tested a documented vulnerability management plan for clinical AI systems or measured effects on breaches or patient harm.

perspectives.view: The only test is a pre-post study without a comparator, involving nine AI agents in an unreported setting. It counts findings and remediations but does not measure breaches prevented.
