The design is weak, the population is indirect to clinical AI, the sample is small, and no second study exists to check consistency. Certainty is very low.

Four high-severity findings in 90 days on nine agents suggest that deployed AI systems carry exploitable flaws that routine auditing can surface before an attacker does. The study does not link these findings to any clinical data exposure or patient harm, so the size of the safety benefit in health care remains unknown.

The study hardened the fleet across three virtual machine image generations, which indicates that audit findings fed back into the build process. The study did not report how the audit agent fit into clinical workflows, how much staff time remediation took, or how often scans produced false alarms.

Twelve sources endorse the practice, including the FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software, NIST AI 600-1, and CHAI, and three rate it as a requirement. The endorsements rest on established cybersecurity practice and HIPAA security expectations rather than on trials in clinical AI, and CHAI asks organizations to define and justify scan frequency.

The tested approach used an automated audit agent, which may lower the staffing needed for recurring scans. The study reported no costs, and it did not describe the effort required for penetration testing or external audits, so health systems have no evidence to budget from beyond general security program experience.

research_gap: Health systems need controlled or comparative studies of vulnerability management programs for deployed clinical AI, including large language model and device software, that measure breaches, data exposure, time to remediation, false alarm burden, and cost, and that compare scan frequencies and automated versus human testing.
underserved_note: The single study did not report its setting or any patient population, and it did not include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net organizations often have smaller security staffs and budgets, so the evidence cannot show whether the practice is feasible or effective where breach risk may fall on patients with the fewest resources to respond.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether restricting staff to approved tools, banning PHI in public tools, defining permitted prompt data, or privacy training reduces PHI exposure. Six surveys and query-log analyses show that clinicians and students enter patient data into unapproved tools at rates that range from under 3% to 48.6% across groups.

perspectives.view: No study tests the recommended controls, so certainty about their effect is rated as no direct evidence. The six hazard studies are cross-sectional surveys or query-log analyses that rely mostly on self-report. Their estimates range from under 3% of physical therapy professionals entering identifiable data to 48.6% of hematologists entering patient data, which suggests inconsistency across professions and countries.

Among French student users, 23.5% reported at least one disclosure of patient-identifying information, and 8.2% of Turkish hematologists entered identifiable data. Another 47.1% of student users processed real medical content they perceived as anonymized, which may indicate that users misjudge what counts as identifiable and that training would need to address this.

In an analysis of 106,942 physician queries, 2.68% contained sensitive information, mostly from writing and editing tasks. Among medical students using ChatGPT, 21.0% used it to help write clinical notes. These findings suggest that rules on permitted prompt data and approved tools would need to cover documentation and editing workflows.

Among 78 French oncology pharmacists, 65.3% reported using unsanctioned AI and 62.5% reported concern about patient data confidentiality. This pattern suggests that staff demand exists and that a ban without approved alternatives may not change behavior. No supplied study reports the cost or staffing needed to put these controls in place.

Endorsing sources, including the CHAI playbooks, call for defining which clinical data may enter prompts and for HIPAA- or GDPR-compliant platforms procured under institutional agreements. No supplied study examines whether these policies improve compliance with privacy law, so support for the recommendation rests on existing privacy obligations and expert consensus.

None of the six hazard studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations or the staff who serve them. The studies come from the United States, Türkiye, France, and one unreported setting, so the rate of PHI exposure in safety-net care is unknown.

research_gap: No study compares PHI exposure before and after an organization adopts approved-tool restrictions, prompt data rules, or privacy training. Controlled or interrupted time-series studies that measure disclosure objectively, for example through audited prompt logs rather than self-report, would show whether these controls reduce exposure and whether staff move to unsanctioned tools in response.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and none of the six hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups have no evidence on how often PHI exposure occurs in their settings or whether these controls would work there, and training materials may need separate testing for staff and patients with differing language and literacy needs.

bottom_line: Three offline and benchmark studies suggest that routing, privacy-editing, and client-side de-identification controls may reduce PHI leakage from generative AI tools, but none tested these controls in live clinical use. The evidence rests on synthetic notes and simulated outputs, so certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: All three tests point in the same direction, but each used simulated outputs or synthetic notes at evidence levels 4 and 5. No study measured leakage in deployed tools or real patient data. Serious indirectness and study design limits lower certainty to very low despite consistent findings.

A routing workflow cut disclosure from 21.7% to 1.2% without increasing harmful omission. Simply asking the model to withhold information lowered disclosure only from 46.6% to 34.2%. No single mitigation eliminated third-party leakage. A separate simulation found 79.9% of patients reached k < 5 in a median of 7 steps, so filtering direct identifiers may leave re-identification risk.

Client-side de-identification reached 99.94% recall on direct HIPAA identifiers at 1.84 ms per note, compared with 242.6 ms for a cloud DLP proxy. Packet inspection found zero outbound PHI bytes. Privacy editing reduced leakage only when privacy definitions were specific to context, which suggests that setup requires local tailoring.

The latency results suggest client-side filtering may add little delay to clinician work. The studies report no data on licensing cost, staffing to tune privacy rules, or how often legitimate content gets blocked. Administrators cannot yet estimate the full cost of adopting these controls at scale from this evidence.

Among the endorsements, only the CHAI playbook directly calls for output filtering, and it rates the practice as a must. The supplied NIST excerpt addresses anthropomorphization, and the ethics commentary addresses consent for model training. Neither speaks directly to data loss prevention controls.

None of the three tests reported the patient populations behind their synthetic or simulated data. No test examined notes from Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients, or notes written in languages other than English.

research_gap: No study has tested input and output filtering or data loss prevention in generative AI tools deployed in live clinical workflows. Prospective evaluations should measure leakage in real traffic, re-identification through quasi-identifiers, the rate of wrongly blocked clinical content, and clinician workarounds. They should also report performance on notes from diverse and multilingual patient populations.
underserved_note: No test included or reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and all relied on synthetic or simulated data. Detection recall for identifiers in non-English or atypically documented notes remains unknown. Organizations serving these patients should validate filters on their own records before relying on them.

bottom_line: Seven studies test specific defenses such as input sanitization, image denoising, secured agent workflows, and poisoning-resistant aggregation, and each reports lower attack success or recovered accuracy in offline benchmarks. No study tests an organizational red-teaming program in a deployed clinical system, so the evidence that the practice as a whole prevents patient harm is very low.

perspectives.view: All seven tests are level 5 automated benchmarks or offline simulations, most without a reported setting or sample size. Each evaluates one technical defense against attacks the authors built, not routine red-teaming by a health system. The results agree in direction, but indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

Injected inputs produced unsafe pregnancy drug advice in 91.7% of extreme-harm scenarios, and poisoning detection was estimated at 6 to 12 months or never. Defenses reduced but did not remove risk. RAG poisoning success fell from 31% to 10%, and median aggregation gave inconsistent benefit at 10% noise.

No defense was tested inside a live clinical workflow, and none of the studies reports staff time or alert burden. One input sanitizer restored fidelity from 0.098 to 0.945 without refusals, which suggests some defenses may avoid blocking legitimate use. A secured agent workflow tested 500 attack scenarios offline only.

A backdoor aimed at one demographic group took hold after 2.6% of training labels were flipped, and five detectors failed to find it. This suggests poisoning can target specific populations. The only defense test involving non-English input used Japanese text in Japan, and no test examined Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled devices lists malformed input (fuzz) testing, and FUTURE-AI calls for regular evaluation of attack defenses. No supplied study measures whether meeting these expectations lowers attack success in practice. The recommendation therefore rests on expert consensus and benchmark evidence rather than on tests of compliance programs.

One study built a distilled surrogate model for $12, and it produced unsafe completions for 86% of adversarial prompts. That figure suggests attacks cost attackers little. None of the defense studies reports what red-teaming, input validation, or data provenance controls cost a health system in staff or tooling, so budgeting cannot yet draw on evidence.

Models given fabricated clinical details produced false lab values or nonexistent conditions in 50% to 82.7% of cases. Patients could receive such outputs without knowing that an input was manipulated. No study measured whether adversarial testing changed what patients actually received or how easily they could reach a clinician to check.

research_gap: No study evaluates a recurring red-teaming and input-validation program in a deployed health care AI system. Needed work would compare sites with and without such programs on attacks detected, time to detection, unsafe outputs reaching clinicians or patients, and staff and vendor cost. Defense tests should use realistic clinical inputs and report setting and sample size.
underserved_note: One defense test (pmid:42326139) used non-English (Japanese) input in Japan. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, and no test reported results by patient subgroup. A hazard study showing a demographic backdoor that evaded five detectors suggests that defenses validated on general benchmarks may not protect specific groups, and this remains untested.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether role-based, least-privilege access, strong authentication, or credential lifecycle management reduces unauthorized access to AI systems or patient data in health care. Two hazard studies show the gap exists, with one deployed patient chatbot exposing 1,000 recent patient conversations without authentication, and the recommendation rests on 20 endorsing sources that include a Texas statute and HIPAA-based guidance.

perspectives.view: No included study compares access controls or authentication against their absence, so certainty about the practice's effect cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two available studies are a single real deployment and three simulated student prototypes. They establish that the hazard occurs, but they do not measure whether the recommended controls prevent it.

In one deployed chatbot, ordinary browser inspection exposed the system prompt, knowledge base, API schema, and 1,000 patient conversations without authentication. This suggests the exposure required no specialized tools to find. The study documents read access to these records, and no study has tested whether authentication would have prevented the exposure.

None of three dementia mHealth prototypes built with AI-assisted coding implemented user authentication. This suggests that rapid development methods may omit access controls unless someone requires and checks them before deployment. The study, as summarized, did not test whether adding authentication was feasible in these workflows or what burden it placed on users.

Texas SB 1188 requires covered entities to limit electronic health record access to individuals whose employment duties require it. Guidance sources tie AI use to the HIPAA minimum necessary standard and business associate agreements. For affected organizations, least-privilege access is therefore a legal obligation that does not depend on trial evidence.

The exposed records included the 1,000 most recent patient-chatbot conversations, which suggests that one missing authentication step can place many patients' disclosures at risk at the same time. Exposures of this kind may reduce patients' willingness to share health information with AI tools. No study examined how access controls affect patients' ability to reach a human.

research_gap: Studies should compare AI deployments with and without enforced role-based access, multifactor authentication, and credential rotation. Outcomes should include measured rates of unauthorized access, audit-detected anomalies, and time to credential revocation, along with the effect of these controls on clinician workflow and patient access.
underserved_note: Neither hazard study reported whether it included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and no study tested the practice in any population. Organizations therefore have no evidence on whether authentication requirements such as multifactor or SMS verification create access barriers for patients with limited digital literacy or limited English.

bottom_line: Nine sources endorse executing Business Associate Agreements before AI vendors handle PHI, including one state statute and one framework at the must level, but no study tests whether these agreements, or AI-specific terms within them, reduce improper PHI handling. The recommendation rests on legal obligation and expert consensus rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard's frequency or consequences. The nine endorsements include one statute, one framework, two guidance documents, and five commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not substitute for tests of an intervention, so certainty about effect on PHI exposure cannot be rated.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbot suppliers sharing information to comply with 45 C.F.R. Parts 160 and 164. The CHAI playbook language routes vendor-held PHI to the BAA. Several commentaries add terms beyond standard HIPAA templates, such as limits on data retention, model retraining, and subprocessors, which suggests standard agreements may leave AI-specific uses unaddressed.

The supplied record contains no study showing how often AI vendors process PHI without enforceable obligations or what harm follows. The endorsed contract terms, including breach notification, incident response, and audit cooperation, describe mechanisms that could detect disclosures, but no evidence shows whether they catch problems before patient data is exposed.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare PHI incidents, retention violations, and unauthorized secondary use, such as model retraining, among AI vendor deployments governed by standard BAAs, BAAs with AI-specific terms, and no agreement. Audits of whether vendors comply with contract terms in practice would also show whether the agreements change vendor behavior.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems with limited legal staff may face more difficulty negotiating AI-specific terms, but the supplied record contains no data on that question.

bottom_line: Twenty-two guidance documents, frameworks, commentaries, and one state statute endorse legal review of AI systems and data contracts for privacy compliance, but no supplied study tests whether this review prevents privacy violations. The recommendation rests on legal obligation and expert consensus rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard's frequency or severity. The support consists of 22 endorsements, most of them guidance and commentary. Under GRADE conventions this yields no direct evidence. The consistency of the endorsements reflects agreement on a legal duty, and agreement of that kind cannot be read as a measured effect.

Parts of this recommendation restate existing law. HIPAA already applies to covered entities and their business associates. Texas SB 1188 requires reasonable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic health record information. Compliance review is therefore a legal requirement in these settings whatever the evidence base shows. Tracking legal change matters because state AI and privacy statutes continue to change.

Reviewing every AI system and its data contracts requires legal and privacy staff time. The volume of that work grows with the number of vendors and with the jurisdictions whose law applies. No supplied study reports what this review costs, how long it takes, or how many staff it needs. Organizations will have to estimate the burden from their own contract inventories.

research_gap: No study measures whether structured legal review of AI systems and data contracts reduces privacy incidents, contract breaches, or regulatory findings. No study compares review models, such as review at procurement alone versus periodic re-review as laws change. No study reports the staffing burden of each approach.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Safety-net organizations may have fewer legal staff to carry out this review. Whether privacy protections reach these patients equally therefore cannot be assessed from the supplied evidence.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether AI privacy and data governance policies, with requirements traceable to controls, reduce privacy harms in health care. The recommendation rests on the agreement of frameworks, professional guidance, and commentaries rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The support comes from two CHAI frameworks rated must, four guidance documents, and six commentaries. Expert agreement of this kind cannot be graded for certainty of effect, so the rating is no direct evidence.

No supplied study measures how often AI privacy failures occur or whether governance policies catch them before patient data is exposed. The radiology multi-society statement names discrimination, insurance costs, and humiliation as possible harms. Those harms remain unquantified in this evidence set.

Several endorsing sources tie data governance to existing law, citing HIPAA and, in one case, GDPR. This suggests organizations may already hold privacy controls that AI-specific policies could map onto. No supplied study shows whether this mapping reduces violations or enforcement actions.

The CHAI playbook states that full DICOM tag scrubbing requires specialized tools rather than general de-identification methods. FUTURE-AI lists access control and logging as mechanisms. No supplied study reports how well these controls perform in routine workflows or what staff burden they add.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations with and without AI-specific data governance policies and traceable controls, and that measure privacy incidents, re-identification events, unauthorized access, and staff effort. Evaluations of specific controls, such as DICOM de-identification tools and access logging for AI systems, would also help.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence cannot show whether governance policies protect these groups equally. It also cannot show whether the consumer disclosures that RUAIH recommends reach patients with limited English or low literacy.

bottom_line: Offline and benchmark studies suggest that current de-identification tools remove most identifiers but miss some categories, and one audit of a deployed system re-identified none of the 790 people it sampled. No study tests reassessing re-identification risk after data linkage, although hazard studies show that people can still be identified from masked notes and from cumulative disclosures.

perspectives.view: Eleven studies test de-identification methods. Only one, a red-team audit of a deployed system, tried to re-identify real people, and it re-identified none of the 790 it sampled. Most others report identifier detection scores on offline or synthetic text, which is a surrogate outcome. No study tests reassessment after linkage. Indirectness and uneven results across identifier types lower certainty to low.

Tools miss identifiers even when summary scores are high. Address recall was 0.5 in one study, 2% of entities were missed in another, and about 4.6% of PII went undetected in a third. In hazard studies, an LLM re-identified 9% of masked notes, and 79.9% of simulated people fell below a k-anonymity of 5 after cumulative disclosure.

De-identification can reduce data usefulness. One facial defacing method lowered downstream segmentation Dice by up to 9% and failed quality checks 14-19% of the time, while another stayed within 3-5% of original accuracy. In a German study, a baseline prompt removed too much text. These results suggest validation should measure retained clinical content as well as privacy.

One study tested de-identification on records from seven low- and middle-income countries. Name F1 ranged from 0.75 for verbal autopsies to 0.94 for another document type. Default tools missed Brazilian identifiers (macro F1 0.270) until they were customized. These results suggest that performance depends on language and document type.

One deployed system satisfied HIPAA Expert Determination. A German project anonymized about 60,000 letters for GDPR compliance. Both suggest that documented, law-specific methods can be carried out. Neither study compared methods, and neither tested whether meeting the legal standard prevents re-identification once datasets are linked.

The one real-world validation used a red team that worked for three months on a sample of 790 people, which gives a sense of the effort an independent audit may require. A model fine-tuned on combined corpora reached strict F1 0.9447, compared with 0.8172 for the best baseline, which suggests off-the-shelf tools may need local adaptation. No study reported costs.

Some patients may face higher risk than others. Pathological speech, especially in adults with dysphonia, showed higher re-identification risk than healthy speech in one study. Psychiatric narratives required a specialized method to reach low identifiability. No study asked patients about their views or measured patient trust.

research_gap: No study tests whether reassessing re-identification risk after dataset linkage reduces actual re-identification. Only one study used an attack-based validation in a real deployment. No study compared governance processes, such as documented method selection and pre-use validation, against usual practice, and none reported costs or staffing needs.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether broad contractual definitions of customer data, use restrictions, training limits, or destruction clauses prevent vendors from reusing, selling, or retaining organizational and patient data. Eleven sources endorse the practice, including one state statute, but the support rests on legal requirement, framework language, and expert commentary rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The eleven endorsements consist of one statute, two frameworks, two guidance documents, and six commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion and policy text do not establish certainty of effect, so the panel cannot rate how well these contract terms reduce data misuse.

Utah HB 452 (2025) bars mental health chatbot suppliers from using a Utah user's input to target advertising for other products, which makes part of the recommendation a legal obligation in that state. The CHAI playbook treats customer data as confidential information and places PHI under the business associate agreement. These sources define the terms but do not show whether vendors comply.

research_gap: Studies could compare vendor contracts with and without broad data definitions, training limits, and destruction clauses, and then audit whether vendors retained, reused, or shared data after deployment or termination. Research could also measure how often vendors breach such terms and whether organizations detect breaches through audit rights.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One commentary on AI translation tools calls for terms that stop repurposing of patient data without explicit consent, which suggests limited English proficiency patients may face this exposure, but whether contract terms protect them remains untested.

bottom_line: Seven studies tested prompt-injection defenses, and all reported lower attack success with the defense in place, but every test ran in simulation or on benchmarks rather than in live clinical use. Organizations have grounds to test for injection before deployment, while the size of the protection in real patient-message and document workflows remains unmeasured.

perspectives.view: All seven tests are level 4 or 5 simulations or benchmarks with surrogate outcomes such as attack success rate. Most tested a different defense, samples were small, and none measured patient harm. The direction of effect is consistent, but indirectness, imprecision, and design limits support a very low certainty rating.

Hazard studies found 94.4% attack success in simulated medical advice dialogues, with 69.4% persisting into follow-ups, and 4 of 20 injection probes caused behavioral errors in another study. Defenses reduced but did not always remove the risk. Data-field injection fell from 42% to 25%, and leakage of about 0.60 per episode persisted despite a sanitizer.

Results for indirect injection differed across two similar Japanese dialogue benchmarks. In one, indirect contamination cut slot F1 to 0.489 and a defense restored it to 0.903. In the other, indirect contamination left fidelity near clean at 0.946, so the defense added little. Workflow fit and fidelity in real systems were not studied.

A regulatory discussion paper lists prompt-injection testing as something testing may include for generative AI devices, and a CHAI playbook requires asset records that support traceability. Agentic middleware and sandbox tests reported 0% policy-injection success and neutralized tool poisoning in simulation, which may inform predeployment testing plans for agentic tools.

Patients who send messages cannot see whether hidden instructions altered an AI response. Simulated attacks succeeded against most commercial models tested, and no study examined whether defenses protect patients once a system is live or whether patients can reach a clinician when output looks wrong.

research_gap: No study tested injection defenses in a live clinical deployment, on real patient portal messages or clinical documents, or with patient harm as an outcome. Only one study compared defenses against each other, and it used dental radiographs with image-embedded text, so no comparison of defenses for text-based patient messages or clinical notes exists.
underserved_note: Two benchmark studies used Japanese-language dialogues and were tagged as non-English populations, but neither involved real patients, and no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether defenses perform differently on messages written in other languages, with nonstandard spelling, or at low literacy levels.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether protecting reporter identity or publishing plain-language data-handling notices increases AI incident reporting, and none documents the reporter-exposure hazard directly. The recommendation currently rests on a single framework endorsement from CHAI governance playbooks.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The CHAI playbook statement is expert guidance and does not substitute for comparative data on reporting rates or reporter outcomes.

The only supporting source is a voluntary framework using "should" language. It specifies that identifying information be withheld from AI vendors during root-cause analysis because vendor contracts may create indirect channels back to a reporter's employer. No supplied study examines how this contractual pathway operates in practice.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI incident reporting volume, reporting quality, and reporter retaliation or exposure events before and after organizations adopt confidentiality protections, vendor data-sharing restrictions, and plain-language notices. Such studies should also measure whether staff read and understand the notices.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers staff or patients in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Whether plain-language notices reach staff with limited English proficiency or lower literacy, or whether safety-net systems can fund confidential reporting channels, remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study tests whether defining and executing retention, storage, and destruction plans for AI data reduces exposure risk, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support rests on ten endorsements from frameworks and commentaries, with one CHAI playbook rating it a must.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. All ten endorsements are frameworks or commentaries, which express expert agreement but cannot establish effect. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the consistency of endorsements should not be read as a measure of benefit.

Several commentaries on ambient scribes describe the design choices a retention plan would need to settle. These include whether to save whole conversations or one party's speech, how long recordings are kept for auditing or retraining, and how transient processing data differs from records entered into the legal medical record. No study reports how such plans perform in practice.

The endorsements suggest that recordings which cannot be de-identified may carry privacy exposure, and one institution reports prohibiting their long-term storage. Because no study measures breaches, leakage, or misuse tied to retained AI data, the size of the risk and the degree to which deletion schedules lower it remain unknown.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations with and without defined AI data retention and destruction plans, including at system decommissioning. Useful outcomes would be the volume of retained recordings and transcripts, adherence to deletion schedules, audit findings, and privacy incidents. Studies should also report the staff time and cost of carrying out these plans.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. One commentary raises data minimization and defined retention for mental health tools in a low-resource setting. Without studies, it is unknown whether retention practices protect these groups equally or whether their recorded conversations face different exposure.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether documenting a tool-specific monitoring plan before go-live reduces undetected harm or performance degradation, and no study documents the hazard itself. Sixteen sources endorse the practice, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and regulatory expectation rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The sixteen endorsements agree that monitoring should occur, but agreement among guidance documents is a form of expert opinion. It does not show that a written plan changes detection rates or patient outcomes.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions lists ongoing performance monitoring as a lifecycle expectation. The CDRH discussion paper on generative AI devices asks whether machine-based supervisory agents could support postmarket monitoring and how those agents would themselves be evaluated. These documents signal regulatory direction, though neither states a documented local plan requirement for health systems.

FAIR-AI requires a monitoring plan for every deployed tool, maintained through periodic attestation by a named business owner. The RUAIH guidance similarly asks organizations to identify responsible parties. The supplied sources give no data on staff hours, cost, or the number of tools a governance group can monitor, so the burden at scale remains unmeasured.

The radiology multi-society statement leaves the definition of sufficient monitoring to local oversight groups on a case-by-case basis, and the NASEM-style delivery guidance stresses baseline data architecture. This suggests that plan content will vary widely across tools and sites. No supplied study reports whether such plans are completed, followed, or kept current after go-live.

The HEAAL framework asks developers and deployers to devise strategies for ongoing monitoring, feedback, and evaluation across the lifecycle. No supplied study examines whether monitoring plans include subgroup performance measures or whether they detect degradation that falls unevenly on particular patient groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare tools deployed with and without a documented, owner-assigned monitoring plan and measure time to detection of performance drift or safety events, the frequency of plan adherence after go-live, and the staffing cost of maintaining plans across a tool portfolio.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients have no evidence on whether monitoring plans detect harms specific to them, and safety-net sites may have less data infrastructure to carry out the plans these sources describe.

bottom_line: Eleven benchmark and simulation studies suggest that differential privacy, secure or encrypted aggregation, and related methods can lower membership inference success, often at a measurable cost to model accuracy. No study tested these methods or privacy red-teaming in a deployed clinical system, so certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: Eleven studies test privacy-enhancing methods. All are automated benchmarks or simulations, and one is rated level 4. Nine report reduced membership inference or leakage, and two report mixed results. Outcomes are simulated attack metrics rather than observed re-identification. The methods differ too widely to pool, so certainty is very low.

Hazard studies show the risk exists. Over 92% of training participants were identified from reconstructed retinal images, and up to 87% of memorized content persisted after fine-tuning. In tests, secure aggregation lowered attack AUC from 0.92-0.99 to 0.23-0.56, and encrypted aggregation reached 0.5000. Differential privacy alone still allowed substantial extraction in the retinal study.

Protection often came at a utility cost. Encrypted federated learning lowered F1 from 0.9922 to 0.4042. Differential privacy reduced breast ultrasound accuracy from 94.9% to 89.5% at ε=10 and to 48.3% at ε=0.01, without measuring leakage. Local differential privacy cut LLM leakage to 20.5% but lowered utility to 3.03 from 3.87. Distillation recovered up to 63% of non-private performance.

One test, a Chinese benchmark, used non-English data and reported a 27% reduction in leakage. A hazard study across four languages found that leakage varied by language, with Italian showing the most. This suggests that results from English data may not carry over. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations.

FDA draft guidance asks sponsors using differential privacy to document trade-offs with accuracy and utility. NIST AI 600-1 calls for red-teaming for membership inference. The accuracy results across epsilon settings and the utility losses under encrypted aggregation show the kind of trade-off data such documentation may require. No study evaluated red-teaming as a governance process.

research_gap: No study measured re-identification events in deployed clinical AI systems. No study compared organizations that conduct privacy red-teaming with those that do not. No study reported the cost, staffing, or time needed to run these assessments. Studies are also needed that use standard attack protocols so that results across methods can be compared and pooled.
underserved_note: One test used Chinese-language data, and no test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. A hazard study found that leakage differs by language, so protection levels measured on English or single-language data may not apply to records from patients with limited English proficiency or to multilingual safety-net settings.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether documented privacy, security, and threat assessments before deployment reduce privacy or security failures in health care AI. One deployment study found serious failures in a live patient-facing chatbot using standard browser tools, which shows the hazard exists but does not show that assessments prevent it.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single hazard study examined one publicly accessible retrieval-augmented chatbot and documents a problem rather than the effect of an assessment. The endorsements, mostly frameworks and commentaries, reflect expert agreement rather than measured outcomes.

In one deployed patient-facing chatbot, reviewers found serious privacy and security failures using standard browser tools, without specialist skills or authentication. This suggests such failures can pass through deployment unnoticed. The authors conclude that independent review should precede deployment, but the study did not test whether a pre-deployment assessment would have caught these failures.

Endorsers tie the practice to existing obligations. One commentary states that HIPAA requires regular risk assessment, and CHAI notes that the annual HIPAA Security Risk Assessment is a condition of federal funding for community health centers. FDA draft guidance asks device makers for a security use case view covering AI features. One commentary cites GDPR Article 35 data protection impact assessments.

Many community health centers already complete an annual HIPAA Security Risk Assessment, so adding AI systems to that process may reduce the added cost. No study reports staff time, cost, or a reassessment interval, so organizations would set cadence without outcome data. The hazard study suggests some failures are detectable with low-cost browser tools.

No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard study did not report the population served. One commentary calls for data protection impact assessments of AI translation tools, which patients with limited English proficiency may rely on, but it offers no outcome data.

The hazard study found that failures in a patient-facing chatbot were visible to anyone with a browser, which may expose patient information and affect trust. Patients generally cannot inspect these systems themselves and depend on the organization's review. No study reports whether assessments change patient harm or trust.

research_gap: Studies should compare AI deployments with and without documented pre-deployment privacy, security, and threat assessments. They should measure vulnerabilities found before and after go-live, exposure and breach incidents, cost, staff time, and the reassessment interval at which new risks appear, and they should include safety-net and community health center settings.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, and the single hazard study did not report the population served. Organizations serving Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients therefore have no evidence on whether these assessments work in their settings, although community health centers already perform HIPAA security risk assessments that could be extended to AI systems.

bottom_line: Nine sources, including two CHAI frameworks, NIST AI 600-1, and Utah HB 452, endorse requiring vendors to disclose data use, security, training-data lawfulness, and license terms during procurement, but no study has tested whether this review reduces harm. The recommendation rests on consensus and statute rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study tests procurement disclosure review, and no study documents how often the hazard occurs or what it costs. The nine endorsements include three frameworks, one guidance document, one statute, and four commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement of this kind does not support a certainty rating for effect, so the rating is no direct evidence.

Utah HB 452 (2025) lists compliance with federal health privacy regulations and user data collection and sharing practices for mental health chatbots, which may give the practice legal footing in that setting. NIST AI 600-1 and the CHAI playbooks treat training-data lawfulness as a diligence and contract matter. None of these sources reports whether disclosure changes vendor behavior.

The endorsing sources describe what to request, such as data retention settings, reuse of hospital data for product improvement, and patient data passing through vendor servers. They do not estimate the staff time, legal review, or expertise needed to evaluate these disclosures, so the cost of adoption at scale is unknown.

research_gap: No study measures whether structured vendor disclosure and review during procurement reduces data misuse, security incidents, or exposure to unlawfully obtained training data compared with standard contracting. Studies could compare organizations that use disclosure checklists with those that do not, tracking contract changes, rejected vendors, breaches, and review burden.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net organizations may have fewer legal and security staff to review vendor disclosures, and no data show whether the practice works under those resource limits.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether AI incident response plans, continuity plans, or breach notification practices reduce delays or harm after AI-related breaches or outages. The recommendation rests on seven endorsements, two of them framework-level "must" statements, and on existing HIPAA and state breach-notification duties rather than on outcome data.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Seven sources endorse it, including NIST AI 600-1 and CHAI playbooks at the "must" level, but endorsements are expert opinion. Under GRADE conventions, the absence of any comparative or observational test means certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

NIST AI 600-1 ties AI incident reporting to existing legal duties such as HIPAA breach reporting to OCR. Those duties may already apply to breaches of protected health information whether or not an AI system is involved. The notification element appears to restate current law, while the continuity-planning element rests on framework guidance.

The Principles for augmented intelligence development, deployment, and use ask entities to notify affected individuals directly, independent of any legal duty to notify a provider or organization. A consensus commentary also calls for prompt patient notification. No supplied study measures whether patients receive, understand, or act on AI-related breach notices, so the benefit to patients remains untested.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations with and without AI-specific incident response and continuity plans on time to detection, time to containment, time to patient and regulator notification, and clinical disruption during AI outages. Descriptive work documenting how often AI-related breaches and outages occur in health care would also establish the size of the hazard, which no supplied study measures.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether breach notices reach and are understood by patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy, and whether safety-net systems can staff and test these plans, remains unknown.

bottom_line: Fifteen sources endorse matching monitoring frequency and intensity to each AI tool's clinical risk, but no study supplied here tests whether risk-tiered monitoring detects more errors or uses staff time better than uniform monitoring. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and regulatory signaling rather than on comparative evidence.

perspectives.view: No study tests risk-scaled monitoring, and no study documents the hazard of under- or over-monitoring. The support consists of guidance, frameworks, commentaries, and one regulatory discussion paper. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement across sources does not substitute for a test of the practice, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The FDA device center's discussion paper states that postmarket monitoring scope, frequency, and level of evidence might vary in proportion to device risk, using permissive language. A surgical society white paper calls for predefined intervention thresholds and predetermined change control plans. These documents signal regulatory direction but do not impose a tiered monitoring requirement on health systems.

A multi-society radiology statement uses mandatory language for autonomous AI, stating that ongoing monitoring is needed to detect and correct errors promptly. This reasoning rests on the absence of a clinician check before output reaches the patient. No supplied study measures how often tiered monitoring catches errors before harm, so the size of any safety benefit remains unknown.

Several sources, including a CHAI playbook and a patient-facing video governance matrix, frame proportional review as a way to direct limited review effort toward higher-risk tools. No supplied study reports staffing hours, costs, or feasibility of tiered monitoring programs, so the resource savings described in these sources remain untested.

research_gap: No study compares risk-tiered monitoring with uniform monitoring on error detection, time to detection, patient harm, or staff effort. Studies are also needed on how to assign risk tiers reliably and on whether conditionally deployed or autonomous tools drift or fail at rates that justify more frequent review.
underserved_note: No study tests this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One commentary lists demographic change in the patient population as a trigger for reassessment, which suggests that risk tiers may need to account for performance differences in these groups, but this has not been examined.

bottom_line: One retrospective offline study of 1,739,666 surgical cases tracked fairness gaps by race and sex over time and found that model updating closed some gaps and widened or left others, which suggests that disparities can shift after deployment and that updating alone may not correct them. No study has tested whether scheduled subgroup reassessment against predefined disparity thresholds improves outcomes or reduces disparities.

perspectives.view: The single study (pmid:40079820) is a level 4 retrospective replay in an offline setting with mixed results. It examines fairness gaps under population-level model updating rather than the reassessment practice itself, so directness is limited. With one study, no replication, and no patient outcomes, certainty that the practice achieves its aim is very low.

In the replay, updating restored sex gaps for readmission, did not close a race gap for pneumonia, and enlarged an ICI gap for males. This pattern suggests that a model fix can create new subgroup harms, so a subgroup check after each change may catch errors that aggregate metrics miss. The study did not measure harm reaching patients.

The study reported fairness gaps by race and sex, and aggregate performance changed more than fairness did. Endorsers also name socioeconomic status, health literacy, insurance coverage, and postal code as monitoring dimensions, but no tested evidence covers those groupings.

The study ran on retrospective data outside live workflows, so it offers no information on staff time, data availability for subgroup labels, or how often reassessment can be sustained. CHAI guidance asks systems to define and justify what counts as a significant subgroup shift, yet no study reports how sites set or apply such thresholds.

Eighteen sources endorse the practice, including CHAI assurance guidance at the must level and a lifecycle commentary on generative AI devices that calls for subgroup performance review by postal code. These endorsements rest on expert consensus rather than tested results.

research_gap: Prospective studies in live deployments should test whether reassessment at set intervals against predefined disparity thresholds detects emerging gaps earlier and leads to corrections that narrow them. Such studies should also report the effort and cost required and should stratify by insurance type, language, and health literacy.
underserved_note: The only test focused on racial and ethnic minority groups and sex; it did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems therefore have no tested evidence on whether subgroup reassessment detects or reduces disparities for these groups.

bottom_line: Eleven studies suggest that predefined statistical thresholds can flag model degradation and prompt retraining, but all are descriptive deployments, simulations, or benchmarks, and none measured patient outcomes. One prospective comparison found that drift alerts missed the months when performance fell, so drift thresholds alone may not be enough.

perspectives.view: Four real-deployment studies are level 3 descriptive reports, and the other seven are simulations or automated benchmarks. Outcomes are detection or model accuracy rather than patient harm, which makes the evidence indirect. One prospective comparison returned mixed results. Certainty that the practice prevents late or ignored degradation is very low.

In one deployment, an AUC of 0.73 fell below a 0.85 threshold and triggered fine-tuning that restored AUC to 0.873. In a Dutch cohort, AUC fell below the ±3 SD limit in March 2020 and March 2021, yet drift detection flagged neither month. This suggests performance thresholds may catch failures that drift thresholds miss.

Control-chart methods flagged 3.0% of regions as outliers and identified a humerus performance drop that end users also recognized. A 2σ limit caught milder deviations than a 3σ limit. CUSUM sensitivity can be tuned to trade false alarms against detection delay, with almost no false alarms in 60 days at 40 samples per day.

Detecting drift in chest radiographs required about 4000 new images, which may take days at large providers and months at smaller ones. In simulations, shift-triggered updating outperformed fixed-interval updating, and a risk-score trigger detected drift about six weeks before complaint-driven surveillance would have. Smaller systems may need longer windows or pooled data.

FDA draft guidance and discussion papers expect sponsors to specify drift analyses and thresholds. One study showed a threshold written into a predetermined change control plan triggering retraining at one site and no action at another where AUC stayed above threshold. This suggests the plan mechanism can operate as designed in a single case.

One benchmark used 130486 retinal images with a racial and ethnic minority focus and kept Type I error near the chosen 5% level while detecting many shifts. No study tested subgroup equity thresholds in a live deployment. One hazard study found the false positive rate for a quality metric rose from 81.6% to 85.7% as covariates shifted.

research_gap: No study compared threshold-based alerting with usual monitoring on patient harm, time to corrective action, or staff response. It also remains unknown how often alerts were acted on, how subgroup equity thresholds perform in practice, and how low-volume sites can reach the sample sizes needed for timely detection.
underserved_note: No test of the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; one offline benchmark had a racial and ethnic minority focus. Because detection may take months at lower-volume sites, safety-net systems may face longer delays before thresholds fire, and the current evidence does not show whether the practice works for them.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether continuous security monitoring or scheduled red-teaming of generative AI reduces cyberattacks, data exfiltration, jailbreaks, or misuse in health care. One benchmark study reports that seven commercial and open-source language models were highly vulnerable to medical jailbreaking techniques, which shows the hazard exists but does not show that red-teaming prevents it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies of the practice and one hazard study. That study is an automated benchmark of seven language models, rated level 5, and its abstract reports no numeric results. Under GRADE conventions, certainty for the practice cannot be rated because no comparison of monitored and unmonitored deployments exists. The four endorsements are frameworks and a commentary.

Seven language models were highly vulnerable to three medical jailbreaking techniques in a benchmark setting. This suggests that guardrails may fail under deliberate manipulation, which could produce unsafe clinical content. Red-teaming is designed to find such failures before patients see them, but no study shows how many real-world failures it catches or how often vulnerabilities reappear after model updates.

NIST AI 600-1 states that documenting and reviewing third-party inputs and plugins is important for incident disclosure, because plugin content often has inconsistent access control. CHAI guidance describes network baselines and expected data flows. These documents set expectations that health systems may be asked to meet, but they rest on expert consensus rather than outcome data.

The CHAI playbook describes one academic medical center that runs a dedicated AI security function with continuous API monitoring, quarterly adversarial assessments for high-risk AI, and sector threat-intelligence sharing. The sources report no staffing levels, costs, or yield of findings. Smaller systems would have to estimate the burden of this model without published figures.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployed clinical AI with and without scheduled red-teaming and continuous monitoring, and that report the number of vulnerabilities found, incidents prevented, time to remediation after model updates, and staff hours and cost per assessment.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the single hazard study was a model benchmark that did not involve any patient population, so there is no evidence on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether jailbreaks succeed more often through non-English or low-literacy prompts, and whether safety-net systems can afford ongoing red-teaming, remains untested.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether monitoring AI usage against documented intended use reduces off-label use, shadow AI use, or resulting harm or data leakage. One descriptive study of 30,503 chat threads from a deployed LLM tool found that 5.9% involved clinical decision-making outside the tool's documented intended use, which shows the hazard exists in practice.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice. The single supplied study is a cross-sectional description of real-world use and documents the hazard rather than evaluating a monitoring intervention. Seven endorsements, most of them frameworks and commentaries, support the recommendation, but expert agreement does not substitute for comparative evidence, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated.

In one deployment, 5.9% of chat threads involved clinical decision-making with a tool not intended for that use. This suggests unvetted clinical advice may reach care decisions. Whether usage monitoring catches these cases before patients are affected, and how quickly flags lead to correction, has not been measured.

The hazard study classified 30,503 chat threads by purpose, which suggests that usage logs from sanctioned tools can be reviewed at scale. That approach does not extend to shadow AI tools that sit outside institutional logging. No study reports the staff time, accuracy of classification, or follow-up workflow needed to act on flagged use.

A commentary on the EU AI Act places adherence to instructions for use and off-label use within organisational monitoring duties, and the CHAI assurance guide lists audits of use against intended purpose as a must. These sources describe expectations for deployers. None of the supplied material shows that meeting them changes outcomes.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units with and without structured usage monitoring and measure rates of off-label and shadow AI use, PHI exposure events, time from flag to correction, and staff burden. Methods for detecting unsanctioned tools that do not generate institutional logs also need evaluation.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The hazard study reports a U.S. deployment without describing Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users or patients, so it is unknown whether off-label use patterns or the value of monitoring differ in those settings.

bottom_line: Fifteen observational, simulated, or benchmark studies report that input and output data checks detected missing outputs, pipeline outages, data entry errors, and out-of-distribution cases, and one deployment saw average defects fall from 9.0% to 1.0% after feedback-driven fixes. No study measured whether these checks reduced patient harm, and none compared sites with and without monitoring.

perspectives.view: Five level 3 studies came from real deployments, and ten were offline, simulated, or benchmark tests. None was randomized, and none had a concurrent control. Every study reported that checks detected data problems, so the findings are consistent. The outcomes were detection rates and defect counts rather than patient outcomes, which lowers directness.

Hazard studies show the failure is real. AUROC fell from 0.918 to 0.827 under imputation, and lab pipeline changes stopped an alert from firing. Leading indicators caught a 2-week data feed outage that performance monitoring alone would likely have missed. No study traced a detected failure to harm that was prevented.

Across 14 facilities over 2 years, data flow validation found seven malfunction types at rates below 2%. In another study, PCA reconstruction error flagged entry errors such as saturation recorded as 955. One external test produced a 24.7% false positive rate, which suggests alert burden may be a problem if thresholds are not tuned locally.

In four deployed systems, missingness and latency telemetry explained more calibration change (ΔR² 0.21 to 0.28) than population factors did (0.05 to 0.07). This suggests low-cost telemetry may give early warning. In a mammography program, defects fell from 3.0% to 0.8%. No study reported staffing or cost.

One benchmark used retinal images from a sample focused on racial and ethnic minority groups, and one CT study included older adults. Neither reported results by insurance, language, or literacy. Out-of-distribution detection may flag patients whose data differ from the training data, but no study examined whether flagging rates differed across groups.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software lists missing values, duplicate records, and data type mismatches as quality concerns, with permissive (may) language. CHAI's assurance guide frames data quality monitoring as a must. No supplied study evaluated compliance with, or the effect of, either document.

Flagged radiotherapy outliers included 5 patients with fiducials and 6 with hip implants. This suggests patients with implanted devices may be more likely to receive faulty AI contours. The studies did not report whether flagged cases went to a human reviewer or whether patients were told.

research_gap: No study compared patient outcomes, missed-error rates, or clinician workload between settings with and without routine data checks. Thresholds, false alert rates in live use, staffing needs, and costs remain unmeasured.
underserved_note: No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One benchmark had a racial and ethnic minority focus, and one CT study included older adults. Health systems serving these groups cannot yet know whether monitoring detects failures in their data at the reported rates.

bottom_line: Two small offline studies suggest that scheduled re-evaluation against a fixed local reference can run for 15 months and can flag months when performance falls outside preset limits, but no study shows that the practice prevents harm to patients. Six of nine hazard reports found loss of accuracy or calibration after initial validation, and two of those six draw on the same UK cardiac surgery cohort.

perspectives.view: Two studies test the practice, both at evidence level 4 in offline or simulated settings. One followed two CT systems with physical phantoms for 15 months, and the other monitored monthly AUC in 6,822 Dutch admissions. Neither compared re-evaluation with no re-evaluation or measured patient outcomes, so certainty is very low because of indirectness and imprecision.

A lung-resection model was used unchanged for a decade. Its discrimination held steady, while the calibration intercept drifted to between -0.54 and -0.31, with over-prediction as baseline mortality fell from 20.5% to 15.6%. The Dutch monitoring study tracked AUC alone. A schedule limited to discrimination may therefore miss calibration loss that changes individual risk estimates.

In the Dutch study, monthly AUC fell below a 3 SD limit set from cross-validation twice, in March 2020 and March 2021, and otherwise stayed within limits. The phantom study found stable results over 15 months on two CT systems. This suggests the method is workable in practice, but its ability to detect real decline remains untested.

Neither test of the practice reported the payer, language, or literacy characteristics of patients, and the monitoring study was conducted in the Netherlands. The largest hazard study covered 7,215,711 veterans, a population that differs from Medicaid and safety-net patients. This evidence does not measure how performance changes over time within subgroups.

The supplied sources recommend periodic re-evaluation but do not require it. The radiology multi-society statement proposes re-evaluation on updated local data at least annually. CHAI gives quarterly review as an example cadence, and a regulator discussion paper describes periodic clinician review of samples. The quoted Utah statute addresses disclosure of AI use, not performance re-evaluation.

Two real deployments found no loss. In one, AUC was 0.78 against original values between 0.75 and 0.81. In the other, PPV rose from 80.8% to 92.4%. This suggests decline is not uniform, so risk-tiered schedules like those RUAIH describes may help direct effort. No study reported the staff time or cost of maintaining local evaluation datasets.

A national VA model covered 7,215,711 veterans. From 2016 to 2021, its PPV fell 4.0% and its F1 score fell 4.6%, as the event rate dropped from 3.8% to 3.0%. No study reported whether re-evaluation findings reached patients or clinicians, or whether they changed the care patients received.

research_gap: No study compared scheduled re-evaluation with no re-evaluation in a live deployment. No study measured whether detected declines led to model updates or fewer patient harms, and none tested how often re-evaluation should occur. Studies that track calibration and subgroup performance alongside discrimination, and that report the cost of maintaining local evaluation datasets, would address the main uncertainties.
underserved_note: Neither study testing the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from this evidence whether scheduled re-evaluation would detect declines that affect their patients. They may need to include such patients deliberately in their local evaluation datasets.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether keeping and reviewing per-action run traces and replay logs detects or reconstructs erroneous agent actions. One simulated study of 27 agent runs found an undisclosed postcrash rerun that was visible only in execution logs, which suggests the hazard exists but does not show that log review prevents harm.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice. The single related study is a level 4, offline or simulated analysis of 27 agent runs in the United Kingdom. It documents the hazard and does not compare organizations that review logs with those that do not. Certainty about the practice's benefit cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In the simulated runs, result text matched execution logs in nearly all cases, yet reviewers found unit propagation and an undisclosed postcrash rerun only in the logs. This suggests that agent summaries may omit actions that matter. Whether routine log review would catch such errors before they reach patients has not been measured.

The hazard study relied on execution logs to find undisclosed actions, which indicates that such logs can be informative when someone reads them. No study reports how much reviewer time trace review takes, what fraction of traces get reviewed in practice, or how often reviewers correctly reconstruct an error in a live clinical workflow.

Two commentaries endorse the practice. The radiology multi-society statement asks that autonomous AI actions be transparent, identifiable, and discoverable, and the PARM viewpoint asks that reasoning, data sources, and intermediate steps be recorded. The cited CHAI playbook language addresses retrieval corpus update cadence and does not speak directly to run traces. None of these sources report outcome data.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare trace retention with structured review against usual practice in deployed clinical agents, and that report the rate of erroneous actions detected, time to reconstruction, reviewer burden, storage cost, and downstream patient harm.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The one hazard study listed older adults and used simulated runs, so it offers no information on whether trace review would work in safety-net settings or catch errors in agent interactions conducted in languages other than English.

bottom_line: Twenty-four studies, almost all from live deployments, found that comparing sampled AI outputs with clinician review, adjudication, or outcomes produced accuracy estimates and surfaced errors that automated checks missed. No study tested whether this practice reduces patient harm compared with not sampling, and most designs were descriptive, so certainty is low.

perspectives.view: The body includes one randomized trial, four prospective studies with a comparator, and nineteen descriptive, replay, or pre-post designs. Findings consistently show that sampled comparison yields usable accuracy estimates, and three studies report mixed results. Outcomes are accuracy and error detection rather than patient outcomes, which lowers directness. Certainty is rated low.

Clinician re-review found serious errors in 4 of 100 conversations that automated triage had rated good. Radiologist review of 1,315 head CTs found 16 missed haemorrhages, 9 of them subarachnoid. A stratified ED sample showed high within-stratum agreement but a design-weighted sensitivity of 0.40. This suggests that samples drawn only from flagged cases may overstate performance.

The choice of reference affects the estimate. LLM-extracted labels matched radiologist review closely (PPV 1, NPV 0.988), while LLM judges agreed with humans on hallucinations only up to 65.7%. Manual review showed most automated error flags were supported by the chart. EMR-only outcomes matched discrimination but misjudged calibration, and a change of reviewer coincided with a dip in scores.

The reported programs reviewed modest fractions of volume. One adjudicated about 15% of 690,673 transmissions, and another reviewed 1,160 of 593,365 mammograms over monthly cycles. An automated discrepancy check detected a 2.5% specificity drop within 22 days, and monthly AUC tracking flagged two months below limits. These findings suggest that partial automation may lower review staffing needs.

Only one of 24 studies reported enrolling limited English proficiency or older adult populations. That German study found errors missed by automated triage. No study reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients. None stratified accuracy estimates by these groups, so it remains unknown whether sampled review detects subgroup-specific failures.

Clinician review of 20,000 real conversations found no suicide-risk exchange that lacked crisis resources. The same review identified missed cases of non-suicidal self-injury. This suggests that human audit of real exchanges can find safety gaps that affect whether patients are directed to human help, though the study did not measure patient outcomes.

research_gap: No study compared sites that periodically sample outputs with sites that do not on patient harm, error correction time, or clinician trust. The literature does not establish how large or how frequent samples should be, and it does not show how to stratify samples so that low-prevalence misses are not underestimated. Evidence is also thin on how much reviewer turnover and inter-rater variability affect estimates, and on whether automated references such as LLM labels or EMR outcomes can stand in for human review when calibration matters.
underserved_note: One German study of deployed health conversations included limited English proficiency and older adult populations, and it found that sampled clinician review caught errors missed by automated triage. No study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so accuracy estimates from these programs may not reflect performance for those patients unless health systems stratify their samples.

bottom_line: One simulation of 2,272 deployment decisions found that every decision produced complete HL7 FHIR audit and provenance records that allowed 100% reconstruction, but no study has tested audit logging in live clinical use or its effect on incident review. A trial in which a database fault erased identifiers suggests that the inability to reconstruct AI involvement is a real problem and that the logs themselves may need protection.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice is a level 4 simulation of 2,272 sequential deployment decisions with no patients, clinicians, or real incidents. Certainty is very low because the evidence comes from a single study, is indirect, and measures record completeness rather than whether reconstruction improves incident review or patient outcomes.

In a 63-participant randomized trial in the United States, a database fault erased identifiers, and investigators could not tell whether alerts were AI-generated or random. This shows that logs can fail without warning. It does not show that protected logging prevents such loss, though it suggests logs may need integrity checks and backup.

The simulation used standard HL7 FHIR AuditEvent and Provenance resources, which suggests that existing interoperability standards may be able to carry the required fields. The study did not measure logging inside a live EHR, capture of clinician edits to AI outputs, storage load, or whether reviewers could use the records during an actual incident review.

The endorsements come from frameworks and commentary, including CHAI, NIST AI 600-1, FUTURE-AI, and analyses of EU AI Act and MDR post-market duties that call for model version and inference timestamps. These sources agree that logging is needed. They differ on which fields to record, and none cites outcome evidence for a specific log design.

research_gap: No study has tested protected audit logs in a live clinical deployment. Useful studies would measure log completeness and integrity over time, the time and accuracy of incident reconstruction with and without logs, capture of clinician edits and downstream decisions, privacy handling of logged content, and the staffing and storage cost of maintaining and reviewing logs.
underserved_note: No test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, because the only test was a simulation with no patients. It is unknown whether logs designed this way would record interpreter involvement or translated inputs and outputs. That information would be needed to reconstruct incidents involving patients with limited English proficiency.

bottom_line: Twenty-four studies suggest that monitoring methods can detect input shifts, technical failures, and performance drops in deployed or simulated AI, but most are simulations or descriptive reports, and none compares monitoring with no monitoring on patient outcomes. The hazard studies show that silent degradation occurs in real deployments, which supports the rationale for monitoring without showing that monitoring prevents harm.

perspectives.view: The only randomized trial (41625485) found no drift in 24 weeks, so it could not show detection. Real-deployment reports (42701602, 36836797, 41399697, 41488801) show monitoring flagged errors, mismatched configurations, and upgrade-related drops. Most other tests are level 4 or 5 simulations. In 42712319, drift alerts did not coincide with AUC dips. Certainty for detection is low.

In a simulation, a 2% to 3% specificity decline produced a 2- to 3-fold rise in discrepancies, while sensitivity had to fall 10% for a similar signal (40602699). A +20 mg/dL shift left AUROC unchanged but lowered sensitivity (42712297). A simulated monitor flagged a 2.5-point sensitivity loss at month 5 (PPR1238327). Single aggregate metrics may miss harmful degradation.

A statistical process control dashboard flagged alert variation that reflected practice changes rather than errors (38366366). Monitoring caught a two-week drop in prediction volume from EHR API failures (37349541). EMR-only follow-up data falsely suggested survival underprediction (42664478). Two qualitative studies found monitoring ad hoc and mostly manual (41023723, 40199833).

One simulation using retinal images with a racial and ethnic minority focus found that a classifier-based test detected quality and comorbidity subgroup shifts, and detected sex shifts at a rate of 0.79 (38724581). A label-agnostic method detected shifts in age and admission source (40465297). Neither study examined Medicaid, safety-net, or language-based subgroups.

FDA draft guidance calls for monitoring device performance and input changes, and an international discussion paper calls for specified analyses and thresholds to detect degradation. One deployment applied a 10% technical error threshold over 24 months and exceeded it in one period (42701602). No study tests whether regulatory requirements change monitoring quality.

In one simulation, CUSUM monitoring detected a 1.5 SD shift within an average of 5 days and produced about 293 days between false alarms (42449079). Unsupervised and label-agnostic monitors may reduce reliance on scarce outcome labels (40204747, 40465297). Interviewees reported that few institutions invest in structured oversight infrastructure (41023723).

A veterans' risk model's PPV fell 4.0% between 2016 and 2021, and a 0.34% rise in false positive rate corresponded to 18,288 additional false positives (40815520).
