Two surgical errors arose from AI that had not been updated for new lens types (39613452). No study shows that monitoring would have caught these problems sooner.

research_gap: No study compares monitored with unmonitored deployments on time to detection, time to correction, or patient harm. Prospective real-deployment studies should report the sensitivity and false alarm rates of monitoring methods, the staff time they require, and whether detected drift led to recalibration that changed outcomes.
underserved_note: No test of the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only test with a population focus was a simulation using racial and ethnic minority retinal data (38724581). Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that published detection performance applies to their patients and may need subgroup-level monitoring.

bottom_line: Seventeen frameworks, guidance documents, and commentaries endorse version and configuration control with re-review after material changes, but no study has tested whether this practice detects or prevents harmful changes. Three hazard studies show that template, coding, and prompt changes can shift performance.

perspectives.view: No study tests version control or change-triggered re-review. Three studies document the hazard: one quasi-experimental deployment study and two automated benchmarks. These show that the problem exists. They do not show that the safeguard works, so the evidence for the practice itself is absent and cannot be graded.

In one deployment with 66 providers, a note template configuration change reduced ICD-10 documentation accuracy from 79% to 35%. This suggests that changes outside the model itself can cause large drops in accuracy that go unnoticed. No study has examined whether change control would catch such a drop before it affects patients.

In a benchmark of 239,246 admissions, the ICD-9-to-ICD-10 coding transition acted as a dataset shift and was associated with performance degradation. A prompt-family change produced 3 reversals among 36 hardness pairs, with 91.7% agreement. These results suggest that data and prompt changes may belong in a change inventory. The staff burden of re-review has not been measured.

The prompt sensitivity benchmark included limited English proficiency or non-English trial populations and found 91.7% agreement across prompt families. No study examined Medicaid or safety-net settings. No study tested whether re-review after changes protects these groups. An obstetric equity commentary argues that configuration shifts can redistribute delays, but no study has tested this claim.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions asks manufacturers for installation and maintenance procedures. An EU AI Act tutorial calls for refreshing the technical file and rerunning conformance tests before redeployment. These sources set expectations for documenting changes. None of them reports outcomes from applying those expectations in health systems.

research_gap: No study compares health systems with and without version control and change-triggered re-review. Such a study would measure whether performance shifts are detected, how quickly they are found, and whether patients are harmed. Research should also measure the staff time that re-review requires and whether vendor-initiated updates are captured in local inventories.
underserved_note: No study tests the practice, so no test has included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard benchmark involved limited English proficiency or non-English populations, which suggests that prompt changes may affect these groups. Whether change control protects them is unknown.

bottom_line: Three before-and-after studies in which health systems tracked defined metrics after deploying an AI tool reported gains in reporting time, postoperative pain, dialysis complications, and cost, but none compared KPI tracking against no tracking. The evidence suggests that outcome-linked KPIs can be measured in real deployments, while whether defining them prevents low-value tools from persisting remains untested.

perspectives.view: One quasi-experimental study and two pre-post studies without comparators report favorable results. Observational designs start at low certainty, and certainty drops further because each study tests an AI tool with metrics attached rather than the practice of KPI tracking itself. No study reports whether tracking led a system to modify or retire a tool.

In 14,747 surgical patients, moderate-to-severe pain fell from 26.3% to 21.7% under AI-guided performance monitoring, while total adverse events changed from 18.1% to 19.2% (P = 0.09). Tracking a safety metric next to the target metric allowed that possible signal to be seen. The dialysis study reported fewer falls and CPR events, although it did not give rates.

The dialysis program tracked clinical, financial, and staff-satisfaction measures across 213,071 sessions, which suggests that measuring several domains at once may be workable in routine operations. None of the three studies reports the staff time, data infrastructure, or analytic effort needed to maintain the metrics over time.

Median chest CT reporting time fell from 21.3 to 18.2 minutes, and exploratory modeling projected about 0.5 FTE of radiologist workload reduction. The dialysis program estimated USD 115,658 in annual savings. These figures show that financial and workforce effects can be estimated, but the estimates are modeled, not audited, and they omit the cost of the monitoring.

The studies took place in China, Taiwan, and one setting the authors did not report. None stratified KPIs by payer, language, or literacy, so the data cannot show whether aggregate gains extended to disadvantaged patients or hid differences between groups.

research_gap: No study compares health systems or tools with outcome-linked KPI programs against those without them. Such a study would need to measure whether tracking leads to earlier detection of tools that underperform, to decommissioning decisions, or to recovery of hidden costs. Studies should also report what it costs to run the monitoring and should present KPIs by patient subgroup.
underserved_note: No test reported enrolling or stratifying Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one study did not report its setting. Health systems serving these patients cannot assume that the reported benefits apply to them and may need to break their own KPIs down by these groups to find out.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether periodic maintain, refine, or retire decisions, or protocols to disable, roll back, recall, or decommission AI tools, reduce continued use of harmful or obsolete tools. Support for the practice rests on 11 endorsements, most of them commentaries and frameworks, and no study documenting the hazard was supplied.

perspectives.view: Eleven sources endorse the practice. Two are CHAI frameworks rated must, one is a multi-society radiology statement, and most of the rest are commentaries. No study tests the practice or documents the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. Agreement among endorsers reflects expert opinion rather than measured effect.

Several commentaries describe staged controls, including conditional suspension, rollback to a prior validated version, reversion to shadow mode, and full withdrawal. They tie each control to monitoring triggers. None of these sources reports whether such protocols caught a failing tool before it harmed patients, and so the safety benefit remains an untested assumption.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without scheduled lifecycle reviews and decommissioning protocols. They should measure time from detected performance degradation or vendor recall to disablement, patient harms during that interval, and staff effort required to carry out rollback or retirement.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot tell from this evidence whether lifecycle reviews detect degradation that falls mainly on these groups, or whether retiring a tool leaves safety-net sites without a working alternative.

bottom_line: One retrospective study found that clinicians' decisions to use AI-drafted text tracked closely with automated quality metrics, which suggests logged dispositions may carry usable signal, but no study has tested whether monitoring override, edit, or reliance rates improves combined human-AI performance. Seven hazard studies show that over-reliance, non-adherence, and undocumented overrides occur in real deployments.

perspectives.view: A single level 3 retrospective replay study tests one part of the practice. It reports that clinicians' use of AI drafts correlated with quantitative metrics. The study measures agreement rather than patient outcomes or changes in combined performance after monitoring began, and it gives no effect size. Indirectness and imprecision place certainty at very low.

In one sepsis program, only 28% (555/1977) of huddles occurred without an alert firing, which suggests clinicians may defer to the alert. In surgery, four of five post-implementation errors occurred in cases where AI authentication was not used. These studies show that reliance and disuse both carry harm, but none shows that monitoring these rates catches errors earlier.

Physicians changed a median 9.0% (IQR 2.5%-21.9%) of AI note words, left 14.9% (143/960) of notes unedited, and averaged between 1.9% and 69.3% edits individually. About a third of physicians did not follow a UTI recommendation tool. This spread suggests clinician-level baselines may be needed before edit or override rates can be read as reliance signals.

A study in the United States that included patients with limited English proficiency found that clinician launches of a prediction screen did not differ by race, ethnicity, or primary language. In Israel, physicians in the Arabic sector were less likely to follow recommendations (OR 3.474). Disposition logs stratified by patient and clinician group could detect such differences, though no study has tested this.

Intensive care nurses in one qualitative study (n=23) described overriding early warning alerts without documentation under workload pressure. This suggests override logs that depend on manual entry may undercount overrides where staffing is tight. The draft-use study suggests automated metrics could reduce human review effort, though no study reported staffing needs or costs.

research_gap: No study has compared units that monitor disposition, override, and edit rates with units that do not, using combined human-AI accuracy, missed diagnoses, or patient harm as outcomes. Studies also need to establish which override or edit rates signal over-reliance and which reflect appropriate skepticism for a given tool.
underserved_note: The one study that tests the practice did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A hazard study included patients with limited English proficiency and racial and ethnic minority patients, but it described usage patterns rather than testing monitoring, so health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether disposition monitoring performs as intended for them.

bottom_line: Nine sources, including CHAI, NIST, FUTURE-AI, and the European Society of Radiology, endorse scheduled governance review of monitoring reports and dashboards, but no supplied study tests the practice or documents the hazard it targets. Adoption would rest on expert consensus alone.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests whether scheduled committee review of monitoring reports changes decisions or patient outcomes, and no study documents how often monitoring data go unused. The nine endorsements come from frameworks, guidance, and commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not count as evidence of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The European Society of Radiology recommends periodic review of post-market surveillance data every 6 to 12 months, presented to deployers. NIST AI 600-1 asks that monitoring staff be able to escalate issues promptly. These sources describe expected oversight practice, but none reports whether such review met regulatory aims in any tested setting.

The endorsements propose cadences that range from weekly or monthly dashboard huddles to quarterly cross-service reviews and reviews every 6 to 12 months. No supplied study reports the staff time, cost, or committee capacity required, so a health system cannot yet estimate the resources needed to sustain this practice across many deployed tools.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without scheduled governance review of AI monitoring data and that measure the time from a detected performance problem to a logged corrective action, the share of flagged issues that receive a response, and downstream patient outcomes. Research should also examine which review cadence fits which type of tool and what committee staffing the practice requires.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One commentary on obstetric resource allocation proposes monthly review of stratified run charts, which suggests dashboards could be built to show subgroup differences, but whether governance review of such data reduces disparities has not been tested.

bottom_line: Twelve sources endorse monitoring deployed generative AI, and one descriptive study of a German deployment found that human review of flagged and sampled conversations detected high-severity failures that automated metrics alone did not reveal. No study compares monitoring with no monitoring or measures its effect on patient harm.

perspectives.view: One descriptive study of 2,035 conversations in a real deployment tests post-market monitoring. It has no comparison group and reports detected events rather than patient outcomes, so certainty is very low. Hazard studies report deployed hallucination rates from 3.4% of records to 21% of hospital courses. These show the problem exists but do not test whether monitoring reduces it.

In the German deployment, reviewers confirmed 5 high-severity events among 45 flagged conversations and 4 among 100 sampled ones. Automated metrics alone did not reveal these failures. In a separate study, LLM judges caught 2 of 9 expert-identified hallucinations. These results suggest that monitoring may need human review and sampling as well as automated flags.

Deployed EHR summarization tools showed 0.73 hallucinations per summary across 1,075 users and a hallucination rate of 11.79% of content units. An automated detector agreed with physicians on 96.95% of units in validation. Automated tools may help triage outputs for review, but another study found that automatic metrics correlated weakly with expert scores (0.10 to 0.23).

The one test included non-English-speaking users and older adults in Germany. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. A Kenyan deployment reported hallucinations in 3.4% of records, most often mis-expanded acronyms or drug names. No study has tested whether monitoring detects failures that fall more heavily on these groups.

The FDA CDRH discussion paper calls for monitoring the underlying foundation model where applicable, and NIST AI 600-1 calls for continuous monitoring of third-party systems in deployment. Ten commentaries make similar recommendations. These sources state expectations rather than evidence. No supplied study tested monitoring of vendor foundation model updates specifically.

The German study reviewed 45 flagged and 100 sampled conversations out of 2,035 and confirmed 9 high-severity events. The study summary does not report reviewer time, staffing, or cost. The current evidence therefore does not allow an estimate of what monitoring at scale would require.

research_gap: No study compares monitoring with no monitoring or links monitoring to fewer errors reaching clinicians or patients. No study tracks drift after vendor foundation model updates in real deployments or reports the staff time and cost of human review. The only study that tests monitoring took place in Germany, and no test of monitoring has been reported from a US health system, although several US studies document the hazard.
underserved_note: The single test included limited English proficiency or non-English users and older adults, but it took place in Germany and did not include Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving those groups in the United States have no direct evidence that monitoring detects the failures most likely to affect their patients.

bottom_line: One uncontrolled pre-post study tested an AI feedback pathway, and it received no patient complaints in five months, which cannot distinguish absent harms from unused channels. Two hazard studies suggest that reporting channels are often missing and that voluntary feedback declines as use grows, but no study tested training or non-retaliation protections.

perspectives.view: A single pre-post study without a comparator (64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions) tested the practice and found zero patient complaints over five months. The design, the absence of a control, and an outcome that cannot separate true absence of harm from non-use support very low certainty. User training and non-retaliation components have no direct tests.

Of 424 nurses who met an AI safety concern, 83 (19.6%) reported no formal channel. Harms that go unreported cannot be traced or corrected. Whether adding a channel raises detection of errors before they reach patients remains untested, and the one test produced no reports to assess.

In one hospital, voluntary feedback fell after a 28-physician pilot as routine use expanded to 1,028 users and 14,910 conversations. This suggests that passive reporting channels may lose fidelity at scale, and the authors concluded that automated monitoring may be needed alongside user reports.

Non-hospital nurses had higher odds of lacking any reporting channel (OR 2.54; 95% CI 1.54-4.19). Care settings outside hospitals may therefore carry larger reporting gaps. No study examined whether patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy can use AI feedback channels.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbot operators to document actions taken to mitigate harmful interactions, and FDA draft guidance encourages users to report device issues within 48 hours. NIST AI 600-1 and several European sources call for feedback processes. None of these sources cites outcome evidence that reporting channels reduce harm.

One site added AI feedback to existing patient feedback systems, which suggests the channel can be built on current infrastructure at modest cost. The pathway produced no complaints in five months. Separately, falling voluntary feedback at scale suggests staff time spent on channels may yield diminishing returns without automated monitoring.

Zero patient complaints in five months may reflect that patients did not know the pathway existed or did not recognize AI involvement in their care. The study did not report patient awareness. Patients cannot report an AI error they cannot see, so disclosure of AI use may be a precondition for this safeguard.

research_gap: Controlled studies should compare report volume, report quality, and time to error correction between sites with and without AI reporting channels. These studies should test user training and non-retaliation protections as separate components, and they should measure staff and patient awareness of the channel so that low report counts can be interpreted.
underserved_note: No study, including the single test of the practice, reported enrolling or analyzing Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The nurse survey found larger channel gaps outside hospitals. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether standard feedback channels reach their patients and may need to evaluate language access and plain-language design locally.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether AI incident response plans, or rehearsing them, shorten or reduce harm during AI incidents, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on five framework, guidance, and commentary endorsements, only some of which address incident response directly.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions this yields no direct evidence. The five endorsements reflect expert consensus rather than measured outcomes, and two of them (the CHAI playbook item on model cards and the portal disclosure commentary) do not speak to incident response.

Of the five sources, the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide most directly asks whether an organization has a documented incident response plan updated at appropriate frequency. NIST AI 600-1 calls for reviewing procedures as new uses arise, and the multi-society radiology statement asks for a process to address failures. None of these sources are binding regulation.

No supplied study measures how long AI-related harm persists with or without a response plan, so the size of the benefit is unknown. The radiology statement frames failure handling as a way to prevent repeated mistakes, which is a plausible mechanism that has not been tested in the supplied evidence.

research_gap: Studies are needed that document how often AI incidents occur in health care, how long they take to detect and contain, and whether organizations with documented and rehearsed response plans achieve shorter time to containment or fewer patient harms than organizations without them. Tabletop or simulation studies comparing rehearsed and unrehearsed teams would provide a feasible first test.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Organizations serving these groups may have fewer staff to build and rehearse response plans, and whether incidents affect these patients differently remains unmeasured.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether a documented, tiered AI escalation chain with suspension authority reduces the time harmful tools stay in use, so support rests on seven endorsements from frameworks and commentaries. No study documenting the hazard was supplied either.

perspectives.view: The supplied record contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The seven endorsements come from two frameworks and five commentaries, and two of the commentaries are the same multi-society radiology statement listed twice. Expert agreement of this kind cannot be graded as evidence of effect under GRADE conventions.

The CHAI playbook frames escalation protocols as a must, and NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to give stakeholders remediation timelines. Both documents are voluntary frameworks. None of the supplied sources ties escalation chains or suspension authority to a binding federal or state requirement.

The radiology statement asks institutions to define the mode of operation while a failing model is assessed. No supplied study measures how often escalation steps are completed in practice, how long acknowledgment takes, or what staff burden a tiered chain adds. Implementation fidelity therefore remains unknown.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems with and without documented escalation chains and measure time from incident report to acknowledgment, time to suspension of a harmful tool, reporter follow-up rates, and patient harm during the interval. No study documenting how often harmful tools remain active for lack of authority was supplied, so the size of the hazard is also unmeasured.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot tell from the supplied record whether escalation chains work in their settings or whether reports from these patients reach the escalation process at all.

bottom_line: Two deployment studies that tracked outcome and balancing measures after AI rollout report favorable results, but neither compares monitoring with no monitoring, so evidence that this practice prevents downstream harm is indirect. Three hazard studies show that unintended effects on care quality and clinician workload occur and can be measured with outcome proxies.

perspectives.view: The two supporting studies are a quasi-experimental sepsis alert evaluation (n=4517 alerts) and an uncontrolled pre-post study. Both measured outcomes after deployment, yet neither isolates monitoring as the intervention being tested. Observational designs and indirectness each lower certainty, and the panel rates it very low.

In the sepsis study, median alert-to-antibiotic time fell from 140.4 to 112.1 minutes, and a balancing measure found no antibiotic delay. Hazard studies suggest harms may go unseen without surveillance, including lower odds of psychiatric intervention with ambient scribes (aOR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72-0.95) and declining counseling quality in an RCT of 51 patients.

A study of 40 clinicians found NASA Task Load Index scores rose from 43 to 57 after AI deployment, which suggests workload can move opposite to intent. A neonatal pre-post study tracked balancing measures such as ventilator days (10.8 to 7.0) as proxies. Neither study reports the staff time needed to run the monitoring.

None of the five supplied studies reports results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The ambient scribe study shows AI can shift clinical decisions, and monitoring that does not report results by payer or language group would be unable to detect whether such shifts differ across populations.

In the ambient scribe study, notes documented more symptoms, yet psychiatric intervention was less likely, while human scribes showed no difference (aOR 1.01). This suggests a tool may record a patient's concern without the concern being acted on. None of the supplied studies reports collecting feedback from patients as part of monitoring.

research_gap: No study compares a structured post-deployment monitoring program with usual oversight to test whether monitoring detects harms earlier or leads to corrective action. Studies are also needed on which outcome proxies and end-user engagement methods detect safety and workflow signals, and at what staff cost.
underserved_note: None of the studies testing the practice or documenting the hazard reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether monitoring detects harms in their patients and may need to stratify monitoring results by payer, language, and literacy to find out.

bottom_line: Seven sources, including NIST, CHAI, and a European Society of Radiology consensus statement, recommend protocols for communicating AI incidents and disclosing AI errors to affected people, but no supplied study tests whether such protocols work. No supplied study documents how often patients or users remain unaware of AI errors that affect them.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests incident communication or disclosure protocols for AI errors, and no study measures the hazard. The seven endorsements are frameworks, guidance, and commentaries, which reflect expert agreement rather than tested effects. Certainty about benefit therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The endorsing sources describe steps such as preserving AI outputs, documenting clinical impact, and informing clinicians or patients when an event is serious. No supplied study shows whether these steps shorten the time to correct a missed or delayed diagnosis, so their effect on harm remains untested.

The European Society of Radiology statement ties patient notification to events that would be reportable under post-market clinical follow-up rules, which links disclosure to existing device law. The supplied material contains no study of how U.S. or EU reporting rules perform when applied to AI incidents.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations with and without AI incident disclosure protocols. They should measure how often affected patients and clinicians learn of AI errors, how long notification takes, whether follow-up care is changed, and what happens to patient trust and complaints. Separate work should first estimate how often AI errors go undisclosed.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Disclosure templates written without testing in these groups may not reach or be understood by the patients least likely to detect an AI error on their own.

bottom_line: Eight of nine studies of corrective-action cycles after AI errors report fewer errors or better performance, but most lack a comparison group and none isolates the effect of root-cause analysis itself. Consistent endorsement by frameworks and regulators supports adopting the practice, while the size of its benefit remains uncertain.

perspectives.view: Two studies had comparators. In PET/CT, off-centering over 2.5 cm fell from 49% to 27% after recalibration, while the manual comparator stayed flat. In mammography, AUC rose from 0.83 to 0.92, though the study could not isolate single updates. The other seven are uncontrolled or offline, and one found no change, so certainty is low.

Corrective changes can introduce new failures. In one study, false positive alerts fell from a median of 35 to 15 per month, yet a department code added 7 new ones per month. A German chatbot study confirmed on re-test that one missed suicidality conversation now triggered the protocol, but this check covered only that failure.

In one mammography program, technical defects fell from 9.0% to 1.0% over repeated cycles of testing, feedback, and updates. In the null study, alert dismissal without further action stayed at 88% after iterative modifications, which suggests that model fixes may not change clinician response. One offline report found that investigating data-feed outages returned data-health metrics to expected ranges.

A closed-loop system across thirteen US hospital sites resolved 42 physician complaints with zero regressions, but it required 1,089 optimization iterations, which implies sustained engineering effort. Correct advice in the Polaris calls rose from about 80.0% to 99.38% over three versions, measured offline without a comparator. No study reported the staffing or cost of root-cause review.

Only the German chatbot study included limited English proficiency users and older adults, and it was descriptive and verified a single fix. No study reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. It is therefore unknown whether corrective cycles catch failures that occur more often in those groups.

Eleven sources endorse the practice. FDA draft guidance for AI-enabled devices expects corrective and preventive action that draws on complaints and other quality data. Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbot operators to document actions taken to mitigate harmful interactions. CHAI, FUTURE-AI, and NIST frameworks rest on expert consensus rather than trial evidence.

research_gap: No study compared sites that performed structured root-cause analysis with sites that did not, and none separated the effect of the investigation from concurrent model or configuration updates. Controlled or stepped-wedge designs could close this gap if they measured recurrence of the original failure, new failures introduced by fixes, staff time, and outcomes in Medicaid and limited English proficiency populations.
underserved_note: One descriptive study from Germany included limited English proficiency users and older adults, and no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving those groups cannot yet assume that corrective cycles will prevent recurring failures in their patients.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether health system reporting of AI adverse events or cross-site sharing of lessons reduces harm, so support rests on 13 endorsements and one descriptive study showing that FDA-cleared AI devices generate adverse events and recalls. Systems may adopt reporting to meet existing FDA and state obligations, but its value for detecting systemic hazards across sites remains unproven.

perspectives.view: No study tests whether reporting AI adverse events or sharing de-identified lessons with peer sites speeds recognition of systemic hazards or reduces harm. One descriptive study of 691 FDA-cleared devices documents the hazard, which is indirect evidence for the practice. The 13 endorsing sources are mostly frameworks and commentaries, and they reflect expert judgment rather than tested outcomes.

The FDA database analysis recorded 489 adverse events across 36 (5.2%) devices, including 458 malfunctions, 30 injuries, and 1 death, along with 113 recalls of 40 devices, mostly for software issues. These counts suggest that failures surface after clearance. Passive reports may undercount events, and the study does not show that more reporting catches errors before they reach patients.

The FDA draft guidance states that manufacturers must report deaths and serious injuries, and New York already requires reporting of certain adverse events through NYPORTS. In these sources, health system submission to patient safety organizations and sharing with peer sites remains voluntary. Several commentaries call for mandatory reporting or a national AI clinical decision support safety clearinghouse.

research_gap: Studies should compare sites with and without structured AI adverse event reporting and peer sharing. Useful outcomes include time to detection of a systemic hazard, time to vendor fix or recall, and repeat events at other sites. Studies should also measure how completely voluntary reports capture AI-related harms when checked against chart review.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The single hazard study used national FDA device data and did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. It is therefore unknown whether current reporting channels capture AI harms in these groups, where events may be less often recognized or reported.

bottom_line: Three deployment studies in the United States show that post-deployment surveys of patients and clinicians can be run and can register small differences, such as an odds ratio of 1.13 for perceived time with the provider, but none compared surveying with not surveying, measured trust directly, or tracked patient opt-out rates. The evidence speaks more to the feasibility of the practice than to its value in catching eroded trust.

perspectives.view: Two quasi-experimental studies (8120 and 31917 patient surveys) and one pre-post clinician survey used post-deployment surveys to measure the effects of AI scribes. None tested whether surveying detects harm or changes decisions, and none tracked opt-out rates. Findings were mixed and the outcomes are indirect for this practice, so certainty is very low.

Across two patient studies, surveys found one small difference (OR 1.13, 95% CI 1.01-1.26) and otherwise no detectable change. Surveys may therefore miss erosion of trust unless shifts are large. A Sierra Leone study found client frustration during rapid AI-assisted scans, which shows the problem can occur but does not show that surveys catch it.

The clinician survey had a 26.4% response rate at 45 days after activation, so its reported gains in satisfaction and work-life balance may reflect the views of those who chose to respond. The patient studies drew on existing post-visit survey programs, which suggests the practice can fit current workflows where experience data are already collected.

All three tests took place in the United States and did not report results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The only study in a limited English and rural population, from Sierra Leone, documented patient frustration with AI-assisted encounters. Written surveys may miss such patients unless they are offered in other languages and formats.

The two patient studies analyzed 8120 and 31917 surveys, which suggests health systems can reuse existing patient experience instruments at scale. Detecting small effects required these large samples and a control group of physicians. No study reported the cost or staff time needed to run surveys or track opt-outs.

No study measured how often patients declined AI use or whether they could reach a human instead. Most hazard studies found no harm to patient experience, including a randomized trial of 279 patients. The Sierra Leone study reported frustration from a lack of communication and emotional support. Opt-out tracking remains untested as a signal of patient trust.

research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without structured post-deployment surveys, measured trust as a distinct construct, or tracked patient opt-out rates as an early warning signal. Studies are needed that test whether survey and opt-out signals lead to timely changes in how AI is used, and that report response rates by language, insurance type, and literacy.
underserved_note: None of the three studies testing the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The one study in a limited English and rural population documented the hazard but did not test surveying, so the value of this practice for underserved patients is unknown.

bottom_line: Six frameworks and guidance documents endorse requiring vendor documentation of intended use, technical requirements, configuration, interoperability, and data quality before purchase, but no study has tested whether this practice reduces unsafe deployment of AI tools. No study supplied here documents the hazard itself, so the recommendation currently rests on expert consensus alone.

perspectives.view: No comparative, observational, or descriptive study evaluates vendor documentation requirements against any outcome. The six endorsements range from a framework mandate to a permissive statement, and none reports data. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not count as evidence of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The targeted failure is a tool used outside its intended population, setting, or technical specification. No study in this set measures how often that failure occurs or whether written documentation helps purchasers detect a mismatch before deployment. The safety benefit therefore remains a plausible mechanism that has not been observed.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks manufacturers to list compatible input devices and acceptable acquisition protocols, and CHAI frameworks call for documentation of model versions, configurations, and change history. These sources describe expectations for vendors rather than tested requirements, and the FDA document remains in draft form.

research_gap: Studies should compare deployments with and without structured vendor documentation and measure outcomes such as detected specification mismatches, performance drift after configuration changes, and patient harm events. Researchers should also assess how often documentation is kept current after updates and whether purchasing staff can use it to judge fit with local populations and infrastructure.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Documentation of intended populations may matter most where local patients differ from development data, but that possibility has not been examined.

bottom_line: No study tests whether requiring vendors to supply model cards or equivalent documentation improves assessment of fitness, bias, or safety, or changes patient outcomes. Three hazard studies and ten endorsing sources suggest that vendor documentation is often missing or incomplete, so the recommendation rests on consensus and observed gaps rather than on tests of the practice.

perspectives.view: No study compares procurement with and without required model documentation. The three available studies are one pre-post evaluation without a comparator, one qualitative interview study, and one descriptive rating of four chatbots. Each shows that the documentation gap exists. None measures whether supplying documentation changes decisions or harms, so certainty about the practice cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

In 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions, reviewers found deferred risk acknowledgement and human oversight offered in place of documented safety design. These patterns suggest that reviewers may be unable to identify failure modes before deployment. Whether a model card would bring those failure modes to light before they reach patients has not been tested.

In 65 Norwegian interviews, staff described limited documentation for CE-marked fracture detection software as a major barrier during procurement and implementation. This suggests that regulatory marking alone may not give implementation teams the information they need. The studies do not report how much effort documentation review would add, or whether local teams can act on what a model card contains.

All four chatbots in one descriptive study scored 0 on training data and knowledge base transparency. Without training data provenance, a health system cannot judge whether a tool was developed on populations similar to its own patients. No study examined whether documentation helps detect bias affecting underserved groups.

Utah HB 452 requires mental health chatbot developers to document foundation models and training data. FDA draft guidance asks for explanation of synthetic data used in submissions. These provisions cover narrow product types or regulatory filings. The Norwegian findings suggest that market authorization does not by itself guarantee that deployers receive usable documentation.

The pre-post evaluation found limited vendor transparency about validation methodology across many solutions, though frequencies were not reported. A documentation requirement would likely need contract language and reviewer time to enforce. The studies do not estimate those costs or show whether vendors comply when asked.

research_gap: Studies should compare procurement and deployment outcomes when model cards are required versus not required. Useful outcomes include detection of bias or performance limits before go-live, rates of tool rejection or modification, reviewer time, vendor compliance, and downstream safety events. Studies should also test which documentation fields evaluators actually use.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and none of the three hazard studies reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no evidence on whether model documentation helps them assess fit for their patients. The training data provenance fields may matter most for these systems, but that remains untested.

bottom_line: One uncontrolled US deployment study found that adding AI-involvement flags to an existing patient safety event reporting system captured 13 low severity AI-related events over six months. The study had no comparison period or group, so it cannot show whether flags raise detection or improve classification, and support for standard definitions and minimum report fields rests on endorsing frameworks and commentaries.

perspectives.view: The single test (epmc:PPR1258899) uses a pre-post design without a comparator and covers 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions in a US deployment. It reports counts of flagged events but no baseline capture rate and no test of standard definitions or minimum fields. Risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

All 13 events captured in six months were low severity. This suggests the flag can surface minor AI concerns, but the study does not show whether serious harms are reported, whether near misses are recognized as AI-related, or whether reports led to fixes before patients were affected. The share of AI incidents that went unreported was not measured.

The study added a flag to an existing reporting system rather than building a new one, which matches the CHAI and RUAIH advice to use current structures. The available findings do not describe reporter burden, how staff judged AI involvement, or agreement between reviewers on classification, so the fidelity of flagging in routine workflow is unknown.

The study shows that an AI-involvement flag was added to an existing reporting system in a deployment covering 55 AI solutions. It does not report staffing, review time, or cost, so administrators cannot yet estimate the resources needed to triage and analyze AI-flagged reports or to add the structured prompts that CHAI recommends.

NIST AI 600-1 ties generative AI incident reporting to existing legal duties such as HIPAA breach reporting. No study examined whether AI tags in internal systems help organizations meet external reporting obligations or align with device adverse event reporting, so the regulatory value of the practice is untested.

research_gap: Studies should compare AI-tagged reporting against a baseline period or an independent detection method such as chart review or trigger tools to estimate capture rates. They should also test whether standard definitions and minimum report fields produce consistent classification across reviewers, whether higher-severity events and near misses are reported, what staff time the process requires, and whether tagged reports lead to corrective actions.
underserved_note: The one test did not report whether its setting or reported events involved Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Because harms in these groups, such as the AI translation errors raised in one commentary, may be less visible to the clinicians who file reports, the study gives no assurance that tagging captures incidents affecting these patients.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether vendor disclosure of foundation models, third-party components, agent capabilities, and a software bill of materials at intake reduces unassessed failures or outages, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on three governance and regulatory documents, only one of which directly calls for disclosure of embedded AI technology.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsements are expert consensus documents, which GRADE treats as opinion rather than evidence of effect. The claim that disclosure prevents failure modes or outages remains an untested hypothesis.

The CHAI playbook lists disclosure of all embedded AI technology as a must-level contract term, but it does not name a software bill of materials. The NIST Generative AI Profile asks that relevant AI actors join risk identification, which may imply upstream disclosure. The FDA discussion paper addresses escalation behavior and bears only indirectly on supply-chain transparency.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or procurements with and without structured upstream disclosure and software bills of materials at intake, measuring outcomes such as the number of dependency-related incidents, time to identify an affected product when an upstream model changes or fails, unplanned downtime, and the staff time required to review disclosures. Even descriptive studies documenting how often hidden upstream models cause clinical AI failures would establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Safety-net systems often have fewer staff to review vendor disclosures, and whether a disclosure requirement yields any benefit for them, or adds review burden without matching capacity, is unknown.

bottom_line: Eleven guidance documents, frameworks, and commentaries endorse a structured pre-procurement assessment of feasibility, workflow fit, total cost of ownership, and return on investment, but no supplied study tests whether such assessments improve outcomes. The recommendation rests on expert consensus, and no supplied study documents the hazard of unassessed purchasing.

perspectives.view: No supplied study compares procurement with and without a structured assessment, and none measures the hazard. The 11 endorsements are guidance, frameworks, and commentaries, and several radiology statements come from one multi-society source listed three times. Under GRADE conventions, consensus agreement does not substitute for tested effects, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The endorsements describe the assessment components, including build-versus-buy choice, competitive analysis, and total cost of ownership, but none reports the staff time or cost of performing them. One framework calls for a lighter path for low-risk use cases, which suggests assessment effort may need to scale with risk. No supplied data show whether assessment costs are recovered through avoided purchases.

research_gap: No study tests whether structured pre-procurement assessment changes purchase decisions, tool abandonment, workflow adoption, or realized return on investment. Comparative or before-and-after studies of health systems that adopt such assessments, with measures of assessment cost and of tools later retired for poor fit, would address this gap.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems with limited analytic staff may find the assessment harder to perform, and the endorsements offer no guidance tested in those settings.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether contract terms requiring vendor monitoring, timed notification of incidents and model changes, and shared monitoring evidence reduce hidden degradation of deployed AI. The recommendation rests on 12 listed endorsements, made up of one framework rated must and 11 guidance or commentary sources rated should.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice and none documents the hazard, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. Of the 12 listed endorsements, 8 are commentaries, 3 are guidance documents, and 1 is a framework, and only the CHAI framework uses must language. Agreement across these sources reflects expert opinion, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect.

The supplied record contains no measurement of how often vendor-side changes or degradation go undetected by deploying sites, or of any harm that followed. Without such data, the size of the failure mode and the share of problems a notification clause might catch before they reach patients remain unknown.

The endorsements differ in scope. The CHAI language addresses misuse and unauthorized disclosure, while one commentary calls for mandatory notification of model updates and defined revalidation triggers. None of the listed sources specifies notification timeframes or the form that shared monitoring evidence should take, so health systems drafting contracts would need to set these terms themselves.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare sites with and without contractual monitoring and notification terms, measuring time from a vendor model change or degradation to site awareness, the frequency of unplanned performance checks, and downstream patient outcomes. Descriptive work on how often vendor changes currently go unreported would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on its effect in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One commentary on rural Australian hospitals calls for vendor monitoring tools suited to rural services, which suggests that smaller or under-resourced systems may face different contracting conditions, though this remains untested.

bottom_line: Ten deployment studies, three of them randomized, measured documentation time, burnout, or coding after AI scribe rollout, and their results varied by site, specialty, and tool, which suggests that local measurement may be needed to know whether a given deployment reduces burden or shifts coding. Only one quasi-experimental study shows that monitoring itself caught a problem, when coding audits detected ICD-10 accuracy falling from 79% to 35% after a template change and recovering after remediation.

perspectives.view: No study compares systems that measure these outcomes with systems that do not, so the three randomized trials test the scribe rather than the monitoring practice. Burnout or work exhaustion fell in all three, but time in notes did not change in one, and burnout rose across follow-up in a large survey. This inconsistency lowers certainty about expected effects.

Coding audits in one quasi-experimental study detected an accuracy drop from 79% to 35% after a template change, and accuracy returned to baseline after remediation. This is the only supplied example of measurement catching an error that would otherwise have persisted. A separate study found psychiatric intervention less likely in AI-scribed visits (aOR 0.83), a change that coding and time metrics may not detect.

Studies measured time in different ways, including EHR log time in notes, work outside of work, and self-reported minutes per note, which limits comparison across sites. One site found note time fell 26.2% while note length rose 28.8% and did not measure coding. Inpatient note time did not change where ambient AI utilization was 3%, suggesting that usage should be tracked alongside outcomes.

Coding intensity results differed across sites. wRVUs rose 12.1% by day 50 in one study, level 4 established visits rose 3.8% in another, and a trial found billing per day rose with more visits but no change in diagnostic codes per visit. Other sites found no billing change. Measuring coding intensity separately from visit volume may help distinguish these patterns.

One pre-post study without a comparator was conducted in Sweden in a non-English setting and reported per-note documentation time falling from 6.69 to 4.72 minutes. No test measured outcomes in Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy settings, where visit complexity and interpreter use may change both documentation time and coding patterns.

The recommended measures track clinicians and billing, and none of the tests reported patient-level outcomes. One hazard study found fewer psychiatric referrals, new diagnoses, or antidepressant starts in AI-scribed visits. This suggests that monitoring limited to time, burnout, and coding may miss changes in the care patients receive.

research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without structured monitoring, so the benefit of measurement itself remains untested beyond a single audit that detected and corrected a coding accuracy drop. Studies are needed that report coding accuracy against audit standards separately from coding intensity and visit volume, that report net documentation minutes after subtracting verification time, and that use common validated burnout instruments over follow-up longer than six months.
underserved_note: Only one test, conducted in a Swedish non-English setting, fell into an underserved category, and no test included Medicaid, safety-net, US limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these populations have no direct evidence on how scribe deployment affects coding, documentation time, or burnout in their settings and would depend on their own measurement.

bottom_line: No study supplied here tests whether pre-engagement privacy, security, supply-chain, or generative AI risk assessments of third-party AI vendors reduce harm, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation currently rests on two framework endorsements, the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide and NIST AI 600-1, both phrased as "should."

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the effect of vendor risk assessment on privacy breaches, security incidents, or harmful outputs remains unmeasured. Framework endorsements reflect expert consensus and do not substitute for outcome data.

Two frameworks endorse the practice at the "should" level. CHAI states that vendor tracking tools may go undiscovered without specific due diligence. NIST AI 600-1 calls for a use-case-based supplier risk assessment covering content provenance, value chain risk, and legal compliance. Neither source is binding, and neither cites outcome evidence in the excerpts supplied.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or procurements with and without structured pre-engagement AI vendor risk assessment and that measure downstream privacy incidents, security events, intellectual property disputes, and harmful generative outputs. Descriptive work documenting how often unassessed vendor AI introduces these problems in health care would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot determine from this evidence whether vendor assessments address risks that may fall differently on these groups, such as data sharing with third parties or generative outputs in languages other than English.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether requiring vendors to disclose limitations, error rates, and subgroup performance before contracting reduces errors or inequitable harm. Ten frameworks and professional statements endorse the practice, and two hazard studies suggest that vendor and product disclosures are often incomplete.

perspectives.view: The evidence contains no study that compares outcomes with and without pre-contract disclosure requirements. The two available studies document the hazard. One is a pre-post study without a comparator, and the other is a descriptive benchmark of 24 questions. Neither measures the effect of disclosure, so certainty about the practice is rated as no direct evidence.

Across 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions, vendors deferred risk acknowledgement, invoked human-in-the-loop review as a proxy for safety design, and gave limited validation detail. These gaps suggest that failure conditions may go unrecognized at purchase. Whether a disclosure requirement would surface these conditions before patients are exposed has not been studied.

Responsible-AI vendor surveys were used in a U.S. real-world deployment covering 64 evaluations of 55 AI solutions, which suggests that a structured vendor questionnaire can be administered at that volume. The study reports what vendors disclosed. It does not report whether the answers changed purchasing decisions, local validation, or clinician use of the tools.

In the vendor survey study, fairness scores were the lowest reported (55%, 57%, 61%). This suggests that fairness, including subgroup performance, may be the area vendors are least prepared to document. No study examined whether requiring such disclosure improves performance or safety for Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients.

In a Brazilian benchmark of 24 patient questions, no chatbot response met the JAMA benchmark criteria, and DISCERN means were 58.7 ± 4.0 for ChatGPT and 56.3 ± 3.5 for Gemini. Patients reading such output may be unable to judge its reliability. The study does not show that vendor disclosure to purchasers would change what patients receive.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare procurement with and without mandatory disclosure of error rates, failure conditions, and subgroup performance, and that follow downstream outcomes such as rejected or modified contracts, local validation findings, detected errors, and subgroup-specific harm after deployment.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One hazard study used patient questions from a non-English setting in Brazil, which shows the reliability problem exists outside English but provides no evidence on whether disclosure requirements protect these groups.

bottom_line: Six sources endorse vendor security questionnaires, independent certification, and contractual security commitments, but no study supplied here tests whether these requirements reduce breaches of patient data or systems. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and analogy to general information-security practice rather than on outcome data from health care AI deployments.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard in AI vendor settings. The six endorsements include two frameworks, two guidance documents, and two commentaries, and only the CHAI playbook states the requirement as a must. Consistent agreement among sources reflects consensus, which GRADE does not treat as evidence of effect.

The supplied record contains no data on how often AI vendors cause breaches, which failure points questionnaires or certification would catch, or how much harm follows. Without hazard or outcome studies, the size of the risk this safeguard addresses and the share of it the safeguard removes both remain unmeasured.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare breach incidents, security findings, or time to remediation between health systems that require vendor questionnaires, independent certification, and contractual testing rights and those that do not. Research should also measure how often AI vendors fail these assessments and whether contract terms such as testing rights are exercised in practice.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether defined procurement requirements and competitive vendor selection reduce the rate of unsupported, poorly integrated, or unstable AI products, and no study documents how often ad hoc selection produces those outcomes. The adoption report on AI in delivery systems states that common data pipelines and interoperable enterprise systems are needed as AI tools multiply. research_gap: Health systems lack studies that compare structured, competitive AI procurement with ad hoc selection on outcomes such as integration failures, vendor exit or product discontinuation, support responsiveness, clinician adoption, and total cost. Such studies would show whether the hazard is common enough to justify the process burden.

Whether a formal competitive process is feasible for them, or whether selection criteria should cover language access and readability of patient-facing outputs, remains untested.

underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard in the material supplied. research_gap: No study has measured whether subprocessor disclosure, change notification, and contractual flow-down reduce unauthorized or unprotected downstream data access, and no study supplied documents how often such access occurs with AI vendors. Useful work would include audits of AI vendor contracts for flow-down clauses, counts of undisclosed subprocessors found during review, and comparisons of data incidents between organizations that do and do not enforce these terms.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the support consists of expert consensus in two framework documents from a single organization.

research_gap: No study measures how often vendor exit, acquisition, or insolvency interrupts clinical AI or strands data, and none compares organizations with and without sunset notice, wind-down, data return, or escrow clauses on outcomes such as service continuity, time to replacement, or data recovery. Case series of vendor exits and comparative contract audits would be reasonable first steps.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether safety-net systems, which may have less negotiating power with vendors, can obtain these contract protections remains untested.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether contractual change-notice, documentation, and local review requirements reduce harm from silent vendor model changes, and no study documents the hazard itself. perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The three endorsements come from a playbook, a regulatory discussion paper, and a commentary, and they represent expert opinion rather than comparative data.

The CHAI playbook states that change notification should be a contractual obligation at procurement, not a matter of vendor goodwill. A MENA liability commentary recommends vendor commitments to version control and update and change-control procedures. The generative AI device discussion paper describes oversight checkpoints but does not directly address contract terms. None of these sources reports tested effects.

research_gap: No study measures how often vendor model updates, retraining, upstream changes, or newly activated AI features occur without customer awareness, or whether contract clauses requiring advance notice and local review change detection rates, performance drift, or patient harm. Studies could compare organizations with and without such clauses on time to detect model changes and on post-update performance.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there is no evidence on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Safety-net systems may hold less contract bargaining power with vendors, and it remains unknown whether this practice is feasible or effective for them.

bottom_line: Four governance frameworks endorse contract terms that assign ownership of AI outputs, derivative data, locally trained models, and performance data, with endorsement strength ranging from must to may. No supplied study tests whether such terms protect organizational rights or reduce infringement exposure, and no supplied study measures how often the targeted hazard occurs.

perspectives.view: No study in this evidence map tests whether ownership and indemnification clauses change outcomes for health systems. No study documents how often unclear terms lead to lost rights or infringement claims. The recommendation rests on four endorsements that reflect expert consensus rather than measured effect, so certainty cannot be rated under GRADE conventions.

The endorsements differ in strength. The CHAI playbooks list ownership and derivative rights as a must. RUAIH guidance and NIST AI 600-1 say should, and the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide says may. NIST AI 600-1 places these terms in contracts and service level agreements for generative AI and adds content provenance. None of the sources reports data on whether the terms prevent disputes.

research_gap: No study describes current AI vendor contract terms in health care, the frequency of ownership or infringement disputes, or whether specific clauses such as indemnification or retained rights to locally trained models change dispute rates, costs, or an organization's ability to reuse its own performance data. Contract audits across health systems and case series of disputes would be a first step.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence includes Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations or the organizations that serve them. It is unknown whether safety-net systems, which may have fewer legal staff and less bargaining power with vendors, can obtain these terms at the same rate as larger systems.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether tiered enforcement, cure periods, or suspension and termination clauses in AI vendor contracts lead to vendor remediation or a safe exit, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on two endorsements, and only one of them addresses enforcement directly.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements are expert guidance, and guidance does not substitute for comparative data on outcomes such as time to remediation or contract exit.

The RUAIH guidance tells organizations to reserve audit rights and impose penalties for noncompliance with data use agreements, which partly supports tiered enforcement. The CHAI playbook statement requires an explicit clause on model training restrictions. It concerns contract content rather than enforcement triggers, timelines, or termination rights, so it supports R407 only indirectly.

research_gap: No study measures whether specific enforcement clauses, such as defined performance triggers, cure timelines, or suspension rights, change vendor behavior after an AI failure or breach. Useful designs would compare remediation time, frequency of exercised termination, and patient-facing disruption across health systems with and without such clauses, or would analyze a series of actual contract disputes involving AI vendors.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net systems may hold less negotiating power with vendors, and whether they can obtain and use these contract terms remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study in this map tests whether BAAs or DUAs that list permitted and prohibited AI data uses, require minimum necessary data, and bar re-identification reduce vendor secondary use or re-identification of patient data. Five sources endorse the practice, and two of them, one framework and one statute, use mandatory language.

perspectives.view: The map lists zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Certainty therefore rests at no direct evidence. The recommendation draws on frameworks, guidance, and one statute. These sources reflect expert consensus, but they do not show that contract terms change vendor behavior or reduce harm to patients.

CHAI playbooks state that permitted uses must be limited to defined functions, and Utah HB 452 uses mandatory language tied to provider request with user consent. RUAIH guidance says organizations should execute BAAs and apply minimum necessary. The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide says vendors should be asked about predicting identity information, and the augmented intelligence principles treat BAAs as optional.

research_gap: No study has compared AI vendor agreements that contain enumerated use limits, minimum necessary terms, and re-identification bans against generic agreements. Useful studies would measure audited vendor secondary use, data volumes transferred, retention beyond contract terms, and re-identification incidents. They would also test whether contract language is monitored and enforced after signing.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot yet tell whether these contract terms protect those patients to the same degree as other patients.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether obtaining vendor validation evidence and independently verifying claims leads to better local performance or fewer harms, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus from 14 sources and on three studies showing that vendor claims often exceed measured performance. In those studies, vendor-reported accuracy averaged 91.5% against 67.3% in real-world use, and a second vendor model and a proprietary risk score also fell short of their reported figures.

perspectives.view: No included study compares sites that verified vendor claims with sites that did not. The three hazard studies use descriptive, pre-post, or simulated designs at levels 3 and 4. They consistently show a gap between claimed and measured performance, but they cannot show that local verification closes that gap or changes outcomes.

A mean gap of 24.2 percentage points (95% CI 21.5 to 26.9) across six systems suggests that a tool chosen on vendor figures alone may miss or misclassify many more patients than expected. Pre-deployment verification is a plausible way to catch this before patients are exposed, though no study confirms that it does.

In a study of 599,163 emergency department visits, a vendor model's performance differed substantially from vendor-reported metrics once it was tailored for real-world use. This suggests that verification may need to take place in the configured local workflow, and that checks against the vendor's reference data alone may be insufficient.

A study of six systems in rural Nigeria covering 52,000 patients found gaps of 17 to 35 percentage points, significant for every system. An opioid risk score also underperformed on California PDMP and commercial claims data even with socioeconomic covariates added. These findings suggest that vendor validation cohorts may not reflect the populations a health system serves.

The radiology multi-society statement notes that vendors test tools during regulatory approval but still advises local validation before clinical use. The endorsing sources treat regulatory clearance as insufficient on its own. The supplied studies do not examine whether cleared and uncleared tools differ in the size of the performance gap.

One endorsing report describes health systems that support pilots but lack the analytics and measurement tools to assess impact. Independent verification therefore requires data, staff time, and methods that many systems may not have. No supplied study reports the cost or staffing needed to verify a vendor tool.

research_gap: No study compares deployment outcomes, local performance, or patient harms between health systems that independently verified vendor claims before purchase and those that relied on vendor documentation. Studies are also needed on which verification methods, sample sizes, and comparability criteria predict local performance, and on what verification costs.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. One hazard study was conducted in rural Nigeria and found gaps of 17 to 35 percentage points, but none of the studies reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. How far vendor claims diverge from measured performance for these groups in U.S. settings therefore remains unknown.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice, and no supplied study documents the hazard. The European Society of Radiology states that a surveillance system should be available when a device is deployed. These positions suggest that contract terms may fill a gap that regulation does not yet close. No supplied study examines enforcement or outcomes.

The recommendation assumes that vendor data would reveal model drift before it harms patients. The supplied record contains no study showing how often degradation occurs in deployed tools or whether vendor reports detected it. Without such data, the size of the harm this safeguard might prevent remains unknown.

research_gap: No study compares health systems with and without contractual vendor monitoring terms on time to detection of performance degradation, frequency of detected drift, or downstream patient harm. Studies are also needed on whether vendors deliver the promised data, on its completeness and timeliness, and on the staff effort required to review it.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Performance degradation may differ across patient subgroups, and vendor reports that omit subgroup-level results may miss drift affecting these populations. Contracts could specify subgroup reporting, though no supplied evidence tests that approach.

The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and analogy to general IT procurement practice rather than on outcome data from health care AI deployments.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard's frequency or consequences in health care AI. research_gap: No study compares health systems with and without enforceable AI service and performance terms on outcomes such as downtime duration, time to remediate performance drift, vendor response times, or patient-facing disruptions. The source is a single-site account without a stated design or comparison group. It suggests that the practice is feasible in one setting, but it does not measure whether validation or monitoring were completed.

A MENA liability commentary lists change-control triggers, audit rights, and incident reporting timelines as contract terms. These sources describe what a contract should contain, and none reports whether such terms changed compliance or liability outcomes.
