The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide limits patient representation to cases where patients may be end users. The RUAIH guidance uses "may." These sources suggest that patient membership is an expectation that sources state with varying force.

research_gap: No supplied study compares governance committees with and without patient or community members on measurable results such as which tools are approved or rejected, how often bias or safety concerns are raised, or how patients later report trust. Studies are also needed on how representatives are recruited, supported, and compensated, and on whether their input changes decisions or remains advisory.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Several commentaries call for community health workers, community-based organizations, or people with lived experience on governance bodies. Whether representatives drawn from these groups change decisions affecting them remains untested.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether evaluating workplace AI tools for surveillance risk protects employee dignity, morale, or trust, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on one framework (CHAI Responsible AI Guide) and one commentary, both phrased as expert judgment.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Two endorsements, a framework and a commentary, support the recommendation through expert opinion only. Under GRADE conventions this yields no direct evidence, and certainty cannot be rated for any outcome, including morale, turnover, or employee trust.

The CHAI guide states that surveillance tools may prompt employee evasions or workarounds that create unsafe or counterproductive situations. That pathway would link workplace monitoring to patient harm, but no supplied study measures workaround frequency, their effect on care, or whether a pre-deployment review reduces them.

The commentary proposes that governance separate tools built to reduce avoidable workload from tools built to monitor employee behavior. This distinction may give review committees a usable sorting rule, although no study reports how reliably reviewers apply it or what the review costs in staff time.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units that screen workplace AI tools for surveillance risk against those that do not, with measured outcomes such as staff-reported dignity and trust, burnout, turnover, documented workarounds, and downstream patient-safety events. Descriptive work documenting how often monitoring features appear in productivity and safety tools would also establish whether the hazard occurs at meaningful rates.
underserved_note: No study was supplied, so no test included staff at Medicaid-serving or safety-net facilities, workers with limited English proficiency, or workers with low literacy. Lower-wage and hourly health care workers, who may be more exposed to productivity monitoring, have no evidence describing either the hazard or the safeguard in their settings.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether consulting patient and family advisory councils improves the clarity or usefulness of AI disclosure materials, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The one endorsing source, a CHAI playbook, speaks to maintaining an AI inventory with opt-out designations rather than to advisory council review.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement whose quoted text does not describe advisory council consultation.

The CHAI playbook language requires that a health delivery organization keep an AI inventory marking each tool as opt-out eligible or not. That provision supports disclosure infrastructure, but it does not state who should design or review patient-facing materials. The link between the endorsement and advisory council consultation is therefore indirect.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI disclosure materials developed with and without patient and family advisory council input, measuring patient comprehension, perceived usefulness, trust, and opt-out decisions. A descriptive study establishing how often patients find current AI disclosures unclear would also help confirm the hazard.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Advisory councils may not reflect these groups unless recruited deliberately, and any future evaluation would need to report council composition and test materials with these patients.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether informing patient and community advisory bodies about higher-risk AI decisions, incidents, and governance updates preserves community trust, and no supplied study documents the trust hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from CHAI, which describes the practice without reporting outcome data.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. A framework that describes a practice is expert opinion, and it cannot be graded for effect. Certainty about whether advisory-body reporting changes trust, engagement, or incident response therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The only endorsing source is the CHAI governance playbook, which is a voluntary framework. It lists advisory councils as recipients of incident reports, material changes, periodic updates, and pre-deployment, pilot, and sunset decisions for higher-risk tools. The supplied material cites no statute or regulation that requires this reporting, so adoption would rest on institutional policy.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems that report AI deployment, pilot, sunset, and incident decisions to patient and community advisory bodies with systems that do not. Useful outcomes would include measured patient and community trust, advisory-body influence on deployment or sunset decisions, and time from incident to public disclosure. The hazard itself, loss of trust when AI decisions go unshared, also lacks documentation in the supplied evidence.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Nothing in the supplied evidence shows whether advisory bodies represent these groups or whether reports reach them in usable languages and reading levels. Systems that adopt the practice may need to check advisory-body membership and report formats on their own, because the evidence offers no guidance.

bottom_line: Eight sources endorse training clinicians and staff to explain AI use, disclosures, privacy practices, and opt-out options to patients, but no supplied study tests whether such training improves patient understanding, trust, or consent. The recommendation rests on expert guidance, frameworks, and commentary alone.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard. Five of the eight endorsements are commentaries, two are CHAI frameworks, and one is a guidance document. The guidance excerpt addresses liability for system failure and misdiagnosis rather than staff training or patient communication, so its support for this recommendation is indirect.

One nursing commentary calls for explaining AI tools to families in clear, non-technical language, and one CHAI playbook calls for plain-language statements in admission paperwork. These endorsements suggest attention to health literacy. No supplied study examines whether trained staff explain AI use accurately to patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy, so the effect in those groups is unknown.

research_gap: Trials or controlled evaluations should compare trained and untrained staff on patient comprehension of AI use, awareness of opt-out options, consent quality, and trust. These evaluations should also measure staff time and training fidelity in routine workflows.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no data on whether staff training produces accurate explanations for their patients and may need to evaluate it locally.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether assessing awareness of AI feedback and reporting channels increases their use or improves safety, and no supplied study documents the hazard of unused channels. The one endorsement comes from a NIST framework whose quoted text addresses content provenance and traceability rather than awareness of feedback channels.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation currently rests on a single framework endorsement and on reasoning about how feedback systems work, not on observed outcomes.

NIST AI 600-1 is a voluntary framework, and its quoted language uses "should." The passage calls for documenting when content is generated, modified, or shared so that history can be traced. That supports transparency in general terms, but it does not directly instruct organizations to measure whether patients or communities know that reporting channels exist.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure baseline awareness of AI feedback channels among patients, clinicians, and community members, then test whether awareness assessments and the outreach they prompt change reporting volume, report quality, and the time it takes to detect AI-related errors. Such studies should report results separately by language, literacy level, and insurance type.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. These groups may be least likely to learn about reporting channels through standard notices, and the absence of data means health systems cannot tell whether awareness efforts reach them.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether a patient feedback or reporting channel for AI-assisted care leads to more concerns being reported or addressed, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support for the practice rests on eight framework and commentary endorsements, one of which (NIST AI 600-1) addresses training data rather than patient feedback.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The eight sources are three frameworks, one consensus guideline, and four commentaries, and these reflect expert opinion rather than measured effects. The quoted NIST AI 600-1 text concerns synthetic training data and does not bear on patient reporting channels, so seven sources apply directly.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide asks whether a feedback mechanism is equally accessible to all relevant subgroups, and the conversational AI equity roadmap calls for an easy way to report safety concerns. Neither source reports data on whether such channels reach patients with limited English proficiency, low literacy, or Medicaid coverage.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide lists this practice at the must level, while the CHAI playbooks list it at the may level, and the remaining sources say should. These are voluntary frameworks. The Health Equity Considerations commentary calls on policy frameworks to create reporting pathways for bias or inaccurate outputs, which suggests such pathways are not yet a settled requirement.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare sites with and without a patient-facing AI feedback channel and measure the volume of concerns reported, time to response, the share of reports that lead to a change in the AI tool or care process, and patient-reported trust. Such studies would also need to establish how often AI-related harms currently go unreported.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two endorsing sources raise equal access across subgroups as a design goal, but health systems have no evidence on which channel formats these patients can use and would need to collect their own uptake data by language, literacy, and payer.

bottom_line: No study supplied here tests whether a patient and family advisory council improves an organization's decisions about AI or the outcomes of AI use, and no study documents harm from the absence of such a forum. The recommendation rests on one governance framework and seven commentaries.

perspectives.view: Eight sources endorse the practice, and all use "should" language. One is a framework (CHAI) and seven are commentaries. No included study tests an advisory council for AI oversight, and none measures the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, expert opinion without empirical tests cannot support a certainty rating, so this recommendation has no direct evidence.

Four commentaries ask that councils reflect the population served or include people from lower socioeconomic backgrounds and people without insurance. One describes sessions organized by language and held at accessible times for migrant workers. No supplied study tests these proposals or shows whether such councils recruit or retain underserved members or whether their input changes AI decisions.

research_gap: Studies could compare organizations with and without AI-focused patient councils on measurable outcomes, such as changes to AI tool selection or configuration, patient-reported trust, complaint rates, and detection of AI-related safety events. They could also record council composition, meeting burden, and cost. Descriptive work documenting how often the absence of a patient forum leads to missed problems would establish whether the hazard occurs in practice.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Several endorsing commentaries call for including these groups, but whether councils reach them or represent their concerns in AI decisions remains untested.

bottom_line: Studies of AI-integrated clinical education show mixed effects on unaided skills, and no study tests whether a health system that assesses deskilling risk tool by tool prevents skill loss. Colonoscopy studies report both declines and gains in unaided detection after AI exposure, which suggests the risk may vary by tool, clinician, and setting.

perspectives.view: Six studies test AI-integrated training, and none tests a health system assessing deskilling risk tool by tool. Two randomized trials in simulated settings disagree. One trial (n=68) found higher unassisted reasoning scores (7.32 vs 5.12), and the other (n=91) found no group difference (p = .936). Small samples, indirect outcomes, and inconsistent results lower certainty to very low.

After CAD introduction, unaided adenoma detection fell from 28.4% to 22.4% in one study and from 31.6% to 13.5% in another. A propensity-matched study found no decline, and CADe-trained endoscopists detected more adenomas without AI (35.5% vs 30.3%). In contouring, 3 of 25 physicians declined. These findings suggest deskilling risk may differ by tool and clinician.

Two tests ran in real workflows. Emergency interns trained with AI assistance reached 82.4% accuracy versus 87.1% with blended learning (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.41–1.16), and unaided retention was not measured. A telehealth program reported rubric gains of 19% to 37% without a comparator. No study measured the staff time or fidelity needed to run deskilling assessments.

No study testing the practice enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The one hazard study in such a setting, covering 81 providers at 7 facilities in rural Sierra Leone, found providers omitting physical examinations and vital sign checks while relying on a scanning device. Whether training safeguards work in low-resource settings has not been tested.

The Sierra Leone report of skipped physical examinations and vital sign checks shows that reliance on a device can reach patients directly. The telehealth study, measured on 468 real patient calls, suggests AI-supported training may improve how clinicians communicate with patients, though it lacked a comparator group.

research_gap: No study evaluates a health system process for assessing deskilling risk before or after an AI tool is deployed, and few education studies measure unaided performance after AI withdrawal in real practice. Prospective studies with comparators that track unaided performance over time, including during AI downtime, and that report cost and staff time would address this gap.
underserved_note: None of the six studies testing the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only hazard study in such a setting, in rural Sierra Leone with non-English-speaking populations, found providers skipping basic examinations. Health systems serving these populations therefore have no direct evidence on whether deskilling assessments or AI-supported training protect clinician skills in their settings.

bottom_line: No study in this evidence map tests whether adding intended users and affected community members to red-teaming of generative AI finds harms that expert red teams miss. The recommendation currently rests on one federal framework and one commentary.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice, and zero studies document the hazard it targets. Certainty therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsing sources are a framework and a commentary, and neither reports outcome data on whether community participation changes what red teams detect.

NIST AI 600-1 uses "should" language and names red-teaming as one of several ways to gather direct feedback from affected communities. The framework is voluntary. A health system that adopts the practice would be following federal guidance rather than meeting a binding requirement, and the guidance does not specify how participants should be recruited or compensated.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare red-teaming with and without intended users and affected community members on the same generative AI system. Such studies would report the number, type, and clinical severity of harms each group identifies, along with recruitment cost and the time participants contribute. Separate work is needed to document how often expert-only red teams miss harms that affected users later report.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether the practice surfaces harms specific to these groups, and whether recruitment of these groups into red-teaming is feasible, remains unmeasured.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether identifying affected stakeholder groups and tracking their involvement reduces unassessed risks from AI tools, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support for the practice rests on five endorsing sources, four of them frameworks or guidance and one a commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero documenting the hazard. The five endorsements reflect expert consensus rather than measured effects. The NIST AI 600-1 excerpt addresses the rate at which security recommendations are implemented, which bears only indirectly on stakeholder tracking. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The dementia care commentary calls for involving people with ADRD, caregivers, clinicians, ethicists, and developers from the early stages. No supplied study measures whether such involvement changes patient safety, trust, or access to a human, so the benefit to patients remains an expectation rather than a finding.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI deployments with and without a documented stakeholder identification and tracking process, measuring whether risks to specific groups are detected before go-live and whether post-deployment harms differ. Such studies should also record the staff time and cost of maintaining involvement logs.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot yet tell from the evidence whether stakeholder tracking surfaces the risks these groups face, although the practice's stated purpose is to keep such groups from being overlooked.

bottom_line: No study in this evidence map tests whether engaging affected stakeholders before selecting an AI solution leads to tools that better address the actual problem. Support for R458 currently rests on one framework rated as a must and eight commentaries rated as should.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The nine endorsements consist of the CHAI guide and eight commentaries, which express expert agreement but supply no comparative data. Under GRADE conventions, consistent opinion cannot substitute for tested outcomes, so certainty about benefit cannot be rated.

One commentary describes a partnership table and needs assessment for diabetes AI tools, and another calls for co-framing problems with patients and caregivers, but neither commentary reports outcomes from that work. No supplied study measures whether early engagement changes tool fit for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI projects with and without structured pre-selection stakeholder engagement, such as needs assessments, interviews, or pre-design surveys, and that measure whether the selected tool addresses the defined problem, gets used, and changes patient or workflow outcomes. Such studies should also report the time and staff cost of engagement.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether, or how, early engagement improves the fit of AI tools for them.

bottom_line: Three studies of patient-facing chatbots suggest that feedback-driven refinement may improve user ratings and engagement, but the one before-and-after measure of reach showed no change except in the Spanish-language version. No study compared feedback use against no feedback use in clinical AI, so the recommendation rests mainly on 20 framework and commentary endorsements.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial (n=2113) reported that user ratings reached the 3.5/5 benchmark on all metrics except health awareness after iterative refinement. The trial appears to test the chatbot rather than the feedback process itself, which lowers directness. Two descriptive studies lack comparators, and one showed null reach results. These limitations support a rating of low certainty.

Stakeholders interviewed about machine-learning decision support named missing feedback loops as a barrier to integration. This shows the gap exists but does not show that closing it prevents harm. None of the tested studies measured errors, adverse events, or whether feedback caught unsafe outputs before they reached patients.

All three tests took place in real deployments of consumer chatbots for maternal, newborn, or general health use. In the United States study, postpartum reach moved from 64.1% to 62.8% (OR 0.95, 0.85-1.05) after content and outreach were revised based on feedback. Collecting feedback and changing content may not by itself increase use.

The trial enrolled older, rural, low-literacy, and non-English-speaking participants in China. In the United States study, the Spanish version raised newborn reach from 58% to 66.2% (OR 1.42) while the English results stayed flat. This suggests that feedback from language-minority users may yield gains that pooled measures would hide.

The endorsements come from voluntary frameworks and guidance. CHAI states that feedback should be solicited, considered, and used, and FUTURE-AI recommends qualitative methods. No endorsement listed here cites a statute or FDA or ONC requirement, so health systems would adopt the practice as good governance rather than as a legal obligation.

In the India deployment, 64% of 110 mothers engaged with a nurse through the chatbot. Feedback-responsive designs may therefore generate human follow-up work that requires staffing. None of the studies reported the cost or staff time needed to collect, review, and act on feedback.

In the India study, 80% of users replied at least once and 64% reached a nurse. This suggests that patients will use a feedback channel when a human responds. The studies did not report whether patients saw their feedback change the tool, which affects trust.

research_gap: No study randomized or compared deployments that acted on feedback against deployments that did not, and none addressed clinician-facing or diagnostic AI. The studies also did not measure safety outcomes, the time from feedback to correction, or staffing cost.
underserved_note: The trial included limited English proficiency, low health literacy, rural, minority, and older adult participants, and the United States study included Spanish-speaking and minority recipients. No study reported Medicaid or safety-net enrollment, so applying these findings to those settings remains an inference.

bottom_line: Forty-six sources endorse continuous multidisciplinary and patient engagement across the AI lifecycle, but no supplied study tests whether such engagement identifies emerging risks or prevents harm. One descriptive survey of WHO European Member States found that patients and the public were engaged less often than government, providers, and developers.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests whether continuous stakeholder engagement detects new risks or improves outcomes. The single study is a descriptive survey of 50 WHO European Member States. It documents who is engaged, not what engagement achieves. The endorsements are mostly commentaries, so the support rests on expert opinion rather than tests of the practice.

Of 36 Member States that reported engagement, 15 (42%) engaged patient associations and 8 (22%) engaged the general public. By comparison, 81% engaged government actors and 75% engaged providers and developers. These figures suggest that patient and public voices may be the groups most often absent from national AI engagement.

The survey did not report whether marginalized, low-income, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups took part. Several endorsing commentaries call for community champions and representatives of marginalised groups. No supplied study examines whether engaging these groups changes AI design, deployment decisions, or outcomes for them.

The endorsements include a consensus guideline (FUTURE-AI), an industry assurance guide (CHAI), and NIST AI 600-1. The NIST passage quoted here addresses risk tolerance and model decommissioning rather than stakeholder engagement. None of the supplied sources describes a binding legal requirement to engage patients or communities.

research_gap: No study compares AI deployments with and without structured, ongoing stakeholder engagement. Future work should measure the number and timing of risks identified after initial design, downstream patient harms, and the staff time and cost of engagement. It should also report which formats of patient and community representation were used and which populations the representatives came from.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The one hazard survey reports national-level engagement in European countries and does not describe these groups. Its relevance to U.S. safety-net settings is therefore uncertain, and health systems serving these populations have no evidence on which engagement approaches reach them.

bottom_line: One controlled deployment study measured patient experience across 31,917 surveys and found no difference attributable to AI, and one 10-person pilot met an acceptability threshold, but no study tests whether measuring experience detects or prevents harm. Hazard studies suggest that some problems, such as patients withholding sensitive information, may not appear in general satisfaction scores.

perspectives.view: Two deployment studies measured patient experience with AI services. A quasi-experimental comparison of 31,917 surveys found no significant difference in pre-post rating change between pilot and control physicians, and a 10-person pre-post pilot found 80% exceeded the acceptability threshold. Neither study tests whether measuring experience changes decisions or detects harm, so certainty is very low.

In a qualitative study, 35.0% to 51.5% of patients anticipated self-censoring about mental health, sexual health, or illicit activity with ambient documentation. Satisfaction in other studies was similar or higher with AI. This pattern suggests general satisfaction items may miss withheld information, a failure mode that tailored questions would need to target.

Press Ganey scores rose after ambient scribe use across 49 providers, with only provider concern reaching significance (+1.9, P=.01). Generic instruments are easy to reuse but were not built for AI-specific questions. In a Swiss screening study, feeling of safety scored 7.7 with AI alone versus 9.5 with augmented intelligence, which suggests tailored items can separate configurations.

Both studies that tested the practice were in the United States and reported no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy subgroups. Hazard studies in China, Turkey, and Sierra Leone enrolled limited English proficiency, rural, or low-income patients. In Sierra Leone, clients trusted scan results but reported absent counselling. Survey validity across languages and literacy levels remains untested.

None of the five endorsing sources is a regulation or statute; three are commentaries and two are guidance or frameworks. One commentary calls for patient-reported outcome and experience measures developed with patient partners. The NIST profile excerpt addresses misuse testing rather than patient experience, so its support for this practice is indirect.

The largest test drew on 31,917 routine patient surveys, 7,164 from pilot physicians, which suggests existing survey programs can support comparisons against a control group with modest added effort. A pre-post design without controls, as in the 49-provider Press Ganey analysis, may attribute secular trends to the AI tool.

In Sierra Leone, combined antenatal assessments and scanning averaged 3 to 5 minutes against a 30 to 40 minute standard, and clients reported poor communication. Patients rated AI-alone skin screening lower on feeling of safety than dermatologist screening. Asking patients directly may be the main route by which such experiences reach decision makers.

research_gap: No study compares AI evaluations that include patient-experience measurement with evaluations that do not, and none tests whether standard satisfaction instruments detect specific harms such as self-censorship or lost counselling time. Controlled studies are needed that validate tailored survey items against observed outcomes and that report response rates and results by language, literacy, and insurance status.
underserved_note: Neither study that tested the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Hazard studies with limited English proficiency, low-literacy, low-income, and rural patients came from outside the United States, so a health system cannot assume that validated English-language surveys capture experience in these groups or reach them at adequate rates.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether structured, risk-prioritized public-feedback exercises with representative participants change AI deployment or decommissioning decisions, and no supplied study documents the hazard. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement whose quoted text addresses risk ranking and provenance rather than public feedback itself.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The one endorsement is a framework statement, which reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for empirical tests of effect.

NIST AI 600-1 uses "should" language, so it is voluntary guidance rather than a binding requirement. Its quoted text asks organizations to rank risks by likelihood and impact and to assess provenance solutions. It does not specify public-feedback methods, participant representativeness, or documentation of how feedback informs decommissioning, so the recommendation extends beyond the quoted source.

The recommendation calls for representative participants, yet no supplied study measures who takes part in public-feedback exercises for health AI or whether feedback from underrepresented groups changes decisions. Without such data, a health system cannot tell whether its feedback process reaches Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare structured, risk-prioritized public-feedback exercises against usual practice and measure participant representativeness, the share of feedback that leads to documented changes in deployment or decommissioning, and downstream effects on patient harm and trust. Studies documenting how often current public feedback on health AI is unrepresentative or unused would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so none included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. This means there is no evidence on whether feedback exercises reach these groups or whether their input shapes decisions, which is the gap the recommendation's call for representative participants aims to close.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether obtaining stakeholder community input to define unacceptable generative AI uses reduces inappropriate deployments, and no study documents the hazard itself. The only support comes from one voluntary federal framework whose quoted text calls for a maintained risk hierarchy rather than for community input specifically.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is a framework statement, which reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative data on outcomes.

NIST AI 600-1 uses "should" language and asks organizations to maintain an updated hierarchy of generative AI risks tied to contexts of use. The quoted passage does not name stakeholder communities as the source of that hierarchy, so the link to this recommendation is indirect. The framework is voluntary and carries no enforcement mechanism.

research_gap: No study compares organizations that solicit community input on prohibited generative AI uses with those that do not, and none measures whether such input changes deployment decisions, patient complaints, or trust. Studies are also needed on which engagement methods produce usable lists of unacceptable uses and at what staff cost.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether community input processes reach these groups, or instead reflect the views of more easily engaged patients, remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether applying human-subjects protections or IRB review to AI feedback and engagement participants prevents unethical treatment, and no study documents the hazard itself. Support rests on two endorsements, a federal framework that frames structured feedback as permissive and a research ethics guide from Uganda that recommends committee review.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two endorsements are a framework and a commentary, and neither reports outcome data on participant harm or protection.

NIST AI 600-1 uses permissive language and describes structured public feedback as a way to evaluate generative AI systems, without addressing participant protections directly. The Uganda research ethics guide states that engagement strategies should be reviewed by a research ethics committee to protect participants' values, interests, and dignity. The two sources differ in strength and jurisdiction.

With no studies supplied, no data describe how feedback participants from Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups are treated, or whether review processes change their experience. The Uganda guide refers to research communities' values, but it offers guidance rather than measured results.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI feedback and engagement activities conducted with and without human-subjects review, measuring consent quality, participant understanding, complaints, reported harms, and withdrawal rates. Descriptive work documenting how often these activities currently receive IRB or ethics committee review would also establish whether the hazard occurs in practice.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. Health systems that recruit these groups for AI feedback activities cannot draw on data showing whether review protects them, and any protections adopted would rest on ethical principle and endorsement rather than measured effect.

bottom_line: Two offline rater studies found that parents and patient or public readers judged AI-generated text differently from clinicians, which suggests that including them in evaluation surfaces information clinicians alone may miss. No study measured whether this inclusion changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Two level 4 retrospective replay studies with raters test the practice, with 50 and 60 source documents. Both report that patient-side raters differed from clinicians. The design is offline, the outcomes are rater preferences rather than harms or benefits, and one abstract gives no numbers. Certainty is very low because of indirectness and imprecision.

In the pediatric study, clinicians contributed judgments on clinical accuracy while parents contributed judgments on readability. In the UK study, public readers preferred a different report version than radiologists did in the lung cohort. This suggests patient raters may catch comprehension problems that clinician review misses. No study tested whether patient raters catch errors that could reach patients.

PPI readers in the UK study completed 180 reads and preferred the full-length version B (P<0.0001), which differed from radiologist preferences in the lung cohort. This suggests structured patient rating can be added to an offline evaluation protocol. Neither study reports time, recruitment effort, or fidelity in a live pilot.

The HEAAL framework asks that fitness-for-purpose assessment engage patient community members from the target population. Neither study reports participant income, insurance, language, or literacy, so it is unknown whether the patient raters resembled the populations HEAAL is meant to protect.

The endorsements come from voluntary frameworks such as the CHAI guides and HEAAL, and from commentaries. The CHAI language ranges from should to may. None of the supplied sources cites a federal or state requirement to include patients in AI evaluation.

Parents in a pediatric cardiac intensive care setting rated helpfulness differently from clinicians, and UK public readers preferred a different report version than radiologists in the lung cohort. This suggests evaluations that exclude patients may approve outputs patients find less useful. The studies did not measure trust or access to a human.

research_gap: No study has compared AI pilots conducted with and without patient or community participants on deployment decisions, detected errors, patient comprehension, or harm, and no study reports the staffing or cost of recruiting and compensating patient evaluators.
underserved_note: Neither study reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, and the pediatric study did not report its country. Patient raters who were more literate or English-proficient than the target population may have missed readability problems that affect underserved patients most.

bottom_line: Seven sources, one federal framework and six commentaries, endorse paying participants in AI feedback and engagement work, but no supplied study tests whether compensation reduces exploitation or changes who takes part. The recommendation rests on ethical reasoning and research-ethics norms rather than on outcome data.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests compensation, and no study documents the hazard of exploitation in AI engagement activities. All seven endorsements are a framework or commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Certainty that compensation achieves its intended effect therefore cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

NIST AI 600-1 frames compensation as part of following human subjects research requirements during feedback activities. This places the practice within existing research-ethics expectations rather than a new legal mandate. One commentary points to a fair market value calculator as a reference, and another reports that unclear reimbursement guidance for young people raised concerns about coercion.

One commentary on safety-net organizations suggests compensating patients or their organizations to sustain engagement, and another describes payment as a way to help ensure all voices are heard. These are arguments about who can afford to participate. No supplied data show whether payment changes participation by low-income, limited English proficiency, or younger groups.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare compensated and uncompensated AI engagement activities on who enrolls, who stays, perceived coercion, and whether participant input changes the deployed tool, along with work on setting payment levels for minors and for people receiving public benefits.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One endorsing commentary centers safety-net organizations and their patients, but the effect of compensation on participation from these groups remains untested.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether dedicated time and funding for outreach, feedback, and recourse processes improve how generative AI systems perform or how patients fare. The recommendation rests on one federal framework and one commentary, so health systems adopting it would be acting on expert judgment rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Both endorsements are a framework and a commentary, which GRADE treats as expert opinion rather than evidence. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and any expected benefit remains a hypothesis.

NIST AI 600-1 says organizations should verify feedback and information-sharing mechanisms about negative impacts from generative AI. This language is voluntary guidance, and nothing supplied here ties it to an FDA, ONC, or state statutory requirement. Systems may cite it as a reference standard, but it does not set a funding level.

The commentary calls for dedicated money and a named coordinator so that patient partners can take part in chatbot projects, including when distressing topics arise. The source reflects a stated patient-engagement priority. No data show whether funded recourse channels help patients reach a human or correct AI errors faster.

research_gap: No study measures whether allocating staff time or budget to feedback and recourse processes changes the volume of reported generative AI problems, the speed of their resolution, patient trust, or harm rates. Evaluations comparing funded engagement structures with ad hoc processes, and reporting the cost per resolved issue, would give administrators a basis for sizing these investments.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. These groups may face greater barriers to using feedback and recourse channels, and whether dedicated resources reduce those barriers is unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether a process for privacy complaints and questions about AI data processing changes how often individual concerns are heard or resolved. The recommendation rests on one framework endorsement from the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, which describes the practice without reporting outcome data.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence when no comparative or observational test exists. The single endorsement is expert consensus, which describes an expected practice but does not measure its effect.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide item GV.MT-P7 calls for policies to receive, track, and respond to individual complaints and questions about privacy practices. This is the only supplied source, and it is a voluntary framework. The materials provided do not link the item to any statute or rule, so its standing rests on framework adoption.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations with and without a defined AI privacy complaint process and measure complaint volume, time to response, resolution rates, and patient trust. No supplied study documents how often AI-related privacy concerns currently go unheard, so the size of the hazard is also unmeasured.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether a complaint process reaches people who face language, literacy, or access barriers remains unknown, and health systems adopting it may need to collect their own data on who uses it.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether gathering patient feedback on AI data processing and privacy preferences changes design decisions or brings AI data practices closer to patient expectations. The recommendation currently rests on a single framework endorsement from the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Without comparative or even descriptive data, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsement reflects expert consensus, which GRADE treats as distinct from evidence of effect.

The one endorsing source, the CHAI Responsible AI Guide, lists feedback mechanisms such as surveys or focus groups as a practice that should be established (CM.AW-P2). This is a voluntary framework expectation and is not a binding regulatory requirement among the sources supplied here.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI products developed with and without structured patient privacy feedback, measuring whether feedback alters data handling choices, patient-reported trust, or privacy complaints. Descriptive work documenting how often AI data practices diverge from stated patient privacy expectations would also establish the size of the hazard.
underserved_note: No test of this practice was supplied, so no evidence includes Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Feedback methods such as surveys and focus groups may underrepresent these groups unless they are offered in multiple languages and accessible formats, and that possibility remains untested.

bottom_line: One guidance document recommends that AI vendors describe how impacted populations were engaged during the AI lifecycle, but no supplied study tests whether requiring this documentation changes the AI that health systems buy or the outcomes patients experience. No supplied study documents the hazard either, so the recommendation currently rests on expert guidance alone.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single endorsement is a guidance statement using "should" language, which reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative data on procurement or patient outcomes.

The only supporting source is one set of principles for augmented intelligence that lists a description of population engagement as a documentation item. That source is guidance, not a statute or regulation, so a health system adopting this requirement would be setting a contractual expectation rather than enforcing an existing legal duty.

research_gap: No study examines whether vendor documentation of population engagement is accurate, whether it differs across products, or whether requiring it in procurement is associated with differences in model performance, bias, patient trust, or harm. A useful first step would compare AI tools procured with and without such documentation on subgroup performance and patient-reported experience after deployment.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these populations have no evidence on whether vendor engagement documentation reflects their patients or predicts how the AI will perform for them.

bottom_line: No study in this map tests whether bias-reporting mechanisms for users and affected populations lead to more reports or less harm, or whether those procedures are fair in themselves. Two frameworks, FUTURE-AI and HEAAL, endorse stakeholder engagement and structured equity procedures, but that support rests on consensus rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard. The support comes from one consensus guideline and one framework, and GRADE does not treat either type of source as evidence of effect. Certainty about whether reporting mechanisms surface bias, or whether the procedures change fairness, cannot be rated.

The recommendation asks that feedback procedures be checked for their own fairness. This matters because reporting channels may favor people with time, digital access, or English fluency. No study here measures who uses such channels or who is left out, so the risk of uneven reporting remains untested.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare bias-reporting channels (for example, clinician portals, patient hotlines, and community advisory input) on report volume, the demographics of reporters, how often reports are confirmed, and later changes in model performance across subgroups. The same studies should measure whether some groups report less often than others.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so there are no data on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. The populations that may face the most bias are also the ones whose ability to use reporting channels has not been measured.

bottom_line: Seven sources, one framework and six commentaries, recommend consulting experts, community members, and people with knowledge of patient experience when assessing AI bias, but no supplied study tests whether this consultation detects bias or reduces inequity. The recommendation currently rests on expert opinion and on the reasoning that affected groups can surface concerns developers miss.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests stakeholder or community consultation as a bias-assessment method, and no study documents the hazard itself. The seven endorsements consist of the CHAI framework and six commentaries, all phrased as should statements. Under GRADE conventions, expert agreement of this kind does not establish certainty about effect, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence.

Several endorsing commentaries argue that community members and social researchers can identify historical bias in data sources and variables. None of the supplied sources reports a test of this claim in any population. Health systems therefore cannot yet say which consultation methods, if any, reach Medicaid, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients well enough to change what bias assessments find.

research_gap: No study compares bias assessments conducted with and without input from community members, patients, or subject matter experts. Useful designs would measure whether consultation identifies biases or baseline inequities that technical audits alone miss, whether those findings change model design or deployment decisions, and what consultation costs in staff time and participant compensation. Studies should also specify who was consulted, how they were recruited, and how their input was recorded and acted upon.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested this practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Because these groups are often the intended voices in community consultation, the absence of tests means health systems have no data on whether consultation methods actually reach them or reflect their concerns.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether collecting user and community feedback on content provenance improves provenance design, trust, or effectiveness, and no study documents the hazard itself. The recommendation rests on a single framework endorsement from NIST AI 600-1.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no certainty rating can be assigned to any outcome. The only support is one framework statement using "should" language. A framework endorsement reflects expert judgment and does not substitute for comparative evidence on whether feedback changes provenance design or user trust.

NIST AI 600-1 advises organizations to record and integrate structured feedback on content provenance from operators, users, and potentially impacted communities, naming user research, focus groups, and community forums as methods. The framework is voluntary. No supplied source ties this practice to a binding federal or state requirement.

The framework names potentially impacted communities as feedback sources, but no supplied study examines who participates in such feedback or whether their input alters provenance design. Without data, a health system cannot tell whether Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients would be represented.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare provenance designs developed with and without structured user and community feedback, measuring whether users correctly recognize AI-generated clinical content, whether their trust matches the content's actual origin, and what the feedback process costs in staff time. Studies documenting how often provenance labels fail or go unnoticed in health care settings are also absent.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems that adopt this practice would need to recruit these groups deliberately and track their participation, because nothing in the supplied evidence shows that feedback processes reach them or reflect their provenance expectations.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether community town halls or listening sessions surface concerns about higher-risk AI before or during deployment, and no study documents the hazard itself. The single endorsing source, a CHAI governance playbook, is quoted on root cause analysis of human-factor contributors and does not speak directly to community listening sessions.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The one endorsement comes from a framework, and its quoted text addresses root cause analysis rather than community engagement, so it offers indirect support at most.

Because no study was supplied, there is no information on whether listening sessions reach Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy communities. Any claim that town halls capture the concerns of these groups currently rests on assumption rather than data.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare organizations holding community town halls or listening sessions on higher-risk AI with those that do not. Useful outcomes include the number and type of concerns raised before deployment, changes made to deployment plans in response, attendance by demographic group, and later measures of patient trust or complaints. No such study appears in the supplied evidence.
underserved_note: No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. This means organizations cannot assume that listening sessions reach these groups, and those that adopt the practice may need to track who attends and who does not.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether clinician counseling about consumer chatbots changes how patients use chatbot advice or whether it prevents harm. Support comes from five endorsements, four of them commentaries, and from four studies that document inaccurate chatbot output and low patient disclosure of chatbot use.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests clinician counseling on consumer chatbots. The four hazard studies are cross-sectional, vignette, or simulated designs, three rated level 4. They show that inaccurate chatbot output occurs, but they do not show that counseling reduces patient reliance or harm. Four of the five endorsements are commentaries, so the recommendation rests mainly on expert opinion.

Inaccurate output appeared across different tasks. Between 62.5% and 73.8% of chatbot ophthalmologist recommendations were wrong. ChatGPT showed 0% specificity for scoliosis on photographs. Exercise plans for type 2 diabetes were judged not fully safe. These studies describe the failure mode, and none tests whether counseling catches such errors before patients act on them.

In one clinic survey of 59 patients, 28.6% used an LLM to learn about their condition before the visit, and 93.8% did not disclose it. This suggests clinicians may not know when counseling is needed unless they ask directly. No study reports how such questions fit into visit workflow or how much time they add.

None of the hazard studies reports enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants, and one study did not report its country. The supplied evidence cannot show whether counseling would reach these patients as well as others, or whether chatbot errors affect them differently.

Most surveyed patients who used chatbots did not tell their clinicians, which suggests clinicians may need to start the conversation. Counseling could give patients a person to check chatbot advice with. No study has measured its effect on patient trust, disclosure, or access to a human clinician.

research_gap: No study compares structured clinician counseling about consumer chatbots with usual care. A trial or pragmatic evaluation should measure patient disclosure of chatbot use, reliance on chatbot advice, harmful actions taken, and visit time. It should enroll patients across literacy levels and languages and include safety-net settings.
underserved_note: No study tests the practice. None of the four hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence gives no basis for judging whether counseling would work for these groups or whether they face different chatbot risks.

bottom_line: Five studies test end-user or community involvement in AI design, and all report favorable findings, but none compares a co-designed tool with one built without such input, and samples are small (8 to 33 participants in the evaluated steps). The evidence suggests that participatory design is feasible and acceptable to participants, while its effect on patient outcomes, safety, or equity remains untested.

perspectives.view: The one study labeled an RCT reports its design-related findings as a pre-post analysis and an 8-user pilot. The other four are qualitative or uncontrolled pilots. None has a comparator, outcomes are intermediate (comprehension, acceptability, stakeholder approval), and samples are small. Risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision each lower certainty to very low.

Co-design took several forms, including community-informed chatbot changes, nurse input on camera monitoring, a design sprint, and focus groups with engagement studios. Among 10 pilot users of one co-developed chatbot, 100% used it and 80% scored above 4 on acceptability. One study ended at a simulated prototype and another at an implementation plan, so routine workflow uptake remains largely unmeasured.

A focus group of 19 clinicians, developers, administrators, and patient advocates named limited patient involvement as a challenge, which shows the gap exists. No study testing co-design measured errors, adverse events, or harm. Whether participatory input catches unsafe design choices before deployment is therefore unknown.

After community-informed adaptations, one chatbot's health literacy demands fell 66.7% (12 of 18 items), and all 8 pilot users reported better comprehension. That study enrolled rural, older, minority, limited English proficiency, and low health literacy participants in China. Its small pilot and non-US setting may limit transfer to US Medicaid and safety-net patients.

None of the five studies reports the cost, staff time, or duration of co-design activities. One study recruited 17 adolescents and young adults plus families and clinicians, and another held a 12-provider focus group and community studios with 21 patients. Planners have no published basis for estimating resource needs at scale.

Patients in community engagement studios reported positively about being engaged, and their input shaped algorithm development and a pilot plan. Patient advocates in a separate focus group described limited patient involvement in AI decisions. No study examined whether involvement changed patients' trust in the deployed tool or their access to a human.

Endorsements come from voluntary frameworks such as the CHAI guide and the FUTURE-AI consensus, which state that representative end users should take part in design. The supplied sources cite no binding federal or state requirement for participatory design, and no study examined regulatory compliance outcomes.

research_gap: No study compares AI tools designed with and without end-user or disadvantaged-group input on clinical outcomes, safety events, uptake, or performance gaps across subgroups. Studies also do not report the cost and staff time that co-design requires.
underserved_note: One test, a small pilot in China, included limited English proficiency, low health literacy, rural, older, and minority participants and found lower literacy demands and better reported comprehension. No test reported including Medicaid or US safety-net populations, so benefits for those groups remain inferred rather than shown.

bottom_line: Two randomized trials, one in a real deployment in China with 2,113 participants and one simulated in Australia with 592, found that AI literacy education increased health awareness and knowledge and reduced intention to use a chatbot for higher-risk questions. Neither trial measured whether patients went on to question or challenge AI in their own care, so certainty in the practice is low.

perspectives.view: Both studies are randomized, which would start certainty high. Certainty drops for indirectness because the outcomes are awareness, knowledge, and stated intention rather than patient engagement with AI in care. Only one trial used a real deployment, and the Australian trial appears to be a preprint in a simulated setting. The two trials agree in direction.

In the Australian trial, animation and image interventions lowered intention to use ChatGPT for higher-risk scenarios (means 2.42 and 2.69 vs 3.12, p<0.001). This suggests education may steer patients away from unsafe chatbot use. The trial measured intention, not behavior or harm, so it cannot show that errors were caught before reaching patients.

The Chinese trial placed AI literacy e-learning before consultations in a live deployment and reported higher objective health awareness (2.95 vs 2.34, P<0.001) and better consultation quality on secondary outcomes. This suggests a preparatory module can fit into a visit workflow. Completion rates, time burden, and fidelity were not reported in the summary provided.

The larger trial enrolled participants with limited or non-English proficiency, low health literacy, rural residence, older age, and racial or ethnic minority status, and it found benefit. Because the trial ran in China, its results may not transfer directly to Medicaid or US safety-net populations, whose language needs and access to digital education differ.

A UK survey of 120 women at breast clinics found that 80% had no knowledge of AI use there and 37% would trust AI findings. That gap suggests patients often cannot question tools they do not know exist. The Australian trial also found lower trust after education, which may reflect more calibrated judgment rather than loss of confidence in care.

Neither trial summary reports cost, staffing, or content maintenance needs. The Chinese trial used e-learning at scale with 2,113 participants, which suggests a digital format can reach large numbers, but health systems have no cost data from these studies to budget for tool-specific materials.

research_gap: No trial has measured whether AI literacy education changes what patients do in their own care, such as asking about AI use, declining a tool, or requesting a human reviewer, or whether it reduces harm. Trials in US settings, including Medicaid and safety-net systems, should compare formats, report cost and staff time, and test how long effects last and whether tool-specific education outperforms general AI education.
underserved_note: The randomized trial in China included participants with limited or non-English proficiency, low health literacy, rural residence, older age, and racial or ethnic minority status, and it found benefit. No test included Medicaid or US safety-net populations, so health systems serving those groups should treat the findings as indirect and evaluate local adaptations.

bottom_line: One automated benchmark reports that an evidence ledger reduced stale citations from 14.7% to 1.2% across 3,200 guideline-change events, but it did not test a defined update schedule or documentation of cut-off dates. Seventeen studies show that outdated sources produce obsolete recommendations, so support for this practice rests on framework endorsement and indirect evidence.

perspectives.view: Only one study, a level 5 automated benchmark, tests a related intervention, and its abstract does not evaluate a scheduled update policy. Certainty is very low because the evidence is indirect, comes from a single study, and relies on benchmark design. The hazard studies show that stale content causes errors, but they do not show that scheduled updates prevent them.

In a German chatbot study, 6 of 104 answers (5.8%) were rated potentially harmful because of outdated or contextually inappropriate recommendations. A corpus containing superseded sepsis definitions increased superseded vocabulary in all four models tested. This suggests that an unmaintained retrieval corpus may introduce errors instead of preventing them.

A United States COVID-19 chatbot's intent-matching accuracy ranged from 54% to 91.1%. Accuracy lagged when new information emerged and rose after new content was added. A retrieval system answered a glofitamab question incorrectly because the key trial was missing from its corpus. These observations suggest that corpus currency affects output, although neither study tests a formal schedule.

An AI-generated CMV prophylaxis protocol relied on outdated evidence. In a simulation built from 165 patients, it cost a mean $4,740 more per patient (P < .01) than guideline-based and institutional protocols. No study reports the staffing or cost of maintaining a corpus on a schedule, so the return on that investment has not been measured.

Both CHAI frameworks list this practice as a must. The CHAI guide calls for continuous checks on how often data on trials, indications, guidelines, and biomarker criteria are updated. The CHAI playbook states that a retrieval corpus needs its own governance policy, separate from model retraining. These are consensus positions and have not been tested against outcomes.

The single test does not report the populations or care settings behind its guideline-change events. The only study involving limited English proficiency or non-English users documents the hazard and does not test the practice. Whether update schedules reduce obsolete advice for Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients is unknown.

In one study, all three ChatGPT-4o responses to a COPD pharmacotherapy question cited a retired guideline. Documented cut-off dates could help clinicians and patients judge how current an answer is. No study measures whether such disclosure affects trust or prompts people to seek a human.

research_gap: No study compares a defined corpus update schedule, or documentation of source databases and cut-off dates, against unmanaged corpora on clinical accuracy, patient outcomes, or cost. Prospective evaluations in deployed retrieval systems could measure stale-recommendation rates at different update intervals and record the staff time each interval requires.
underserved_note: The one test (epmc:PPR1157120) reports no information on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. A German hazard study included limited English proficiency or non-English users but did not test the practice. The effect of scheduled updates in underserved populations is therefore unknown.

bottom_line: Two offline vignette studies suggest that documenting data provenance and auditing retrieval sources may reduce unsupported model claims, but neither study measured patient outcomes or tested expert review of clinical fine-tuning pairs. The recommendation rests mainly on framework endorsements, with very low certainty that the practice improves care.

perspectives.view: One simulation reported unsupported claims at 8.4% (95% CI 6.7–10.3%) with structured artifacts, a 40% relative reduction versus baseline (p = 0.02). A second audited 200 entities and 200 relationships and found 100% guideline-presence precision. Both are single, offline studies of synthetic or scripted cases, so indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

A benchmark of more than 800,000 synthetic data points showed erosion of pathological variability and diagnostic reliability, which shows the contamination hazard exists. It does not show that provenance checks prevent it. The 8.4% residual unsupported claim rate suggests documentation may reduce, but does not remove, errors that could reach clinicians.

The knowledge-graph audit suggests retrieval sources can be checked against guidelines at the entity and relationship level. The study did not report reviewer hours, expert staffing, or how often audits must repeat as guidelines change, so the burden of sustaining this in production remains unknown.

One study was conducted in China and the other did not report a setting, and both used synthetic or scripted scenarios. Neither examined whether curated or audited data represent Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so provenance review could certify data that still underrepresent these groups.

NIST AI 600-1 and the CHAI Assurance Standards Guide advise verifying training, fine-tuning, and retrieval data provenance. The CHAI playbook states that persistent agent memory must fall under data governance, including BAA coverage. No supplied study tests documentation formats or compliance with these provisions.

research_gap: No study compares deployed models built with and without documented data lineage or expert-reviewed fine-tuning pairs in live clinical use, and none reports reviewer workload, cost, or effects on patient-level errors.
underserved_note: Neither test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; both used synthetic or scripted cases. Health systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that provenance review improves output fidelity for their patients.

bottom_line: Eleven studies test input quality checks, and most report that detectors flag poor-quality or incomplete inputs, with AUCs up to 0.77 in one study and as high as 0.999 in another, but all are offline or benchmark evaluations and one found no gain from gating. No study measured whether notifying users during live care changes clinical decisions or patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: All 11 tests are level 4 or 5 offline or benchmark studies. Reported AUCs were 0.933 to 0.995 for infant fundus images, 0.984 to 0.999 for smartphone cornea images, up to 0.77 for OCT scans, and 0.80 for anomalous documents. One study found that gating out poor images did not improve performance. Indirectness and inconsistency lower certainty to very low.

Hazard studies show that failures can pass silently. LLMs erred in 45% of neurology cases missing key information and hallucinated in 50 to 82.7% of cases after one fabricated detail. Filtering retinal images raised gene prediction accuracy from 33.8% to 68.9%, which suggests gating may prevent some errors, though no test tracked harm reaching patients.

In a replay of 28,185 visits, a confidence gate released forecasts at 32.7% to 48.1% of visits, and 51.5% of suppressions came from incomplete assessments rather than model uncertainty (0.2%). Input checks may therefore withhold output often. Clarification prompts improved LLM accuracy in automated benchmarks, and no study tested them in clinical workflows.

In routine use, a prostate AI tool failed on 10% of cases because of pre-analytical artifacts, and 21.7% to 26.5% of joint images were unsuitable for another algorithm. These figures suggest input checks will return a measurable share of cases to staff for rework or manual review, a cost that no testing study quantified.

Only one test involved non-English material. It used Japanese safety reports translated to English, and anomaly detection reached an AUROC of 0.80 with three counterexamples. A hazard study of German records traced most model discrepancies to incomplete documentation. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations.

FDA draft guidance asks developers to list compatible devices and acceptable acquisition protocols, and FUTURE-AI and CHAI frameworks call for mechanisms that identify erroneous or missing inputs. All four sources use should-level language. No study tested whether specifying protocols in device labeling reduces use with incompatible inputs.

In one vignette study, GPT-4o asked for missing acne medication details and OpenBioLLM-70B did not. In another, models failed to detect ambiguity in weekday-phrased patient questions. Patients may receive advice built on incomplete information without knowing it, and no study examined whether patients understood or acted on input-quality notices.

research_gap: No study deployed input quality checks with user notification in live clinical care and compared error rates, clinician responses, workload, or patient outcomes against a setting without checks. Studies are also needed that test whether published protocol specifications hold across device vendors and how often clinicians override or ignore quality notifications.
underserved_note: One test used Japanese safety reports that had been translated to English, but these were regulatory case reports and did not involve patients with limited English proficiency. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the performance of input checks on records and images from those settings remains unknown.

bottom_line: Two offline studies suggest that vetted, documented retrieval corpora may reduce hallucinations and make citations traceable, but neither tests the act of defining and registering corpus criteria in live care. Hazard studies show that poor sources and indexing degrade retrieval, which supports the concern without showing that a registry solves it.

perspectives.view: Two studies test the practice, and both are offline or benchmark evaluations with surrogate outcomes. In one, Google-retrieval chatbots hallucinated in 18% of answered questions versus 2% for CIS chatbots using a vetted corpus (OR 9.4, 95% CI 1.2-17.5). Neither study tests registration itself, so certainty is very low for indirectness and imprecision.

Hazard studies show retrieval failures that can reach answers. Only 22% of top-16 passages were relevant in one study, and off-target articles retrieved for a DLBCL question led to an incorrect answer in another. A documented guideline corpus raised citation groundedness from 0% to 51-89%, which suggests documentation may make errors traceable. No study measured patient harm.

Indexing choices appear to affect retrieval quality. Fixed-size chunking yielded precision 0.17 and recall 0.40, and a German study of 100 cases attributed most errors to automated chunk splitting. One real deployment grounded in embedded institutional protocols recorded 1 hallucination in 240 queries. No study measured the staff time needed to document and maintain a corpus registry.
