Studies conducted in Japan and Germany, including one test of the practice, were classified as covering limited English or non-English populations. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients, and none examined whether registered corpora contain materials suited to those groups.

The CHAI playbook states that organizations must keep data preparation procedures for data input into models, even when they do not train models. The other three endorsements are commentaries. No study examined whether a corpus registry satisfies FDA, ONC, or state requirements, so the policy case rests on framework guidance rather than tested outcomes.

research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without documented, registered corpus inclusion criteria, sources, and indexing methods. Prospective evaluations in live clinical workflows should measure hallucination rates, citation traceability, audit time, and maintenance burden, and they should include safety-net and limited English proficiency settings.
underserved_note: One testing study, conducted in Japan, was classified as including a limited English or non-English population, but no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients. That classification does not establish relevance to limited English proficiency patients in U.S. care, so the benefit for those groups remains untested.

bottom_line: Twelve offline or benchmark studies show that hallucination, omission, and term-recall metrics can be applied to AI-generated notes, but rater agreement is inconsistent and no study tested whether a health system evaluation program reduces errors that reach patients. No testing study measured speaker misattribution or coding accuracy.

perspectives.view: All 12 studies that test the practice are level 4 or 5 and use offline replays, simulated encounters, or automated benchmarks. They show that defined metrics can be applied and produce error rates. None measured whether a health system's evaluation program reduces errors in signed notes or harm to patients. Indirectness and inconsistent rater agreement lower certainty.

In 450 UK transcript-note pairs, 1.47% of note sentences contained hallucinations, 44% of them major, and 3.45% of transcript sentences were omitted. Iterative refinement cut major omissions from 61 to 0. Across 59,819 transcription errors, no frequency metric tracked serious clinical risk (|ρ|<0.16), which suggests severity grading may be needed beyond word error rate.

Rater agreement varied across studies. Ten clinicians adjudicating 434 flagged items reached an inter-clinician AC1 of 0.24, and an automated judge agreed with clinicians 64% of the time. An LLM jury reached κ of 81% against a seven-physician panel, compared with 67% for a single expert. A vision-enabled scribe recorded 98% medication data accuracy in simulation.

Health system executives in the guidance source asked for shared metric definitions so that systems can compare results. Clinician adjudication takes staff time, and one study used 10 clinicians for 565 adjudications. Automated judges could lower that cost, but agreement of 64% in one study and κ of 81% in another suggests local validation may be needed before they replace clinician review.

Two testing studies involved non-English or limited English proficiency material, and both were benchmark-only. One used 30 synthetic Brazilian teleconsultations, and the other used a UK transcription-error set. A Belgian hazard study reported that dialect and accent problems produced incomplete transcripts, which suggests quality metrics may perform differently for these speakers.

One endorsing commentary proposes patient-reported accuracy under open notes as a quality measure, but no testing study asked patients to review their notes. In 200 breast oncology consultations, patient-level fabrication was 8% for AI summaries versus 3% for staff summaries. This suggests patients may benefit from a way to flag errors in their records.

research_gap: No study compared live deployments with and without a structured note-evaluation program on errors in signed notes, downstream diagnosis documentation, coding accuracy, or patient harm. Validated and reliable metrics for speaker misattribution and coding accuracy are absent, and inter-rater agreement standards for clinician and automated judges have not been established.
underserved_note: Two testing studies included non-English or limited English proficiency material, and both were benchmark-only studies without real patients. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that published error rates or metric validity carry over to accented speech, interpreted visits, or low-literacy encounters without local evaluation.

bottom_line: Eleven sources endorse clinician verification of AI output, and ten studies show that AI notes and summaries omit, misstate, or add content, but only one small offline study tests review itself. In that study, pharmacist correction of 80 AI medication logs raised a text-similarity score from 0.68 to 0.71, which says little about whether review prevents harm to patients.

perspectives.view: One retrospective replay study of 80 medication logs tests the practice. Its outcome is a machine similarity score (BERT F1 0.68 to 0.71) rather than errors caught or patient outcomes. The design, indirect outcome, single setting, and small sample suggest very low certainty. The ten hazard studies establish the problem but do not show that verification solves it.

Hazard studies report safety concerns in 6% of 50 real ED handoff summaries, risk-fact omission of 4% to 26% in psychiatric summaries, and major omissions up to 5.5% in simplified spine MRI reports. In a study of 104 medical students, hybrid notes scored lower on chief complaint (P=.05), which the authors attributed to automation bias. This suggests review alone may miss omissions.

A qualitative analysis of 2,267 clinician forum segments found that whether scribe errors were caught or carried forward depended on integration quality, governance clarity, and review capacity. Median numeric-token preservation in generated admission notes ranged from 33.3% to 70.0% by model. This suggests reviewers may need to check numbers against source data.

The single test of the practice used non-English medication logs in China, and one hazard study translated 60 neuroradiology impressions into Spanish. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore does not show how verification performs for those groups.

The qualitative study linked error propagation to review capacity, and a transcription benchmark found clinically significant errors from 2% to 66% depending on system and background noise. These findings suggest the review effort needed may vary by tool and setting. No study measured how much clinician time verification requires.

In radiology reports simplified to a 7th-grade level, inaccuracies with potential to alter management included inappropriate generalization in 40% (8/20), omission in 35% (7/20), and incorrect conversion in 35% (7/20). About 30% of one model's myopia education responses were rated slightly harmful. Patients may receive flawed content if no clinician checks it first.

research_gap: No study measures whether clinician verification of AI notes or answers catches omissions, misattributions, or unsupported content before they affect care in real deployment. Studies comparing structured, source-linked review against usual review, with errors caught, review time, and patient outcomes as endpoints, would address this gap.
underserved_note: The only test of the practice used non-English medication logs in China, but it was offline and measured text similarity rather than safety. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the benefit of verification for those groups is unknown.

bottom_line: Offline studies suggest that AI tools can attach sources that point to the correct passage in most cases, and clinicians rate such answers as more verifiable and more trustworthy. In one simulation, displayed citations also made physicians more likely to accept wrong answers, and no study has tested labeling of chart-verified versus model-assumed content in live care.

perspectives.view: Nineteen studies test source display, and all are offline or benchmark-based. Two randomized trials measured ratings rather than errors caught. Trust rose from 2.59 to 3.80 with claim-level linking, and verifiability ratings rose from 35% to 84%. Indirect outcomes, small samples, and mixed results in four studies support a low certainty rating.

In a 46-physician simulation, correct answers carried supporting citations more often (87.7% vs 65.5%). When a citation supported an incorrect answer, physicians resisted it 34.8% of the time rather than 92%. Attached quotes fully substantiated 37.1% of claims for one model and 48.0% to 78.8% in two other studies. A displayed source may increase reliance without confirming the claim.

Retrieval tools located the correct source passage in 90% to 95% of simulated cases. One tool failed to retrieve in eight of 100 cases. Two studies labeled general-knowledge answers separately from sourced content, and experts valued that layering. No study tested labels for chart-verified versus model-assumed content inside an electronic health record workflow.

One test, a Chinese-language evaluation of 60 questions, used non-English content, and it enrolled no patients. In hazard studies, all outputs written for low-literacy readers lacked citations and dates, and Chinese-language answers scored low on sourcing. No test of source display included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users.

Adding guideline retrieval raised citation groundedness from 0% to between 51% and 89% across six models. This suggests the feature can work with more than one vendor's model. No study measured how much clinician time it takes to open and check sources, so the staffing cost of verification is unknown.

In a trial with 127 caregivers, only one of four public chatbots gave source citations. Clinician trust rose when answers linked claims to sources. No study tested whether patients or caregivers can use displayed sources to check answers or to decide when to contact a clinician.

research_gap: No study measures whether displayed sources lead clinicians to catch errors before they reach patients in a live deployment. No study tests visible labeling of chart-verified versus model-assumed content within an electronic health record. Trials should measure error detection, automation bias toward cited but incorrect answers, and the time clinicians spend on verification.
underserved_note: One test used Chinese-language content, but it evaluated questions and enrolled no patients or clinicians from underserved settings. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Hazard studies show that sourcing is absent in low-literacy and non-English outputs, so benefits for these groups remain untested.

bottom_line: Five offline or benchmark studies test parts of this practice: two detection classifiers report high accuracy, one study finds detection systems inefficient, and two benchmarks find that watermarking degrades medical text. No study tests whether labels or provenance tracking help clinicians or patients judge authenticity in real use.

perspectives.view: All five tests are level 4 or 5 designs in offline or benchmark settings, and none measures a user or patient outcome. The detector studies disagree, with one classifier reaching accuracy 0.98 and another an F1 above 95%, while a third study found detection inefficient. Indirectness, inconsistency, and design limits support very low certainty.

Two benchmarks report that watermarking can introduce hallucinated terminology, lexical corruption, and misattributed image findings in medical text. The provenance mechanism itself may therefore create a new route for errors to reach clinicians. A hazard study found experts misclassified synthetic CT images with a 67% false positive rate, but it does not show that labels would prevent this.

In a Swiss simulation, an automated classifier reached accuracy 0.98 on medical reports, compared with 0.60 for nine experts. This suggests tools may outperform human review. No study reports how detection or labeling fits into clinical workflows. None addresses alert burden or the handling of false positives in live systems.

The Swiss detection study included non-English medical reports. A Chinese randomized trial found that only 7.3% of participants identified LLM-generated materials. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy groups, and these groups may depend most on labels they can read and interpret.

NIST AI 600-1 conditions its guidance on auditing tools that can be demonstrated to aid lineage and authenticity tracking. The current evidence shows mixed detector performance and, in benchmarks, watermarking harms to medical factuality. This evidence may not yet meet that demonstration condition for clinical content.

In a real deployment dataset, patient advisors identified AI-generated responses 24% of the time and attributed 50% to humans. Patients may therefore not know when a machine wrote a message to them. No study tested whether a label changes patient trust or understanding, or whether it affects patients' ability to reach a clinician.

research_gap: No study deploys labeling or provenance tracking in live patient portals or clinical documentation. Such studies should measure whether users correctly judge authenticity, whether trust and reliance change, and whether watermarking alters the factual accuracy of clinical text. They should also report detector false-positive rates on human-written content and enroll diverse patient populations.
underserved_note: One detection test (pmid:42097830) included non-English medical reports, but no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. No evidence shows whether patients with limited literacy or limited English proficiency understand content labels, so effects in those groups cannot be inferred.

bottom_line: Thirteen simulated or benchmark studies suggest that automated pre-delivery filters and judge agents may reduce harmful generated output, but several found that harm persisted and one found that a guardrail stack increased omission of safety-relevant information. No study tested filtering of copyright-infringing or unlawful content, and none was conducted with live patients.

perspectives.view: All 13 tests used synthetic dialogues, vignettes, or automated benchmarks, and none measured patient outcomes. Eight reported support and five reported null or mixed results. Many abstracts gave no numbers. Certainty is very low because of indirectness, inconsistency across models and designs, and imprecision.

In one benchmark, a four-component guardrail stack lowered commission errors but raised omission of safety-relevant information from 17.6% to 30.1%. A safety filter cut harmful output for Mistral from 13.1% to 4.4% but changed GPT-4.1 only from 9/250 to 8/250. These results suggest filters may shift harm rather than remove it.

Resistance to circumvention varied. One defense-in-depth system gave safe responses to all 206 attacks, while another study found existing control protocols could be subverted. In a hazard study, Copilot blocked disinformation prompts initially but not at 12 weeks, which suggests one-time testing may not hold as models change.

One benchmark reported full interception of unsafe prompts at baseline cost and latency. A validation-agent study found accuracy of 0.40 to 0.82 across 12 models, and only models of 27B parameters or larger exceeded 0.80. This suggests that dependable checking may require larger models and the compute costs that come with them.

Two tests included non-English or limited English proficiency content. A safety-oriented system prompt lowered harmful answers from 56% to 30%, though a system prompt differs from a post-generation filter. A validation agent in Qatar did not dependably block unscientific advice. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users.

NIST AI 600-1, the CHAI guide, and one commentary endorse output checks. No supplied study tested whether filters block copyright-infringing or otherwise unlawful content, so that part of the recommendation rests on endorsement alone.

The rise in omitted safety information under a guardrail stack means a filtered answer can leave patients without warnings they need. No study measured what patients see when output is blocked or whether they are directed to a human.

research_gap: Prospective evaluations in live clinical or patient-facing deployments should measure harmful output, omission of needed safety information, and false blocking together, repeat circumvention testing over time as models update, and include tests of copyright and legal-compliance filtering, which no current study addresses.
underserved_note: Two tests included non-English or limited English proficiency content, one in Qatar, and neither was run with real patients. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so performance of these filters for those users is unknown.

bottom_line: Across 85 studies, mostly offline and level 4, uncertainty signals tended to separate correct from incorrect AI outputs and supported deferral or abstention, but no study measured whether calibrated uncertainty expression reduces patient harm in real care. How clinicians respond to uncertainty displays varied by display format, so developers and evaluators should test the display as well as the calibration.

perspectives.view: One level 2 real-deployment study found mean confidence of 0.97 for correct versus 0.81 for incorrect medication and lab mappings. The rest are level 4, mostly offline, and report surrogate outcomes such as error separation. Uncertain nodules had an AUC of 0.62 versus 0.93 for certain ones. One study found entropy ran in the opposite direction, which lowers consistency.

In chest X-rays, AI accuracy was 0.596 on images the AI flagged as uncertain, while physicians reached 0.698 on those images, which suggests deferral may catch errors. An uncertainty-acknowledgement prompt lowered hallucination rates from 65.9% to 44.2% without eliminating them. In a hazard study, one model conveyed high confidence on 100% of responses at 45-65% accuracy.

In a 192-participant trial, token-level uncertainty displays increased agreement with the AI. Relation-level displays reduced users' external verification. In a separate trial of 64 clinicians, trust was lower when the AI performed worst. These findings suggest that display format may shape clinician behavior as much as calibration does, and both trials were simulated.

Uncertainty thresholds shift work to human reviewers. Reviewing fewer than 10% of patients captured all extraction errors for two conditions, but capturing all seizure errors required reviewing 19.6%. Certainty thresholds raised accuracy above 90%, but fewer than half of items were then covered automatically. Abstention rose from 9.6% to 22% as the required confidence increased.

A regulatory discussion paper asks whether a device defers when uncertain without over-deferring, and FUTURE-AI calls for calibrated uncertainty estimates. Across models built on the same data, the share of cases flagged as uncertain ranged from 0.3% to 59.9%. This spread suggests that any standard would need to address the amount of deferral as well as coverage.

Three tests used non-English clinical text, from Finland, Switzerland, and Japan. One of these found that the entropy signal ran counter to expectations after translation. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Whether uncertainty signals hold up across these patient groups is therefore unknown.

In a real deployment of 2,035 patient conversations, a chatbot gave confident answers that filled gaps in its evidence rather than signaling uncertainty. No practice test measured patient understanding, trust, or whether patients reached a human after an uncertainty flag.

research_gap: No study tested calibrated uncertainty expression in live clinical use with outcomes such as intercepted errors, clinician verification behavior, or patient harm. Evaluations of generative model outputs and of patient-facing uncertainty messages remain sparse. Head-to-head comparisons of display formats in real workflows are also needed.
underserved_note: Three tests used non-English source text from European and Japanese settings, and one included older adults. None included Medicaid, safety-net, US limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether calibration and error flagging perform equally for these groups, or whether patients in these groups understand uncertainty messages.

bottom_line: Seven studies test citation verification, and all report that it catches or prevents fabricated and misattributed references, but six are automated benchmarks and one is an uncontrolled review of 20 synthetic cases. None measures whether verification during deployment reduces errors that reach clinicians or patients, or what it costs in reviewer time.

perspectives.view: Six of seven tests are level 5 automated benchmarks, and the seventh is a pre-post study without a comparator using 20 synthetic cases. The results point in one direction, but the evidence is indirect because it tests verification tools in offline settings rather than evaluators working in deployment. Samples are small or unrepresentative, so certainty is very low.

In one hazard study, 68.9% of ChatGPT neurosurgical references were inaccurate and 33.9% were falsified. Chain-of-Verification detected 60 of 62 problematic references (sensitivity 96.8%, specificity 98.6%). One agent verifier caught all injected attribution swaps, yet its source-plus-relation accuracy fell to 0.229 on a harder multi-source benchmark, which suggests detection may weaken as outputs grow complex.

Live PMID verification alone produced 0.0% fabricated and 0.0% wrong-topic citations, compared with 95.9% wrong-topic citations in unguided output. Adding programmatic citation checks moved one system from last (55.5) to first (81.8), which suggests evaluation design can change conclusions. In the one deployment test, 56 of 60 source-attributed statements were fully covered by the cited excerpt.

One Brazilian benchmark of 500 non-English clinical queries found 461 of 500 correct citations with deterministic verification versus 1 of 500 with prompt-based citation. A Turkish hazard study reported ChatGPT perfect-reference rates of 78.5% in Turkish and 71.4% in English, which suggests citation reliability may vary by language.

The NIST Generative AI Profile states that organizations should review and verify sources and citations during pre-deployment measurement and ongoing monitoring. This framework is voluntary guidance, and none of the supplied studies evaluates adherence to it or its effect on outcomes.

No study reports staff time, cost, or the effort needed to verify citations at scale. The tested methods were largely automated, including one that screened 8,050 references against expert adjudication, which suggests automation could reduce manual review, though no study measured workload directly.

In ratings and interviews involving oncology physicians, trust declined when citations did not match claims or provenance was buried. Two studies found chatbot answers scored 0 on JAMA source-attribution benchmarks, so patients reading such answers may have had no way to check where claims came from.

research_gap: No study compares deployed systems monitored with and without citation verification. Such a study would measure the rate of fabricated or misattributed citations reaching clinicians or patients, reviewer time per output, and the performance of manual versus automated checks on multi-source clinical answers. It would also report results separately for non-English and patient-facing use.
underserved_note: One test, a Brazilian benchmark, used non-English clinical queries, and no test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving those groups have almost no evidence on whether verification performs as reported for their patients, particularly for patient-facing content in languages other than English.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether pre-deployment evaluation of dosing, unit conversion, lab interpretation, and implausible-value detection reduces medication harm. Sixty-three hazard studies, nearly all offline simulations, report numeric and dosing error rates that range from none to 90% of cases depending on model, task, and configuration.

perspectives.view: None of the 63 supplied studies compares deployment with and without pre-deployment numeric testing, so certainty about the practice cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The hazard evidence is mostly level 4 vignette or replay work with small samples, and findings are inconsistent. One study found no dosage difference from experts (p=0.975), while another found 79.2% errors in kidney disease.

The documented failures fall into categories that pre-deployment tests could target. ChatGPT exceeded maximum local anesthetic doses in 9 of 10 cases. A vancomycin tool with fully accurate calculations still produced safety violations in 17% of cases, including doses above 4 g/day. No model caught diazepam's 7-day prescription limit. These studies show the hazard, not that testing prevents it.

Performance shifted with configuration. Dosing guidance raised potassium dosing accuracy from 45% to 65%. Retrieval augmentation removed the 8% hallucination rate seen in a base model. Pediatric dose accuracy ranged from 66 to 100 across three models. These results suggest that a test may only hold for the exact model version, prompt, and retrieval setup that is deployed.

The only real-deployment hazard study comes from Kenya, where neonatologists rated 75% of complex neonatal dosing outputs correct. Three offline studies involved non-English or limited English proficiency settings and reported nutrient underestimation of up to 54% and occasional high-risk drug answers. None of these studies tested whether evaluation protects these groups.

The single endorsing source is a regulatory discussion paper that describes, rather than requires, assessing whether a device interprets numerical and measurement information correctly under noisy or ambiguous input. No binding standard among the supplied sources sets test content, pass thresholds, or retesting after model updates.

Several hazards reach patients directly when they use these tools on their own. Large carbohydrate overestimations that could lead to insulin overdosing occurred in 13% to 38% of meals across three models, compared with 3% for dietitians. AI-generated medication instruction images scored 16.7%, compared with 85% for written responses.

research_gap: No study tests whether a structured pre-deployment numeric evaluation predicts or reduces dosing errors after deployment. Such a study would compare tools that passed or failed defined tests of unit handling, implausible or unit-less inputs, and dose limits, then track medication errors in live use and after model updates.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. A few hazard studies involved non-English settings or a Kenyan deployment. This suggests that numeric errors occur in these contexts, and test suites built only on English, well-formatted inputs may miss them.

bottom_line: One Swedish deployment study audited random samples of AI-excluded records and found no confirmed false negatives among 600 records, which suggests that sample-based spot-checks can be run at scale and can document AI error rates. No study tested whether periodic spot-checking detects errors that accumulate over time or improves reporting accuracy, so the evidence for the practice as written remains thin.

perspectives.view: A single prospective study with a comparator (n=74,679 records) tested a random-sample audit. Its design starts at low certainty. It measured errors at one point rather than monitoring over time, which makes it indirect. Zero events in 600 records gives an imprecise estimate. These limits lead to a very low rating.

In the 600-record audit, no AI-excluded record was confirmed as a final false negative, and all 38 retained records in the 680-record audit had been AI flagged. By the rule of three, a zero count in 600 is still compatible with a miss rate near 0.5%. Detection of rare errors would therefore require larger or repeated samples.

The study embedded random-sample audits in a live deployment, which suggests that spot-checks can run alongside AI-assisted record handling. The report does not describe how often audits recurred, who performed them, or how data completeness was tracked. Fidelity over time therefore remains untested.

Audits of 600 and 680 records against a pool of 74,679 represent a small fraction of volume. This suggests that sample-based checking may cost far less than full manual review. The study did not report staff hours or cost per audit, so budgeting would have to rely on local estimates.

The only test took place in Sweden, and the summary gives no breakdown by insurance, language, or literacy. Error rates in a pooled random sample can mask higher error rates in small subgroups. Health systems may need to stratify their samples to see errors concentrated in underserved patients.

research_gap: No study has measured whether periodic spot-checks and ongoing error-rate and completeness monitoring detect drift or accumulating errors after deployment, particularly in quality reporting. The field also lacks data on the sample sizes and audit frequency needed to detect low error rates, and on the staff time and cost of sustained auditing.
underserved_note: The single test was conducted in Sweden and reported no data on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether random audits capture errors that fall disproportionately on these groups is unknown, and pooled audit results should not be assumed to apply to them.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether governance policies on incorrect, falsified, outdated, or unverifiable generative AI output reduce the harm from such output, and the support for this recommendation rests on one guidance document and two commentaries. One offline study found that every language model it examined produced hallucinations (2 to 8 occurrences) across 10 pediatric nephrology cases, which shows the problem exists but does not show that a policy addresses it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice. The single hazard study is a level 4 simulation of 10 clinical cases in France, so it is indirect, small, and offline. Endorsements come from one guidance document and two commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, certainty that governance policies change outcomes cannot be rated because no direct test exists.

All models in the pediatric nephrology simulation produced hallucinations, ranging from 2 to 8 occurrences across 10 cases. This suggests that incorrect generated content may reach clinicians if no check is in place. The study did not examine whether any institutional rule, review step, or verification requirement would catch these errors before they affect care.

The guidance source states that health care organizations should develop governance policies covering incorrect or falsified responses and the inability to verify sources. The two commentaries call for accountability frameworks and mechanisms to limit misinformation. These statements express expert expectation, and none of them reports a test of how such policies perform once adopted.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare health systems or units with and without written policies on inaccurate generative AI output and measure error detection rates, errors reaching patients, clinician verification behavior, and the time and staff cost of policy compliance in live clinical workflows.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and the one hazard study used 10 simulated pediatric nephrology cases in France without reporting Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore says nothing about whether such policies would work for these groups, who may face added risk if hallucinated content appears in translated or simplified patient materials.

bottom_line: Six small offline or benchmark studies suggest that testing AI output against current guidelines and scoring differentials for serious conditions can reveal knowledge gaps and error rates that vary by model, topic, and patient group. No study shows that this testing, once adopted, reduces missed diagnoses or contraindications in patient care.

perspectives.view: All six tests are level 4 or 5 designs, mostly vignettes or question sets of 30 to 384 items, and none measured patient outcomes. Findings are inconsistent: guideline accuracy ranged from 80% to 86% in two studies, while antibiotic answers were complete and correct in only 27.5% to 38.1% of special-population cases. Indirectness and imprecision support a very low rating.

In one hazard study, errors of omission made up more than 80% of severe errors, which is the failure this testing targets. A replay of 43 emergency notes found a must-not-miss condition in the top three in 78.0% of cases with one system versus 52.0% for a standalone model. This suggests prioritization scoring can separate safer from less safe configurations.

In a dental trauma chatbot, initial completeness of 53% for primary tooth fractures rose to 100% in most cases after code adjustments. This suggests guideline testing may be most useful as an iterative development loop. Retrieval grounding lowered major guideline deviations from 38.1% to 7.9% in one hazard study, which evaluators could use as a comparator.

Error rates in one test reached 79.2% for kidney disease and 25% for older adults, compared with 11.9% for pregnancy. Evaluation sets that omit such subgroups may overstate accuracy. One test used Chinese-language guidelines. In a Rwanda deployment with community health workers, both models missed important conditions, and no test examined similar settings.

A regulatory discussion paper names differential completeness and prioritization of serious diagnoses as possible device testing, using permissive language. The supplied studies do not show which test design or threshold would satisfy a reviewer. Accuracy moved from 84% to 86% over 30 days in one benchmark, which suggests repeat testing after model updates may be needed.

The physician's most probable diagnosis was omitted in 19.6% of consultations in one real-world symptom tool. Patients who use such tools may not know which conditions were left out. Published guideline and differential test results could help patients and clinicians judge how far to rely on the output.

research_gap: No study compares deployments that underwent guideline and differential testing with those that did not, and none links test scores to missed diagnoses, contraindication errors, or harm in live care. Evaluators also lack evidence on how often to retest after guideline or model changes.
underserved_note: One test used non-English questions scored against Chinese guidelines, and one included older adults, where error rates were higher. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so health systems serving these groups cannot assume published accuracy figures apply to their patients.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether requiring vendors to show evidence-constrained outputs and hallucination mitigation reduces inaccurate AI output reaching clinicians or patients, and no supplied study documents the hazard itself. The two endorsing sources address data rights and external validation rather than hallucination evidence specifically, so support for this recommendation rests on indirect expert guidance.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no comparative or observational test exists. The recommendation currently rests on expert endorsement alone, and the endorsements do not describe what counts as adequate vendor evidence.

The CHAI playbook text requires vendors to warrant that training, validation, and operating data were lawfully obtained. The augmented intelligence principles call for external validation that accounts for model drift and degradation. Neither quoted passage names hallucination or evidence-constrained output, so the recommendation extends these sources rather than restating them.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare procurement processes requiring vendor evidence of hallucination mitigation against processes that do not, measuring the rate of inaccurate outputs detected after deployment and any resulting patient harm. Work is also needed to define what form of vendor evidence, such as benchmark results, citation grounding tests, or independent audits, predicts accuracy in local use.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Vendor accuracy evidence drawn from other settings may not reflect error rates for patients who communicate in languages other than English or whose records differ from vendor test data, and health systems serving these groups may need local validation.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether documenting and testing validation of tool-call outputs reduces harm from agentic AI. Six benchmark and simulation studies show that agents often accept erroneous, tampered, or poisoned tool outputs and carry them forward, which establishes the hazard but not the remedy.

perspectives.view: None of the six studies evaluates a validation step, so certainty about the practice is rated as no direct evidence. The hazard studies are level 4 and 5 designs. Most are automated benchmarks, and the one replay study included 8 patients. They consistently show error propagation, but they are indirect for the question of whether validation works.

Unsupported observations affected 16.63% of 14,400 audited cases and propagated downstream. Models chose a sham guideline in 40.6% of 10,500 decisions. Subtle chart tampering, such as MRN or age changes, passed almost entirely undetected. These failures could reach patients through record writes and treatment choices, yet no study shows that validation catches them.

In an 8-patient replay, agents selected and executed tools correctly, and most errors came from wrong arguments or misread tool results. A separate benchmark found that 91% of reasoning traces scored above a rubric threshold while decorrelating from accuracy. This suggests that reviewing an agent's rationale may miss bad tool outputs, so validation may need to check the outputs directly.

The generative AI device discussion paper describes assessing whether an agentic device recognizes when an action sequence would exceed its safety envelope. The CHAI playbook requires documentation of retrieval design. Neither source specifies how tool-output validation should be tested, and no supplied study offers a test method that reviewers could adopt.

Frontier models failed in 1 to 3% of 1,200 simulated scenarios because of unverified tool outputs, and the weakest models reported actions they never executed. Patients and clinicians may be unable to tell a fabricated action from a real one. This may argue for making validation records available to the people who review agent actions.

research_gap: No study compares agents with and without a documented tool-output validation step on outcomes such as error propagation, detection of tampered records, or rejection of poisoned retrieved content. Prospective tests in live clinical workflows that measure detection rates, missed errors, and clinician burden are absent.
underserved_note: No study tests the practice. None of the hazard studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and only one reports a country (United States). Health systems serving these groups therefore have no evidence on whether validation performs differently with their records, languages, or documentation patterns.

bottom_line: Twenty-four studies test automated fact-checking or hallucination detection on generative AI outputs, but all were offline or benchmark evaluations, and none measured whether flagging kept inaccurate content from reaching patients or staff. Purpose-built detectors reported F1 values of 0.80 to 0.98 on benchmarks, while general LLM-as-judge approaches agreed with experts roughly half to two thirds of the time.

perspectives.view: All 24 studies use level 4 or 5 designs run offline or on benchmarks, so they apply only indirectly to real dissemination. Results are inconsistent across methods. Fine-tuned detectors scored higher than LLM judges, and no study reports patient or staff outcomes. Certainty that the practice prevents misinformation from spreading is very low.

Detection reduced errors but did not remove them. Automated filtering lowered error rates without eliminating harmful responses. In-agent safeguards filtered 89.9% of hallucinations, yet hallucinations remained prevalent. A verifier corrected 85.6% of identified hallucinations while the hallucination rate stayed near 0.61. These results suggest flagging may serve as one layer that still requires human review.

Checker performance depended on the evidence it could consult. A strong LLM scored 91% with gold evidence and 35% with wrong evidence, and expert clinicians reached 53.3% macro F1. Early detection rates were 0.352 to 0.390 under strict false-positive caps. CARE surfaced up to 5 times fewer sentences for review, which may reduce reviewer burden.

In one small study, GPT-4o checked claims in 42 seconds versus 18 minutes for expert pharmacists and agreed on all 20 claims. It missed an internal inconsistency in a longer response. Atomic fact-checking improved answer quality across 16 models. No study reports implementation cost, staffing needs, or tool maintenance.

Two studies used non-English source material, Japanese safety reports and Russian EHR summaries. The drug-name checker caught every hallucinated name in 20 cases but missed errors caused by dictionary gaps and spelling. LLM judges on the Russian summaries showed Kendall W of 0.37 to 0.55. No study tested patient-facing content for low-literacy readers.

NIST AI 600-1 advises integrating tools that identify patterns of misinformation. The Principles for augmented intelligence guidance assigns authors responsibility for validating the veracity of AI-generated referenced content. Neither source sets performance thresholds, and the supplied studies do not establish a validated benchmark against which an organization could judge a documented tool.

Every evaluation stopped before content reached patients. In simulated patient-coach dialogues, harmful responses remained after filtering. On 1,500 patient messages, the best error-checking F1 was 0.500. These findings suggest patients may still receive inaccurate content even when checking tools are in place.

research_gap: No study deployed a fact-checking tool in a live workflow and compared how much inaccurate content reached patients or staff with and without flagging. Prospective comparisons in patient-facing channels would address this gap if they reported false-positive burden on reviewers, missed harmful content, and performance on non-English and plain-language materials.
underserved_note: Two tests used non-English source content. One caught all hallucinated drug names in 20 Japanese case safety reports but missed errors from dictionary gaps and spelling, and the other found low agreement among LLM judges on Russian EHR summaries. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence cannot show whether these tools catch misinformation in materials written for those patients.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether drawing biological sex from the statutorily designated EHR field changes the accuracy of treatment recommendations, and no supplied study documents the hazard. The practice rests on a single Texas statute that requires it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for R501 contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. Any claim that the requirement reduces distorted recommendations remains untested in the material supplied.

Texas SB 1188 uses mandatory language. It requires that any algorithm or decision assistance tool in an EHR that assists treatment decisions include biological sex as recorded in the field the statute designates. For systems operating in Texas, compliance is a legal obligation regardless of the evidence gap.

No supplied study measures how often incorrect sex inputs reach decision algorithms or what harm follows. Without hazard data, the panel cannot estimate the frequency or severity of the failure this requirement targets. The panel also cannot say whether one designated field catches or introduces errors.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare treatment recommendations generated from the designated biological sex field against those generated from other sex or gender fields. These studies should measure how often recommendations differ, whether they lead to clinical errors, and how records for patients whose sex-linked physiology differs from the recorded value are handled.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The effect of the requirement on the accuracy of recommendations for these groups is unknown.

bottom_line: Most comparative tests, largely small and offline, suggest that grounding outputs in curated sources lowers hallucination and raises rated accuracy, and one real deployment reported hallucinations in 10% of grounded versus 38% of ungrounded answers. Two tests found that grounding degraded outputs or failed to prevent errors, and grounded systems still produced errors, so certainty is low.

perspectives.view: One real-deployment quasi-experiment found hallucinations in 5/52 (10%) of RAG answers versus 15/39 (38%) native answers (P=.002). Most other tests are offline, small, or confounded by model changes. One study with 80,502 expert annotations found that standard RAG lowered factuality by up to 6%. Inconsistency, indirectness, and risk of bias suggest low certainty.

Grounding appears to lower hallucination frequency without removing it. The grounded arm still hallucinated in 10% of answers in one deployment, and a model given source passages hallucinated in 19.7% of answers. A RAG chatbot produced unverified contact details in 4/20 distress probes. A RAG mental health classifier raised more false alarms. Grounded output may still need review.

Retrieval quality appears to determine whether grounding helps. In one evaluation only 22% of the top-16 retrieved passages were relevant. A guideline RAG produced zero verifiable citations, while a knowledge-graph design reached 100%. In one deployment, accuracy rose from 67% to 82% as knowledge hit rates rose from 86% to 100% across tuning rounds, which suggests curation requires sustained work.

Tests ran in Germany, Slovenia, China, Bangladesh, and India, and three were tagged as including non-English-speaking patients. One Caribbean tool cited verified local facilities in 28/28 queries versus 10/28 for ChatGPT. No test enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients in the United States. A descriptive RAG chatbot study with Medicaid caregivers reported 99% intent accuracy without an ungrounded comparator.

NIST AI 600-1 lists grounding and retrieval-augmented generation as one control among several that organizations may apply. The CHAI guide treats knowledge-base integration as a requirement for treatment-selection use cases. The endorsing sources are frameworks and commentaries, and none of the supplied tests addresses regulatory compliance or liability.

Cost and speed data are sparse. One oncology study found that a fixed high-end model cost more and received lower expert ratings than automatic model selection with context. One graph-grounded design reported lower latency than text-only RAG but gave no numbers. Repeated tuning rounds in one deployment suggest that knowledge-base upkeep requires ongoing staff time.

Three reported cases describe patients and families misled by false LLM information. Grounding in verified directories may help patients reach real services, since one Caribbean tool cited verified facilities in 28/28 queries. A RAG chatbot still invented contact details in 4/20 distress scenarios, which suggests that patients in crisis may need a direct route to a human.

research_gap: No randomized or controlled deployment study measures patient harm, clinician error correction, or downstream care outcomes for grounded versus ungrounded outputs. Few studies report retrieval precision alongside output quality, and few separate the effect of grounding from concurrent changes to the model or prompt. Head-to-head comparisons of retrieval designs, such as text RAG versus knowledge graphs, are rare, and no tests have been run in safety-net settings in the United States.
underserved_note: Several tests of the practice ran in Germany, Slovenia, China, Bangladesh, India, and the Caribbean, and three were tagged as including non-English-speaking patients. No test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, low-literacy, or limited English proficiency patients within health systems in the United States. The only study involving Medicaid caregivers was descriptive and lacked an ungrounded comparator, so it remains untested whether curated sources cover the services and languages these patients use.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether basing AI-assisted coverage and prior-authorization decisions on current evidence-based criteria and individual patient circumstances, with criteria visible in clinician workflow, changes denial accuracy or patient outcomes. Support for R502 rests on two endorsements, one guidance document and one framework, and no supplied study documents the hazard of algorithmic denials either.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no test exists. The two endorsements express expert agreement, which a methodologist treats as opinion rather than evidence of effect.

The augmented intelligence principles state that payors should decide on particular patient care needs rather than on algorithms built from similar patients. The CHAI guide describes access to patient data, communication of payer treatment guidelines, and human review. Neither source reports measured compliance or outcomes, so the recommendation currently rests on professional guidance alone.

The CHAI guide lists human review and decision-making as part of the coverage process, which aligns with patients' interest in reaching a person when a claim is denied. No supplied study measures whether patients actually receive individualized review or whether accessible criteria reduce inappropriate denials.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare AI-assisted prior-authorization programs using current evidence-based criteria and individual patient review against programs without these features, measuring inappropriate denial rates, overturn rates on appeal, time to treatment, clinician burden, and patient harm. Studies should also test whether displaying payer criteria inside the clinician workflow changes submission completeness and approval accuracy.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems therefore have no evidence on whether individualized, criteria-based AI coverage review performs equally across these groups, whose members may face higher administrative barriers when appealing denials.

bottom_line: One offline study of 50 hospital stays found that a summarization approach produced hospital course summaries rated more complete and correct, but no study tested whether documenting truncation or reconciliation rules changes model outputs or patient outcomes. Four hazard studies show that long or truncated records can drop facts or cause model failure, which supports the concern but does not show that the practice resolves it.

perspectives.view: The single test is a retrospective rater study of 50 stays. It reports completeness of 4.28 vs 4.01 and correctness of 4.37 vs 4.17. It evaluates a summarization method rather than the act of documenting rules, and no study addresses reconciling conflicting EHR values. Indirectness and imprecision lower certainty to very low.

In a benchmark of 100 conversations, an allergy fact survived memory compression 0 to 1% of the time, compared with 97% with full memory. This suggests truncation can silently remove safety facts. Written rules may help reviewers see what a model never received, but no study shows that documentation catches such omissions before they reach patients.

In the MIMIC-IV study, 99.7% of admissions exceeded 512 tokens, and truncated BioClinicalBERT scored F1-micro 0.4645 against 0.5528 for TF-IDF. Llama 3.1 70B failed on all complex synthetic FHIR records within its nominal window, and an 8-patient EHR tool study found long, repetitive responses risked exceeding it. Rules may need to address complexity as well as length.

The only endorsement comes from the CHAI governance playbooks, which list documentation of truncation and summarization rules as a must. The supplied sources contain no federal or state requirement on input truncation or on reconciling conflicting EHR values. The practice therefore rests on voluntary governance guidance.

No study reports the payer mix, language, or literacy of included patients, and the one test did not report its setting. The largest hazard dataset uses MIMIC-IV admissions with a Taiwan DRG approximation. Whether truncation or reconciliation rules perform differently for Medicaid, safety-net, or limited English proficiency patients has not been tested.

research_gap: No study compares model outputs or clinical outcomes with and without documented truncation, summarization, or reconciliation rules, and none tests methods for resolving conflicting EHR values. The burden of maintaining such rules is also unmeasured. A prospective evaluation in live workflows that measures omitted safety facts, such as allergies, and whether reviewers detect those omissions would address this gap.
underserved_note: None of the tests or hazard studies reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients cannot assume that the reported gains in the completeness and correctness of summaries apply to their records.

bottom_line: Four studies, two in real deployments, suggest that pairing AI diagnostic output with additional imaging, laboratory testing, or clinician review may catch errors that AI alone misses, including 9 breast cancers found by supplementary ultrasound after both AI and radiologists missed them. None of the studies were randomized, two were offline reader studies, and none reported outcomes for underserved populations.

perspectives.view: All four tests point the same direction, but none is randomized. The two real-deployment studies are prospective or quasi-experimental, and the breast study rests on 9 cancers. The two reader studies compare radiologists plus AI against AI alone rather than AI plus added tests, which makes them indirect. Consistency supports low certainty, while imprecision and indirectness limit it.

Standalone AI-CAD missed 10 of 29 cancers (34%), and same-day ultrasound found 9 of them. In pulmonary embolism CT review, AI alone made 43 errors and the combined read made 7. Other hazard studies report a best F1 of 28.11% at 0.4% prevalence and 16.7% specificity for hip fractures, which suggests false positives are common when AI stands alone.

In a live bloodstream infection workflow, molecular-AI and phenotypic-AI recommendations agreed in 81.4% of episodes (κ=0.55). Resistance discordance predicted therapeutic discordance (aOR 7.70), and phenotypic confirmation was reported to ensure appropriate therapy in all cases. This suggests discordance itself may serve as a trigger for confirmatory testing. The two reader studies ran offline, so their workflow fidelity is unknown.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide frames this practice as optional, stating that results "can be combined" with imaging or laboratory tests for the specific cancer type. The guide offers no threshold for when combination is required, so health systems would need to set local rules for which AI outputs require confirmation.

The breast study screened 2,061 examinations with supplementary ultrasound and found 9 additional cancers, all in women with dense breasts. No study reported staffing time, added test costs, or the rate of extra biopsies from false-positive confirmatory tests. Administrators therefore have no cost data to judge the burden of routine confirmation at scale.

In each tested workflow a clinician or a confirmatory test stood between the AI output and the diagnosis, and biopsies confirmed the cancers that ultrasound flagged. No study measured patient experience, delays from added testing, or how results were explained to patients.

research_gap: No randomized or cluster-randomized trial compares AI-alone diagnosis with AI plus protocolized confirmatory imaging or laboratory testing on patient outcomes, added costs, false-positive workups, or time to treatment. Studies also do not define which AI outputs or discordance patterns should trigger confirmation.
underserved_note: No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The studies came from South Korea, China, and one unreported setting, so it is unknown whether access to supplementary imaging or laboratory confirmation is feasible or equally protective in under-resourced U.S. settings, where these added tests may be harder to obtain.

bottom_line: No study tests whether journal policies requiring authors to verify AI-generated text and references reduce fabricated or erroneous content in medical literature. Five descriptive and benchmark studies document the hazard, with problematic reference rates ranging from 2.9% to 69% depending on the system and design.

perspectives.view: No study compares manuscripts or journals with and without an author verification requirement, so certainty about the practice cannot be rated. The five hazard studies use descriptive or benchmark designs, and three rest on small samples (6 questions, 17 responses, 6 systems). They measure the size of the problem, not the effect of any remedy.

One study found 69% of 59 references fabricated and 5 major factual errors among 17 responses. A benchmark reported citation hallucination rates of 2.9% to 36.8% across six systems. These figures suggest unverified AI text may carry errors into literature clinicians rely on, though no study traces such errors to patient harm.

A benchmark that checked 8,050 references against PubMed found that misattribution made up 77% of errors and fabrication 0.6%. This suggests a check limited to whether a reference exists may miss most problems. Verification would need to confirm that each source supports its attached claim, and no study has measured the time or fidelity of that step.

One of the two endorsing sources addresses automated coverage denials and does not speak to manuscript verification. The other is a commentary urging manual checking with librarians or methodologists. The recommendation therefore rests on one directly relevant endorsement, and neither source describes how journals would enforce or audit author attestations.

None of the five studies involves patients or reports whether its test questions concerned Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether reference errors occur more often in research on these groups, where the literature base may be thinner, has not been examined.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare reference accuracy and factual error rates in published manuscripts before and after journals adopt AI verification requirements, or between journals with and without such policies. Audits should measure author compliance with attestations, distinguish fabrication from misattribution, and record the reviewer and author time that verification requires.
underserved_note: No study tests the practice, and none of the hazard studies included or reported on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence cannot show whether verification policies would protect the literature that informs care for these groups.

bottom_line: Nine sources endorse telling patients, physicians, and staff that AI output can be inaccurate or incomplete, but the single trial of a warning found no change in advice-taking among 186 medical students (15.3% vs 15.9%; OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.46-2.59). Forty-one studies document errors and omissions in AI answers, so the hazard is established while the effect of disclosure on user behavior remains largely untested.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial tests the practice. Among 186 fourth-year medical students in a simulated task, diagnostic changes after AI advice were 15.3% without and 15.9% with a 'ChatGPT can make mistakes' warning (OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.46-2.59). The population, setting, and outcome are indirect, and the interval is wide, so certainty is very low.

Across 888 answers to patient questions, problematic responses ranged from 21.6% to 43.2% and unsafe responses from 5% to 13%. In one survey, predicted delay in care rose from 11.6% to 30.5% with high trust and frequent use. A generic warning did not change advice-taking in the one trial, so it may not catch errors by itself.

Disclaimers already appear in many outputs, and one study found disclaimer rates of 88% to 100% across three models. In the one trial, a one-line warning shown during a diagnostic task did not change how often students revised diagnoses. This suggests a fixed label may be passed over in workflow, and the format and timing of disclosure deserve testing.

The trial enrolled medical students and did not report country. Hazard studies in Chinese-language settings found that 12.5% of answers deviated from guidelines and that high trust with frequent use was associated with higher predicted delay in care among 2,460 adults. No test of disclosure included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users.

In one study, 73.1% of parents trusted ChatGPT medical information while over a quarter of responses had expert-identified inaccuracies. Community respondents rated chatbot quality similar to or better than physicians even when answers omitted when to consult a professional in 27.2% to 40.8% of cases. No study tested whether disclosure helps patients detect these gaps.

research_gap: No study has tested disclosure of AI limitations among patients or practicing clinicians in a real deployment. Trials should compare generic warnings with specific, in-context statements of known limitations and with user training, and should measure verification behavior, delayed care, and errors that reach patients rather than advice-taking in a simulated task.
underserved_note: The only test of the practice enrolled fourth-year medical students in a simulated setting and included no Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy participants. Three hazard studies drew on non-English-speaking populations, and one linked high trust to predicted delay in care, so the groups that may rely most on chatbot advice are the least represented in tests of whether disclosure changes behavior.

bottom_line: Most tests of automated output checks ran offline or in simulation, where the checks caught fabricated entities and implausible values at reported detection rates between 72% and 100%. Two small real-deployment reports and one mixed result on harmful errors suggest the checks reduce errors but do not remove them when no human reviews the output.

perspectives.view: In a 25-case ablation, 166 deterministic rules eliminated all 6 fabrication failures, and red-flag routing cut vignette safety violations from 8/56 to 0/56. An LLM-judge filter left harmful errors nearly unchanged for o3 (4.3% to 3.9%). A drug-name dictionary check missed some drug error categories because of dictionary limits and misspellings.

Performance varied by output type. Deterministic SCORE2 recalculation raised agreement from κw 0.15-0.61 to 0.85-0.90, and rule-based verification raised accuracy from 64.9% to 74.8%. An image screener flagged synthetic CT hallucinations at specificity 0.78 to 0.98 depending on a distance parameter, which suggests thresholds may need local tuning before use.

Portuguese vignettes and Korean clinical records showed gains in agreement and accuracy after checks, and emergency vignettes from Japan showed fewer safety violations. A fourth study used Japanese safety reports translated to English. None enrolled Medicaid, safety-net, low-literacy, or US limited English proficiency patients, so performance for those groups is unknown.

CHAI states that teams should add a human to the workflow or else implement additional quality control processes. FUTURE-AI recommends mechanisms to detect implausible outputs without tying this to the absence of human review. Neither source sets performance thresholds, and no supplied study evaluates checks against a regulatory standard.

One deployment report described a 30% reduction in report creation time with automated verification. A postprocessing filter cut order set suggestions by 29% while keeping 92% of useful ones, and an offline regeneration step reduced signal loss from 15.55% to 8.48% without extra LLM calls. Staffing and rule-maintenance costs were not reported.

The LLM-judge filter replaced flagged answers with a deferral to a provider, which gives patients a route to a human. Harmful errors still appeared in 3.9% to 7.6% of simulated responses after filtering, so patients may need to be told that automated checks lower risk but do not remove it.

research_gap: No randomized or controlled prospective study compares deployed AI with and without automated checks on patient outcomes. Future work should measure errors that reach patients, false alarm burden on staff, and rule maintenance costs in live deployments, including settings that serve Medicaid and limited English proficiency patients.
underserved_note: Two tests used Portuguese vignettes or Korean clinical records, one used emergency vignettes from Japan, and one used Japanese safety reports translated to English, which offers limited evidence that checks work outside US English-language data. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, low-literacy, or US limited English proficiency patient populations, so health systems serving those groups cannot assume the reported detection rates will hold and may need to validate checks locally.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether showing users the active operating point or configuration of an AI device, with instructions on when to choose alternatives, reduces misinterpretation of outputs. The recommendation currently rests on a single FDA draft guidance that asks developers to explain how users can tell which operating point the device is using.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The link between display of the operating point and fewer interpretation errors remains a plausible assumption that no supplied study has measured.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions states that, when operating points are configurable, a submission should describe how end users can discern the operating point currently in use. Draft guidance is nonbinding, and the text addresses discernibility of the active setting more directly than instructions for selecting alternatives.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare clinician interpretation accuracy, and downstream decisions, when a configurable AI device does or does not display its active threshold and guidance on alternative settings. Such studies should also first establish how often users misread outputs because they do not know the active configuration, since no supplied study documents the frequency of this hazard.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups have no information on whether configuration displays are understood by their staff or affect outcomes for their patients, and any displays should be checked for clarity in those settings.

bottom_line: Seventy-one studies apply reference-standard evaluation to AI outputs and find accuracy that varies widely by task and model, and in several studies automated and expert methods disagreed on what counts as an error. No study tests whether evaluation before deployment reduces patient harm or whether predefined organizational risk tolerances change deployment decisions.

perspectives.view: Among the summarized tests, three are level 2 prospective real-deployment comparisons, one is a level 3 real-deployment pre-post study without a comparator, and the rest are offline level 4 designs. Precision was 0.33 for trial matching, while field accuracy for RCT summaries ranged from 85.4% to 97.9%. No study compares evaluated with unevaluated deployment, so certainty is very low.

Expert review flagged five potentially dangerous chatbot responses in one study and placed 4.2% of responses in the lowest safety category in another. Hazard studies report harmful plans in 16% of infectious disease cases and high harm risk in 26% of drug answers. Evaluation can detect errors, but no study shows it stopped errors from reaching patients.

Evaluation methods did not always agree. Automated completeness correlated with expert usability at rho ≈ 0.393, and relevance metrics correlated weakly or negatively with correctness. An automated checking tool found 1 error in 2,067 checks while raters found soft errors in 32% of briefs. A judge LLM reached AC1=0.80 with experts. Layered methods may capture different error types.

Reference standards require expert labor. One team annotated 50 of 4,762 notes as ground truth, which suggests evaluation on samples may be feasible. Another reached 93.6% agreement only on the fourth iteration after early scores as low as 0.26, which implies repeated evaluation cycles and staff time before deployment.

Three tests involved non-English or translation settings, including layered evaluation of translated discharge instructions, extraction from Chinese records, and scoring of German patient records. One study extracted housing instability from notes of pregnant women. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so the performance of evaluation methods in those groups is unknown.

NIST AI 600-1 advises comparing output with ground truth using several methods, and CHAI playbooks tie project pathways to risk category. No supplied study sets or tests a predefined organizational risk tolerance, so the threshold component of this recommendation rests on framework consensus rather than empirical tests.

In one study otolaryngologists rated ChatGPT empathy at 4.28 of 5 but accuracy at 3.76 and flagged five responses as potentially dangerous. Patients may trust fluent answers that contain errors, which suggests evaluations should score accuracy and safety separately from tone.

research_gap: No study compares AI deployments that underwent benchmarked, multi-method evaluation against predefined risk thresholds with deployments that did not, using patient harm or error interception as outcomes. Studies are also needed that validate automated and LLM-as-judge methods against clinician review across tasks, that report how organizations set risk tolerances, and that measure the staff time and cost of building reference standards.
underserved_note: Three tests included non-English or limited English proficiency settings (translated discharge instructions, Chinese eCRF extraction, German patient records), and one assessed housing instability in notes from pregnant women. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations, so health systems serving those patients cannot assume that reference standards or error rates from these studies transfer and may need evaluation samples drawn from their own populations.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether developer documentation of intended workflow, workflow phase, interface sequence, and output incorporation reduces misuse or ignored outputs at deploying sites. The recommendation currently rests on one FDA draft guidance and one safety-case commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Both endorsements are expert opinion, one in draft regulatory guidance and one in a commentary. Under GRADE conventions, no certainty rating can be assigned to the effect of workflow documentation on misuse or ignored outputs.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions states that the device description should cover all functions across connected applications for patients, caregivers, and providers and explain how they connect. Because the guidance is a draft, it signals agency expectations for marketing submissions but does not yet carry final status.

A deployment safety case for AI-assisted prostate cancer diagnosis names mapping the intended clinical workflow as the first step of its method. This places workflow documentation at the start of hazard analysis, but the commentary does not report whether the step caught errors before they reached patients.

research_gap: Studies should compare sites that receive structured developer workflow documentation with sites that do not, and measure off-label workflow use, rates of ignored or overridden outputs, and downstream patient harm. Researchers should also study documentation fidelity and the effort required for sites to map vendor workflows onto local practice.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net sites often run workflows that differ from those at developer partner sites, and whether workflow documentation helps them adapt tools safely remains unknown.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether an explicit error or unavailable indication keeps clinicians from reading a missing or invalid AI result as normal, and no study documents how often that misreading occurs. The recommendation currently rests on an FDA draft guidance and the CHAI assurance guide, both of which describe the practice rather than evaluate it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Both endorsements are descriptive examples within guidance documents. Under GRADE conventions no certainty rating can be assigned, and the effect on clinician interpretation or patient outcomes remains unmeasured.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions gives an example in which an error message appears when inputs fail requirements. This suggests reviewers may expect manufacturers to describe such behavior in submissions. The guidance is a draft and uses the language of illustration, so it does not by itself establish a binding requirement for deployers.

The CHAI guide lists an incomplete or absent risk score as a failure mode that delays clinician review and patient communication, with an unavailable value shown. This framework identifies the failure pathway, but no supplied data show whether the indication shortens that delay or prevents a missing score from being read as low risk.

research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how often clinicians misread blank, stale, or invalid AI outputs as normal findings, and that compare explicit error or unavailable displays against current interfaces for detection rates, time to clinician follow-up, and downstream patient events.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether error indications work equally well in understaffed settings, or for patient-facing tools used by people with limited English or literacy, is unknown.

bottom_line: Six studies found that giving AI tools more complete patient data improved output quality, including one randomized trial in which fuller discharge-summary inputs raised coding F-scores from 0.786 to 0.798. No study tested cross-system retrieval as a deployment safeguard or measured patient outcomes, so the evidence supports the direction of the practice more than its specific form.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial in real deployment showed F-score gains of about 0.01 to 0.015 with full-section inputs. The other five studies are offline replays or benchmarks that rely on rater scores, accuracy, or recall. All six point in the same direction, but indirectness and surrogate outcomes lower certainty to low.

In a live deployment, withheld data lowered AUROC, and restoring the data raised it from 0.896 to 0.918. One tool recommended genetic testing a patient had already completed. In a benchmark, recall of inserted interpretation errors rose from 2.67% to 43.33% when the panoramic radiographs were provided. None of these studies measured harm that reached patients.

Adding historical EHR data to ambient notes raised composite quality from 80.1 to 94.8. Multi-source inputs also improved pharmacist-rated medication logs. Two benchmarks traced missing note content to inter-hospital transfers, which suggests retrieval across systems may matter. No study measured retrieval burden, latency, or fidelity within clinical workflow.

The only test with a flagged population was a non-English offline replay of 80 medication logs from China. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients. Patients whose care is split across unaffiliated systems may have more fragmented records, and no study examined whether retrieval closes that gap for them.
