Adding personal health record context improved the rated helpfulness of answers to 2,257 queries (p < 0.001). This suggests patients may receive more relevant answers when their own data are used. No study asked patients about consent to cross-system retrieval, or whether fuller data changed their trust or their access to a clinician.

research_gap: No study compared deployments with and without cross-system retrieval. None measured how often retrieval fills missing fields in routine practice, and none tracked clinical errors or patient outcomes. A pragmatic trial at sites with high inter-hospital transfer rates would test the practice directly if it reported retrieval completeness, staff workload, and downstream errors.
underserved_note: One test, the pharmacist-rated medication-log study, took place in a non-English setting in China. No test included Medicaid or safety-net patients, patients with limited English proficiency in English-dominant health systems, or low-literacy populations. Systems serving these groups have no direct evidence that the reported gains apply to their records or patients.

bottom_line: Four guidance and framework documents endorse automatic drift and anomaly notifications to responsible staff, but no supplied study tests whether such notifications lead to earlier detection or fewer patient harms. Health systems adopting this practice would be acting on expert consensus and regulatory examples rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied evidence tests automatic drift or anomaly notifications, and no study documents how often unnoticed degradation occurs. The four endorsements come from two guidelines, one assurance framework, and one commentary. Under GRADE conventions, consensus statements do not raise certainty, so the effect of this practice on detection time or patient outcomes remains unmeasured.

The FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software describes an example in which performance is calculated automatically every 6 months and an e-mail goes to the site administrator and sponsor when results fall outside the expected range. This draft language describes a practice without mandating it. CHAI and FUTURE-AI frame notification as a should-level expectation.

The obesity-prediction commentary warns that alerts without an explicit alert budget, batched summaries, and threshold-based suppression may erode clinician trust. That concern concerns patient-level alerts, but the same design question applies to drift notifications sent to administrators. No supplied study measures notification burden, response rates, or fidelity in real operational settings.

The FDA example suggests a low-frequency design, with checks every 6 months and a single e-mail, which would place modest demands on staff. A 6-month interval may miss faster drift, however. No supplied evidence reports the cost, staffing, or response workflow needed to act on notifications once they arrive.

research_gap: Studies should compare deployments with and without automatic drift and anomaly notifications and measure time from performance change to detection, the share of alerts that prompt action, false-alarm rates, and downstream patient outcomes. They should also examine how monitoring frequency and alert thresholds affect alert fatigue among the staff who receive them.
underserved_note: No study tests this practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Drift that affects only a subgroup may not trigger notifications built on aggregate performance, and without subgroup-level evidence health systems cannot know whether these alerts would detect degradation concentrated in underserved patients.

bottom_line: Five offline or benchmark studies suggest that postprocessing checks can flag failed or implausible segmentation and dosimetry outputs, but none measured whether blocking those outputs changed clinician decisions or patient outcomes. Support for the practice comes from one consensus guideline and from technical performance data in imaging and radiotherapy.

perspectives.view: All five tests of the practice were offline or benchmark evaluations. Samples ranged from 5 to 500 cases, and outcomes were limited to detection accuracy or risk scores. The results point in the same direction, but indirectness, small samples, and the absence of clinical endpoints lower certainty to very low.

In an English retinal clinic replay, 18 of 37 (48.6%) AI errors not made in real-world care involved non-anatomical fluid segmentations, which shows the failure mode exists. A failure mode analysis reported that an automated check lowered the risk priority number from 186.2 to 35.3. A multinational benchmark detected segmentation failures with sensitivity 1.00.

No study placed a check inside a live workflow, so alert burden and clinician response remain unmeasured. The French cohort reported recall 0.75 and precision 0.88, which implies that about one in four failures would pass and some valid outputs would be flagged. Balanced accuracy fell from 0.94 internally to 0.88 externally, which suggests performance may drop at new sites.

No test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and two tests did not report a country. Only the hazard study described its population, which was older adults. No study examined whether detection thresholds hold across different scanners or across patient groups at under-resourced sites.

research_gap: No study has embedded output checks in a deployed clinical system. Such studies should measure how often implausible outputs are blocked, how often valid outputs are wrongly rejected, and whether clinician decisions and patient outcomes change. Tests outside imaging and radiotherapy, and tests in safety-net settings, are also needed.
underserved_note: None of the five tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore cannot show whether these checks perform equally well for those patients or at sites with older equipment and different case mixes.

bottom_line: Three offline studies, two of which appear to report the same UK dementia cohort, suggest that grouping model outputs into risk categories can keep or improve statistical performance and track outcomes. No study tested whether clinicians interpret or act on categories better than on raw probabilities, which is the hazard this recommendation targets.

perspectives.view: All three studies are offline or automated benchmarks at evidence levels 4 and 5. The two UK reports share 63 participants and 32,896 person-days, so they likely count as one dataset. The outcomes are model metrics, not clinician judgment or patient outcomes. Indirectness and imprecision support a very low certainty rating.

In the Korean stroke cohort (n=796), four large vessel occlusion categories were associated with infarct volume and 3-month mRS. This suggests the categories carry prognostic signal. No study measured missed escalations, delayed treatment, or harm from patients placed just below a cutoff, so the effect on errors reaching patients is unknown.

Traffic-light categories raised accuracy from 71.36 to 78.87 and specificity from 75.28 to 90.33 against binary classification. These gains come from how the output is thresholded, not from observed use in a workflow. No study examined alert burden, how cutoffs were set with clinicians, or whether staff followed tiered next steps.

The UK studies enrolled people living with dementia, a population of older adults with disability. No study reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups. The studies also did not examine whether fixed cutoffs perform differently across subgroups.

research_gap: No study randomized or compared clinicians viewing risk categories with clinicians viewing raw probabilities to measure risk judgment, action rates, or patient outcomes. Deployers also lack tests of how cutoff placement and linked next-step pathways affect missed cases and overtreatment in live care.
underserved_note: The tests included older adults and people with disability through a UK dementia cohort. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Evidence on whether category labels help these patients and their clinicians is therefore absent, and cutoffs set in other populations may not transfer.

bottom_line: Nine distinct studies suggest that surfacing AI outputs and alerts inside the workflow at the point of decision may increase clinician action and shorten response times, though one trial found that adding predictive alerts to threshold alerts did not improve glucose control. Certainty is low because most studies are nonrandomized, outcomes are mostly process measures, and no study compares in-interface delivery with labeling alone.

perspectives.view: Two of the ten records appear to report the same 596-encounter suicide-screening trial, so the base is nine studies. In that trial, screening rose from 4% to 42% with interruptive alerts. The glucose trial found a 3.9% gain for threshold alerts and a -0.8% difference for predictive alerts. The remaining studies are nonrandomized, which supports a low rating.

Patient-level outcomes are sparse. Arrests without return of circulation fell from 1.4 to 0.4 per 1000 patient days after a display launched, and nephrotoxin discontinuation rose from 25% to 54%. Both studies lack comparators, so secular trends may explain part of the change. Electronic notification sped oxygen for pneumothorax by 143.8 minutes but did not speed procedures.

PACS-integrated alerts cut median pneumothorax reporting time from 186 to 100 minutes, and smartphone notification shortened stroke and hemorrhage workflows by 15 to 57 minutes. Hazard studies found 18.6% acknowledgment of passive alerts, 3% use of a tool with a hard-to-find launch button, and 37% report review. These show the problem exists but do not test the fix.

No study reports enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and several do not report the country. Interface effects measured among clinicians at the sites studied may not carry over to settings with different staffing, EHR configurations, or patient mixes.

FDA draft guidance states that information should be communicated at the time it is needed, and FUTURE-AI lists user warnings among possible mitigations. Neither source specifies interruptive or passive formats. The suicide-screening trial compared formats at the same point in the workflow, which suggests that interface documentation may need to address display format as well as timing.

The studies do not report cost, alert fatigue, or clinician time spent responding to alerts. In the glucose trial, predictive alerts added no benefit beyond threshold alerts, which suggests that more alerts do not always yield more gain. Systems considering interruptive designs have no data here on the workload those designs impose.

In a vignette study of 203 nephrologists, displayed risk shifted follow-up recommendations downward for low risk and upward for high risk. This suggests that what appears on screen can change the care patients receive. No study measured patient understanding, patient trust, or patients' ability to reach a clinician about an AI-driven decision.

research_gap: No study directly compares delivering AI outputs and safety information in the interface at the point of decision with delivering them only in labeling or documentation. Trials that vary timing and format separately, measure patient outcomes alongside alert burden and override rates, and report results for underserved populations would address the main gaps.
underserved_note: None of the studies reports including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and several do not report the setting. The findings therefore cannot show whether in-workflow delivery works the same way, or carries the same burden, in the settings where these patients receive care.

bottom_line: Structured or refined prompts improved accuracy, guideline adherence, or clinician acceptance in most of the 52 tests, and one deployment study tracked iterative, versioned prompt changes, but no study tested governance review of templates. Several studies found that structured prompts added hallucinations, lowered accuracy on some tasks, or helped some models and not others, so templates may need validation for each task and model.

perspectives.view: One randomized trial (n=60) and three real-deployment before-after or quasi-experimental studies support refined prompts, and a fourth deployment study had mixed results. Most other tests are simulations comparing structured with simple prompts, which is indirect to governance-reviewed templates. The endorsing framework quote addresses fine-tuning data ratios, and the other two endorsements are education commentaries.

Structured prompts cut major hallucinations in notes from 4 to 1 and major omissions from 24 to 10. In stroke vignettes, unsafe recommendations fell from 16.7% to 0%. One study found that structured prompts introduced more hallucinations and bias, and another found prompt engineering counterproductive for some tasks. Templates may therefore need safety review for each task.

After iterative, versioned prompt changes, physician acceptance of drafted replies rose from 62% to 84%. Draft token retention also increased across refinement phases. A second deployment found that negative sentiment fell from 12.0% to 8.2% while draft usage decreased (beta -0.10). Better-rated drafts may not translate into more use.

A language-simplification prompt lowered accuracy for Kimi from 70.0% to 48.8% and for DouBao from 57.5% to 7.5%. In texts for older and low-literacy readers, DISCERN scores differed by prompt for all 6 models. Plain-language templates may trade accuracy for readability. Positive tests in China involved general and stroke patients, not US safety-net groups.

No study reported the staff time or cost of building, reviewing, or maintaining a template library. Template gains varied by model. Role-play templates helped GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 but not Gemini or Claude, and GPT-3.5 error stayed at 0.42 after refinement. A template may need revalidation whenever the underlying model changes.

In the one randomized trial, patients who used a structured question outline reached knowledge scores of 95.3, close to 95.6 with a physician and above 82.1 with free use. In a hazard study, framing a prompt as coming from a patient produced under-triage in 41.7% of responses, compared with 12.5% for specialist framing.

research_gap: No study compared a governance-reviewed, versioned template library with ad hoc prompting on patient outcomes, error rates reaching patients, or clinician workload in routine care. No study measured how template performance changes after model updates, or the cost of maintaining templates across sites.
underserved_note: Six tests of the practice were conducted in China or Germany, four of which were tagged as using non-English data, and one included older stroke survivors. No test of the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, US limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Hazard studies suggest that simplification prompts can reduce accuracy, so templates aimed at these groups would need separate validation.

bottom_line: Sixteen studies tested input detectors, and all reported that flagging missing, low-quality, or out-of-distribution inputs improved detection of unreliable outputs or downstream model accuracy, but every test ran offline, in simulation, or on benchmarks. No study measured whether detectors change clinical decisions or patient outcomes in live care.

perspectives.view: All 16 tests are level 4 or 5 designs run offline or on benchmarks. They measure detector AUROC or downstream accuracy rather than patient outcomes. Results point in one direction, though one study found benefit inconsistent across detectors and age subgroups. Certainty is very low because of indirectness and risk of bias.

In a Belgian failure-mode analysis, a case-specific report flagging out-of-training-distribution inputs lowered the lack-of-detectability score for bad predictions from 8.17 to 3.51. About 3% residual risk remained that staff overlook the report. Correct predictions appeared in all reliability categories in one external validation, so flags may also withhold usable outputs.

On uncurated glioma images, rejecting uninformative regions raised accuracy from 72.59% to 90.10%. Fundus quality filtering separated drusen sensitivity of 0.853 in good images from 0.494 in poor images. These studies suggest filters may work on real image streams, but none measured clinician response to flags or workflow burden in deployment.

No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. In a safety-net, rural deployment in India, an AI gradability check had 8% specificity and labeled 21 (42%) human-ungradable cataract eyes as gradable. This hazard study suggests detectors may fail where image quality is poorest.

One Mahalanobis-distance detector ran in seconds on a CPU with 92% AUROC for failed segmentations, which suggests low computing cost. A simulation estimated that runtime verifiers cut expected per-patient cost by upwards of 40% in polyp segmentation. No study reported staffing or review time needed to handle flagged cases.

Hazard studies show that missing inputs degraded performance across 20,334 silently deployed laboratory models and that 8 of 1,570 CTA cases produced errors from poor-quality images. No test examined whether patients learn that an input was flagged or whether a flag sends their case to a clinician.

research_gap: No study deployed an input detector in live care with a comparison group, so its effect on clinician decisions, missed diagnoses, and patient harm is unknown. Prospective or stepped-wedge studies should measure flag rates, clinician handling of flagged cases, false-flag burden, and patient outcomes, including in settings with frequent missing data or poor image quality.
underserved_note: None of the 16 tests included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The only safety-net data come from a hazard study in rural India, where an AI gradability check classified 42% of human-ungradable cataract eyes as gradable. Health systems serving these groups should not assume that benchmark detector performance will transfer to their patients.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this map tests whether real-time point-of-care nudges built on ambient scribe outputs and EHR data close documentation gaps. The only support is one guidance report describing a single health system's request for such nudges after it observed risk profile degradation in scribe-assisted visits.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies measuring the hazard. The single endorsing source describes one system's request, which is an observation rather than an evaluation. Under GRADE conventions, no certainty rating can be assigned because no comparison of nudged and unnudged documentation exists.

The guidance reports that Ochsner Health asked its vendor for real-time nudges on HCC documentation after noticing risk profile degradation in visits using the ambient scribe. The report does not state whether the nudges were built, what they cost, how often they fired, or whether risk scores recovered, so adopters cannot yet estimate return or clinician burden.

research_gap: Health systems need controlled or stepped-wedge evaluations that compare scribe-assisted visits with and without point-of-care nudges, measuring diagnosis capture, coding accuracy, false-positive prompt rates, clinician time and alert fatigue, and whether added diagnoses are clinically supported rather than driven by payment incentives. Studies should first quantify how often ambient scribe notes omit diagnoses relative to clinician-authored notes.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether scribe omissions or nudge performance differ for patients with non-English or interpreter-mediated visits remains unknown, and systems serving these patients should not assume the Ochsner experience applies to them.

bottom_line: Two uncontrolled before-after studies suggest that automated routing may shorten result turnaround and usually delivers images and AI outputs between sites, but transmission still failed for 2 of 22 referred patients in one study. The evidence favors automation paired with checks for failed transfers, and certainty is very low.

perspectives.view: Two before-after studies without comparators test the practice. One reports shorter urine culture turnaround after automatic result release but does not quantify the added effect. The other reports successful CT transfer for 90.9% (20/22) of patients. Risk of bias, indirectness, and imprecision each lower certainty, which leaves it at very low.

Hazard studies show that data flows fail in real deployments. A randomized trial recorded 3 AI integration failures from a software error, and another deployment missed patients whose admitting service was misclassified. These studies show that the problem exists, not that automation prevents it. The China study suggests that automated transfer still needs a way to detect failed uploads.

The Canadian study suggests that sending results directly into the chart may reduce delay beyond process changes alone. In a separate deployment, routing missed patients because eligibility depended on one admitting service, and the team widened eligibility in November 2022. Automated routing depends on the accuracy of the upstream fields it reads.

Neither study that tests the practice reports cost, staff time, or interface maintenance effort. The China deployment covered 1291 patients and still relied on a manual fallback, physical films, when PACS transfer failed. Health systems adopting automated routing may need to budget for failure alerts and a staffed backup path.

When automated transfer failed in the China study, two patients had to carry physical CT films to the tertiary hospital. This finding suggests that failed data flows can shift work and delay onto patients. Patients may be better served when a staff member confirms that results arrived and patients know whom to contact when they do not.

research_gap: No study compares automated routing with manual routing using a concurrent control group, and none reports how often wrong studies or wrong patients reach a model. Future studies could measure misrouting, undelivered results, and time to result delivery across several sites and report the size of each effect.
underserved_note: Neither study that tests the practice reports enrolling or analyzing Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The evidence therefore does not show whether automated routing performs as well in safety-net settings, where interface resources and record linkage may differ.

bottom_line: Five randomized trials in real deployments suggest that risk-targeted outreach may reduce no-shows, hospitalizations, and time to palliative care consultation, though two of those trials found null or mixed results. Only one trial paired risk scores with an explicit eligibility check, and no trial reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations.

perspectives.view: Five randomized trials tested risk-targeted outreach in real deployments, and three supported it, including a 26.2% no-show reduction among highest-risk patients. The Swiss trial found 21.9% versus 22.0%, and the kidney trial found mixed outcomes. Outcomes differ across trials, and only one trial added specialist-confirmed eligibility, so inconsistency and indirectness lower certainty to moderate.

In a cluster trial, risk-flagged enrollment was associated with a hospitalization RR of 0.70 (0.51-0.96). A matched historical comparison reported AKI falling from 11.3% to 8.8% and readmission from 12% to 8.9%. A pre-post study reported 18% fewer monthly ED visits, but it had no control group, so secular trends may explain part of that change.

Delivery fidelity appears to limit effects. In the Swiss trial, 42.3% of targeted patients were not reached by phone, and in the kidney trial 71% of flagged patients were screened. An automated IVR trial of 59,994 patients reported a 1.7-point lower no-show rate, and the effect held over 6 months in 244,000 patients.

Only the kidney trial reported a named underserved group, rural patients. No trial reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Phone outreach reached 57.7% of targeted patients in one trial, which suggests that patients without reliable phone access may be missed when outreach is routed by risk score.

The IVR trial found its largest effect in the highest-risk quartile, which suggests that focusing contact on top-risk patients may stretch limited staff further. A simulation found that model-based selection sent remote monitoring equipment to more high-risk patients than random allocation, but it reported no numbers. No study reported cost or staffing effort.

The kidney trial found no gain in patient empowerment, self-efficacy, or self-care choice, although preference documentation rose (IRR 1.34). Palliative care consultation orders came sooner when risk-based identification was paired with specialist-confirmed eligibility, at 42.8 versus 63.9 days. These results suggest that faster routing may not change how patients experience their care.

research_gap: No trial compared routing by risk score plus eligibility criteria against eligibility criteria alone, and none reported cost, staff time, or effects in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The two simulation studies, including the Malawi ART retention model (epmc:PPR1271675), would need testing in real deployments before they could inform practice.
underserved_note: Only one trial reported a named underserved group (rural patients in the kidney trial), and no test reported inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume the reported reductions will carry over, especially where phone-based outreach reaches fewer patients.

bottom_line: Studies of threshold adjustment suggest that cutoffs chosen with response capacity in mind can reduce alert volume without a clear loss of detection, but only one retrospective study tested clinician involvement directly. Certainty is low because most evidence is simulated and no study compared clinician-selected cutoffs with default cutoffs on patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Of 15 studies, one cluster RCT (n=9887) reported a 12% decrease in administered high-risk drug combinations, and two prospective comparisons reported lower alert volume after threshold adjustment. No study compared clinician-selected cutoffs with default cutoffs, and most were simulated. Certainty is therefore low because of indirectness and study design.

Raising cutoffs lowers alert volume but can miss patients. In one simulation, a cutoff of 4 raised estimated sepsis deaths from 9 to 18 cases. In another model, lowering the threshold to 0.33 raised sensitivity from 38.5% to 51.3%, and false positives rose from 119 to 207. These trade-offs suggest that teams need explicit agreement on acceptable misses.

Only one study, from Singapore, set a threshold with physicians and radiologists. In a retrospective replay, that threshold retained 93.19% sensitivity and 35.85% operational improvement. Silent alert simulations across four models supported capacity-aligned thresholds but predicted postimplementation performance poorly. A Korean ward study found that a cutoff of 94 rather than 91 better discriminated physician intervention, which suggests cutoffs may need revision after go-live.

In a screening program of 145,848 patients, adjusting the operating point cut alerts from 4.4% to 2.3%, with no difference in enrolment rate among reviewed alerts. In Hungarian mammography, moving the threshold to match workload capacity reduced flagged cases from 10.6–11.2% to 7.4%, while additional cancer detection stayed at 0.7 per 1,000. One trial of alert follow-up described staff burden as high.

Two tests included rural populations, in Hungary and China. One obstetric replay had a racial and ethnic minority focus, and in that study a 0.2 threshold missed fewer at-risk patients than 0.3. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups, so it is unknown whether capacity-driven cutoffs shift missed cases toward these patients.

research_gap: No study randomized or prospectively compared cutoffs selected with clinician input and capacity data against statistically derived or vendor-default cutoffs in live deployment. None measured missed high-risk patients, patient outcomes, and staff workload together over time.
underserved_note: Three tests included rural populations or had a racial and ethnic minority focus. None included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups should not assume that cutoffs tuned elsewhere will balance missed patients and alert burden the same way for their patients.

bottom_line: Three studies tested integration, and each found lower burden or higher use when the AI tool sat inside the EHR, PACS, or main monitor, but none had a concurrent comparator in routine practice. Ten hazard studies consistently link separate interfaces to low use, which suggests the problem is real while the size of any benefit from integration remains uncertain.

perspectives.view: Two pre-post studies without concurrent comparators and one simulation with 23 clinicians test the practice. Caries risk assessment completion rose from under 5% to a peak of 89% after EHR integration, and 93.3% (14/15) of clinicians reported that PACS-integrated AI did not interfere with practice. Risk of bias, small samples, and indirectness lower certainty to very low.

In a simulation, a secondary monitor raised NASA-TLX physical demand by 17.33 points and frustration by 14.33 points compared with an overlay on the main surgical monitor. Strain was reported by 60% versus 6.7%. Hazard studies name separate EHR tabs and external platforms as barriers, and 67% of staff rarely or never used one unintegrated tool.

None of the three tests measured diagnostic errors, missed findings, or patient harm. With a separate referral platform, only 28% of referral records were complete and 44.4% of feedback was reviewed. This suggests information may be lost at handoffs, but no study shows that integration closes that gap.

No test reported enrolling Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. An endorsing framework describes EHR integration at an FQHC network, but that account does not measure outcomes. Whether integration changes use or burden for clinicians serving these patients has not been tested.

No study reported integration cost, build time, vendor dependence, or staffing needs. The caries risk assessment gains appeared over roughly 20 months after the July 2022 launch, which may indicate that benefits accrue slowly. One operational guide proposes a quick standalone front end for pilots before EHR integration, and no study has tested that tradeoff.

research_gap: No study compares the same AI tool delivered inside versus outside the EHR or PACS with a concurrent control. Stepped-wedge or cluster designs that measure use, clinician time and workload, errors, patient outcomes, and integration cost would address this, and they should include safety-net settings.
underserved_note: None of the three tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The settings were Chinese hospitals, a US dental program, and a Canadian surgical simulation. The findings may not transfer to under-resourced sites, where EHR build capacity and vendor support can differ.

bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether a pre-deployment review of AI-triggered actions and follow-up capacity prevents inequitable effects, and no supplied study documents the hazard. Four sources endorse the practice, one framework and three commentaries, so adoption rests on expert judgment rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. The four endorsements come from a framework and three commentaries, which GRADE treats as expert opinion. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence until a comparative study measures equity outcomes with and without the assessment.

The HEAAL framework reports that a workflow double-booking patients predicted to miss appointments was judged to worsen inequities, and one commentary calls for mapping exclusion risks in low-resource maternal and child health settings. These statements describe a concern, but no supplied study measures who was harmed or whether a prior assessment would have changed the result.

One commentary recommends that risk thresholds be co-designed to match service capacity and reviewed as capacity changes, and that evaluation track workload and referral churn. No supplied study reports the staff time, cost, or feasibility of conducting such capacity reviews before deployment, so resource planning has no empirical benchmark.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare deployments with and without a structured pre-deployment review of triggered actions and follow-up capacity, measuring outcomes such as missed follow-up, appointment access, and referral completion by payer, language, and literacy group. A first step would be observational documentation of how often prediction-triggered workflows, such as double-booking or referrals without staffed follow-up, produce differential access.
underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. The endorsements focus on these groups conceptually, yet health systems serving them have no outcome data showing whether the assessment reduces harm.

bottom_line: Two small studies suggest that pre-go-live simulation may help deployers set alert thresholds, surface workflow problems, and identify training needs. One of them found that silent simulation did not predict how alerts performed once clinicians interacted with them, and no study measured patient harm or alert fatigue after go-live.

perspectives.view: The evidence comprises one descriptive study of 4 predictive models and one qualitative study of 17 nurses. Neither study had a comparison group or measured patient outcomes. The silent-mode study tests a related but different practice, since alerts were not shown to clinicians, which adds indirectness. Certainty is very low.

Six simulation sessions with 17 nurses yielded four debriefing themes that led to CDS changes before go-live, which suggests that rehearsal can catch some design problems before they reach patients. The silent simulation study found limited ability to predict post-implementation performance, so errors that arise from human-alert interaction may still appear only in live care.

Silent simulations helped teams choose thresholds that matched clinical capacity and workflows in a real deployment. Silent mode does not capture how clinicians respond to alerts, and that gap may explain why it predicted post-implementation performance poorly. Simulation sessions with nurses produced workflow and training inputs, which suggests the two approaches answer different questions.

The studies report no data on staff time, cost, or disruption from simulation periods. One framework describes a mandatory two-week shadowing period at each hospital, but no study measured what that period required or whether its length was sufficient. Threshold selection aligned with clinical capacity may help with staffing planning, though the studies did not measure this.

Neither study reported the patient population, payer mix, or setting type. The 17 nurses in the simulation study may not reflect staff in safety-net hospitals, and no study examined whether simulated workflows accounted for patients with limited English proficiency or low literacy.

research_gap: No study compares go-live with and without a clinician-facing shadowing or simulation period on outcomes such as alert override rates, alert fatigue, clinician errors, or patient harm. Studies are also needed on how long a shadowing period should last, what it costs in staff time, and whether combining silent-mode threshold testing with clinician rehearsal improves prediction of live performance.
underserved_note: Neither study reported its population or setting, so no test is known to have included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Deployers serving these groups have no direct evidence on whether simulation periods surface workflow problems specific to their patients or staffing conditions.

bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether standardizing response team staffing and documentation across sites before expanding an AI early warning system improves alert effectiveness or model performance. The recommendation rests on one governance framework that describes a pilot in which variation in rapid response team staffing, training, and documentation led planners to build standard operations before expansion.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The only support is a framework description of a single pilot, which counts as expert opinion under GRADE. Certainty about the effect of cross-site standardization on patient outcomes or model performance cannot be rated.

The CHAI playbook reports that one pilot found variation in rapid response team staffing, training standards, and documentation across hospitals. The source does not report the cost, staffing hours, or time needed to standardize these processes. Leaders planning expansion have no measured estimate of the effort involved or of the benefit it returns.

research_gap: Multisite studies are needed that compare early warning system performance, response times, and patient outcomes at sites with and without standardized response team staffing and documentation. These studies should also measure the cost and time of standardization and test whether documentation variation biases model inputs or outcome labels.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net hospitals may have different rapid response staffing levels than the pilot sites, and it remains unknown whether a standard built at better-resourced sites would be feasible or effective for them.

bottom_line: Three studies suggest that AI components fitting existing workflows are used more and disrupt less, but none tests whether assessing fit before purchase changes uptake, burden, or patient outcomes. Fourteen hazard studies document low uptake and added burden when fit is poor, which supports the concern but does not show that the recommended assessment solves it.

perspectives.view: The one real-deployment test is a quasi-experimental study in which components built into pharmacist workflows were used and reduced antimicrobial use, while a new multistage hand hygiene behavior failed. The other two tests are offline simulations. No study compares pre-purchase fit assessment with no assessment, so certainty is very low because of design and indirectness.

Wrong-recipient alerts accounted for nearly 50% of negative user feedback in one deployment, and charge nurses documented acknowledgment of alerts in 18.6% of cases in another. Alerts that go unread may allow deterioration to pass unnoticed. No study shows that a pre-deployment fit review prevents these failures.

Utilization averaged 29% in one trial, with a separate EHR tab cited as a barrier, and 11% of presented message drafts were used in another deployment. Workload scores rose from 43 to 57 after one rollout. A reader study found concurrent AI reading cut mean time by 13.5 seconds versus independent reading, which suggests integration design affects burden.

None of the three tests reports Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. In Sierra Leone, observers found a provider-to-client ratio of 1:23 despite reported easy integration, and in Kenya duplicative paper-based data entry was the main barrier to adoption. These findings suggest fit problems may be larger in low-resource settings.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software asks what else users might be doing at the same time, and a multi-society radiology statement says workflow integration must be considered. These documents are endorsements rather than binding duties for deployers, and no supplied study evaluates whether following them changes outcomes.

A simulation found that isolated automation raised time to treatment to 37.1 days from 29.4 and lowered throughput to 647 from 1022 per year. Another simulation estimated a 4% drop in daily patient volume or 2% longer operating time. A Danish emergency department recorded 6 to 23 minute delays before AI reports were available.

Primary care physicians reported excessive prompts and added cognitive and emotional strain, and 21% of responding physicians in one trial said alert timing did not match patient care. Burdened clinicians may have less attention for patients, although no supplied study measured patient-reported effects.

research_gap: No study compares deployments that underwent structured pre-purchase assessment of workflow, technology fit, user acceptance, and clinician burden with deployments that did not. A prospective multisite comparison that measures uptake, clinician workload, and patient outcomes, and that includes safety-net and limited English proficiency settings, would address this gap.
underserved_note: None of the three studies testing the practice included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations; only a hazard study in Sierra Leone included limited English proficiency and rural populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume the findings transfer to their staffing levels and workflows.

bottom_line: Three FDA documents support submitting a predetermined change control plan through a marketing submission and obtaining authorization before relying on it, with the final guidance stating this as a requirement. No study has tested whether this practice reduces unreviewed model modifications or patient harm, and no study documents how often the targeted hazard occurs.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard it targets. The recommendation rests entirely on regulatory guidance and a discussion paper. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about any effect on unauthorized model changes or patient outcomes cannot be rated, so the evidence base is best described as absent.

The final PCCP guidance states that manufacturers need a new marketing submission containing the plan, which makes authorization a precondition rather than an option. The draft lifecycle guidance encourages early Q-Submission discussion for continuously updating models. The generative AI discussion paper describes the plan as one possible mechanism, which suggests its scope for generative models remains unsettled.

research_gap: No study measures how often manufacturers implement model changes under plans that FDA has not authorized, or whether the authorization requirement changes post-market performance, safety signals, or recall rates. Studies comparing devices modified under authorized plans with devices modified through new submissions would help establish whether the process affects patient outcomes.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice in any population, so there is no evidence on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Health systems cannot tell from current evidence whether authorized change control plans address performance shifts that may fall unevenly on these groups after a model is updated.

bottom_line: Two real-deployment studies found better documentation after locally tailored templates, but each bundled template changes with training or workflow changes, so the template effect alone is unknown. The certainty that collaborative template customization by itself improves ambient scribe notes is very low.

perspectives.view: The US study of 66 providers used a quasi-experimental design. The Singapore study compared 150 investigation reports before and after the change without a comparator. Neither study isolated the template component, and supervisor investigation reports are indirect evidence for clinical notes. Risk of bias, indirectness, and bundled interventions lower certainty to very low.

In a simulated study of 104 medical students, chief complaint scores fell because AI notes often omitted symptom duration, a locally required element. This shows that generic formats can drop required content. It does not show that customization prevents such omissions, and no study linked template changes to patient harm or near misses.

In one deployment, ICD-10 documentation accuracy fell from 79% (95% CI, 72 to 86%) to 35% (95% CI, 28 to 42%). It returned to baseline after template redesign combined with user training. The recovery suggests that local redesign may work in live workflows. Because training accompanied the redesign, the template's separate contribution cannot be estimated.

A locally tailored ambient scribe workflow was associated with higher report completeness (adjusted difference 1.95, 95% CI 0.91 to 3.00). It was also associated with higher adapted PDQI scores (difference 0.53, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.69). Participation was voluntary, which may have selected motivated users.

Both deployments paired customization with other work, including user training at one site and a bundled workflow change at the other. The study summaries do not report staff time, vendor effort, or cost. Administrators therefore have no data on the resources that collaborative customization requires or how it scales across specialties.

research_gap: No study has compared customized with generic ambient scribe templates while holding training and workflow constant. No study has measured the cost of customization or linked template changes to omissions that reach patients.
underserved_note: Neither test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It is unknown whether locally customized templates capture content these patients need, such as interpreter use or social needs, or whether the reported gains would hold in those settings.

bottom_line: Two FDA guidance documents encourage manufacturers to discuss proposed predetermined change control plans through the Pre-Submission (Q-Submission) process, especially for models that update automatically, but no study has tested whether early engagement improves plan adequacy or review outcomes. The recommendation rests on regulatory expectation rather than measured effect.

perspectives.view: No study in this map compares predetermined change control plans that went through a Pre-Submission with those that did not. No study documents how often regulators find plans inadequate. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the endorsements count as expert and agency opinion.

The final PCCP guidance strongly encourages Pre-Submission discussion for plans containing automatically implemented modifications, and the draft lifecycle guidance encourages Q-Submission use early in development for continuously updating models. Both use should-level language, so the practice is voluntary, and neither document reports data on whether this engagement changes authorization outcomes or timelines.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare marketing submissions with and without prior Pre-Submission discussion of a change control plan, measuring additional-information requests, review time, authorization rates, and the scope of modifications FDA accepts. FDA or manufacturers could report aggregate data on how often proposed modification types are narrowed or rejected and whether early feedback reduces that rate.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Neither guidance excerpt addresses whether Pre-Submission discussions should examine how automatic modifications perform in these groups, which leaves any effect on them unknown.

bottom_line: Two FDA guidance documents direct manufacturers to assess modifications against existing 510(k) change guidance and to file a new marketing submission for significant changes outside an authorized predetermined change control plan, and the final PCCP guidance states this as a requirement. No study supplied here tests whether this practice prevents unreviewed changes from reaching the market or affects patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study tests this practice, and no study documents how often significant unreviewed changes reach market. The recommendation rests on regulatory guidance alone. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence, and the size of any benefit remains unknown.

The final PCCP guidance states that a manufacturer must submit a new marketing submission when a modification falls outside the plan and could significantly affect safety or effectiveness. The draft lifecycle guidance points manufacturers to the existing 510(k) change guidances for this assessment. The practice therefore restates an existing legal obligation rather than adding a new one.

research_gap: Studies could measure how often AI-enabled device modifications are marketed without a required submission, how consistently manufacturers apply the 510(k) change guidances to AI model updates, and whether PCCP boundaries lower the rate of unreviewed significant changes compared with devices that have no plan.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether unreviewed changes, such as retraining on new data, affect performance differently in these groups.

bottom_line: Three studies test some form of filtering alerts before they reach frontline staff, and only one, a retrospective analysis across 184 skilled nursing facilities, examines a remote clinical review team, reporting a positive predictive value of 35.4%. No study compares remote nurse review against direct alerting on alert fatigue or patient outcomes, so support for this practice rests on thin evidence.

perspectives.view: The one comparative test enrolled 28 residents over seven days and evaluated automated context-aware filtering rather than a nurse team, which makes it indirect. The other two tests lack a concurrent comparator. Imprecision, indirectness, and design limits place certainty for remote nurse review at very low.

In remote fetal surveillance, therapeutic cooling went from 6 (0.25%) to 2 (0.08%) cases, p = .10, with no significant differences in neonatal outcomes. These data do not show whether remote review catches deterioration earlier. Reported PPVs of 9.8% to 13.9% for single-threshold alerts suggest a filtering layer has many false alarms to remove.

Across 184 skilled nursing facilities, remote team review preceded on-site alerts and yielded 23.9 unique patients alerted per 100 beds per month, which authors described as manageable. A Spanish trial reported that automatic AI alert management handled 61,827 alerts without overloading staff, which suggests automated filtering may serve as an alternative to a human review layer.

Two of the three tests enrolled older adults in nursing homes or skilled nursing facilities, and none reported Medicaid status, safety-net setting, preferred language, or literacy. Whether remote review performs equally for these groups has not been examined.

The practice requires a staffed remote nurse team, and no study reports its cost, staffing ratio, or reviewer workload. In the fetal surveillance program, 78.8% of responding nurses said the remote hub improved safety, which suggests staff acceptance but does not measure efficiency or return on investment.

research_gap: No study randomizes or concurrently compares routing AI early-warning alerts through a remote nurse team with sending them directly to frontline clinicians. Such a study would measure alert fatigue, time to clinical response, patient outcomes, and staffing cost, and it would also compare remote human review with automated alert filtering.
underserved_note: None of the three tests reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Two studied older adults in residential or skilled nursing care, and the third described its sample only as births. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume the reported alert burden or acceptance figures will apply to their patients.

bottom_line: Seven randomized trials in real deployments found that pairing AI outputs with a specified clinical action improved process or clinical outcomes in six, though most compared the bundle against usual care rather than isolating the defined response. One trial that separated the two found that decision support alone gave no improvement, while decision support linked to patient outreach raised follow-up completion.

perspectives.view: Seven randomized trials support high starting certainty, lowered one level for indirectness because most tested AI output plus a defined action against no AI. Trial 40935221 isolates the element and found no gain from decision support alone. A small suicide-alert trial was null (OR 1.22, 95% CI 0.41 to 3.65). Observational and simulation studies point the same direction.

In one trial, hypotension prediction paired with a treatment protocol reduced hypotensive episodes and their duration (p = 0.01), and a small pre-post study reported similar reductions. Two hazard studies found that clinicians avoided tools lacking a clear consequence. In one small trial, alerts recommending suicide risk assessment did not significantly raise completion (20.3% vs 17.4%).

Where risk categories were tied to a workflow, goals-of-care documentation for high-risk patients rose from 17.6% to 70.8%. Antibiotic treatment of sepsis cases stayed near 10% without a huddle and reached 22.7% with one. Initial aneurysm evaluation rose from 18% to 42% with a defined referral workflow. These pre-post designs lack concurrent controls.

A trial of risk-informed prompts for serious illness conversations reported adjusted savings of $13,747 per decedent in end-of-life spending. In trial 40935221 the gain came from outreach paired with the output, which suggests that the specified action may carry staffing costs that the software alone does not cover.

The largest trial included Medicaid patients and found that serious illness conversation rates rose from 3.4% to 13.5% (aOR 2.62). The only other trial reporting Medicaid enrollment was null and enrolled 115 patients. No study reported results for safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups.

When alerts triggered a call from a peer recovery specialist, participants reported modest reductions in anxiety, stress, depression, and craving, although some calls followed random rather than anomaly-triggered alerts. In a vignette study, clinicians trusted AI risk output more when it came with specific treatment advice (β = .262). None of these studies measured patients' own trust.

research_gap: Few trials randomize the same AI output with and without a specified response, so the separate contribution of defining the action remains uncertain. Studies have not compared ways of specifying actions (owner, timeframe, escalation rules), measured staffing burden, or reported patient-reported trust and access to a human.
underserved_note: Two trials included Medicaid patients: one large trial with positive results and one small trial with null results. No test reported safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the effect of defined response workflows in these groups is unknown.

bottom_line: One cluster randomized trial and several nonrandomized deployments suggest that automated detection paired with real-time team alerts may shorten time to treatment for stroke and some other emergencies, while the effects of deterioration alerts on escalation were mixed. For conversational or generative AI escalating a crisis, the only test is one simulated benchmark, and hazard studies show that current tools often miss emergencies.

perspectives.view: The one cluster randomized trial (n=243) found that door-to-groin time fell 11.2 minutes (95% CI, -18.22 to -4.2). Nonrandomized studies of stroke and neurosurgical alerts point the same way, but the deterioration-alert and pneumothorax studies gave mixed results. Most tests involve imaging triage rather than generative devices, so certainty is low for indirectness, inconsistency, and imprecision.

In one deterioration study, sending alerts did not change escalation (12.3 vs. 11.3 per 1000 bed days), while mortality was 7% vs. 9.3%. A live STEMI tool missed 25.8% of cases. In chatbot vignettes, the most common recommendation for red-flag symptoms was self-care. Escalation helps only when recognition works, so testing sensitivity may matter as much as alert design.

In one pre-post study, clinicians typically acted before the alert fired (469 vs. 359 minutes before the alert). This suggests that alerts may arrive too late to change care. In the pneumothorax study, adding electronic notification cut time to oxygen by 143.8 minutes, but time to tube thoracostomy and to surgical consultation did not change significantly.

Only one simulated benchmark and one hazard vignette study included limited English proficiency or non-English inputs. In the benchmark, a cannot-miss prompt reduced under-triage discordant pairs from 31 to 10. No real deployment reported including Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy patients, and several studies did not report their country.

A regulatory discussion paper lists timely, clear, and actionable escalation as a review consideration for generative AI devices. None of the products tested in real use were generative conversational tools. The only generative test was an offline benchmark, which cannot show how a marketed device performs with patients in crisis.

A fall study in older adults reported 0.82 vs. 2.14 falls per person-month with active warnings. The authors describe this as an exploratory association. For patients using chatbots, the tested evidence does not show whether they reach a human or a crisis service quickly, which is the outcome the endorsing commentaries call for.

research_gap: No study tested a deployed generative or conversational AI that detects crisis states, such as suicidality or perinatal emergencies, and routes patients to a human. Such a study would need outcomes such as time to clinician contact, missed emergencies, and false alarms. No trial compared escalation designs, and no study reported cost or staff burden.
underserved_note: Only one offline benchmark tested the practice with limited English proficiency inputs, and no real-world test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume that the reported time savings apply to their patients and may need local validation.

bottom_line: FDA final guidance on predetermined change control plans asks manufacturers to describe data management, retraining, performance evaluation, and update procedures for each planned modification. No study supplied here tests whether this documentation prevents modified models from being deployed without predefined methods, and no study documents how often that hazard occurs.

perspectives.view: No study in this map tests the practice, and none measures the hazard it targets. The recommendation rests on a single regulatory guidance document. Under GRADE conventions, expert or regulatory consensus does not count as evidence of effect, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence.

The FDA final guidance states that each modification protocol in a PCCP should address four areas: data management, retraining, performance evaluation, and update procedures. The guidance uses "should" language. Manufacturers seeking an authorized PCCP will likely treat the four areas as expected content, although the guidance itself does not show that the protocols improve device safety.

research_gap: Studies could compare devices authorized with detailed modification protocols against devices modified through new submissions, measuring post-update performance drift, adverse event reports, and recall rates. Audits of authorized PCCPs could also test whether documented procedures match what manufacturers actually do when they retrain and release updates.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these patients cannot tell from the current record whether documented performance evaluation plans include data drawn from their populations, and they may need to ask manufacturers directly how subgroup performance is checked after each update.

bottom_line: Three uncontrolled before-after studies in live deployments report that reviewing alert dispositions was followed by higher alert acceptance or response in two cases and by no significant change in an 88% dismissal rate in the third. These studies suggest the practice is feasible, but they cannot show that disposition review caused the gains.

perspectives.view: All three tests of the practice are before-after studies without a comparison group. Under GRADE these start at low certainty and drop further for risk of bias and inconsistent results. One reported a 41.3% rise in the prescription-to-alert ratio, one reported improved acceptance for some diagnoses, and one found no significant fall in dismissals.

Hazard studies show that alert dispositions affect patients. In one, 14 of 26 highest-risk patients did not receive HIT testing despite an advisory, and eight had possible complications. Another found that 78% of non-adherence flags were not followed up. Disposition logs could reveal such gaps, but no included study shows that logging reduced harm events.

At one site, iterative logic changes left 88% of alerts dismissed while firing rose from 53.8 to 61 per 1,000 patient days. A potassium CDSS blocked 42.9% of prescriptions, and the blocking rate trended upward. These results suggest that disposition review may need to reduce alert volume as well as revise alert logic.

The targeted-email approach, applied across 2,161 providers, suggests one low-cost response to disposition data. The Tanzania and Rwanda study adapted algorithms from override findings across 27,593 consultations. Neither study reported the staff time or cost of reviewing dispositions, so resource needs at scale remain unknown.

One test took place in Tanzania and Rwanda, and the other two did not report their country or population. No test reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. It is therefore unknown whether override patterns, or the response to disposition review, differ for these groups.

AI pulmonary embolism notifications had a 71.5% false positive rate, which raised concern about fatigue among response teams. Such fatigue may delay care for patients whose alerts are real. Disposition review may give patients some assurance that ignored alerts are examined, though no study measured patient outcomes or trust.

research_gap: No study compared units with and without disposition logging and review, and none measured patient harm, staff time, or cost. A cluster-randomized or stepped-wedge trial across sites would address this gap if it reported dismissal rates, harm events, and results stratified by payer and language.
underserved_note: No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. One test took place in Tanzania and Rwanda, and two did not report their setting. Health systems serving these groups therefore have no direct evidence on whether disposition review works the same way for their patients.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether documenting the authorized device version and the change control plan title and version number, as stated in the authorization letter, reduces confusion about which plan and version are in use. The recommendation rests on two FDA guidance documents, one draft and one final, rather than on empirical evidence.

perspectives.view: The supplied record contains no studies that test the practice and no studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated when no test exists. The two endorsements are regulatory guidance, and they express expected practice rather than measured effects on version ambiguity or downstream harm.

The draft lifecycle guidance states that a new UDI is required when there is a new version or model, which ties version identity to an existing identifier system. The final PCCP guidance asks sponsors to attach the modification description, protocol, and impact assessment. Neither document reports evidence that version documentation prevents deployment of unauthorized versions.

research_gap: Studies could audit deployed AI-enabled devices to measure how often the version in clinical use differs from the version and change control plan named in the authorization letter, and could compare mismatch rates before and after structured version documentation or UDI linkage is adopted.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net hospitals that may run older device versions longer have no data showing whether version documentation reduces mismatches in their settings.

bottom_line: FDA final guidance on predetermined change control plans asks manufacturers to assess the benefits and risks of each planned modification and of the plan as a whole, and to document the associated risk mitigations. No study supplied here tests whether this assessment prevents unrecognized risks from individual or combined modifications, so the recommendation rests on regulatory expectation rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in this map tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard of unrecognized risk from single or combined modifications. Under GRADE conventions, certainty about the effect of benefit-risk impact assessment on patient outcomes or device performance cannot be rated. The single endorsement is a guidance document, which reflects expert and regulatory judgment rather than empirical evidence.

The FDA final guidance places the benefit-risk assessment and documentation of mitigations in the impact assessment section of a predetermined change control plan. For manufacturers seeking an authorized plan, this functions as a submission expectation. The guidance uses "should" language, and its content describes what reviewers expect to see rather than evidence that the assessment reduces harm.

research_gap: No study has examined whether documented benefit-risk assessments within change control plans identify risks that would otherwise go unrecognized, particularly risks arising from the interaction of several modifications. Useful studies could compare postmarket performance, adverse event reports, or field corrections for AI-enabled devices modified under plans with differing depth of impact assessment, and could test whether assessments of combined modifications detect performance shifts in subgroups that single-modification assessments miss.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether manufacturers' benefit-risk assessments account for how modifications may change device performance in these groups, and health systems serving them cannot rely on published evidence that the assessments protect their patients.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether updating device labeling after AI model modifications keeps users informed of current performance. One descriptive review of 26 FDA-authorized devices with change control plans found user manuals online for 54% of them, and many manuals lacked performance details or any mention of the plan.

perspectives.view: No study compares updated labeling with outdated or absent labeling on any outcome. The single available study is a cross-sectional review of 26 devices that documents the hazard. It shows that labeling gaps exist and does not show that revised labeling closes them. Certainty about the practice's effect cannot be rated from this evidence.

FDA's final guidance on predetermined change control plans says the public-facing document should summarize planned modifications, testing, validation, performance requirements, and how users will be informed. The review of 26 authorized devices suggests that labeling in circulation may not yet reflect this expectation, since manuals were found online for only 54% of devices.

When a model changes and the manual does not, clinicians may calibrate their trust to performance figures that no longer apply. The review found that many manuals omitted performance details altogether, which means users of those devices had no baseline to compare against even before any modification. Whether updated labeling reduces misuse remains untested.

Patients depend on their clinicians knowing how a device performs now. The finding that roughly half of manuals could not be located online suggests that patients and outside reviewers may also lack a way to learn whether a tool changed after authorization.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare user understanding, reliance, and error rates when labeling is updated after a model change versus when it is not. Useful designs would also measure how quickly labeling is revised after a modification and whether clinicians receive and read the notices.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. The hazard study reviewed device documents and did not report on Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy users. Readability and language access of updated labeling are therefore unexamined, and administrators serving these populations cannot assume that labeling updates will reach or be understood by their staff and patients.

bottom_line: No study has tested whether manufacturer documentation of user-configurable elements, setting levels, and appropriate conditions for change prevents inappropriate configuration changes. Two simulated studies show that configuration settings can shift AI outputs, and one FDA draft guidance endorses the practice.

perspectives.view: Zero studies evaluate the documentation practice itself, so certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The two available studies are level 4, offline or simulated designs that document the hazard. They show that outputs vary with configuration, but they do not show whether documenting configurations changes user behavior or patient outcomes.

In a simulation of 5,000,000 binary decisions, persona prompts shifted affirmative rates from 36.9% to 46.4% under fixed evidence. In 86 radiology cases, changing temperature and top-p settings raised accuracy to 73%. Both results suggest that an unrecorded setting change could alter clinical recommendations without anyone noticing, which is the failure mode that documentation is meant to expose.

The two studies vary settings, such as prompt persona, temperature, and top-p, that sites or vendors may adjust during deployment. Neither study examines how configuration is managed in live workflows. Whether clinicians or IT staff would read and follow documentation about appropriate operating points is therefore unknown.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions recommends that submissions describe the level at which each configuration is defined, whether patient, clinical site, or hospital network. The guidance is in draft form and uses "should" language. It sets an expectation for marketing submissions, but it does not by itself create evidence that the practice works.

research_gap: No study compares deployments with and without structured configuration documentation. Such a study could measure the rate of inappropriate setting changes, performance drift after reconfiguration, or downstream clinical errors. Studies in live clinical settings with site-level and network-level configuration changes are needed.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, and neither hazard study reported inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The effect of configuration changes on these groups, and the value of documentation for sites serving them, remains unexamined.

bottom_line: Two FDA guidance documents direct manufacturers to confirm that a modification falls within the authorized predetermined change control plan (PCCP) and follows its methods and specifications before implementation, and one ties this to the design-change requirement in 21 CFR 820.30(i). No study has tested whether this pre-implementation check prevents out-of-scope or nonconforming changes, and no study documents how often such deviations occur.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The recommendation rests on regulatory expectation rather than on measured effects on deviation rates or patient outcomes.

The draft lifecycle guidance treats this verification as a mandatory design-control step under 21 CFR 820.30(i), which requires procedures to identify, document, validate or verify, review, and approve design changes before implementation. The final PCCP guidance uses advisory language and asks manufacturers to first consider whether a modification is consistent with the authorized plan.

research_gap: No study has measured how often manufacturers implement AI device modifications that fall outside an authorized PCCP or depart from its methods and performance specifications. No study has compared deviation rates, recall rates, or post-change performance between manufacturers with and without a formal pre-implementation consistency check. Reviews of FDA inspection findings or postmarket reports for PCCP-authorized devices could supply a first estimate of how often the hazard occurs.
underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence exists for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Whether a change that stays within an authorized plan preserves performance for these groups may depend on whether the plan's performance specifications include subgroup criteria, which this recommendation does not address.

bottom_line: No study supplied for this recommendation tests whether a documented change management process that assigns developer, vendor, and implementer responsibilities reduces risk from code, data, environment, or model changes. The recommendation rests on four endorsements, including FDA draft guidance and two CHAI frameworks, rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The four endorsements reflect expert and regulatory consensus, and consensus of this kind does not substitute for comparative data on whether assigned change responsibilities reduce undetected performance shifts after updates.

FDA draft lifecycle guidance lists change management strategies among its recommendations, and one CHAI playbook asks parties to specify who reports changes to FDA authorization. A commentary on US and EU approaches assigns update documentation to developers and incident reporting to institutions. These sources describe expected roles, and none reports outcomes from applying them.

research_gap: Studies are needed that compare sites with and without documented, role-assigned change management plans and measure outcomes such as time to detect post-update performance degradation, the share of updates that receive revalidation, version-tracking errors, and patient-level harm events. No study, including any study of the underlying hazard, was supplied to establish how often unclear update accountability leads to harm.
underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. It remains unknown whether change management processes perform differently in safety-net settings, where bargaining power with vendors and informatics staffing may be more limited and where post-update performance shifts could affect these populations without being detected.

bottom_line: Five sources endorse predefined performance-change thresholds for continuously adaptive AI, but no supplied study tests whether such thresholds catch silent performance change or reduce harm. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and regulatory analogy rather than on evaluated outcomes.

perspectives.view: No supplied study tests the practice, and no supplied study documents the hazard. The five endorsements consist of one multi-society guidance statement, two frameworks, and two commentaries. Under GRADE conventions, expert statements do not count as evidence of effect, so the certainty that thresholds improve detection or patient outcomes cannot be rated.

Three sources draw on FDA concepts, including predetermined change control plans, postmarket adverse event reporting, and prespecified update triggers with rollback criteria. The CHAI playbook asks vendors to state whether calibration changes trigger risk recategorization. These sources describe how the practice fits existing oversight models, but none reports whether the approach has worked when applied.

The endorsing sources describe threshold-triggered notification as a way to surface performance change before it reaches patients. No supplied study measures how often self-calibrating models drift, how often thresholds would fire, or whether notification leads to timely correction, so the size of the safety benefit remains unknown.
